  • A contaminated airstream carries solids, moisture, corrosives, flammables or hazardous fumes. Ask what is in the air before selecting a fan, because it changes the impeller, the arrangement, the accessories and the construction.

You Can Read a Duty Statement

You can now take a line like "12,000 CFM at 3.0 in. wg, 1,173 RPM, 7.9 BHP, standard air" and say what every number means, check the horsepower and the velocity yourself, and correct the pressure for a hot airstream or a high-altitude site. That vocabulary is the foundation for every chapter that follows.

docs.title: Airstreams, Total Pressure and Standard Air
Summary
docs.text: This chapter completes the air fundamentals: velocity pressure and its equation, total pressure, pressure rise, air power, the continuity equation, and the standard air condition that catalog ratings assume. It then classifies the airstreams fans must handle (hot, wet, corrosive, particulate-laden, and explosive) because those conditions drive many construction choices later in the book. After completing it, readers can describe an application's air conditions in the terms a fan specification uses.

docs.title: Concepts Covered
docs.text:
This chapter covers the following 16 concepts from the learning graph:

Concept Concept Impact Score Wet Airstream 35 Duct System 235 Blower 6 Pressure Rise 3 Feet Per Minute 3 Velocity Pressure 85 Standard Air 66 Corrosive Airstream 46 Particulate-Laden Airstream 26 Hot Airstream 120 Explosive Atmosphere 77 Air Power 2 Airflow Continuity Equation 3 Barometric Pressure 34 Total Pressure 62 Velocity Pressure Equation 2

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
This chapter builds on concepts from:

  • Chapter 1: Air, Pressure and the Fan

Two Questions on Every Fan Inquiry

Every fan inquiry eventually asks two questions: how hard does the fan have to push, and what exactly is it pushing? This chapter gives you the vocabulary to answer both in the terms a catalog and a specification use. By the end you will be able to turn a job-site description into air conditions an application engineer can select from. Let's follow the airflow.

docs.title: Where This Chapter Picks Up
docs.text:
Chapter 1 described air with four measurements: airflow volume in cubic feet per minute (CFM), air velocity, static pressure in inches of water gauge (in. wg), and air density. Those are enough to say what a fan delivers, but not enough to read a performance table or write an order. A catalog rating also assumes a particular air condition, and a real job almost never matches it exactly. And the air itself may be hot, wet, corrosive, dusty or flammable, any one of which changes how the fan has to be built.

The chapter is in two halves. The first half finishes the pressure story: it adds velocity pressure to static pressure to get total pressure, shows how a fan's pressure rise and air power follow, and places the fan inside the duct system it serves. The second half covers barometric pressure and standard air, then the five airstream conditions that appear on almost every industrial inquiry.

docs.title: Velocity, Area and Continuity
docs.text:
Air velocity in the fan industry is stated in feet per minute (fpm): the distance, in feet, that air travels along a duct or through an opening in one minute. Fpm pairs with CFM, which also uses minutes, so no unit conversion is needed between them. One fpm is 1/60 of a foot per second. Typical values range from a few hundred fpm across a filter bank, to 1,500–3,000 fpm in ventilation ductwork, to 4,000 fpm or more in ducts that carry dust.

Velocity, area and airflow are tied together by the airflow continuity equation. Air that enters one end of a duct with no branches or leaks must come out the other end, so the volume flowing past every cross-section is the same. Multiplying the cross-sectional area by the average velocity gives the airflow.

docs.title: Airflow Continuity Equation
docs.text:
\[ Q = A \times V \]

where:

  • \( Q \) is the airflow volume, in CFM (ft³/min)
  • \( A \) is the inside cross-sectional area of the duct or opening, in ft²
  • \( V \) is the average air velocity across that area, in fpm

Strictly, continuity conserves mass. Treating it as conserving volume is accurate in ductwork because fan pressures change air density by only a few percent. The practical consequence is simple: when the same airflow moves from a large duct into a small one, the velocity rises in proportion to the area ratio. A 10,000 CFM airstream in a 24 in. × 24 in. duct (4.00 ft²) moves at 2,500 fpm; squeezed into a 20 in. × 20 in. duct (2.78 ft²), it moves at 3,600 fpm.

docs.title: Velocity Pressure
docs.text:
Moving air carries kinetic energy, and that energy can be measured as a pressure. Velocity pressure (VP) is the pressure that would be produced if a moving airstream were brought to a stop. You can feel it by holding your hand flat against a strong wind: the push on your palm is velocity pressure being recovered. Velocity pressure is measured in in. wg, the same unit as static pressure, and it is always positive in the direction the air is moving.

Static pressure and velocity pressure answer different questions. Static pressure is the bursting or collapsing pressure that pushes outward or inward on the duct walls in every direction, and it is what overcomes the resistance of filters, coils, dampers and duct friction. Velocity pressure exists only because the air is moving, and it acts only in the direction of motion. A Pitot tube inserted into a duct, facing upstream, senses both; a side-wall tap senses static pressure alone. The difference between the two readings is the velocity pressure.

docs.title: The Velocity Pressure Equation
docs.text: The velocity pressure equation converts between velocity and velocity pressure. For standard air (defined later in this chapter as air with a density of 0.075 lb/ft³), it takes a form every application engineer memorizes:

docs.title: Velocity Pressure Equation (Standard Air)
docs.text:
\[ VP = \left( \frac{V}{4005} \right)^2 \qquad \text{or} \qquad V = 4005\sqrt{VP} \]

where:

  • \( VP \) is the velocity pressure, in in. wg
  • \( V \) is the average air velocity, in fpm
  • 4005 is the constant that makes the units work for air at 0.075 lb/ft³

For air at any other density \( \rho \) (lb/ft³), the general form is \( VP = \rho \left( V / 1096 \right)^2 \). Substituting \( \rho = 0.075 \) recovers the 4005 version.

The equation is a square law. Doubling the velocity quadruples the velocity pressure, and that is why small, high-velocity ducts are expensive to run.

Worked example: velocity pressure in two ducts. Use the 10,000 CFM airstream from the continuity section.

  1. In the 24 in. × 24 in. duct, \( V = 10{,}000 / 4.00 = 2{,}500 \) fpm. Then \( VP = (2{,}500 / 4005)^2 = (0.624)^2 = 0.39 \) in. wg.
  2. In the 20 in. × 20 in. duct, \( V = 10{,}000 / 2.78 = 3{,}600 \) fpm. Then \( VP = (3{,}600 / 4005)^2 = (0.899)^2 = 0.81 \) in. wg.
  3. Going the other way, a Pitot traverse that averages 0.25 in. wg of velocity pressure means \( V = 4005 \times \sqrt{0.25} = 4005 \times 0.5 = 2{,}003 \) fpm.

The duct area dropped by about 30 percent, but the velocity pressure roughly doubled. That energy has to come from the fan.

A Number Worth Memorizing

At standard air, 4,005 fpm is exactly 1.00 in. wg of velocity pressure, so 2,000 fpm is about 0.25 in. and 3,000 fpm is about 0.56 in. Keep those three points in your head and you can sanity-check any velocity pressure on a drawing or test report in seconds.

docs.title: Total Pressure
docs.text: Total pressure (TP) is the sum of static pressure and velocity pressure at a point in the airstream. It represents all of the energy the air carries at that point, measured as pressure.

docs.title: Total Pressure
docs.text:
\[ TP = SP + VP \]

where:

  • \( TP \) is the total pressure, in in. wg
  • \( SP \) is the static pressure, in in. wg (positive above atmospheric pressure, negative below)
  • \( VP \) is the velocity pressure, in in. wg (always positive)

The sign convention matters. On the inlet side of a fan, the fan is pulling air through the system, so static pressure is below atmospheric and is written as a negative number. Velocity pressure is still positive. The total pressure on the inlet side is therefore usually negative but smaller in magnitude than the static pressure.

Total pressure is the quantity that steadily falls along a duct in the direction of flow, because friction and fittings turn some of the air's energy into heat. Static pressure alone does not behave that simply: where a duct gets larger and the air slows down, some velocity pressure converts back into static pressure, and static pressure can actually rise downstream. Total pressure never rises unless a fan adds energy.

Static and Velocity Pressure Trade Places

Think of total pressure as the air's energy budget, with static and velocity pressure as two accounts it can move money between. A duct reducer moves energy from the static account to the velocity account; an expansion moves some of it back. Only the fan makes a deposit; every fitting and filter makes a withdrawal.

docs.title: Pressure Rise and Air Power
docs.text: The pressure rise of a fan is the increase in pressure the fan produces between its inlet and its outlet. The most complete measure is fan total pressure (FTP): the total pressure at the outlet minus the total pressure at the inlet. Catalogs more often list fan static pressure (FSP), which by industry convention is the fan total pressure minus the velocity pressure at the fan outlet. Chapter 10 shows how both appear on a performance curve; here the point is that both describe the same pressure rise, measured two ways.

docs.title: Fan Pressure Rise
docs.text:
\[ FTP = TP_{\text{outlet}} - TP_{\text{inlet}} \qquad FSP = FTP - VP_{\text{outlet}} \]

where:

  • \( FTP \) is the fan total pressure, in in. wg
  • \( FSP \) is the fan static pressure, in in. wg
  • \( TP_{\text{outlet}} \) and \( TP_{\text{inlet}} \) are the total pressures measured at the fan outlet and inlet
  • \( VP_{\text{outlet}} \) is the velocity pressure at the fan outlet

Air power is the rate at which the fan delivers energy to the air: the useful output of the fan, before any losses inside the fan, bearings or drive. In U.S. units it is calculated in horsepower from airflow and fan total pressure. The shaft power a fan draws, its brake horsepower, is always larger than its air power; the ratio of the two is the fan's total efficiency, which Chapter 10 covers.

docs.title: Air Power
docs.text:
\[ AHP = \frac{Q \times FTP}{6356} \]

where:

  • \( AHP \) is the air power, in horsepower
  • \( Q \) is the airflow, in CFM
  • \( FTP \) is the fan total pressure, in in. wg
  • 6356 is the unit conversion between CFM × in. wg and horsepower

Worked example: an exhaust fan's pressure rise and air power. A fan exhausts 10,000 CFM. Its inlet duct is 24 in. × 24 in.; its outlet duct is 20 in. × 20 in. A field reading gives a static pressure of −1.20 in. wg at the inlet and +2.00 in. wg at the outlet. Using the velocity pressures already calculated (0.39 in. at the inlet and 0.81 in. at the outlet):

Quantity Inlet Outlet Static pressure, SP (in. wg) −1.20 +2.00 Velocity pressure, VP (in. wg) 0.39 0.81 Total pressure, TP = SP + VP (in. wg) −0.81 +2.81
  1. Fan total pressure: \( FTP = 2.81 - (-0.81) = 3.62 \) in. wg.
  2. Fan static pressure: \( FSP = 3.62 - 0.81 = 2.81 \) in. wg.
  3. Air power: \( AHP = 10{,}000 \times 3.62 / 6356 = 5.70 \) hp.
  4. If the fan's total efficiency were 75 percent (an illustrative value), the shaft would need \( 5.70 / 0.75 = 7.59 \) hp.

Notice that subtracting a negative inlet pressure adds to the pressure rise. A fan that must pull hard on its inlet works just as hard as one that must push hard on its outlet.

Watch the Inlet Sign

A common trap is adding inlet and outlet static pressures as if both were positive, or dropping the inlet reading entirely because "the fan only blows." Write every reading with its sign before you subtract, and check that your inlet total pressure is negative on an exhaust or ducted-inlet fan; if it is not, recheck the gauge connection.

docs.title: The Duct System
docs.text:
A fan never works alone. The duct system is everything the air passes through on its way to and from the fan: hoods, grilles, louvers, filters, coils, dampers, elbows, transitions, straight duct runs and the final discharge, together with the fan's own inlet and outlet connections. A system can be very short (a wall fan with a louver) or very long (a dust-collection network with dozens of hoods). The duct system is the reason a fan must produce pressure at all: every component takes away some total pressure, and the fan must put back exactly as much as the system uses at the airflow being moved.

Duct-system resistance depends on velocity, and velocity depends on airflow. Friction and fitting losses scale with velocity pressure, which scales with the square of velocity. The result is the most useful rule in system work: for a fixed duct system, the pressure required rises with the square of the airflow.

docs.title: System Resistance Relation
docs.text:
\[ \frac{P_2}{P_1} = \left( \frac{Q_2}{Q_1} \right)^2 \]

where:

  • \( P_1 \) is the pressure the system requires at airflow \( Q_1 \), in in. wg
  • \( P_2 \) is the pressure the system requires at airflow \( Q_2 \), in in. wg

Plotting that relation for every airflow gives the system curve. Chapter 10 lays it over the fan curve to find the operating point, and Chapter 25 covers the "system effect" losses caused by poor inlet and outlet connections. Duct-system design itself is outside the scope of this book; what the book needs from it is the airflow and the pressure the system requires, stated at the actual air conditions.

Worked example: a requested airflow increase. The plant running the exhaust system from the previous example wants 20 percent more airflow, 12,000 CFM, through the same ductwork.

  1. Airflow ratio: \( 12{,}000 / 10{,}000 = 1.20 \).
  2. Pressure ratio: \( 1.20^2 = 1.44 \).
  3. New fan total pressure: \( 3.62 \times 1.44 = 5.21 \) in. wg.
  4. New air power: \( 12{,}000 \times 5.21 / 6356 = 9.84 \) hp, which is \( 1.20^3 = 1.73 \) times the original 5.70 hp.

A 20 percent airflow increase costs 44 percent more pressure and 73 percent more air power. Customers who ask for "just a bit more air" from an existing system are often surprised by that arithmetic, and it is why the duct system has to be described before a fan can be selected.

The MicroSim below lets you change the airflow in this same exhaust system and watch velocity, velocity pressure, static pressure and total pressure respond at both fan connections.

docs.title: Diagram: Duct System Pressure Explorer
docs.text:
Duct System Pressure Explorer

Type: microsim sim-id: ch02-duct-system-pressure-explorer Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Apply Bloom Verb: calculate Learning Objective: The learner will calculate duct velocity, velocity pressure, total pressure, fan total pressure and air power for a simple exhaust duct system, to within the tolerances stated in Feedback.

Prerequisites: airflow continuity equation, feet per minute, velocity pressure, velocity pressure equation, static pressure, total pressure, fan total pressure, fan static pressure, air power, duct system, system resistance relation (all defined in the sections above).

Evidence of Mastery: The learner answers five calculation challenges by typing a number before the sim reveals it. An answer is correct when it is within the tolerance listed for that challenge. Mastery is at least 4 of 5 correct on the first attempt. Moving the airflow control and reading the live values is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) Inlet static pressure is added as a positive number, so the fan pressure rise is underestimated. (2) Velocity pressure is proportional to velocity rather than to velocity squared. (3) A 20 percent airflow increase needs only 20 percent more pressure. (4) Static pressure always falls in the direction of flow.

Instructional Rationale: Apply-level calculation needs practice with a check, so each challenge locks the live readout of the target value until the learner commits an answer. Free exploration of the airflow afterwards lets the learner see the square law and the sign convention hold at every airflow, which confronts misconceptions 2 and 3 with numbers.

Content:

A labeled schematic of one exhaust system, in flow order: Hood → Inlet duct (24 in. × 24 in., area 4.00 ft²) → Station 1 (fan inlet) → Fan → Station 2 (fan outlet) → Outlet duct (20 in. × 20 in., area 2.78 ft²) → Discharge stack.

Values shown at each station: velocity V (fpm), velocity pressure VP (in. wg), static pressure SP (in. wg), total pressure TP (in. wg). Values shown for the fan: fan total pressure FTP (in. wg), fan static pressure FSP (in. wg), air power AHP (hp).

Clicking a schematic label reveals its definition:

  • Hood: the entry point where air and contaminant are captured from the room.
  • Inlet duct: the duct between the hood and the fan; the fan pulls on it, so its static pressure is negative.
  • Station 1 (fan inlet): the measurement point just upstream of the fan.
  • Fan: the only component that adds total pressure to the air.
  • Station 2 (fan outlet): the measurement point just downstream of the fan.
  • Outlet duct: the duct between the fan and the stack; the fan pushes into it, so its static pressure is positive.
  • Discharge stack: where the air leaves the system at atmospheric pressure.

Challenges, in this order:

# Question shown Correct answer Tolerance Feedback when wrong 1 At 10,000 CFM, what is the velocity in the inlet duct (fpm)? 2,500 ±25 Use Q = A × V: 10,000 ÷ 4.00 ft² = 2,500 fpm. 2 At 10,000 CFM the outlet velocity is 3,600 fpm. What is the outlet velocity pressure (in. wg)? 0.81 ±0.02 VP = (V ÷ 4005)²: (3,600 ÷ 4005)² = 0.899² = 0.81 in. wg. Velocity pressure goes with the square of velocity. 3 At 10,000 CFM, inlet SP is −1.20 and inlet VP is 0.39; outlet SP is +2.00 and outlet VP is 0.81. What is the fan total pressure (in. wg)? 3.62 ±0.03 TP inlet = −1.20 + 0.39 = −0.81; TP outlet = 2.00 + 0.81 = 2.81; FTP = 2.81 − (−0.81) = 3.62 in. wg. Keep the inlet sign. 4 What is the air power at 10,000 CFM and 3.62 in. wg fan total pressure (hp)? 5.70 ±0.05 AHP = Q × FTP ÷ 6356 = 10,000 × 3.62 ÷ 6356 = 5.70 hp. 5 The airflow is raised to 12,000 CFM in the same system. What fan total pressure is now required (in. wg)? 5.21 ±0.05 Pressure goes with the square of airflow: (12,000 ÷ 10,000)² = 1.44, and 3.62 × 1.44 = 5.21 in. wg, not 3.62 × 1.20.

Provenance: All values come from the chapter sections "Velocity Pressure", "Pressure Rise and Air Power" and "The Duct System". The system model is illustrative, chosen so that 10,000 CFM reproduces the chapter's worked example; the sim labels it "illustrative system".

Rules:

  • Airflow Q: min 4,000, max 14,000, step 500, default 10,000, unit CFM.
  • Air is standard air (0.075 lb/ft³) throughout.
  • V1 = Q ÷ 4.00; V2 = Q ÷ 2.78 (fpm). VP = (V ÷ 4005)² (in. wg).
  • Total pressure at each station follows the system resistance relation: TP1 = −0.81 × (Q ÷ 10,000)²; TP2 = +2.81 × (Q ÷ 10,000)² (in. wg).
  • SP1 = TP1 − VP1; SP2 = TP2 − VP2.
  • FTP = TP2 − TP1; FSP = FTP − VP2; AHP = Q × FTP ÷ 6356.
  • Display velocities to the nearest 10 fpm, pressures to 0.01 in. wg and air power to 0.01 hp. Display computed values from unrounded intermediates.
  • At the default airflow the sim shows V1 = 2,500, VP1 = 0.39, SP1 = −1.20, TP1 = −0.81, V2 = 3,600, VP2 = 0.81, SP2 = 2.00, TP2 = 2.81, FTP = 3.62, FSP = 2.81, AHP = 5.70 (matches the chapter table; small rounding differences of ±0.01 are acceptable).

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner reads challenge 1 and types an answer. The value the challenge asks for is hidden in the live readout until the answer is checked.
  2. The learner presses Check. The sim marks the answer, shows the correct value and its worked calculation, and moves to the next challenge.
  3. For challenge 5, the airflow control moves to 12,000 CFM before the question appears, and the FTP readout is hidden until the answer is checked.
  4. After challenge 5, free exploration unlocks: the learner changes the airflow and every station value and fan value updates at once. The learner should notice that SP1 is always negative, that TP1 is always smaller in magnitude than SP1, and that doubling the airflow from 5,000 to 10,000 CFM multiplies FTP by 4 and AHP by 8.

Feedback: Five challenges, fixed order, two attempts each. Correct: "Correct: ." Incorrect: the "Feedback when wrong" text for that challenge. After the second wrong attempt the correct value and worked calculation are shown and the challenge counts as missed. A running count "Challenges correct: n of 5" is shown, counting only first-attempt answers.

Starting State: Airflow at 10,000 CFM, the schematic with all labels, and challenge 1 displayed with the inlet velocity readout hidden. The prompt reads "How fast is the air moving in the inlet duct?"

Chapter Anchors: 10,000 CFM; 24 in. × 24 in. duct, 4.00 ft², 2,500 fpm, VP 0.39 in. wg; 20 in. × 20 in. duct, 2.78 ft², 3,600 fpm, VP 0.81 in. wg; inlet SP −1.20, outlet SP +2.00; TP −0.81 and +2.81; FTP 3.62 in. wg; FSP 2.81 in. wg; air power 5.70 hp; 12,000 CFM needs FTP 5.21 in. wg and 9.84 hp; airflow ratio 1.20, pressure ratio 1.44, power ratio 1.73.

docs.title: Fans and Blowers
docs.text:
The word blower appears on nameplates, catalogs and company names, including Twin City Fan & Blower, so a new engineer needs to know what it signals. In everyday use, "blower" means a fan built to produce comparatively high pressure, usually a centrifugal design. Twin City Fan's current catalog describes its pressure blowers as "ideal for applications requiring high pressures at relatively low volumes of air," with performance that stays stable through the operating range and can be turned down to zero flow with a discharge damper. FanPedia notes that pressure blowers have narrower housings and impeller widths than standard centrifugal fans (FanPedia p. 4).

Engineering standards draw the line more precisely, using the pressure ratio: the absolute pressure at the outlet divided by the absolute pressure at the inlet. The commonly cited ASME definitions are:

  • Fan: pressure ratio up to 1.11
  • Blower: pressure ratio from 1.11 to 1.20
  • Compressor: pressure ratio above 1.20

Absolute pressure is atmospheric pressure plus gauge pressure. At sea level the atmosphere is about 407 in. wg (the next section explains where that number comes from).

Worked example: is a 40 in. wg pressure blower a fan or a blower? Take a machine drawing air from the room at sea level and discharging at 40 in. wg.

  1. Inlet absolute pressure: 407 in. wg (atmospheric).
  2. Outlet absolute pressure: \( 407 + 40 = 447 \) in. wg.
  3. Pressure ratio: \( 447 / 407 = 1.098 \).

At 1.098, the machine is technically a fan under the ASME definition, even though its product line is called a pressure blower. The ratio reaches 1.11 only near 45 in. wg (\( 0.11 \times 407 \)), and 1.20 near 81 in. wg. The lesson for a specification is to state the airflow and pressure required, never just the word "blower"; the word tells you the customer expects high pressure, not which product family fits.

docs.title: Barometric Pressure
docs.text:
Barometric pressure is the absolute pressure of the atmosphere at a location, the weight of the column of air above it. Weather reports and fan calculations state it in inches of mercury (in. Hg). At sea level under standard conditions it is 29.92 in. Hg. Since mercury is about 13.6 times denser than water, that equals roughly 29.92 × 13.6 = 407 in. wg: the atmosphere presses on everything with a force equal to a column of water nearly 34 feet tall.

Barometric pressure falls with altitude, because there is less air overhead. It also moves a little with weather, but for fan work the site elevation is what matters. Using the standard atmosphere, approximate values are:

Elevation (ft) Barometric pressure (in. Hg) Ratio to sea level 0 29.92 1.000 2,500 27.31 0.913 5,000 24.89 0.832 7,500 22.65 0.757

Air density is directly proportional to absolute pressure, as Chapter 1 explained, so the ratio column is also the ratio of air density at that elevation to air density at sea level, at the same temperature. That ratio is what corrects a fan's catalog performance for altitude.

Worked example: a fan for a plant at 5,000 feet. A catalog rating (illustrative values) says a fan at a certain speed moves 8,000 CFM against 2.00 in. wg static pressure and draws 4.00 bhp at sea level and 70°F. The fan will be installed at 5,000 ft, and the air will be at 70°F.

  1. Barometric ratio at 5,000 ft: \( 24.89 / 29.92 = 0.832 \).
  2. A fan is a constant-volume machine: at the same speed it moves the same 8,000 CFM, whatever the air density.
  3. Pressure scales with density: \( 2.00 \times 0.832 = 1.66 \) in. wg.
  4. Power scales with density: \( 4.00 \times 0.832 = 3.33 \) bhp.

If the duct system at the plant genuinely needs 2.00 in. wg at that airflow, this selection falls short. The fan must be selected from the catalog at \( 2.00 / 0.832 = 2.40 \) in. wg to deliver 2.00 in. at altitude.

docs.title: Standard Air
docs.text:
Every fan catalog has to rate its fans at some air condition, and the industry agreed on one: standard air, air with a density of 0.075 lb/ft³. Dry air at 70°F and a barometric pressure of 29.92 in. Hg (sea level) has very nearly this density, so standard air is often described simply as "70°F at sea level." Unless a table says otherwise, the static pressures and brake horsepower in a fan catalog are standard-air values, and the 4005 constant in the velocity pressure equation assumes standard air too.

Real air rarely matches. The correction combines the altitude effect from the previous section with the temperature effect from Chapter 1 into one density ratio:

docs.title: Density Ratio
docs.text:
\[ \frac{\rho}{0.075} = \frac{P_b}{29.92} \times \frac{530}{T + 460} \]

where:

  • \( \rho \) is the actual air density, in lb/ft³
  • \( P_b \) is the actual barometric pressure, in in. Hg
  • \( T \) is the actual air temperature, in °F
  • 530 is 70°F expressed in absolute degrees Rankine (70 + 460)

Three rules follow from the fact that a fan moves a fixed volume at a fixed speed. At the same speed, airflow (CFM) does not change with density. Pressure changes in direct proportion to the density ratio. Brake horsepower also changes in direct proportion to the density ratio. The worked examples in the barometric pressure section above and the hot airstream section below both apply these rules; the table below collects them in one place.

Quantity, same fan at same speed Effect of lower density (hot air or high altitude) Airflow, CFM Unchanged Pressure, in. wg Multiplied by the density ratio (falls) Brake horsepower Multiplied by the density ratio (falls) Mass of air moved, lb/min Multiplied by the density ratio (falls)

Two Directions, One Ratio

If density corrections feel slippery, that is normal; the hard part is remembering which way to apply the ratio, not the arithmetic. Use one rule: going from the catalog to the job, multiply by the density ratio; going from the job's required pressure back to the catalog, divide by it. Try it on the 5,000-foot example above until both directions feel automatic.

docs.title: The Airstreams Fans Handle
docs.text: Chapter 1 introduced the airstream, the air or gas mixture that actually passes through the fan, and the idea of a contaminated airstream. Specifications go further and name the specific condition, because each condition points toward specific construction, materials, arrangements and accessories. Five conditions cover nearly every industrial inquiry: hot, wet, corrosive, particulate-laden and explosive. An airstream can have more than one of them at once, and a good inquiry form asks about each separately. The construction details are covered in later chapters; this section teaches you to recognize each condition and to ask the right questions about it.

docs.title: Hot Airstreams
docs.text:
A hot airstream is one whose temperature is high enough to change the fan's performance or to call for construction beyond the standard catalog build. There is no single threshold temperature, because the limit depends on the fan design. FanPedia's high-temperature pages show where special construction begins for different designs (FanPedia pp. 110–116):

Fan design (FanPedia page) Airstream temperatures covered by high-temperature packages Centrifugal fans, Arrangements 1, 8, 9, 9F, 10 (p. 110) 276°F to 1,000+°F; packages from 301–500°F up to 1,001°F and over Centrifugal fans, Arrangement 4 (p. 111) 181°F to 1,000+°F; packages 181–300°F and 301°F and over Arrangement 4 plug fans (p. 114) 181°F to 1,000+°F; 301°F and over requires engineering review Axial fans (p. 116) 106°F to 600°F, in packages starting at 106–150°F

Other limits show up in the technical descriptions. A standard double-width, double-inlet fan in Arrangement 3 has both bearings in the airstream and is limited to clean air at 130°F (FanPedia p. 167). Arrangement 1 keeps the bearings on a pedestal outside the airstream, "which makes them ideal for high temperature or contaminated air applications" (FanPedia p. 162), while for an Arrangement 4 plug fan, with the impeller on the motor shaft, "high airstream temperatures may limit the use of this arrangement" (FanPedia p. 171). High-temperature construction adds features such as shaft coolers, heat shields, insulation, high-temperature grease and fixed-and-floating bearings; Chapter 21 covers them.

Hot air also changes performance, through density. Hot air is lighter, so a fan running at the same speed develops less pressure and draws less power in service than its standard-air catalog rating shows.

Worked example: selecting a fan for a 300°F oven exhaust at sea level. The duct system needs 3.00 in. wg static pressure at the operating temperature of 300°F.

  1. Density ratio: \( \dfrac{29.92}{29.92} \times \dfrac{530}{300 + 460} = \dfrac{530}{760} = 0.697 \). The actual density is \( 0.075 \times 0.697 = 0.0523 \) lb/ft³.
  2. Catalog (standard-air) pressure to select at: \( 3.00 / 0.697 = 4.30 \) in. wg, at the required CFM.
  3. Suppose the catalog shows 10.0 bhp at that point (an illustrative value). The operating power at 300°F is \( 10.0 \times 0.697 = 6.97 \) bhp.
  4. The catch: when the oven starts cold, the air is near 70°F and the fan draws the full 10.0 bhp until the air heats up. A motor sized only for the 6.97 bhp hot condition would be overloaded at every cold start. The order must state both the operating temperature and whether the fan must start and run on cold air, so the motor can be sized for cold start or protected by a damper or speed control.

The density ratio grows smaller as temperature rises and altitude increases. The chart below plots it, so you can read the correction for any combination before you calculate it.

docs.title: Diagram: Density Ratio by Temperature and Altitude
docs.text:
Density Ratio by Temperature and Altitude

Type: chart sim-id: ch02-density-ratio-temperature-altitude Library: Plotly Status: Specified Bloom Level: Apply Bloom Verb: calculate Learning Objective: The learner will calculate the air density ratio for a given airstream temperature and site elevation, to within ±0.01, and use it to convert a required pressure into a standard-air catalog pressure.

Prerequisites: standard air, barometric pressure, air density, density ratio, hot airstream, the rule that pressure and power scale with the density ratio (defined in the sections "Barometric Pressure", "Standard Air" and "Hot Airstreams" above).

Evidence of Mastery: The learner answers five challenges by typing a value before the chart marks the point. A density ratio answer is correct within ±0.01; a pressure answer is correct within ±0.05 in. wg. Mastery is at least 4 of 5 correct on the first attempt. Hovering curves and moving the temperature marker is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) Temperature in °F can be used directly in the ratio without adding 460. (2) Hot air raises the pressure a fan develops. (3) To find the catalog pressure, multiply the required pressure by the density ratio instead of dividing. (4) Altitude and temperature corrections cannot be combined.

Instructional Rationale: The chart makes the shape of the correction visible (steep at moderate temperatures, flattening at high ones; each altitude curve a fixed fraction of the sea-level curve), and the challenges then require the learner to compute values the chart can confirm, so the learner practices the calculation rather than reading answers off the plot.

Content:

  • x-axis: airstream temperature, °F, from 0 to 1,000.
  • y-axis: density ratio (actual density ÷ 0.075 lb/ft³), dimensionless.
  • Four curves, one per elevation: 0 ft (29.92 in. Hg), 2,500 ft (27.31 in. Hg), 5,000 ft (24.89 in. Hg), 7,500 ft (22.65 in. Hg).
  • A horizontal reference line at ratio 1.000 labeled "standard air".
  • Hovering any point shows: elevation, barometric pressure, temperature, density ratio to three decimals, and density in lb/ft³ to four decimals.
  • Reference points the chart can mark: 70°F at 0 ft = 1.000; 0°F at 0 ft = 1.152; 300°F at 0 ft = 0.697; 600°F at 0 ft = 0.500; 1,000°F at 0 ft = 0.363; 70°F at 5,000 ft = 0.832; 300°F at 5,000 ft = 0.580.

Challenges, in this order:

# Question shown Correct answer Feedback when wrong 1 Density ratio at 300°F, sea level? 0.697 530 ÷ (300 + 460) = 530 ÷ 760 = 0.697. Add 460 to °F before dividing. 2 Density ratio at 70°F, 5,000 ft? 0.832 24.89 ÷ 29.92 = 0.832; at 70°F the temperature factor is 1.000. 3 Density ratio at 300°F, 5,000 ft? 0.580 Multiply the two factors: 0.832 × 0.697 = 0.580. 4 Density ratio at 600°F, sea level? 0.500 530 ÷ (600 + 460) = 530 ÷ 1,060 = 0.500. 5 A system needs 3.00 in. wg at 300°F, sea level. What standard-air pressure do you select from the catalog (in. wg)? 4.30 Divide by the density ratio when going from the job to the catalog: 3.00 ÷ 0.697 = 4.30 in. wg. Multiplying gives 2.09, which would under-select the fan.

Provenance: The density ratio formula and the 0.075 lb/ft³ standard are from the chapter section "Standard Air". Barometric pressures are from the chapter's elevation table, computed from the standard atmosphere. Challenge 5 is the chapter's 300°F worked example.

Rules: density ratio = (Pb ÷ 29.92) × (530 ÷ (T + 460)), with T in °F and Pb in in. Hg. Density = 0.075 × ratio. Temperature marker: min 0, max 1,000, step 10, default 70, unit °F. Elevation selector: 0, 2,500, 5,000, 7,500 ft; default 0 ft. Ratios display to three decimals.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner moves the temperature marker and switches the elevation; the marked point and its hover readout update. The learner should notice that the ratio at 600°F is exactly half the ratio at 70°F, and that each elevation curve is the sea-level curve multiplied by a constant.
  2. The learner opens the challenges. For each, the learner types an answer and presses Check; the chart then marks the correct point on the correct curve.
  3. After the five challenges the learner may continue exploring.

Feedback: Five challenges, fixed order, two attempts each. Correct: "Correct: ." Incorrect: the "Feedback when wrong" text. After the second wrong attempt the answer is shown, the point is marked and the challenge counts as missed. A score "n of 5 correct on first attempt" is shown at the end.

Starting State: The sea-level curve with the marker at 70°F and a ratio of 1.000, the other three curves visible, and the question "How much lighter is 300°F air than standard air?"

Chapter Anchors: 0.075 lb/ft³; 70°F; 29.92 in. Hg; 530; 460; 300°F at sea level = 0.697 and 0.0523 lb/ft³; 5,000 ft = 24.89 in. Hg and 0.832; 2,500 ft = 27.31 in. Hg (0.913); 7,500 ft = 22.65 in. Hg (0.757); required 3.00 in. wg at 300°F selects at 4.30 in. wg.

docs.title: Wet Airstreams
docs.text:
A wet airstream carries enough water vapor, mist or steam that liquid water can condense and collect inside the fan. Typical sources are dishwashing and laundry exhaust, swimming-pool exhaust, cooling and washing processes, and any process that vents steam. Water vapor changes air density only slightly, so the main concern is not performance but what the water does to the fan: it pools in the housing, attacks steel and coatings, and can reach motors and bearings.

FanPedia lists several provisions for wet service:

  • Drains and weep holes. Fan housings typically need an opening at the lowest point for draining moisture; most come standard with a weep hole, and a drain (a half-coupling pipe welded to the scroll, with an optional plug or valve) can be added. Inlet boxes may also get drains (FanPedia p. 147).
  • High moisture construction, used "in applications where steam or condensation may collect in the fan housing." It applies to Arrangement 9 axial fans only and cannot be combined with high temperature construction (FanPedia p. 122).
  • Motor enclosure. An open drip-proof (ODP) motor "should not be used in dirty and wet atmospheres"; a totally enclosed motor is the usual choice (FanPedia p. 73).

Worked example: reading a wet-service inquiry. A customer asks for an exhaust fan for a commercial laundry: warm, steam-laden air, ducted to the roof, with the fan mounted in the duct at its low point. Work through it the way an application engineer would:

  1. Will liquid collect in the fan? Yes: the fan sits at the duct's low point and the air is near saturation. Specify a housing drain at the lowest point, piped to a floor drain, rather than relying on a weep hole.
  2. Does the air pass over the motor? If the design puts the motor in the airstream, choose an arrangement that moves it out, or a totally enclosed motor; never ODP.
  3. Is the moisture carrying anything else? Laundry exhaust also carries lint, which makes the airstream particulate-laden as well (see below). Note both conditions on the order.

docs.title: Corrosive Airstreams
docs.text:
A corrosive airstream contains gases, vapors or mists that chemically attack the fan's materials: acids, alkalis, chlorine, solvents and similar compounds, often made worse by moisture and heat. Mild steel, the standard material, can lose metal quickly in such service. The defense is material selection: coatings, stainless steel (SST) or fiberglass-reinforced plastic (FRP). Twin City Fan's current catalog states that its fiberglass fans "are specifically designed for the exhaust of moisture-laden, corrosive or chemically contaminated air" and that FRP "offers a more economical solution compared to stainless steel or other exotic alloys."

Mixing materials needs care. FanPedia lists buffer strips for use "when customer specifies that corrosion resistant (i.e. stainless steel) housing may not be welded to a mild steel pedestal" (FanPedia p. 85). Motors near corrosive air may call for a Severe Duty or chemical-duty motor (FanPedia p. 73).

Worked example: choosing a material path. An inquiry reads: "Exhaust from a chemical storage room; chlorine-bearing air; room temperature; humid." Before any material can be chosen, the application engineer needs four facts:

Question Why it matters Which chemicals, and at what concentration? Material compatibility is chemical-specific; "corrosive" alone cannot be quoted. What is the airstream temperature, normal and maximum? Every coating and FRP resin has a temperature limit that must be checked against the catalog. Is the air wet or dry? Moisture usually accelerates attack, and it adds the wet-airstream questions. Where is the motor, and is it in the airstream? It decides whether the motor needs protection or a severe-duty enclosure.

For this inquiry, humid, chlorine-bearing air at room temperature points first toward the fiberglass fan line, with stainless steel as the alternative if the catalog's FRP limits or the customer's standard rule it out. The final choice is confirmed against the current catalog, not against a general rule.

docs.title: Particulate-Laden Airstreams
docs.text:
A particulate-laden airstream carries solid material: dust, grit, chips, fibers, lint, paper trim or granular product. Particles cause two problems. They wear (erode) blades and housings, and they build up on surfaces, which unbalances the impeller and causes vibration. Fibrous and stringy material can also wrap around impeller parts. Particulate service therefore pushes toward rugged impellers, wear-resistant construction and bearings kept out of the airstream. FanPedia shows radial-bladed impellers designed for this work, including the open paddle impeller, the material handling impeller (wool) and the paper handling impeller (FanPedia p. 32), and taconite bearing seals "designed for dirty or abrasive environments" (FanPedia p. 100). Twin City Fan's current catalog offers pressure blowers "to meet clean or particulate-laden airstream applications."

Ducts that carry material must keep the air moving fast enough that particles stay suspended instead of settling and plugging the duct. That minimum is the conveying velocity, and for many dusts it is on the order of 3,500–4,500 fpm (a general industrial ventilation range; the right value depends on the material).

Worked example: airflow for a dust-collection branch. An 8 in. round duct must carry dust at 4,000 fpm (illustrative).

  1. Area: \( \pi (8/12)^2 / 4 = 0.349 \) ft².
  2. Airflow from continuity: \( Q = 0.349 \times 4{,}000 = 1{,}396 \) CFM.
  3. Velocity pressure: \( (4{,}000 / 4005)^2 = 1.00 \) in. wg.

That velocity pressure, about 1 in. wg in every branch, is lost at every hood entry and recovered nowhere. This is why dust-collection fans run at higher pressures than ventilation fans of the same airflow, and why the airstream description must say what the material is, not just "dusty."

docs.title: Explosive Atmospheres
docs.text:
An explosive atmosphere is air that contains flammable gases, vapors, mists or combustible dusts in concentrations that a spark or hot surface could ignite. Solvent vapors, fuel vapors and fine grain, wood or metal dust are common examples. A fan in such service must not become the ignition source: a steel impeller rubbing a steel inlet can throw sparks. Twin City Fan addresses this with spark-resistant construction in three types, summarized here from FanPedia (p. 193):

  • Type A, the highest degree of spark resistance: all fan components in the airstream are non-ferrous, assembled to reduce the possibility of contact between stationary and rotating parts.
  • Type B: the impeller is non-ferrous, typically aluminum with an aluminum rub plate, and the airstream parts are assembled to reduce the possibility of contact.
  • Type C, a minimal level: only reduces possible contact between rotating and stationary parts, typically with an aluminum inlet cone and an aluminum rub plate where the shaft passes through the housing.

Spark resistance concerns the fan's airstream parts. The motor is a separate decision: an explosion-proof (EXPL) motor is designed so that an internal arc or explosion cannot ignite a surrounding atmosphere of flammable dust or gas, and its rating is specified under the National Electrical Code by class, division and group (FanPedia p. 73). Chapter 20 treats the spark-resistant types in detail, including what each one does not protect against.

Worked example: separating the two decisions. An inquiry reads: "Exhaust for a solvent-recovery room; flammable vapors present; motor to be mounted in the same room."

  1. Is the airstream an explosive atmosphere? Yes, flammable vapors are present. The specification needs spark-resistant construction, and the type (A, B or C) must come from the customer's specification or engineer, because it sets how much of the fan must be non-ferrous.
  2. Is the motor in a hazardous location? Yes, it is in the same room. It needs an explosion-proof motor rated for the area's NEC class, division and group, which the owner or the authority having jurisdiction determines; the fan supplier does not assign it.
  3. If the motor could instead be placed outside the hazardous area, for example with a belt-driven arrangement and the motor beyond a wall, the motor decision changes, but the spark-resistance decision does not.

Spark Resistant Is Not Explosion Proof

Watch out for orders that say "explosion-proof fan." Spark-resistant construction lowers the chance that the fan's moving parts strike a spark; it does not make the fan, or the system, explosion-proof. Ask which spark-resistant type the specification calls for and, separately, what hazardous-location rating the motor needs.

docs.title: Recognizing Conditions Together
docs.text: Real airstreams often combine conditions: a laundry is wet and particulate-laden, a grain elevator is particulate-laden and explosive, a natatorium is wet and corrosive. The sorter below gives ten application descriptions; tag every condition each one has, or mark it clean.

docs.title: Diagram: Airstream Condition Sorter
docs.text:
Airstream Condition Sorter

Type: microsim sim-id: ch02-airstream-condition-sorter Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Understand Bloom Verb: classify Learning Objective: The learner will classify ten application descriptions by every airstream condition they present (hot, wet, corrosive, particulate-laden, explosive atmosphere, or clean), matching the answer key on at least 8 of 10.

Prerequisites: airstream, hot airstream, wet airstream, corrosive airstream, particulate-laden airstream, explosive atmosphere (defined in the section "The Airstreams Fans Handle" above).

Evidence of Mastery: For each description the learner selects one or more condition tags and presses Submit. An item is correct when the selected set exactly matches the answer key. Mastery is at least 8 of 10 correct on the first attempt. Reading definitions by clicking a tag's info button is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) Each airstream has only one condition. (2) Warm, humid air is "hot." (3) Combustible dust is only a particulate problem. (4) Any chemical exhaust is an explosive atmosphere.

Instructional Rationale: Classification with multi-select tags makes the learner judge each condition separately against its definition, which is the Understand-level skill an inquiry form needs. Immediate per-item feedback with a reason corrects the overlap misconceptions while the description is still on screen.

Content:

Tag definitions, shown on each tag's info button:

  • Hot: temperature high enough to change performance or call for construction beyond the standard catalog build.
  • Wet: enough water vapor, mist or steam that liquid can condense and collect in the fan.
  • Corrosive: gases, vapors or mists that chemically attack the fan's materials.
  • Particulate-laden: carries solid material such as dust, grit, chips, fibers or lint.
  • Explosive atmosphere: contains flammable gases, vapors or combustible dusts that a spark could ignite.
  • Clean: none of the above; ordinary air near standard conditions.

Items, shown in shuffled order:

# Description shown to the learner Correct tags Why (shown as feedback) 1 Recirculating air inside a kiln dryer at 450°F. Hot 450°F is well inside FanPedia's high-temperature package ranges; nothing else is described. 2 Exhausting steam-laden air from a commercial dishwashing room. Wet Steam condenses and collects in the housing; it is warm, not hot. 3 Dry, room-temperature exhaust from a chemical storage room containing chlorine compounds. Corrosive Chlorine compounds attack fan materials; the air is dry and at room temperature. 4 Sand and grit from a foundry shakeout, at ambient temperature. Particulate-laden Sand is abrasive solid material; it is not combustible. 5 Exhaust from a solvent-recovery room where flammable vapors are present. Explosive atmosphere Flammable vapors could be ignited by a spark from the fan. 6 Filtered outdoor air supplied to an office floor. Clean Filtered outdoor air near 70°F has none of the five conditions. 7 Exhaust from an indoor swimming pool hall: warm, humid air containing chlorine compounds. Wet, Corrosive The humidity condenses and the chlorine compounds attack materials; the air is warm, not hot. 8 Grain dust drawn from a feed-mill bucket elevator. Particulate-laden, Explosive atmosphere Grain dust is solid material and is also a combustible dust. 9 Clean air leaving a heat-treating oven at 700°F. Hot 700°F calls for high-temperature construction; the air is stated to be clean. 10 Warm, moist exhaust from commercial laundry dryers carrying lint. Wet, Particulate-laden Moisture condenses in the duct and fan, and lint is fibrous solid material.

Provenance: Definitions are from the chapter section "The Airstreams Fans Handle". Item temperatures and descriptions are illustrative applications written for this sim; item 1 and 9 temperature judgments rest on FanPedia pp. 110–116 as summarized in the chapter's high-temperature table.

Rules: Tags are multi-select. Selecting Clean clears all other tags, and selecting any other tag clears Clean. An empty selection cannot be submitted. Correct means exact set match; a partly matching set is incorrect and the feedback names which tags were missing or extra.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner reads a description and may open any tag's info button to read its definition.
  2. The learner selects every tag that applies and presses Submit.
  3. The sim marks the item, shows the correct tags and the "Why" text, and presents the next item.
  4. After ten items the sim lists any missed items with their correct tags.

Feedback: Ten items, shuffled, one attempt each. Correct: "Correct: . ." Incorrect: "Not quite. Missing: . Extra: . ." The correct answer is revealed immediately after each submission. A score "n of 10" is shown at the end; the learner may restart with a new shuffle, and only the first run counts as evidence.

Starting State: The first shuffled description with no tags selected and the prompt "Which conditions does this airstream have? Select all that apply."

Chapter Anchors: Ten descriptions; five conditions plus Clean; the chapter names laundry (wet and particulate-laden), grain elevator (particulate-laden and explosive) and natatorium (wet and corrosive) as combined examples; mastery 8 of 10.

docs.title: Putting It Together on an Inquiry
docs.text:
Everything in this chapter ends up in a few lines of a fan inquiry or specification. A complete air-conditions description states:

  1. Airflow in CFM, and whether it is stated at actual or standard conditions.
  2. Pressure required, identified as static or total, at the stated airflow.
  3. Airstream temperature: normal operating, maximum, and the start-up condition.
  4. Site elevation, or barometric pressure.
  5. Each airstream condition present: hot, wet, corrosive, particulate-laden, explosive, with the material, chemical or hazard named.

With those five items, an application engineer can convert the duty to standard air, read the catalog, and begin choosing the construction the airstream demands.

You Can Describe the Air Now

You can now add velocity pressure to static pressure to find total pressure, work out a fan's pressure rise and air power, and convert a hot, high-altitude duty to the standard air a catalog uses. You can also name the airstream conditions that will steer construction choices in the chapters ahead.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Velocity in fpm, area in ft² and airflow in CFM are linked by continuity, \( Q = A \times V \); for the same airflow, a smaller duct means higher velocity.
  • Velocity pressure is the pressure of moving air brought to rest. At standard air, \( VP = (V/4005)^2 \): 4,005 fpm is 1.00 in. wg, and doubling velocity quadruples VP.
  • Total pressure is \( SP + VP \). On a fan's inlet side, SP is negative; keep the sign when you subtract.
  • A fan's pressure rise is fan total pressure, \( TP_{\text{outlet}} - TP_{\text{inlet}} \); fan static pressure is FTP minus the outlet velocity pressure. Air power is \( Q \times FTP / 6356 \).
  • In a fixed duct system, pressure rises with the square of airflow and air power with its cube, so a 20 percent airflow increase needs 44 percent more pressure.
  • "Blower" usually signals a high-pressure fan; by the ASME pressure-ratio definition, many pressure blowers are still fans. State airflow and pressure, not the word.
  • Barometric pressure is 29.92 in. Hg (about 407 in. wg) at sea level and falls with altitude; air density falls with it.
  • Catalogs rate fans at standard air, 0.075 lb/ft³. At the same speed, CFM does not change with density, but pressure and horsepower scale with the density ratio. Multiply going from catalog to job; divide going from job to catalog.
  • Hot airstreams reduce operating pressure and power, raise cold-start power relative to the hot condition, and call for high-temperature construction whose starting temperature depends on the fan design.
  • Wet, corrosive, particulate-laden and explosive airstreams each point to specific provisions: drains and enclosed motors, corrosion-resistant materials such as FRP or stainless steel, rugged impellers and adequate conveying velocity, and spark-resistant construction plus correctly rated motors. Airstreams often combine conditions, so ask about each one.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: This chapter introduces the parts that every fan shares: the housing, the impeller, the shaft and its bearings, the motor, the inlet and outlet, and the drive train that connects them. It also covers basic housing features such as welded and bolted construction, access doors, inspection ports, split housings, flanges, screens, backdraft dampers, and stack caps. These parts are the building blocks for the fan families in the next three chapters. After completing it, readers can point to and name each major part of a fan.

docs.title: Concepts Covered
docs.text:
This chapter covers the following 19 concepts from the learning graph:

Concept Concept Impact Score Fan Housing 1194 Impeller 5562 Fan Motor 2380 Fan Inlet 147 Fan Outlet 303 Fan Shaft 2742 Access Door 18 Welded Housing 2 Bolted Housing 1 Bearing 1755 Inlet Collar 3 Inlet Flange 11 Outlet Flange 9 Backdraft Damper 16 Bird and Safety Screens 16 Stack Cap 3 Split Housing 5 Inspection Port 1 Drive Train 725

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
This chapter builds on concepts from:

  • Chapter 1: Air, Pressure and the Fan

docs.title: Why Fan Anatomy Comes First
docs.text:
Every fan order, drawing, and field report is written in the vocabulary of fan parts. A specification asks for "an access door on the scroll," a mechanic reports "the drive-side bearing is running hot," and a contractor asks whether the "inlet is a collar or a flange." If you cannot point to each of those parts, you cannot check the order, answer the question, or catch the mistake before the fan ships.

Meet the Parts Before You Meet the Product Lines

Every Twin City Fan model, from a small panel fan to a large industrial blower, is built from the same short list of parts. Learn those parts here and every exploded view, submittal drawing, and field call in the rest of this book gets easier to read. Let's follow the airflow.

In Chapter 1 you learned that a fan is a machine that moves air by turning at some speed and absorbing some power. This chapter opens that machine up. We will follow a single cubic foot of air from the duct, through the fan, and back into the duct, naming each part it touches. Then we will look at the parts that turn the impeller, the parts that hold everything up, and the smaller features that let people inspect, clean, connect, and protect a fan.

The parts fall into four groups, and the chapter follows them in this order:

  • The air path: the housing, the impeller, the inlet, and the outlet, the parts that touch the airstream.
  • The rotating support: the shaft and the bearings that carry it.
  • The power source and the connection to it: the motor and the drive train.
  • The housing features and accessories: welded or bolted construction, split housings, access doors, inspection ports, flanges, collars, screens, backdraft dampers, and stack caps.

Most of the illustrations in this chapter come from the exploded views in FanPedia (pages 9 to 19). An exploded view is a drawing that pulls a machine's parts apart along their assembly lines, so you can see each part and where it goes. Later chapters revisit each group in detail; here the goal is a working map of the whole fan.

docs.title: The Fan Housing
docs.text:
The fan housing is the stationary shell that encloses the impeller and guides the air from the inlet to the outlet. FanPedia describes it as the main structure of the fan: it directs the air (or air carrying particulate) through the system, and it supports the other key components, including the inlet, the outlet, the framing, and the structural supports. Other components may be mounted inside it, outside it, or both. In the field you will also hear the housing called the side, the scroll, or the casing.

The shape of the housing depends on the fan family. A housed centrifugal fan has a snail-shaped housing. A tubeaxial or inline fan has a tubular housing, a straight cylinder with the impeller inside. A square inline fan has a box-shaped housing. Some fans have no housing at all: plenum fans, panel fans, and ring fans do without one, and a plug fan's housing is optional. Those fans still have an inlet and a discharge, but the space around them (an air-handler cabinet, a wall, or a ring) does the job a housing would do.

On a single-width, single-inlet (SWSI) centrifugal fan, the housing is made of several named pieces:

  • The housing scroll is the curved outer wrapper. Its spiral shape gives the air leaving the impeller room to slow down and build pressure as it travels toward the outlet.
  • The two housing sides are the flat plates on either side of the scroll. The inlet side carries the inlet opening; the drive side carries the opening for the shaft.
  • The cutoff is the point where the scroll comes closest to the impeller, just before the outlet. It separates the air that is leaving from the air that is still circling.
  • The wiper bar works near the inlet funnel to direct air through the housing, reducing turbulence and improving efficiency.
  • The framing stiffens the housing and ties it to its supports.
  • The inlet opening is usually round, so it can carry a collar, a funnel, a flange, or a combination of these. The outlet opening, also called the discharge, can be square, rectangular, or round.

The table below reorganizes those pieces by the job each one does, using the terms just defined.

Housing piece What it does Where you see it on a drawing Housing scroll Wraps the impeller and guides air toward the outlet The curved outline in a side view Housing sides Close the scroll and carry the inlet and shaft openings The flat faces in a front view Cutoff Separates outgoing air from recirculating air Just upstream of the outlet Wiper bar Helps direct air near the inlet funnel Near the inlet funnel Framing Stiffens the housing and connects it to supports Angles or bars around the scroll Inlet and outlet openings Let air in and out; carry flanges or collars The two ends of the air path

docs.title: Worked Example: Which of These Fans Has a Housing?
docs.text:
A distributor's quote lists five fans for one building: a SWSI centrifugal fan for a process exhaust, a tubeaxial fan for a parking garage, a plenum fan in an air handler, a plug fan in a second air handler, and a panel fan for a warehouse wall. The customer asks which ones will arrive with a housing that needs space and support.

  1. SWSI centrifugal: scroll housing. Plan for its footprint, outlet flange, and supports.
  2. Tubeaxial: tubular housing, connected into the duct run at both ends.
  3. Plenum fan: no housing; the air-handler cabinet encloses it.
  4. Plug fan: housing optional. If the order lists none, the cabinet encloses it.
  5. Panel fan: no housing; it mounts in a panel that fits a wall opening.

Answer: two fans certainly have housings, one may, and two do not.

The Housing Is Part of the Aerodynamics

It is tempting to think of the housing as a protective box, but on a housed centrifugal fan the scroll and cutoff are part of how the fan builds pressure. That is why a housing change, such as adding a split or an inlet box, is never just a sheet-metal question.

docs.title: Welded and Bolted Housings
docs.text:
Housings are joined together in one of two ways. A welded housing has its scroll, sides, and framing joined by welds, so the housing is one permanent piece. Welding gives a stiff housing with no bolted seams to leak. When FanPedia describes nominally leak-tight construction, it calls for continuous welds, with the weld locations varying by model (page 120).

A bolted housing is assembled from sections joined with bolts through mating flanges, so it can be taken apart. Bolted joints let a housing be shipped in pieces, opened for impeller removal, or replaced in parts. The trade-off is that every bolted seam is a possible leak path. For nominally leak-tight service, FanPedia requires closely spaced bolt holes, on 3-inch to 4-inch centers, and gasketing on bolted connections such as flanges, access doors, inlet funnels, and split housings (page 120). Many fans combine the two: a welded housing with bolted access doors, flanges, and inlet funnels.

docs.title: Split Housings
docs.text: A split housing is a housing built in sections that bolt together along a planned joint, so the housing can be opened or shipped in pieces. FanPedia (pages 156, 157 and 194) names three centrifugal styles. A horizontal split runs along the horizontal centerline; on size 807 and above, the shop may split the housing this way for shipping. A pie split cuts out a wedge of 90 degrees or more so the impeller can be removed without disturbing the inlet or outlet ductwork. A 3-way split divides the housing into three sections, either for shipping or so the fan can pass through an opening of a specific size, and it takes extra drafting and engineering time. Specify a split when the fan must enter a small room or when the impeller will be pulled for service.

docs.title: The Impeller
docs.text:
The impeller is the rotating part that does the work on the air. It is the only part of the fan that adds energy to the airstream; every other part either guides the air, supports the impeller, or turns it. In older literature and on some job sites it is called the wheel, and on axial fans it is sometimes called the propeller or rotor.

A centrifugal impeller is built from a few standard pieces. The blades are the curved or flat vanes that push the air. The back plate is the solid disk on the drive side that the blades are attached to. The impeller front plate (also called the shroud) is the ring on the inlet side that holds the blade tips and matches the inlet funnel. The hub is the center piece that fastens the impeller to the shaft. Air enters at the center of the impeller, turns 90 degrees, and is flung outward between the blades into the housing scroll.

An axial impeller is built differently. Its blades are attached around a hub, and air passes straight through along the shaft line. FanPedia (page 35) labels the axial parts as the blade, the blade tip, the hub, the hub boss, and, on adjustable-pitch impellers, the shank at the root of each blade that lets the blade angle be set.

The blade shape names the impeller type. FanPedia shows the centrifugal and mixed flow types on pages 31 and 32; you only need their names here, since Chapter 8 compares them in detail.

Impeller type Blade shape in one line Backward inclined Flat, single-thickness blades tilted back from the direction of rotation Backward curved Single-thickness blades curved back from the direction of rotation Airfoil Backward-inclined blades with a wing-shaped (airfoil) cross section Forward curved Single-thickness blades curved forward, toward the direction of rotation Radial tip Curved forward at the entering edge and radial at the tip of the leaving edge Radial bladed Straight paddle blades that point out from the center Mixed flow Airfoil blades that taper from the front plate to the hub end

The impeller also has a position on the shaft. An overhung impeller is mounted on the end of the shaft, with both bearings on one side of it. A center-hung impeller sits between the two bearings. FanPedia (page 30) shows Arrangements 1, 4, 8, 9 and 10 with overhung impellers and Arrangements 3 and 7 with center-hung impellers. We will return to this when we reach the shaft.

docs.title: How Hard Is the Impeller Working?
docs.text: One quick way to compare how hard two impellers are working is tip speed, the speed of the outer edge of the blades as they sweep around. Because the tip travels one circumference per revolution, tip speed grows with both the diameter and the rotational speed. Tip speed matters because both the pressure the impeller can develop and the stress in its metal rise as the tips move faster.

docs.title: Impeller Tip Speed
docs.text:
\[ V_{tip} = \frac{\pi \, D \, N}{12} \]

where:

  • \( V_{tip} \) is the tip speed in feet per minute (ft/min)
  • \( D \) is the impeller diameter in inches
  • \( N \) is the rotational speed in revolutions per minute (RPM)
  • 12 converts inches to feet

docs.title: Worked Example: Tip Speed of a Centrifugal Impeller
docs.text:
An illustrative 30-inch impeller turns at 1,200 RPM.

  1. Multiply the diameter by \( \pi \): \( \pi \times 30 = 94.25 \) inches per revolution.
  2. Multiply by the speed: \( 94.25 \times 1{,}200 = 113{,}097 \) inches per minute.
  3. Divide by 12 to convert to feet: \( 113{,}097 / 12 = 9{,}425 \) ft/min.

If the same impeller were sped up to 2,400 RPM, the tip speed would double to 18,850 ft/min. Speed changes performance quickly, which is why a catalog lists the speed limits for each impeller rather than leaving them to judgment. Chapter 25 covers the fan laws that describe exactly how airflow, pressure, and power follow speed.

docs.title: The Fan Inlet
docs.text:
The fan inlet is the opening where air enters the fan, together with the parts that guide the air into the impeller. On a housed centrifugal fan the inlet is a round opening in the housing side. On an inline or axial fan it is the open upstream end of the tube. On a plenum or plug fan it is the inlet funnel itself, open to the cabinet.

Air arriving at the impeller should be smooth and evenly spread across the opening. If it enters the impeller crowded to one side or spinning, part of the impeller works harder than the rest, and the fan delivers less air and makes more noise than its rating. Three parts at the inlet prevent that:

  • The inlet funnel is an aerodynamically shaped ring that funnels air into the impeller. FanPedia (page 188) says it provides high efficiency and smooth airflow through the fan, is flanged on one end to mount to the housing, and is also called the inlet cone, funnel, or inlet bell. It reaches close to the impeller front plate, so the gap between them stays small.
  • The inlet collar is a short sleeve at the inlet for a slip-fit duct connection.
  • The inlet flange is a flat ring with bolt holes for a bolted duct connection.

The collar and the flange are covered in their own sections below. Many inlets carry more than one of these: FanPedia notes that the round inlet opening supports a collar, a funnel, a flange, or any combination (page 59). Inlet accessories, such as inlet boxes, inlet vanes, silencers, and flex connectors, attach at this same opening and are covered in Chapter 18.

Inlet velocity is the number that tells you whether the inlet connection is likely to cause trouble. You met air velocity and cubic feet per minute (CFM) in Chapter 1: velocity is airflow divided by the area it passes through.

docs.title: Air Velocity Through an Opening
docs.text:
\[ V = \frac{Q}{A} \]

where:

  • \( V \) is the average air velocity in feet per minute (ft/min)
  • \( Q \) is the airflow in cubic feet per minute (CFM)
  • \( A \) is the open area in square feet (ft²)

docs.title: Worked Example: Velocity at an Inlet Collar
docs.text:
An illustrative fan moves 6,000 CFM through a round inlet collar 20 inches in diameter.

  1. Convert the diameter to feet and find the radius: 20 in = 1.667 ft, so the radius is 0.833 ft.
  2. Find the area: \( A = \pi r^2 = \pi \times 0.833^2 = 2.18 \) ft².
  3. Find the velocity: \( V = 6{,}000 / 2.18 = 2{,}750 \) ft/min.

At 2,750 ft/min the air is moving fast enough that an elbow bolted right at the collar would push the air to one side of the impeller. That is the practical reason inlet duct layout matters: the inlet funnel can smooth air that arrives straight, but it cannot fix air that arrives spinning or crowded against one wall.

An Elbow at the Inlet Costs Performance

A common trap is accepting a duct layout with an elbow bolted directly to the inlet collar or flange, because the fan's catalog rating assumes smooth, straight air at the inlet. Flag the layout before the order is placed and ask for a straight duct run, turning vanes, or an inlet box designed for the job.

docs.title: Inlet Collar
docs.text: An inlet collar is a short, plain cylindrical sleeve attached to the fan inlet so a duct or flexible connector can slip over it and be clamped. It has no bolt holes. In the FanPedia exploded views of centrifugal fans (pages 9 and 10), the inlet collar is drawn as one inlet option and the flanged inlet as the other. Collars suit lighter, slip-fit duct connections, such as a flexible sleeve held with clamps. When the connection must be bolted, rigid, or sealed, specify an inlet flange instead.

docs.title: Inlet Flange
docs.text:
An inlet flange is a flat ring or frame around the fan inlet, drilled with a bolt-hole pattern, so a duct or accessory can be bolted to the fan face to face. A flange gives a rigid, sealable joint that can carry load. The matching part on the duct side is the companion flange. FanPedia (page 180) explains that companion flanges are connected to the ductwork in the field to guarantee a matching connection to the fan, and they are shipped loose for field mounting. Companion flanges come round or rectangular.

The inlet flange can also be structural. On Arrangements 4VI and 4HI, direct-drive fans mounted by their inlet, FanPedia notes that the entire fan is supported by the inlet flange only (page 21).

docs.title: Worked Example: Connecting Ductwork to an Inlet Flange
docs.text:
A mechanical contractor will connect a round duct to the inlet of a SWSI centrifugal fan and asks what to order so the bolt holes line up.

  1. Confirm the fan's inlet connection on the submittal drawing. It shows a flanged inlet, not a collar, so the connection is bolted.
  2. Read the inlet flange's bolt-hole count, bolt circle, and hole size from the drawing. These are model-specific; never guess them.
  3. Add a round inlet companion flange to the order. It is drilled to match the fan's inlet flange and is shipped loose.
  4. The contractor attaches the companion flange to the duct in the field, then bolts it to the fan's inlet flange with a gasket between them.

Result: the duct and fan meet with matching bolt patterns, and nobody drills holes on the job site. If the fan were an Arrangement 4HI hung by its inlet, step 4 would also need the contractor to confirm that the duct-side structure can carry the fan's full weight.

docs.title: The Fan Outlet
docs.text:
The fan outlet, also called the discharge, is the opening where air leaves the fan, together with the parts that connect it to the downstream duct or to the open air. On a housed centrifugal fan the outlet is the rectangular or square opening at the end of the scroll, just past the cutoff. On an inline or axial fan it is the downstream end of the tube. The outlet's position on a centrifugal fan, such as top horizontal or up blast, is designated with a discharge code; that system is covered in Chapter 12.

Because the air has just been accelerated by the impeller, it usually leaves faster than it entered and is not yet evenly spread across the opening. Three kinds of parts deal with that:

  • The outlet flange is a flat frame with a bolt-hole pattern for a bolted duct connection (covered in its own section below). On double-width, double-inlet (DWDI) fans, FanPedia shows a setback outlet flange, set back from the end of the outlet (page 61).
  • A transition is a duct piece that changes the opening from one shape to another, such as rectangular to round, or keeps the shape but enlarges or reduces it. FanPedia (page 67) notes a transition can be welded to the fan or bolted on as a separate piece.
  • An evasé is a transition that enlarges the outlet. It is attached, usually bolted, to the discharge, and its outlet is larger than its inlet. FanPedia (page 146) gives its purpose: to reduce the fan's outlet velocity and increase its static pressure capability. For some fans the published ratings include the evasé.

Outlets that discharge to the open air carry their own accessories: backdraft dampers, screens, and stack caps, which are covered near the end of this chapter. The table below summarizes the outlet parts just described.

Outlet part Purpose Typical connection Outlet flange Bolted connection to the duct or an accessory Bolted, with a companion flange Setback outlet flange Outlet flange set back from the end of the outlet (DWDI fans) Bolted Transition Changes the shape or size of the opening to match the duct Welded or bolted Evasé Enlarges the outlet to lower velocity and raise static pressure capability Usually bolted

docs.title: Worked Example: What an Evasé Does to Outlet Velocity
docs.text:
An illustrative centrifugal fan delivers 9,000 CFM through an outlet 18 inches by 24 inches. The engineer is considering an evasé that enlarges the opening to 24 inches by 30 inches.

  1. Outlet area without the evasé: \( (18/12) \times (24/12) = 1.5 \times 2.0 = 3.0 \) ft².
  2. Outlet velocity without the evasé: \( 9{,}000 / 3.0 = 3{,}000 \) ft/min.
  3. Outlet area with the evasé: \( (24/12) \times (30/12) = 2.0 \times 2.5 = 5.0 \) ft².
  4. Velocity leaving the evasé: \( 9{,}000 / 5.0 = 1{,}800 \) ft/min.

The evasé cuts the leaving velocity by 40 percent. Air that leaves more slowly carries less of the fan's energy away as velocity, which is how an evasé lets the fan deliver more useful static pressure. Chapter 2 explains the pressure side of this trade.

docs.title: Outlet Flange
docs.text:
An outlet flange, also called a discharge flange, is a flat frame around the fan outlet with a bolt-hole pattern for a bolted connection to the downstream duct or to an outlet accessory such as a damper, silencer, or evasé. Like the inlet flange, it mates with a companion flange shipped loose for field mounting. On a centrifugal fan the outlet flange is usually rectangular; on an inline or axial fan it is round.

The bolt pattern is where outlet flanges cause trouble. On cast aluminum pressure blowers, FanPedia (pages 125 and 180) shows a blast gate, a wafer-type butterfly valve, that mounts to the outlet flange, and both the blast gate and the flange bolt pattern match the 125# ASA pipe flange standard. For nominally leak-tight fans, every bolted connection, outlet flange included, needs closely spaced holes on 3-inch to 4-inch centers and gaskets (page 120).

docs.title: Worked Example: Matching an Outlet Accessory to the Outlet Flange
docs.text:
A plant engineer wants to add a blast gate to the discharge of a pressure blower and pipe it to process equipment.

  1. Identify the outlet connection on the blower's drawing: a flanged outlet with a 125# ASA pipe flange bolt pattern.
  2. Select the blast gate. Its bolt pattern also matches 125# ASA, so it bolts directly to the outlet flange with no adapter.
  3. Check the downstream pipe. If it ends in a 125# ASA flange of the same size, it bolts to the blast gate; if not, add a transition or companion flange that matches.
  4. Note the blast gate's limit from FanPedia (page 180): maximum temperature 250°F. If the process air is hotter, the blast gate is the wrong accessory.

Result: three parts that bolt together with one shared flange standard, plus one temperature check that a quick read of the outlet flange alone would have missed.

Now that you have seen the inlet, impeller, housing, and outlet, you can trace the complete air path. The MicroSim below asks you to put the parts in the order a cubic foot of air meets them.

docs.title: Diagram: Follow the Airflow Through a Centrifugal Fan
docs.text:
Follow the Airflow Through a Centrifugal Fan

Type: microsim sim-id: ch03-follow-the-airflow Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Remember Bloom Verb: list Learning Objective: The learner will list, in airflow order, the eight parts that air passes through in a ducted, belt-driven SWSI centrifugal fan, and set aside the three parts that stay out of the air path.

Prerequisites: fan housing, housing scroll, cutoff, impeller, inlet funnel, inlet flange, outlet flange, ductwork, shaft, bearing, motor (all defined in "The Fan Housing", "The Impeller", "The Fan Inlet" and "The Fan Outlet" above; shaft, bearing and motor are named in the chapter introduction).

Evidence of Mastery: The learner places all 11 cards: 8 into numbered air-path slots 1 to 8, and 3 into a "Not in the air path" bin, then submits. A placement is correct when it matches the Content table. Mastery is all 11 cards correct within two submissions. Dragging cards around before submitting is exploration and is not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) Air enters the impeller at the blade tips (it enters at the center, through the inlet funnel). (2) The cutoff is at the inlet (it is just upstream of the outlet). (3) Every part of a fan touches the air (in a belt-driven Arrangement 9 fan the bearings and motor sit outside the airstream).

Instructional Rationale: Ordering the parts by the path of the air forces the learner to recall each part's position relative to the others, which is the Remember-level skill an exploded view or field call requires. Including three non-air-path cards makes the learner decide what touches the air, not just recite a list.

Content:

Card Correct place Why (shown as feedback) Inlet ductwork Slot 1 Air arrives from the upstream duct. Inlet flange (with companion flange) Slot 2 The bolted joint where the duct meets the fan inlet. Inlet funnel Slot 3 Funnels the air smoothly into the eye of the impeller. Impeller Slot 4 The only part that adds energy to the air; air enters at the center and is thrown outward between the blades. Housing scroll Slot 5 Collects the air leaving the impeller and guides it toward the outlet. Cutoff Slot 6 The point of the scroll closest to the impeller, just before the outlet; it separates leaving air from circling air. Outlet flange Slot 7 The bolted joint where the fan outlet meets the downstream duct. Outlet ductwork Slot 8 Air leaves the fan system through the downstream duct. Shaft Not in the air path It passes through the housing side to carry the impeller, but it is not a stage the air flows through.
