A mixed flow fan uses a hybrid axial-centrifugal impeller, so air leaves the impeller on a diagonal, partly along the shaft and partly outward. FanPedia groups mixed flow fans with tubular inline centrifugal fans: both are built with tubular housings, both move air straight through the fan, and both use straightening vanes to return the air to the duct direction. FanPedia describes the mixed flow impeller's airfoil blades as tapering from the impeller front plate to the hub end, resulting in a larger tip width. Twin City Fan's current catalog describes its mixed flow fans as giving the performance of a centrifugal fan with the space-saving advantages of an axial-type fan, for large volumes of clean air at low to moderate pressures, and splits the line into high-pressure models such as QSL and low-pressure models such as QCLB. For classification, remember that a mixed flow fan is its own family even though its tube looks like a vaneaxial's.

With the three families and their housings and vanes defined, you can test the impeller-decides rule on seven fan configurations. For each one, you predict two directions: the direction air leaves the impeller, and the direction air leaves the whole fan.

docs.title: Diagram: Airflow Path Explorer
docs.text:
Airflow Path Explorer

Type: microsim sim-id: ch04-airflow-path-explorer Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Understand Bloom Verb: classify Learning Objective: The learner will classify seven fan configurations by the direction air leaves the impeller and the direction air leaves the fan, relative to the fan shaft.

Prerequisites: impeller, fan shaft, fan housing (Chapter 3); fan family, centrifugal fan, axial fan, mixed flow fan, scroll housing, unhoused centrifugal fan, plenum fan, tubular housing, guide vanes, straightening vanes, inline centrifugal fan (all defined in this chapter above this block).

Evidence of Mastery: For each of the 7 configurations, the learner commits two predictions before the airflow animation plays: (a) impeller exit direction and (b) fan exit direction. Each prediction is correct when it matches the answer columns in Content. Mastery is 12 of 14 predictions correct on the first attempt. Watching the animation and replaying it are exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) A fan in a round, straight-through tube must be an axial fan. (2) Air leaves a centrifugal fan in the same direction it leaves the impeller in every case. (3) Guide vanes add pressure by speeding the air up. (4) A mixed flow fan discharges at a diagonal out of the fan.

Instructional Rationale: Classifying by airflow direction is an Understand-level task, so the learner must commit a prediction before the answer is revealed, then see a slowed step-through of the actual path. Separating impeller exit from fan exit forces the learner to see that the housing and vanes, not the impeller, decide where air finally leaves.

Content:

Answer choices for impeller exit direction: "Parallel to the shaft", "At a right angle to the shaft", "Diagonal (between parallel and right angle)".

Answer choices for fan exit direction: "Parallel to the shaft", "At a right angle to the shaft, through one outlet", "Outward in all directions around the impeller".

# Configuration shown (side view, shaft drawn horizontally) Impeller exit Fan exit Why (feedback) 1 Housed centrifugal fan, single width single inlet (SWSI), in a scroll housing At a right angle to the shaft At a right angle to the shaft, through one outlet The centrifugal impeller throws air outward; the scroll gathers it and sends it out one outlet at a right angle to the shaft. 2 Housed centrifugal fan, double width double inlet (DWDI), in a scroll housing At a right angle to the shaft At a right angle to the shaft, through one outlet Air enters from both sides, but the impeller still throws it outward and the scroll still collects it to one outlet. 3 Plenum fan (unhoused centrifugal) inside an air handler cabinet At a right angle to the shaft Outward in all directions around the impeller With no housing, nothing collects the air; it leaves the impeller all the way around and pressurizes the surrounding plenum. 4 Tubular inline centrifugal fan with straightening vanes At a right angle to the shaft Parallel to the shaft The impeller is centrifugal, so air leaves it radially; the tube and straightening vanes turn the air back to flow along the duct. 5 Tubeaxial fan (no guide vanes) Parallel to the shaft Parallel to the shaft An axial impeller pushes air along the shaft; it leaves the fan still swirling because there are no vanes to straighten it. 6 Vaneaxial fan (guide vanes downstream of the impeller) Parallel to the shaft Parallel to the shaft Same axial path as the tubeaxial; the guide vanes remove the swirl but do not change the main direction. 7 Mixed flow fan in a tubular housing with straightening vanes Diagonal (between parallel and right angle) Parallel to the shaft The hybrid impeller sends air out on a diagonal; the tubular housing and vanes return it to the duct direction.

After the two predictions for an item are committed, the animation shows particles entering along the shaft, following the configuration's path through the impeller, and leaving the fan. Swirl is shown as a rotating component of particle motion for items 5 and 6; for item 6 the swirl visibly stops after the guide vanes.

Labels the learner sees on the drawings: "Shaft", "Impeller", "Inlet", "Outlet", plus "Scroll housing" (items 1 and 2), "Plenum wall" (item 3), "Tubular housing" (items 4 to 7), "Straightening vanes" (items 4 and 7), "Guide vanes" (item 6).

Provenance: Airflow paths from FanPedia (Twin City Fan, 2021) pp 4-7 (fan types) and p 186 (technical description of axial versus centrifugal impellers); vane locations from the exploded views on pp 15-17. The animation speed and particle counts are illustrative.

Rules: Items are presented in the fixed order 1 to 7. An item's animation does not play until both predictions are committed. The learner may not change a committed prediction. A replay button replays the current item's animation any number of times. The score counts only first-attempt predictions.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner reads the configuration name and studies the side-view drawing with the impeller blades shown but no airflow.
  2. The learner chooses an impeller exit direction and a fan exit direction, then commits.
  3. The animation plays. Each prediction is marked correct or incorrect, and the "Why" text appears.
  4. The learner advances to the next item. After item 7 a summary shows the score and lists the items missed.
  5. In the summary, the learner should notice that items 4, 6 and 7 all leave the fan parallel to the shaft, but only item 6 is an axial fan.

Feedback: 7 items, fixed order, one attempt per prediction. Correct prediction: "Correct." followed by the "Why" text. Incorrect prediction: "Not quite. The answer is ." followed by the "Why" text. A running count "Predictions correct: n of 14" is shown. The summary after item 7 states "Mastery: 12 of 14 or better" when met, otherwise "Review the Fan Families section, then try again", with a restart button that resets the score.

Starting State: Item 1 is shown with no airflow drawn and both prediction choices empty. The prompt reads "Which way will the air leave the impeller, and which way will it leave the fan?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter names three families: centrifugal, axial and mixed flow. The chapter states that seven configurations are included and that the learner predicts two directions for each. The chapter's Fan Families worked example names a tubular inline centrifugal fan as the look-alike trap for an axial fan.

docs.title: Panel Fans and Ring Fans
docs.text: A panel fan is an axial fan whose impeller is centered in a flat, square panel; a ring fan centers an axial impeller in a ring-shaped housing. FanPedia notes both are typically wall mounted and move air in a straight line through the fan. They are the simplest axial forms: no tube, little or no ductwork, and air simply passes through an opening in a wall. FanPedia's exploded view of a panel fan shows the accessories that usually come with one: a mounting adapter, an inlet safety screen, a backdraft shutter, a weatherhood and a bird screen. Panel fans also serve as the base for some roof units, described below.

docs.title: Wall Mounted Fans and Weatherhoods
docs.text:
A wall mounted fan is a fan designed to be installed in or on a wall to supply or exhaust air directly through it, usually without ductwork. Twin City Fan's current catalog describes its wall mounted fans as built for cost-effective, general ventilation, offered direct and belt driven, with aluminum or steel impellers and fixed or adjustable pitch. The catalog sorts them by construction:

  • Heavy-duty construction: TCWPX (adjustable pitch blades) and TCWPZ (fabricated steel impeller)
  • Medium-duty construction: WPD (direct drive) and WPB (belt driven)
  • Light-duty construction: TCPE (direct drive)
  • Fiberglass construction: TCWPF (panel fan, direct drive)

Their fixed and adjustable pitch impellers mark most of them as panel fans in the axial family.

A weatherhood is a hood mounted over the outdoor side of a wall fan to keep rain and snow out of the opening while letting air pass. In FanPedia's panel fan exploded view, the weatherhood sits on the outside of the wall, with a bird screen across its open side to keep birds out.

docs.title: Power Roof Ventilators
docs.text:
Many building fans live on the roof, where they exhaust air from the spaces below or bring outside air in. A power roof ventilator (PRV) is a motor-driven fan unit built to mount on a roof opening. The word "power" separates it from a gravity ventilator, which has no fan. A PRV can be centrifugal or axial. FanPedia's Centrifugal Power Roof Ventilators page shows five rooftop configurations: upblast and side wall units exhaust air in a straight line through the fan, while downblast, louvered and hooded units move air up through the fan and deflect it down and outward.

Twin City Fan's current catalog splits rooftop products across two sections that are easy to confuse. Centrifugal Roof & Wall Exhausters are the centrifugal PRVs. Roof Ventilators are axial PRVs built on tubeaxial impellers, such as upblast TUD and TUB units, low profile LUD and LUB units, and hooded THD and THB units, along with filtered supply and smoke and heat versions.

docs.title: Worked Example: Decoding "PRV, Hooded, Belt Driven"
docs.text:
A specification schedule lists one exhaust fan as "PRV, hooded, belt driven." A new representative asks which catalog page to open.

  1. PRV does not name a family. Both centrifugal and axial PRVs exist, and both have hooded versions.
  2. Look for the family clue. The current catalog's hooded centrifugal roof exhausters include BCLH (belt driven); the hooded axial roof ventilators include THB (tubeaxial, belt driven).
  3. Use the job to narrow it. A hooded axial roof ventilator suits high-volume, low-pressure general exhaust, or supply in its filtered form. A centrifugal roof exhauster handles more duct resistance and, in the catalog's words, uses backward inclined, non-overloading impellers "for maximum efficiency and quiet operation."
  4. Ask before guessing. If the schedule gives an airflow and a static pressure, the selection can be checked against both lines. If it does not, the representative asks the engineer whether the unit is ducted and what static pressure it must overcome.

The lesson for every rooftop line is the same: "PRV" tells you where the fan sits, not how the air moves through it. Chapter 5 covers the rooftop product lines in detail.

docs.title: Roof Ventilators
docs.text: In Twin City Fan's current catalog, roof ventilators are the axial power roof ventilators: tubeaxial-based units in upblast, low profile upblast, hooded and filtered supply forms. The catalog describes them as providing cost-effective, general purpose exhaust ventilation of commercial buildings as well as a large variety of industrial applications, with direct and belt driven models and cast aluminum, adjustable pitch or fabricated steel, fixed pitch impellers. The term is narrower in the catalog than in everyday speech: on a job site, "roof ventilator" may be said of any roof fan, so confirm the family before quoting.

docs.title: Roof Mounted Axial Fans
docs.text:
A roof mounted axial fan is a tubeaxial fan, used as the base model, with roof accessories added. FanPedia shows two forms, and air moves in a straight line through the fan in both:

  • With a stack cap and curb cap, the air discharges straight up.
  • With a hood and curb cap, the air is deflected down and outward for exhaust; for supply, the flow runs in the reverse direction.

Roof mounted versions of panel fans follow the same pattern, built from a panel fan with a stack cap or a hood.

docs.title: Centrifugal Roof Exhausters
docs.text: A centrifugal roof exhauster is a power roof ventilator with a centrifugal impeller. Air enters from the roof opening below, turns outward through the impeller, and leaves through the unit's shroud, hood or louvers. FanPedia's exploded views show the parts of the upblast and downblast versions: a motor cover and motor housing (downblast), the motor, a bird screen, the impeller, a shroud (upblast) or skirt (downblast), and a curb cap that sits on the roof curb. Twin City Fan's current catalog describes its centrifugal roof and wall exhausters as direct and belt driven, with backward inclined, non-overloading centrifugal impellers, in configurations for relatively clean air and for grease-laden air. Upblast units throw the exhaust up and away from the roof; downblast units turn it down and outward toward the roof surface.

docs.title: Worked Example: Reading the Configuration From the Model List
docs.text:
A distributor is asked for a belt-driven centrifugal exhauster that discharges straight up, for a ducted general exhaust from a warehouse office. The distributor uses the configuration names in the current catalog to narrow the choices.

Requirement Matches Rules out Centrifugal impeller Centrifugal Roof & Wall Exhausters section Axial roof ventilators (TUD, TUB) Discharges straight up Upblast roof exhausters Downblast (DCRD, BCRD, VC), louvered (DCLP, BCLP), hooded (DCLH, BCLH) Belt driven BCRU, VCUB VCU (direct drive) General exhaust, not a kitchen BCRU, VCUB BCRUR (kitchen), BCRUSH (smoke and heat)

The remaining candidates, BCRU and VCUB, are then compared on performance and features. Upblast discharge versus downblast discharge, and why kitchen exhaust uses upblast, are developed in Chapter 5.

docs.title: Roof Curbs
docs.text:
A roof curb is a raised frame built into the roof around the opening, flashed into the roofing so water cannot get in, on which a rooftop fan sits. In FanPedia's centrifugal roof exhauster exploded view, the fan's curb cap, a flat base plate at the bottom of the fan, rests on top of the roof curb. The curb lifts the fan above standing water and snow and gives the roofer a weatherproof seam to work to. When quoting a roof fan, confirm two things:

  1. Whether the curb is supplied with the fan or by others.
  2. That the curb fits the fan's curb cap, so the fan seats and seals on it.

docs.title: Ceiling Ventilators
docs.text: A ceiling ventilator is a small exhaust fan mounted in or above a ceiling, drawing air from the room through a ceiling grille and discharging it into ductwork. Twin City Fan's current catalog groups ceiling and cabinet ventilators together and describes them as designed for commercial applications requiring quiet, continuous and reliable operation, including bathrooms, generator rooms, data centers and general HVAC exhaust. The current lines include T ceiling ventilators and TL inline/ceiling ventilators, which can be mounted in more than one configuration. Ceiling and cabinet ventilators appear only in the catalog's commercial product list, which leads to the next topic.

docs.title: Laboratory Fume Exhaust Fans
docs.text:
A laboratory fume exhaust fan removes contaminated air from fume hoods and discharges it high enough above the building that it does not re-enter through air intakes, windows or doors. Twin City Fan's current catalog explains the requirement: laboratory fumes can be hazardous to human life in concentrated form, and lab exhaust fans must move air at high velocities to achieve a high plume height while entraining clean ambient air to dilute the chemical concentration. The fans are often built from special materials to withstand the fumes.

FanPedia describes how these fans dilute the exhaust. Lab exhaust configurations draw in fresh outside air in two ways: through a bypass air plenum, which produces bypass flow, and through the fan's nozzle or windband, which produces entrained flow. The fresh air mixes with the contaminated air to dilute it and carry it up and away from the building. FanPedia shows lab exhaust configurations in two families: housed centrifugal lab exhaust fans with scroll housings, and inline centrifugal and mixed flow lab exhaust fans with tubular housings.

The current catalog's lab exhaust lines reflect those families:

  • Induced flow, mixed flow: TVIFE (direct drive) and QIFE (belt driven)
  • Induced flow, centrifugal: BAIFE (airfoil) and BCIFE (backward inclined)
  • Venturi nozzle: QFE (mixed flow) and TFE (inline centrifugal)

docs.title: Worked Example: Following the Flows
docs.text:
The numbers here are illustrative, chosen to show how the flows add up; they are not ratings for any Twin City Fan model. FanPedia's lab exhaust drawings label five flows: contaminated air, bypass flow, fan flow, entrained flow and total flow.

A lab building's fume hoods draw 5,000 CFM of contaminated air. The bypass air plenum adds 1,000 CFM of outside air ahead of the fan, and the nozzle entrains another 3,000 CFM of outside air into the discharge plume.

Flow How it is found Illustrative value Contaminated air From the fume hoods 5,000 CFM Bypass flow Outside air through the bypass air plenum 1,000 CFM Fan flow Contaminated air + bypass flow 6,000 CFM Entrained flow Outside air drawn in at the nozzle or windband 3,000 CFM Total flow Fan flow + entrained flow 9,000 CFM

The fan itself handles only the fan flow, 6,000 CFM, so that is the airflow it is selected for. The plume leaving the nozzle carries 9,000 CFM, which is why the discharge is more dilute than the air in the hood ducts: in this example the contaminated air is 5,000 of the 9,000 CFM, or about 56 percent of the plume. How bypass dampers and plume dilution are controlled on real jobs is covered in Chapter 6.

Size the Fan for Fan Flow

Want to save yourself a re-selection? When a lab exhaust schedule lists several airflows, find out which one is the fan flow before you look up a model. The fan is selected for the air that actually passes through the impeller; entrained air joins the plume after it.

docs.title: Bypass Air Plenums
docs.text: A bypass air plenum is a chamber on the inlet side of a laboratory exhaust fan that admits fresh outside air into the fan's inlet alongside the contaminated air from the fume hoods. FanPedia identifies it as the source of bypass flow, and its accessory drawings for lab exhaust models show bypass dampers and isolation dampers with actuators on these units. The bypass air adds to the fan flow, dilutes the contaminated air before it reaches the impeller, and helps keep the discharge moving fast enough for a high plume.

docs.title: Commercial and Industrial Duty
docs.text:
Twin City Fan's current website sorts its product lines into two lists: Commercial Solutions and Industrial Solutions. Many families appear in both lists, including centrifugal fans, axial fans, inline centrifugal fans, mixed flow fans, plenum fans, roof ventilators, wall mounted fans and lab exhaust fans. A few appear in only one. Ceiling and cabinet ventilators and kitchen and restaurant exhaust fans are listed only under commercial. Air kits, plug fans, and radial tip and high efficiency fans are listed only under industrial.

A commercial duty fan is a fan built and rated for building ventilation and HVAC service: comfort air handling, restroom and general exhaust, and similar jobs in offices, schools, hospitals and retail buildings, usually with clean air at normal temperatures, quiet operation and standard construction. The catalog's descriptions of commercial products repeat those priorities: ceiling ventilators for "quiet, continuous and reliable operation," wall mounted fans for "cost-effective, general ventilation." Commercial lines are often offered in standard sizes, with standard accessories, from published performance.

docs.title: Worked Example: Two Calls, Two Duty Classes
docs.text:
A distributor takes two calls in one morning.

  1. Call 1: a school district needs restroom exhaust for a new classroom wing: clean room air, a ceiling grille in each restroom, ducted to the roof. The air is clean and at room temperature, the setting is a building, and quiet matters. This is commercial duty. The distributor looks at ceiling ventilators for the restrooms, or a centrifugal roof exhauster on the roof, both in the commercial product list.
  2. Call 2: a foundry needs a fan to pull hot, dusty air from a process hood to a dust collector. The airstream is hot and particulate-laden, and the fan will run as part of a production process. This is industrial duty. The distributor starts from industrial centrifugal fans and expects the inquiry to need construction options such as the high-temperature, spark-resistant or special-material choices the catalog lists as optional construction.

The two calls might both end in a centrifugal fan, but the duty class changes which lines, construction and accessories are worth considering.

An industrial duty fan is a fan built for process and plant service, where the airstream may be hot, dusty, wet, corrosive or explosive, and the fan is part of a production process that must keep running. Recall these airstream conditions from Chapter 2. Industrial fans are typically heavier in construction and are offered with options matched to the airstream, such as the spark-resistant, high-temperature, nominally leak-tight and special-material constructions on the current catalog's centrifugal fan pages. The construction classes behind those options are covered in Chapter 20 and Chapter 21.

Duty Is About the Airstream and the Building

Notice that duty class and fan family are two separate questions. The family comes from the airflow path through the impeller; the duty comes from the airstream, the setting and how hard the fan must work, so a centrifugal fan can be commercial or industrial.

docs.title: Putting It Together: Sorting Real Product Lines
docs.text: You now have all the pieces: the three families, the housings that can disguise them, and the product lines built on each. The MicroSim below asks you to sort fifteen current Twin City Fan product lines by family, using the clues in each card's description.

docs.title: Diagram: Fan Family Sorter
docs.text:
Run Fan Family Sorter Fullscreen

Fan Family Sorter

Type: microsim sim-id: ch04-fan-family-sorter Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Analyze Bloom Verb: differentiate Learning Objective: The learner will differentiate fifteen Twin City Fan product lines into the centrifugal, axial and mixed flow families from a short description of each, correctly placing at least 13 of 15.

Prerequisites: fan family, centrifugal fan, axial fan, mixed flow fan, scroll housing, tubular housing, guide vanes, unhoused centrifugal fan (plenum and plug types), inline centrifugal fan, panel fan, power roof ventilator, centrifugal roof exhauster, roof ventilator, wall mounted fan, laboratory fume exhaust fan (all defined in this chapter).

Evidence of Mastery: The learner places each of the 15 cards into one of three bins: Centrifugal, Axial, Mixed flow. A placement is correct when it matches the "Correct bin" column in Content. Mastery is 13 of 15 correct on the first placement.

Misconceptions: (1) Any fan in a tubular housing is axial. (2) Any roof fan, or any "PRV," is centrifugal. (3) Lab exhaust fans are their own family rather than centrifugal or mixed flow fans. (4) Fans without a housing cannot be centrifugal.

Instructional Rationale: Differentiating requires the learner to separate the relevant clue (the impeller's airflow path) from irrelevant ones (housing shape, mounting location, application). Mixing look-alike cards, such as a tubular inline centrifugal next to a tubeaxial, forces that separation, and committed placements give a checkable record.

Content: Fifteen cards, each showing the model designation and the description below. Card text must not contain the words "centrifugal," "axial," "mixed flow" or "mixed-flow"; those words appear only in the feedback.

# Card shown to the learner Correct bin Why (feedback) 1 BC-SW: single width, single inlet fan in a snail-shaped housing; air leaves at a right angle to the shaft Centrifugal A scroll housing with a right-angle discharge is a housed centrifugal fan. 2 NFC-DW: double width, double inlet fan with a forward curved wheel in a snail-shaped housing Centrifugal Forward curved wheels throw air outward; DWDI housed fans are centrifugal. 3 Plenum fan: wheel and inlet funnel with no housing, running inside an air handler cabinet Centrifugal An unhoused fan is still centrifugal; the plenum collects the air instead of a scroll. 4 Plug fan: wheel inside an oven wall, mounting panel and motor outside Centrifugal Plug fans are unhoused centrifugal fans plugged into a plenum wall. 5 TSL: airfoil wheel in a round tube, with straightening vanes; air goes straight through Centrifugal A tubular inline centrifugal fan: the wheel throws air outward and the vanes turn it back along the tube. 6 BSI: belt-driven fan in a square housing with removable side panels; straight-through or 90-degree flow Centrifugal A square inline centrifugal fan uses a backward inclined centrifugal wheel. 7 DCRD: direct-drive downblast roof exhauster Centrifugal DCRD is in the catalog's Centrifugal Roof & Wall Exhausters section. 8 BCIFE: induced flow laboratory exhaust fan with a backward inclined wheel Centrifugal Backward inclined wheels are centrifugal; lab exhaust is an application, not a family. 9 TD: direct-drive fan in a plain round tube, propeller-style blades on a hub, no vanes Axial A tubeaxial fan: air goes straight along the shaft and leaves swirling. 10 TCVA: cast aluminum propeller-style impeller in a round tube, with a vane section downstream Axial A vaneaxial fan: the guide vanes straighten the swirl but the path is still along the shaft. 11 WPB: belt-driven wall mounted fan, impeller centered in a flat panel Axial A panel fan centers an axial impeller in a panel and moves air straight through the wall. 12 TUD: direct-drive upblast roof ventilator built on a tube with a propeller-style impeller Axial The catalog's Roof Ventilators are tubeaxial-based PRVs; not every roof fan is centrifugal. 13 QSL: high-pressure airfoil fan in a round tube with straightening vanes; blades taper from the front plate to the hub end Mixed flow Blades that taper from the front plate to the hub end mark the hybrid impeller of a mixed flow fan. 14 QCLB: low-pressure, single-surface-blade fan in a round tube; air leaves the impeller on a diagonal Mixed flow A diagonal impeller exit is the mixed flow signature. 15 TVIFE: direct-drive induced flow laboratory exhaust fan with a hybrid impeller whose air leaves on a diagonal Mixed flow TVIFE is listed as an induced flow, mixed flow lab exhaust fan.

Provenance: Model designations and their family groupings from Twin City Fan's current product catalog pages on tcf.com (products: centrifugal fans, plenum fans, plug fans, inline centrifugal fans, axial fans, wall mounted fans, roof ventilators, centrifugal roof and wall exhausters, mixed flow fans, laboratory and fume exhaust fans), retrieved 2026-10-08. Housing and impeller descriptions from FanPedia (Twin City Fan, 2021) pp 4-8, 17 and 32.

Rules: The 15 cards are presented in a shuffled order. Each card can be placed once; after placement it is locked and marked correct or incorrect. The score counts first placements only. After all 15 cards are placed, the learner may press "Sort again," which reshuffles all cards and resets the score.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner reads the top card and places it into Centrifugal, Axial or Mixed flow.
  2. The card locks into the bin and is marked correct or incorrect, and the "Why" text appears beneath it.
  3. The learner continues until all 15 cards are placed.
  4. A summary shows the score and lists each misplaced card with its correct bin and "Why" text. The learner should notice which clue misled them on each miss: housing shape, roof location or application name.

Feedback: 15 items, shuffled, one attempt each. Correct: "Correct: ." followed by the "Why" text. Incorrect: "This one is ." followed by the "Why" text. The score is shown as "Correct: n of 15". When the score is 13 or more, the summary reads "Mastery reached." Otherwise it reads "Review the sections on tubular housings and power roof ventilators, then sort again."

Starting State: Three empty bins labeled Centrifugal, Axial and Mixed flow, and the first card face up. The prompt reads "Which family does this product line belong to? Look for the airflow path, not the housing."

Chapter Anchors: The chapter states that the sorter holds fifteen current Twin City Fan product lines and three families. The chapter names TSL, BSI and DSI as inline centrifugal lines; TD, TB, TCTA and TCTS as tubeaxial lines; TCVA, TCVX and TCVS as vaneaxial lines; QSL and QCLB as mixed flow lines; TVIFE, QIFE, BAIFE, BCIFE, QFE and TFE as lab exhaust lines; and DCRD, BCRD, VC and BCRU as centrifugal roof exhausters.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• A fan family is defined by the airflow path through the impeller: centrifugal (in along the shaft, out at a right angle), axial (in and out along the shaft, with swirl) or mixed flow (out on a diagonal).
  • The impeller decides the family; the housing does not. Tubular housings carry axial, inline centrifugal and mixed flow impellers alike.
  • A scroll housing collects air from a centrifugal impeller and, by widening from the cutoff to the outlet, slows the air and recovers velocity pressure as static pressure. Tracing the scroll from the cutoff toward the outlet gives the direction of rotation.
  • Unhoused centrifugal fans run without a scroll: plenum types sit inside a plenum, and plug types mount through a plenum wall with the drive outside.
  • Guide vanes straighten the swirl leaving an axial impeller and make a tubeaxial into a vaneaxial. "Inlet guide vanes" on a centrifugal fan usually means the inlet vane flow-control accessory, a different part.
  • Inline centrifugal fans and mixed flow fans keep the duct straight while using centrifugal or hybrid impellers.
  • Panel fans, ring fans and most wall mounted fans are axial; weatherhoods protect their outdoor openings.
  • A power roof ventilator can be centrifugal (centrifugal roof exhausters) or axial (the catalog's roof ventilators and roof mounted axial fans); every rooftop unit sits on a roof curb.
  • Ceiling ventilators serve quiet, continuous commercial exhaust.
  • Laboratory fume exhaust fans dilute contaminated air with bypass flow from a bypass air plenum and entrained flow at the nozzle; the fan is sized for the fan flow, not the total plume flow.
  • Commercial duty and industrial duty describe the service, not the family: the airstream, the setting and the construction options separate them.

You Can Read the Fan Zoo

You can now look at a fan, a drawing or a model list and name its family, its housing and the catalog section it lives in, even when a tubular housing or a rooftop hood tries to hide it. That sorting step is the first line of every fan order you will ever write.

docs.title: Roof, Wall and Specialty Exhaust Fans
Summary
docs.text: This chapter surveys the exhaust and ventilation products that sit on roofs and walls or serve a specific application: kitchen exhaust fans, smoke and heat exhaust fans, fiberglass fans for corrosive service, mancoolers, housed centrifugal and plenum fans, square inline and tubeaxial fans, wall exhausters, gravity relief ventilators, and hooded, louvered, and low-profile roof units. It explains upblast versus downblast discharge and how entrained flow works in lab exhaust. After completing it, readers can match a common building ventilation need to the product line built for it.

docs.title: Concepts Covered
docs.text:
This chapter covers the following 17 concepts from the learning graph:

Concept Concept Impact Score Kitchen Exhaust Fan 3 Smoke and Heat Exhaust Fan 3 Fiberglass Fan 3 Mancooler 1 Upblast Discharge 3 Downblast Discharge 2 Housed Centrifugal Fan 91 Plenum Fan 79 Square Inline Centrifugal Fan 2 Tubeaxial Fan 28 Centrifugal Wall Exhauster 1 Gravity Relief Ventilator 1 Cabinet Ventilator 1 Entrained Flow 6 Hooded Roof Exhauster 1 Louvered Roof Exhauster 1 Low Profile Roof Ventilator 1

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
This chapter builds on concepts from:

  • Chapter 1: Air, Pressure and the Fan
  • Chapter 2: Airstreams, Total Pressure and Standard Air
  • Chapter 3: Basic Fan Anatomy
  • Chapter 4: Centrifugal, Axial and Mixed Flow Fans

docs.title: From Fan Families to Product Lines
docs.text:
Chapter 4 sorted fans into three families by the path air takes through the impeller. A Twin City Fan catalog, however, is not organized by family alone. It is organized by the job: a restaurant hood, an atrium that must be cleared of smoke, a wastewater plant full of corrosive vapor, a hot foundry floor. Each job produced a product line whose housing, discharge, materials and listings were shaped around that job's air and that job's mounting location.

Every Building Has an Exhaust Story

Walk across almost any commercial roof and you will see a dozen fans, each one chosen for a reason. By the end of this chapter you will be able to read that roof like a parts list and name the product line a customer's job calls for. Let's follow the airflow.

The chapter moves in four steps. It starts with the four general-purpose fan styles that appear inside buildings and ductwork, moves up to the roof and the wall to compare discharge directions, then covers the application specialists, and finishes with entrained flow, the trick that lets a laboratory exhaust fan dilute and launch its plume.

docs.title: General-Purpose Building Fans
docs.text: Four fan styles do most of the air moving inside a building's duct system and air-handling equipment. Two are centrifugal and differ in whether they have a housing; two sit in line with the duct.

docs.title: Housed Centrifugal Fan
docs.text:
A housed centrifugal fan is a centrifugal fan whose impeller turns inside a scroll housing. FanPedia (p. 4) describes the type this way: air is drawn in through one side of the housing (single inlet) or both sides (double inlet) and is discharged at a right angle to the fan shaft. The scroll collects the air thrown off the impeller tips, converts part of its velocity into static pressure, and delivers it through a single rectangular outlet that bolts to a duct.

Two width-and-inlet combinations cover most catalog listings:

  • Single width, single inlet (SWSI): one inlet and an impeller of standard width, as in the BC-SW.
  • Double width, double inlet (DWDI): two inlets and a double-width impeller, which roughly doubles the volume a given impeller diameter can move, as in the BC-DW.

The same housed construction accepts backward inclined, airfoil, backward curved, radial tip, forward curved and radial bladed wheels, and it is the base for packaged configurations on FanPedia p. 4: roof-mounted filtered supply units, enclosed duct fans, and the lab exhaust fans covered at the end of this chapter.

Worked example: what leaves the outlet. A customer's drawing shows an SWSI housed fan delivering 6,000 CFM through an outlet that measures 24 in. by 18 in. How fast does the air leave the scroll (values illustrative, standard air)?

  1. Outlet area: \( A = 2.0 \text{ ft} \times 1.5 \text{ ft} = 3.0 \text{ ft}^2 \).
  2. Outlet velocity: \( V = Q / A = 6{,}000 / 3.0 = 2{,}000 \) fpm.
  3. Velocity pressure at standard air, using the relation from Chapter 2:
\[ VP = \left( \frac{V}{4005} \right)^2 = \left( \frac{2000}{4005} \right)^2 = 0.249 \text{ in. wg} \]

where \( VP \) is velocity pressure in inches of water gauge and \( V \) is air velocity in feet per minute.

A DWDI fan handling the same 6,000 CFM would split it, about 3,000 CFM per inlet. Either way, a housed fan concentrates all of its air into one outlet at a known velocity, so the duct connection there matters. Chapter 12 shows how that one outlet can be pointed in many directions.

docs.title: Plenum Fan
docs.text:
A plenum fan is an unhoused centrifugal fan that runs inside an air plenum. FanPedia (p. 5) defines a plenum as an air-filled space within a structure, and the plenum fan's job is to pressurize that space. With no scroll, the impeller discharges air radially in all directions, 360 degrees around the wheel, and the surrounding cabinet does the job a housing would do: it collects the air and sends it to whatever outlets the cabinet has. The fan has an inlet funnel on one side and a frame that carries the impeller, shaft, bearings and drive.

The current Twin City Fan plenum fan line (E-Series EPF, EPFN, EPQ and EPQN, plus commercial, modular and EC versions) uses 9- or 12-blade airfoil impellers for general HVAC duty: large volumes of clean air at low to moderate pressure. A close relative, the plug fan, mounts its panel on the outside wall of the plenum with the impeller inside; Chapter 6 covers it.

The Cabinet Is the Housing

Notice what disappeared when the scroll went away: the fan no longer decides where the air goes, the plenum does. That is why a plenum fan can feed a top opening, two side openings and a bottom opening at once, while a housed fan feeds exactly one outlet.

Worked example: housed or plenum in an air handler. An air-handling unit manufacturer is laying out a cabinet that must deliver supply air through three duct connections: one on top and one on each side. The unit serves a pharmaceutical cleanroom, and the owner wants as little maintenance in the airstream as possible.

  1. Count the outlets. A housed fan would need a discharge plenum and transitions after its one outlet to feed three connections. A plenum fan pressurizes the cabinet section, so all three openings draw from the same space.
  2. Check the air. Clean air at low to moderate pressure is the duty the airfoil plenum line is built for.
  3. Choose the drive. FanPedia (p. 170) states that direct drive Arrangement 4 plenum fans mount the impeller on the motor shaft, eliminate belt residue and need less maintenance, and are therefore widely used in cleanroom and pharmaceutical applications.
  4. Conclusion. A direct drive plenum fan fits. A housed fan stays the better choice for a single ducted outlet or a free-standing fan. Chapter 11 explains arrangement numbers in full.

docs.title: Square Inline Centrifugal Fan
docs.text: A square inline centrifugal fan puts a centrifugal impeller inside a square housing with removable side panels. FanPedia (p. 6) notes that it can move air straight through the fan or turn it 90 degrees, depending on how the ductwork connects. The square shape lets the fan drop into rectangular duct runs and above-ceiling spaces, and the removable panels give service access without taking the fan out of the duct. Twin City Fan's square inline line includes the belt-driven BSI and direct-drive DSI with backward inclined wheels, plus a DSI mixed flow version. Choose it when the duct runs through a tight space, the air is relatively clean, and the installer wants one compact box that can absorb a duct turn.

docs.title: Tubeaxial Fan
docs.text:
A tubeaxial fan is an axial fan in a plain cylindrical housing with no guide vanes. Air enters one end of the tube, passes through the impeller, and leaves the other end moving in the same straight line, carrying some rotational swirl because nothing straightens it. A vaneaxial fan adds a vane section that helps straighten the airflow (FanPedia p. 7). The current catalog positions tubeaxial fans for general ventilation through process air supply, in direct and belt driven models with fixed or adjustable pitch impellers; vaneaxials are aimed at moderate to high pressures.

The tubeaxial is also the base model for roof-mounted axial fans, which add a hood or a stack cap (FanPedia p. 7), such as the TUB upblast and THB hooded roof ventilators. In a belt-driven tubeaxial (FanPedia p. 15), the motor sits on a motor base saddle outside the tube, and a belt tube, also called a belt fairing, shields the belt where it crosses the airstream.

Worked example: duct velocity and duty. A contractor needs 8,000 CFM of exhaust from a warehouse process area through a straight, round duct, and asks whether a 24-in. tubeaxial is a sensible starting point (values illustrative).

  1. Tube area: \( A = \pi r^2 = \pi (1.0 \text{ ft})^2 = 3.14 \text{ ft}^2 \).
  2. Air velocity through the tube: \( V = 8{,}000 / 3.14 = 2{,}546 \) fpm, an ordinary duct velocity for general exhaust.
  3. Duty: a short, straight duct at low pressure points to a tubeaxial. A long duct with filters and higher pressure would point to a vaneaxial.
  4. Drive: if the exhaust carries heat or fumes the motor should not breathe, the belt-driven version keeps the motor outside the tube.

The answer is yes, confirmed against the catalog performance curve (Chapter 10).

The four general-purpose styles compare as follows.

Fan style Housing Air path Typical place in a building Housed centrifugal Scroll In through the side, out at 90 degrees through one outlet Ducted supply and exhaust, utility duty Plenum None; the cabinet acts as the housing In through the funnel, out radially into the plenum Inside air-handling units Square inline centrifugal Square box, removable panels Straight through or a 90-degree turn Rectangular duct, above ceilings Tubeaxial Plain tube, no vanes Straight through, with swirl Short ducted runs, roof ventilators

docs.title: On the Roof and Through the Wall
docs.text: Most exhaust air ends up leaving through the roof or an exterior wall, and the defining choice there is the direction the air leaves the unit. FanPedia (p. 5) describes the centrifugal power roof ventilator family by that direction. Upblast and side wall configurations exhaust air in a straight line through the fan. Downblast, louvered and hooded configurations move air up through the fan and then deflect it down and outward.

docs.title: Upblast Discharge
docs.text: Upblast discharge sends exhaust air straight up, away from the roof surface. The impeller turns on a vertical shaft, the air rises through the wheel and leaves through the top of the unit, and the plume carries contaminants, heat and grease clear of the roof and of nearby air intakes. Because the outlet faces the sky, upblast units carry a weather defense: FanPedia's technical descriptions (p. 181) note that butterfly-type gravity dampers, built into roof-mounted upblast fans, prevent outside air from back-drafting in and provide weather protection when the fan is off. Twin City Fan's VCU, VCUB and BCRU upblast roof exhausters, and the kitchen and smoke versions covered below, all use this discharge.

docs.title: Downblast Discharge
docs.text:
Downblast discharge turns the air leaving the impeller back down toward the roof, out and around the unit. The classic downblast centrifugal roof exhauster has a mushroom-shaped motor cover over a spun aluminum shroud; air rises through the wheel, strikes the inside of the cover, and spills out the bottom edge in all directions. The low silhouette and built-in weather protection suit clean air: restroom, general office and storage exhaust. The current catalog lists the VC and DCRD direct-drive and BCRD belt-driven downblast models. FanPedia's exploded view (p. 19) names the parts common to both roof exhauster types: motor cover, motor housing, motor, impeller, shroud, skirt, bird screen, curb cap and roof curb.

Downblast Means Clean Air Only

A common trap is quoting a downblast exhauster for kitchen, fume or hot exhaust because it is cheaper and lower. A downblast unit lays its discharge back onto the roof, where grease collects and fumes find the nearest outdoor-air intake, so for anything but relatively clean air, switch the quote to an upblast unit.

docs.title: Hooded, Louvered and Low-Profile Roof Units
docs.text:
Three more roof configurations differ mainly in how they shelter the discharge. The hooded and louvered exhausters share the "up, then down and out" path of the downblast; the low profile ventilator comes in both upblast and hooded forms.

A hooded roof exhauster is a centrifugal roof exhauster topped by a weatherhood. Air passes up through the impeller and the hood turns it down and outward around the base, giving full rain and snow protection over the opening. The current catalog lists the DCLH (direct drive) and BCLH (belt driven) models. The same hood idea appears on axial roof units, where the hood deflects exhaust downward or, on a supply unit, admits air from underneath.

A louvered roof exhauster replaces the hood with a louvered penthouse: a box with fixed weather louvers on its sides. Air rises through the impeller into the penthouse and is deflected down and outward through the louvers, which shed rain while keeping the unit's profile boxy and compact. The current catalog lists the DCLP (direct drive) and BCLP (belt driven) models.

A low profile roof ventilator is a propeller-type roof ventilator built to sit close to the roof deck, for roofs where a tall unit would be visible from the street or would catch the wind. The roof ventilator line offers low-profile versions in both discharge styles: the LUD and LUB upblast units (plus the LUBMO, with its motor out of the airstream) and the LHD and LHB hooded units, some of which add filters for supply duty. Like the rest of the roof ventilator line, these use cast aluminum adjustable-pitch or fabricated steel fixed-pitch axial impellers rather than centrifugal wheels.

docs.title: Centrifugal Wall Exhauster
docs.text: A centrifugal wall exhauster is the side-wall version of the centrifugal roof exhauster: the same backward inclined, non-overloading wheel and motor package, mounted on an exterior wall so the shaft is horizontal and air leaves straight out, away from the building face. It serves buildings without convenient roof access and duct runs that end at a wall. Several Twin City Fan models do double duty on a roof or a wall (VCU and VCUB); the BCRW is a dedicated belt-driven wall unit, the BCRWR is its kitchen version, and the fiberglass line includes the HA and HAB wall exhausters.

docs.title: Gravity Relief Ventilator
docs.text: A gravity relief ventilator has no fan at all. It is a weather-protected roof opening that lets air leave (relief) or enter (intake) a building under natural pressure differences: warm air rising inside the building, wind across the roof, or the slight positive pressure created when supply fans run. Twin City Fan offers them as spun aluminum (GRV), modular hooded (MGR relief, MGI intake), louvered (TEL relief, TIL intake) and fiberglass (MA) units. They are often specified beside powered fans: the supply fan pushes air in and the gravity relief ventilator lets it out without a second motor.

docs.title: Cabinet Ventilator
docs.text:
A cabinet ventilator is a small centrifugal blower, usually with a forward curved wheel, packaged in a sheet-metal cabinet that mounts in or above a ceiling, on a wall, or inline in a duct. It is the quiet, continuous-duty fan for bathrooms, small offices, generator rooms and general HVAC exhaust. In Twin City Fan's current catalog the group is called "Ceiling & Cabinet Ventilators" and includes the T ceiling ventilator, the TL inline/ceiling ventilator, and the DBS and DBT forward curved inline duct blowers. It is the indoor relative of the ceiling ventilator introduced in Chapter 4.

Before the next diagram, here is how the roof and wall configurations line up by airflow path.

Configuration Air path out of the unit Fan inside Typical use Upblast roof exhauster Straight up, away from the roof Centrifugal Grease, fumes, heat, contaminated air Downblast roof exhauster Up, then down and out over the roof Centrifugal Clean general exhaust Hooded roof exhauster Up, then down and out under a hood Centrifugal Clean exhaust with full weather cover Louvered roof exhauster Up, then down and out through side louvers Centrifugal Clean exhaust, compact penthouse look Low profile roof ventilator Up (upblast) or down and out (hooded), close to the deck Axial propeller General exhaust or supply on low-profile roofs Centrifugal wall exhauster Straight out, away from the wall Centrifugal Exhaust where the duct ends at a wall Gravity relief ventilator Out or in by natural pressure None Relief or intake without fan energy

docs.title: Diagram: Roof and Wall Exhaust Path Explorer
docs.text:
Roof and Wall Exhaust Path Explorer

Type: microsim sim-id: ch05-roof-wall-exhaust-path-explorer Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Understand Bloom Verb: classify Learning Objective: The learner will classify seven roof and wall ventilation configurations by the path the exhaust air takes as it leaves the unit, given a cutaway of each unit with its discharge hidden.

Prerequisites: upblast discharge, downblast discharge, hooded roof exhauster, louvered roof exhauster, low profile roof ventilator, centrifugal wall exhauster, gravity relief ventilator, roof curb, gravity damper (all defined in the section "On the Roof and Through the Wall").

Evidence of Mastery: For each of the seven configurations, shown one at a time in shuffled order, the learner commits a prediction of the discharge path by choosing one of three paths: "Straight up", "Up, then down and out", "Straight out from the wall". The gravity relief ventilator is asked as a separate yes/no question: "Does this unit need a fan to move air?" A prediction is correct when it matches the Correct path column below. Mastery is 6 of 7 path predictions correct plus the gravity question correct, on first attempts. Clicking parts of a cutaway to read labels is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) Every roof exhauster blows air straight up. (2) A hood or louvers change the fan type inside the unit. (3) Downblast units are suitable for any exhaust because the air still leaves the building. (4) A gravity relief ventilator contains a small fan.

Instructional Rationale: Classifying by predicted airflow path before the path is animated forces the learner to reason from the unit's construction (open top, cover, hood, louvers, wall mount) rather than memorize model names, which is the Understand-level skill the chapter's matching task depends on.

Content:

# Configuration Parts shown in the cutaway (each clickable, with the definition below) Correct path Feedback (why) 1 Upblast centrifugal roof exhauster impeller, motor, open top with butterfly gravity damper, roof curb Straight up The outlet faces the sky, so the plume goes up and away from the roof surface. 2 Downblast centrifugal roof exhauster impeller, motor, motor cover, shroud, skirt, bird screen, curb cap, roof curb Up, then down and out The motor cover turns the rising air back down so it spills out around the base. 3 Hooded roof exhauster impeller, motor, weatherhood, roof curb Up, then down and out The hood deflects the air downward and outward, as the downblast cover does. 4 Louvered roof exhauster impeller, motor, louvered penthouse, roof curb Up, then down and out The air rises into the penthouse and the louvers deflect it down and outward; louvers change the look, not the path. 5 Low profile roof ventilator, upblast version axial propeller impeller, motor, short stack, roof curb Straight up It is an upblast unit built close to the deck; the profile changes, not the path. 6 Centrifugal wall exhauster impeller, motor, wall mounting plate Straight out from the wall It is the side-wall version of the upblast exhauster, so air leaves in a straight line away from the wall. 7 Gravity relief ventilator weather hood, opening, roof curb, no impeller Up, then down and out Relief air rises through the opening and the hood turns it down and out; the gravity question asks whether a fan moves it.

Gravity question (asked after item 7): "Does this unit need a fan to move air?" Correct answer: No. Feedback: "Correct: a gravity relief ventilator relies on natural pressure differences, such as warm air rising or supply fans pressurizing the building." Incorrect feedback: "Look for the impeller: there is none. A gravity relief ventilator moves air only by natural pressure differences."

Part definitions revealed on click:

  • Impeller: the rotating wheel that moves the air (centrifugal wheel in items 1-4 and 6, axial propeller in item 5).
  • Motor: drives the impeller, directly or through a belt.
  • Motor cover: the dome over the motor that also turns the discharge downward on a downblast unit.
  • Shroud: the spun aluminum surround that guides air into and around the impeller.
  • Skirt: the lower edge of the downblast unit, around which the air spills out.
  • Bird screen: a mesh that keeps birds and debris out of the discharge.
  • Curb cap: the base plate that covers the roof curb and carries the fan.
  • Roof curb: the raised frame on the roof that supports the unit above the roof surface.
  • Butterfly gravity damper: hinged blades that open when the fan runs and close by gravity when it stops, blocking backdraft and weather.
  • Weatherhood: a hood over the discharge that turns air downward and sheds rain and snow.
  • Louvered penthouse: a box with fixed weather louvers on its sides.
  • Short stack: a low discharge collar on a low profile unit.
  • Wall mounting plate: the plate that fixes the exhauster to an exterior wall.
  • Opening (gravity unit): the weather-protected roof penetration that air passes through without a fan.

Provenance: Airflow paths for upblast, side wall, downblast, louvered and hooded configurations: FanPedia p. 5 (Centrifugal Power Roof Ventilator Exhaust Fans). Part names for roof exhausters: FanPedia p. 19 exploded view. Butterfly gravity damper: FanPedia p. 181. Low profile units and their impellers: tcf.com Roof Ventilators product page (LUD, LUB, LHD, LHB). Gravity relief ventilators: tcf.com Gravity Relief Ventilators product page.

Rules: Seven path items, shuffled once per session, then the gravity question. Path choices are the same three for every item. The cutaway shows parts but hides the discharge arrows until the learner commits. After a commit the sim reveals the correct path with arrows showing air entering the unit and leaving it.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner sees a cutaway with the discharge hidden and may click any part to read its definition.
  2. The learner chooses one of the three paths and commits.
  3. The sim reveals the true path with flow arrows and shows the feedback text. The learner should notice that the parts above the impeller (open top, cover, hood, louvers) decide the path.
  4. After item 7 the learner answers the gravity question.
  5. A summary table shows all seven configurations with their paths, and the learner can reopen any item to view its path again without changing the score.

Feedback: Seven path items plus one yes/no item, one attempt each, no re-answering. Correct: "Correct: ." followed by the Feedback (why) text. Incorrect: "Not quite: this unit's air goes ." followed by the Feedback (why) text. The correct path is revealed after every commit. A running score "Paths correct: n of 7" is shown.

Starting State: The first shuffled cutaway, discharge hidden, with the question "Where does the exhaust air go when it leaves this unit?"

Chapter Anchors: Seven configurations; upblast and side wall move air in a straight line; downblast, louvered and hooded move air up and then down and outward (FanPedia p. 5); low profile roof ventilators use axial propeller impellers.

docs.title: Application Specialists
docs.text: The next four product lines are defined less by airflow path than by what is in the air, or by where the people are.

docs.title: Kitchen Exhaust Fan
docs.text: A kitchen exhaust fan removes the hot, moist, smoky and grease-laden air that ovens, stoves, grills and dishwashers produce, and discharges it away from building surfaces. Grease is the deciding factor: it coats any surface it lands on and is a fire hazard, so kitchen fans use upblast or wall discharge that throws the plume clear of the roof, and they carry a safety listing for grease-laden air. Twin City Fan's current catalog lists its kitchen exhaust fans to UL 705 Supplement SC (formerly UL 762) and pairs them with grease collection systems. The line includes the BCRUR upblast roof and BCRWR wall exhausters, the VCU and VCUB roof/wall units, a BCVR kitchen utility set, and QCLBR and QSLR mixed flow inline fans.

docs.title: Smoke and Heat Exhaust Fan
docs.text: A smoke and heat exhaust fan is built to keep running while it moves smoke and hot gas out of a burning building, so occupants can escape and firefighters can enter. Its motor, bearings and materials are selected to survive a temperature that would stop an ordinary fan. Twin City Fan's current catalog rates its smoke and heat fans to withstand a minimum of 500°F for four hours or 1,000°F for 15 minutes. The line spans spun aluminum roof exhausters (BCRUSH), utility sets (BCVSH), mixed flow fans (QCLBSH, QSLSH), roof ventilators (LUBSH, TUBSH) and axial fans (TBSH, TCTSSH, TCVSSH); inline versions can be roof-mounted with a stack cap whose butterfly dampers are held by a fusible link designed to stay open in a fire. High-temperature construction in general is covered in Chapter 21.

docs.title: Fiberglass Fan
docs.text: A fiberglass fan has its housing, and often its impeller, molded from fiberglass-reinforced plastic (FRP) so it can exhaust moisture-laden, corrosive or chemically contaminated air that would eat through carbon steel. The current catalog describes FRP as a more economical answer than stainless steel or other exotic alloys, with molded housings that resist denting and cracking. Options let the resin and surface match the chemistry: vinyl ester resin, fire retardant resin, a synthetic surface veil, static grounding, and a stainless steel shaft. Twin City Fan builds fiberglass versions of nearly every fan style in this chapter, from housed centrifugal (BAFF, BCSF, RBOF) and inline centrifugal (ILCF) to tubeaxial (TAHF, TAMF), roof exhausters (WA, WAB), wall exhausters (HA, HAB) and panel fans (TCWPF). Wastewater treatment, plating and chemical process exhaust are typical jobs.

docs.title: Mancooler
docs.text:
A mancooler is an axial fan packaged to blow air directly on workers in a hot industrial space. Twin City Fan's current catalog describes two forms: mounted units on a movable base whose swivel allows a full 360-degree rotation, and stationary units with a predrilled base plate for wall, column, ceiling or floor mounting (TCSM). Both have inlet and outlet screens as standard, fabricated to meet OSHA safety requirements, because the fan runs within reach of people. A mancooler does not exhaust anything; it moves air across the body to speed evaporative and convective cooling at a foundry pour station or a loading dock.

Ask What Is in the Air First

Here is a shortcut for any exhaust inquiry: ask "what is in the air?" before "how much air?" Grease points to a listed kitchen fan, fire duty to a smoke and heat fan, corrosive vapor to fiberglass, and clean air leaves every option open.

docs.title: Entrained Flow in Laboratory Exhaust
docs.text:
Fume hood exhaust can be toxic, corrosive or explosive, and it must not re-enter the building through a nearby intake. Chapter 4 introduced the lab exhaust fan and its bypass air plenum; this section adds the second dilution mechanism FanPedia names (pp. 4 and 6), entrained flow.

Four flows need names before the arithmetic:

  • Contaminated air is the exhaust drawn from the fume hoods.
  • Bypass flow is fresh outside air drawn in through the bypass air plenum and mixed with the contaminated air before it reaches the fan.
  • Fan flow is everything that passes through the impeller: contaminated air plus bypass air.
  • Entrained flow is outside air pulled into the discharge plume by the high-velocity jet leaving the fan's nozzle or windband. It never passes through the impeller; the jet drags it along.

The plume leaving the stack carries the total flow, the fan flow plus the entrained flow:

\[ Q_{\text{fan}} = Q_{\text{contaminated}} + Q_{\text{bypass}} \] \[ Q_{\text{total}} = Q_{\text{fan}} + Q_{\text{entrained}} \]

where each \( Q \) is a volume flow rate in CFM. Because the contaminant amount stays the same while the air volume grows, the concentration in the plume falls in proportion:

\[ C_{\text{plume}} = C_{\text{hood}} \times \frac{Q_{\text{contaminated}}}{Q_{\text{total}}} \]

where \( C_{\text{hood}} \) is the concentration in the hood exhaust and \( C_{\text{plume}} \) is the concentration leaving the stack, in the same units (ppm here).

Free Dilution Air

Think of the nozzle as a pump with no moving parts. Bypass air costs fan capacity because it goes through the impeller; entrained air rides along for free because the jet's own momentum pulls it in, adding mass to the plume and helping it climb.

Worked example: diluting a fume hood plume. A lab exhaust fan serves fume hoods that exhaust 8,000 CFM of contaminated air at an illustrative 100 ppm. The bypass damper admits 2,000 CFM of outside air, and the nozzle entrains 7,000 CFM more (values illustrative; real entrainment is a catalog-rated value for a specific model and nozzle).

  1. Fan flow: \( Q_{\text{fan}} = 8{,}000 + 2{,}000 = 10{,}000 \) CFM. The fan must be selected for this volume.
  2. Total flow: \( Q_{\text{total}} = 10{,}000 + 7{,}000 = 17{,}000 \) CFM leaves the stack.
  3. Plume concentration: \( C_{\text{plume}} = 100 \times 8{,}000 / 17{,}000 = 47.1 \) ppm.
  4. Interpretation: the fan moves 10,000 CFM but the plume carries 17,000 CFM, so entrainment more than halves the hood concentration at no extra fan volume. The larger, faster plume also rises higher, which is why the current catalog stresses discharge velocity and plume height for lab exhaust.

Twin City Fan's current lab exhaust line includes induced flow mixed flow fans (TVIFE, QIFE), induced flow centrifugal fans (BAIFE, BCIFE), and venturi nozzle fans (QFE, TFE). Chapter 6 returns to bypass flow, plume dilution and lab exhaust total flow.

docs.title: Diagram: Lab Exhaust Entrained Flow Calculator
docs.text:
Lab Exhaust Entrained Flow Calculator

Type: microsim sim-id: ch05-lab-exhaust-entrained-flow-calculator Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Apply Bloom Verb: calculate Learning Objective: The learner will calculate the fan flow, total flow and plume concentration of a laboratory exhaust fan from its contaminated, bypass and entrained flows, with flows exact and concentration within 0.5 ppm.

Prerequisites: contaminated air, bypass flow, fan flow, entrained flow, total flow, concentration in ppm, and the three equations in the section "Entrained Flow in Laboratory Exhaust".

Evidence of Mastery: For three challenge cases, the learner types fan flow, total flow and plume concentration before the sim shows the answer. Flows are correct when they equal the model value exactly; concentration is correct when it is within ±0.5 ppm of the model value. Mastery is all nine values correct across the three cases, with at most two attempts per value. Moving the inputs in free-exploration mode is not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) The fan must be sized for the total flow, including entrained air. (2) Entrained air passes through the impeller. (3) Bypass air and entrained air dilute in different ways, so only one of them reduces plume concentration. (4) Doubling the entrained flow halves the plume concentration.

Instructional Rationale: Apply-level calculation needs committed answers with a check. Separating fan flow from total flow in every case makes the learner state which air passes through the impeller, which is the idea the misconceptions get wrong.

Content:

Quantities in free-exploration mode:

Quantity Min Max Step Default Unit Contaminated air from fume hoods 2,000 20,000 500 8,000 CFM Bypass flow 0 10,000 500 2,000 CFM Entrained flow 0 20,000 500 7,000 CFM Hood exhaust concentration 10 500 10 100 ppm

Challenge cases, in this order (hood concentration 100 ppm in every case):

# Contaminated (CFM) Bypass (CFM) Entrained (CFM) Fan flow (CFM) Total flow (CFM) Plume concentration (ppm) Feedback when wrong 1 8,000 2,000 7,000 10,000 17,000 47.1 Fan flow is contaminated plus bypass: 8,000 + 2,000 = 10,000. Total adds entrained: 17,000. Plume: 100 × 8,000 / 17,000 = 47.1 ppm. 2 6,000 0 9,000 6,000 15,000 40.0 With no bypass, fan flow equals the contaminated air, 6,000. Entrained air does not pass through the fan. Total 15,000; plume 100 × 6,000 / 15,000 = 40.0 ppm. 3 12,000 4,000 0 16,000 16,000 75.0 With no entrainment, total flow equals fan flow, 16,000. Bypass air alone still dilutes: 100 × 12,000 / 16,000 = 75.0 ppm.

The sim labels all challenge and default values "illustrative".

Provenance: Flow definitions (bypass flow through a bypass air plenum, entrained flow through the nozzle or windband, fan flow, contaminated air, total flow): FanPedia pp. 4 and 6. Numeric values are illustrative and match the chapter's worked example (case 1).

Rules: Q_fan = Q_contaminated + Q_bypass. Q_total = Q_fan + Q_entrained. C_plume = C_hood × Q_contaminated / Q_total, rounded to 0.1 ppm. Q_total is never zero because Q_contaminated >= 2,000 CFM. Concentration is correct when |answer − model| <= 0.5 ppm.

Learner Activity:

  1. Case 1 is shown as a labeled flow diagram: fume hood air entering, bypass air joining before the fan, the fan, the nozzle, and entrained air joining the plume. The three answer boxes are empty.
  2. The learner types fan flow, total flow and plume concentration and presses Check. Each value is marked correct or incorrect; the flow arrows then fill in with their values.
  3. Cases 2 and 3 follow the same way. The learner should notice in case 2 that fan flow equals the hood air when bypass is zero, and in case 3 that total equals fan flow when entrainment is zero.
  4. After case 3, free exploration unlocks: the learner changes any quantity, and the fan flow, total flow and plume concentration update at once. The first time the learner doubles the entrained flow, the sim shows the before and after concentrations so the learner sees that the concentration does not halve.

Feedback: Three cases, fixed order, three values each, two attempts per value. Correct: "Correct: ." Incorrect, first attempt: "Not yet. Check which air passes through the impeller." Incorrect, second attempt: the "Feedback when wrong" text for that case, then the value is revealed and counted as missed. A running count "Values correct: n of 9" is shown.

Starting State: Case 1 with empty answer boxes and the question "How much air must the fan move, and how much leaves the stack?"

Chapter Anchors: Worked example: 8,000 CFM contaminated at 100 ppm, 2,000 CFM bypass, 7,000 CFM entrained, fan flow 10,000 CFM, total flow 17,000 CFM, plume concentration 47.1 ppm. All values illustrative.

docs.title: Matching the Job to the Product Line
docs.text:
Everything in this chapter comes together when a customer describes a job and expects a product line in return. Work the description from the air outward: what the air carries, where it must go, where the fan can sit, and whether people stand in the airflow.

The sorter below gives you twelve such descriptions. If the product names still blur together, use the two comparison tables above as a checklist and work the sorter a second time.

docs.title: Diagram: Ventilation Job Matcher
docs.text:
Ventilation Job Matcher

Type: microsim sim-id: ch05-ventilation-job-matcher Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Evaluate Bloom Verb: recommend Learning Objective: The learner will recommend the product line that fits each of twelve building ventilation jobs, judged by the air contents, discharge path, mounting location and occupant exposure described in the job.

Prerequisites: housed centrifugal fan, plenum fan, square inline centrifugal fan, tubeaxial fan, upblast discharge, downblast discharge, centrifugal wall exhauster, gravity relief ventilator, cabinet ventilator, kitchen exhaust fan, smoke and heat exhaust fan, fiberglass fan, mancooler, entrained flow (all defined earlier in this chapter).

Evidence of Mastery: The learner assigns each of the twelve job cards to one of twelve product lines and, for each, selects the one deciding factor from four choices (air contents, discharge path, mounting location, occupant exposure). A card is correct when both the product line and the deciding factor match the Content table. Mastery is 10 of 12 product lines correct on the first attempt.

Misconceptions: (1) Any roof exhauster can handle any exhaust air. (2) A smoke exhaust job only needs a large ordinary fan. (3) Stainless steel is the only answer for corrosive air. (4) A mancooler is an exhaust fan. (5) Every relief opening needs a powered fan.

Instructional Rationale: Recommending a product line from a job description is an Evaluate-level judgment against criteria. Requiring the learner to also name the deciding factor makes the reasoning visible, so a correct guess for the wrong reason is caught.

Product lines offered (all twelve shown on every card): Kitchen exhaust fan; Smoke and heat exhaust fan; Fiberglass fan; Mancooler; Downblast centrifugal roof exhauster; Laboratory exhaust fan with entrained flow; Plenum fan; Cabinet ventilator; Gravity relief ventilator; Square inline centrifugal fan; Centrifugal wall exhauster; Tubeaxial fan.

Kitchen exhaust fan Air contents Grease-laden air needs a listed kitchen fan (UL 705 Supplement SC) with upblast discharge away from building surfaces. 2 An atrium must be cleared of smoke during a fire, with the fan still running at high temperature. Mancooler Occupant exposure A mancooler is an axial fan on a 360-degree swivel base with OSHA-compliant inlet and outlet screens; it cools people rather than exhausting air. 5 Restroom exhaust on a flat roof where a low, weather-protected unit is preferred. Tubeaxial fan Discharge path A plain-tube axial fan moves air straight through at low pressure in a short duct run.

Provenance: Kitchen listing, smoke and heat ratings, fiberglass description, mancooler description, cabinet ventilator applications and gravity relief ventilator description: tcf.com product category pages (Kitchen & Restaurant Exhaust Fans; Smoke & Heat Exhaust Fans; Fiberglass Fans; Mancoolers; Ceiling & Cabinet Ventilators; Gravity Relief Ventilators). Downblast and upblast airflow paths: FanPedia p. 5. Plenum fan Arrangement 4: FanPedia p. 170. Square inline centrifugal: FanPedia p. 6. Entrained flow: FanPedia pp. 4 and 6. Job cards are illustrative scenarios written for this chapter.

Rules: Twelve cards, shuffled once per session. Each card has exactly one correct product line and one correct deciding factor, as listed. Product line and factor are scored separately; the mastery count uses product lines only.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner reads a job card and chooses a product line from the twelve.
  2. The learner chooses the deciding factor from the four and commits both.
  3. The sim marks each choice and shows the Why text. The learner should notice that air contents decide cards 1-3, while cards 7, 8, 10 and 11 turn on where the fan can sit.
  4. After all twelve cards, a summary lists each job, the learner's choice and the correct choice, grouped by deciding factor.

Feedback: Twelve cards, shuffled, one attempt each, no re-answering. Correct line: "Correct: ." Incorrect line: "A better fit is ." followed by the Why text. The deciding factor is marked separately: correct "Right reason." or incorrect "The deciding factor here is ." The correct answers are revealed after each commit. Scores "Product lines correct: n of 12" and "Reasons correct: n of 12" are shown.

Starting State: The first shuffled job card with all twelve product lines and four factors available, and the question "Which product line was built for this job, and why?"

Chapter Anchors: Twelve jobs and twelve product lines. Smoke and heat fans withstand 500°F for four hours or 1,000°F for 15 minutes. Kitchen fans are listed to UL 705 Supplement SC (formerly UL 762). Mancoolers swivel a full 360 degrees and have OSHA-compliant screens.

When a real inquiry arrives, the same four questions apply, and the current catalog page for the chosen line supplies the sizes and ratings to quote.

You Can Read a Roof Now

You can now tell an upblast from a downblast at a glance, explain why a plenum fan needs no scroll, and work out how much air a lab exhaust plume really carries. That is the vocabulary behind most of the ventilation inquiries you will ever quote.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• A housed centrifugal fan delivers all its air through one scroll outlet at a right angle to the shaft; a plenum fan has no scroll and pressurizes the cabinet around it, so the cabinet decides where the air goes.
  • A square inline centrifugal fan fits rectangular duct and can turn the air 90 degrees; a tubeaxial fan is a plain-tube axial fan and the base for roof-mounted axial units.
  • Upblast discharge throws air up and away from the roof, for grease, fumes and heat; downblast discharge lays it back over the roof and is for clean air only. Hooded and louvered roof exhausters shelter a down-and-out discharge, and low profile roof ventilators keep axial units close to the deck.
  • A centrifugal wall exhauster discharges straight out from a wall, a gravity relief ventilator moves air with no fan, and a cabinet ventilator is a quiet blower for ceiling or inline duty.
  • Kitchen, smoke and heat, and fiberglass fans are defined by what is in the air: grease, fire, or corrosive vapor. A mancooler blows air on people.
  • Entrained flow joins the lab exhaust plume without passing through the fan, so total flow exceeds fan flow and plume concentration falls in proportion.

docs.title: Industrial Fans and Application Product Lines
Summary
docs.text: This chapter finishes the product-line survey with the heavier-duty and application-specific fans: plug fans, vaneaxial fans, pressure blowers, radial bladed and radial tip fans, duct fans, filtered supply fans, utility sets, air kits, paint booth exhaust fans, and dust collection fans. It closes with how laboratory exhaust fans use bypass flow and plume dilution to discharge contaminated air safely. After completing it, readers know the full range of fan families and product lines the rest of the book refers to.
