  • Tubular housings add straightening vanes, a discharge cone and, on belt drives, a belt tube; a belt guard and motor cover protect people and the motor outside the airstream.
  • Plug fans use a mounting panel and an insulation plug at the plenum wall; roof fans use a curb cap, a roof exhauster shroud, and on lab exhaust a nozzle and windband.

You Can Read the Drawing Now

You can now open any FanPedia exploded view, find the cutoff, the side plates, the straightening vanes or the curb cap, and say what each one is for. That "bent piece near the outlet" from the start of the chapter is most likely the cutoff, and you know to confirm it on p. 60 before anyone orders a part.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: This chapter introduces the impeller, the part that does the work of moving air. It covers blades, back plates, shrouds, and hubs; the main centrifugal types (single width single inlet, backward inclined, and forward curved); mixed flow impellers; and axial impellers with fixed or adjustable pitch, including hub position on the intake or discharge side and reversible impellers. It also covers straight bore and taper lock hubs and why impellers are balanced. After completing it, readers can identify an impeller type and explain how air flows through it.

docs.title: Concepts Covered
docs.text:
This chapter covers the following 22 concepts from the learning graph:

Concept Concept Impact Score Impeller Blade 26 Impeller Back Plate 4 Impeller Shroud 2 Impeller Balancing 47 Blade Leading Edge 1 Impeller Hub 9 Centrifugal Impeller 55 Axial Impeller 17 Impeller Orientation 5 Back Plate Fins 1 Single Width Single Inlet 10 Backward Inclined Impeller 13 Forward Curved Impeller 5 Mixed Flow Impeller 2 Fixed Pitch Impeller 1 Adjustable Pitch Impeller 3 Fiberglass Axial Impeller 2 Hub on Intake Side 2 Hub on Discharge Side 2 Reversible Impeller 1 Straight Bore Hub 2 Taper Lock Hub 2

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
This chapter builds on concepts from:

  • Chapter 2: Airstreams, Total Pressure and Standard Air
  • Chapter 3: Basic Fan Anatomy
  • Chapter 4: Centrifugal, Axial and Mixed Flow Fans
  • Chapter 5: Roof, Wall and Specialty Exhaust Fans

Welcome to the Impeller Chapter

Every fan you will ever quote, specify, or troubleshoot has exactly one part that actually moves the air, and that part is the impeller. By the end of this chapter you will be able to look at a wheel on a shop floor or a picture in a catalog and say what type it is, which way the air goes through it, and what the order has to say about it. Let's follow the airflow.

docs.title: The Part That Does the Work
docs.text:
In Chapter 3 you met the impeller as one part among many: housing, shaft, bearings, motor, inlet, and outlet. Every other part of a fan exists to hold the impeller, spin it, or guide air into and out of it. The impeller is the only part that adds energy to the airstream. When it turns, its blades push on the air, raising the air's velocity and pressure, which is the total pressure rise you studied in Chapter 2.

In Chapter 4 you sorted fans into three families by the path the air takes. That sorting is really a statement about the impeller inside. This chapter opens the fan up and looks at the impeller itself: what its parts are called, how the main centrifugal and axial types differ, how an axial impeller's hub position follows from the airflow direction, how the hub fastens to the shaft, and why every impeller is balanced before it ships. Chapter 9 then goes further into airfoil, backward curved, radial, and material handling designs.

docs.title: Impeller Parts
docs.text: Before comparing impeller types, it helps to name the parts that most of them share. FanPedia's centrifugal impeller drawing (FanPedia PDF p. 31) labels four of them: the blade, the back plate, the impeller front plate, and the hub. A fifth idea, the blade's leading edge, appears on every axial airflow page (FanPedia PDF pp. 37–41).

docs.title: Impeller Blade
docs.text:
An impeller blade is the surface that pushes on the air. Every impeller, centrifugal or axial, has a set of blades arranged evenly around the axis of rotation, and the shape, angle, and number of those blades decide most of what the impeller can do: how much pressure it can build, how efficiently it runs, and how well it tolerates dust. Blade shape is also the quickest way to identify an impeller type in the field. A blade that leans or curves back, away from the direction of rotation, belongs to the backward family; a blade whose tip curves toward the direction of rotation belongs to a forward curved impeller; a blade that runs straight out from the center is radial.

On an axial impeller the blades are shaped like propeller blades. FanPedia describes their action in one sentence: the concave side of the blade "cups the air and pushes it away from the impeller" (FanPedia PDF p. 37). The concave side is the hollow, inside face of the curved blade.

docs.title: Worked Example: Checking Rotation from the Blades
docs.text:
A facilities technician calls about a new housed centrifugal fan that "runs but doesn't move much air." You ask them to lock out the motor, open the access door, and describe the blades. They report flat blades whose outer ends lean back, away from the direction the arrow on the housing shows.

  1. Flat, single-thickness blades that lean backward identify a backward inclined impeller (FanPedia PDF p. 31).
  2. On a backward inclined impeller, the blade tips should trail the direction of rotation. The technician's description says the tips lean away from the arrow, which is correct for the arrow.
  3. You then ask them to bump the motor and watch the shaft. If the shaft turns against the arrow, the wiring is reversed. A centrifugal impeller turning backward still moves some air, but far less than its rating, which matches the complaint.
  4. The fix is to swap two motor leads (a job for an electrician) and recheck the rotation.

The blade shape told you what "correct" looks like before anyone measured anything. Chapter 12 shows how rotation is formally designated on a drawing.

docs.title: Blade Leading Edge
docs.text: The blade leading edge is the edge of the blade that meets the incoming air first. On an axial impeller, FanPedia states that "air is drawn through the impeller from the leading edge of the blades" (FanPedia PDF p. 37), so the leading edge always faces the intake side of the fan. On a centrifugal impeller the leading edge is the inner edge of each blade, near the inlet, and the opposite edge at the outer diameter is the trailing edge, or blade tip, where air leaves. Knowing which edge leads is how you check that an axial impeller is mounted facing the right way: if the leading edges face the discharge, the impeller is backward on its shaft.

docs.title: Impeller Back Plate and Impeller Shroud
docs.text:
The impeller back plate is the solid disc on the closed side of a centrifugal impeller. The blades are welded to it, and on most centrifugal impellers the hub is attached to it, so the back plate carries the blade loads to the hub and shaft. It also forms one wall of the air passage, so air entering the open side has nowhere to go except outward between the blades.

The impeller shroud is the ring-shaped plate on the inlet side of a centrifugal impeller. FanPedia labels it the impeller front plate (FanPedia PDF p. 31), and both names are common in the trade. The shroud has a large hole in its center where air enters, and it closes the other side of the blade passages so air is guided outward instead of leaking around the blade edges. Together, the back plate and shroud sandwich the blades. Not every impeller has both: FanPedia's open paddle impeller has neither, and its material handling impeller has a back plate only (FanPedia PDF p. 32), designs that Chapter 9 covers.

docs.title: Back Plate Fins
docs.text:
Back plate fins are small radial vanes welded to the outside of the back plate, on the side away from the blades. FanPedia lists this accessory as "fins on impeller back plate" and notes that it is also known by these names, any of which may appear on drawings and orders (FanPedia PDF p. 126):

  • thrust fins
  • thrust vanes or anti-thrust vanes
  • back plate fins
  • back pressure fins
  • cooling fins

FanPedia also gives their purpose: the fins "reduce the thrust load on the bearings," and they "can create a negative pressure behind the impeller to draw air into the fan through the shaft hole in the housing," which "helps reduce the possibility of leakage of the airstream to atmosphere" (FanPedia PDF pp. 126, 184). Thrust load is the push along the shaft's axis that the bearings must resist. Back plate fins therefore show up when bearing life or airstream leakage around the shaft is a concern.

docs.title: Impeller Hub
docs.text: The impeller hub is the thick central piece that connects the impeller to the shaft. Its bore, the hole through its center, fits the shaft, and the hub transmits the motor's torque into the blades. On a centrifugal impeller the hub is fastened to the back plate; on an axial impeller the hub is the center body that the blades attach to. FanPedia's axial overview (FanPedia PDF p. 35) names five axial parts: the blade, the blade tip, the hub, the hub boss (the raised center of the hub that holds the bore), and, on adjustable pitch impellers, the shank, which is the root of a blade that fits into the hub.

docs.title: Worked Example: Reading a Hub Callout on a Replacement Order
docs.text:
A plant sends a purchase order for "one replacement impeller, same as existing," with a photo of the old wheel. Before it can be quoted, the hub has to be described. You work through it like this:

  1. What fastens the hub to the shaft? The photo shows set screws on the side of the hub and a keyway in the bore. That is a straight bore hub (defined later in this chapter).
  2. What size is the bore? A straight bore must match the shaft diameter, so you need the shaft size from the nameplate data or the original order. The photo cannot give it.
  3. Is it centrifugal or axial? A back plate and front plate are visible, so it is centrifugal, and the hub sits on the back plate.
  4. Anything attached to the back plate? The photo shows short vanes on the back of the back plate, so the replacement must also have back plate fins.

The order now names the hub type, the bore, and the fins instead of "same as existing." That is the habit to build: name each part, and an order can be checked.

Before moving on, the table below collects the parts you have just read about.

Part Where it is What it does Blade Around the axis, between plates (centrifugal) or on the hub (axial) Pushes on the air Blade leading edge Edge of the blade that meets the incoming air Faces the intake; shows mounting direction Back plate Closed side of a centrifugal impeller Carries blades to the hub; closes the air passage Shroud (front plate) Inlet side of a centrifugal impeller Guides air outward; closes the blade passages Back plate fins Outside of the back plate Reduce bearing thrust; help limit shaft-hole leakage Hub Center of the impeller Connects the impeller to the shaft

docs.title: Centrifugal Impellers
docs.text:
A centrifugal impeller draws air in along the shaft axis and throws it outward, at a right angle to the shaft, off the blade tips. Air enters through the shroud opening, turns, and is flung outward through the passages between the blades by the impeller's rotation. FanPedia's housed centrifugal fan description states the result: air is drawn in through one or both sides and "is discharged at a right angle to the fan shaft" (FanPedia PDF p. 4). In a housed fan the scroll housing collects the air leaving the blade tips and turns its velocity into useful pressure; in a plenum fan, the plenum does that job; in an inline centrifugal fan, the tubular housing turns the air back in line with the duct.

FanPedia lists the centrifugal impeller types built into housed centrifugal fans: backward inclined, airfoil, backward curved, radial tip, forward curved, and radial bladed (FanPedia PDF p. 4). This chapter covers backward inclined and forward curved; the others are in Chapter 9.

One number connects impeller size and speed to how hard the impeller works on the air: the tip speed, the velocity of the blade tips as they travel around the circle. Higher tip speed means the blades can build more pressure, and it also means more stress in the impeller. For an impeller diameter \( D \) in inches turning at \( N \) revolutions per minute, the circumference in feet is \( \pi D / 12 \), and the tip speed is:

\[ V_{tip} = \frac{\pi D N}{12} \]

where \( V_{tip} \) is the tip speed in feet per minute (ft/min), \( D \) is the impeller diameter in inches, and \( N \) is the speed in rpm.

docs.title: Worked Example: Tip Speed of a Centrifugal Impeller
docs.text:
A 30-inch centrifugal impeller runs at 1,200 rpm (illustrative values, not a specific catalog size).

\[ V_{tip} = \frac{\pi \times 30 \times 1200}{12} = 9{,}425 \text{ ft/min} \]

If a belt change raises the speed to 1,800 rpm, the tip speed rises in proportion to 14,137 ft/min, 50% higher. The fan laws in Chapter 25 show that pressure rises with the square of speed, so this change raises the pressure the impeller can develop by a factor of \( 1.5^2 = 2.25 \). The impeller's structure has to be rated for that speed, which is why a speed increase is always checked against the maximum speed the current catalog allows for that fan and its construction.

Same Spin, Different Path

A centrifugal impeller works mostly by flinging air outward, so its pressure comes from the radius the air travels through. An axial impeller works by lifting air along the shaft, like a propeller. Once you see which way the air leaves the wheel, the housing, the arrangement, and even the drawing conventions start to make sense.

docs.title: Single Width Single Inlet
docs.text:
A single width single inlet (SWSI) impeller takes air in through one side only. It has one back plate, one shroud, and one inlet opening, and its housing has one inlet. The alternative is the double width double inlet (DWDI) impeller, which is essentially two single-width impellers placed back to back on a common center plate, drawing air in from both sides; it is covered in Chapter 9. FanPedia's housed centrifugal fan figure shows both (FanPedia PDF p. 4), and the arrangement pages list the SWSI arrangements separately (FanPedia PDF pp. 20–22).

Because a SWSI impeller has one open side and one closed side, its shaft can come in through the closed side. That allows the impeller to hang on the end of the shaft, with no bearing on the inlet side to block the airflow.

docs.title: Worked Example: Can This Be Arrangement 4?
docs.text:
A mechanical contractor asks for "a direct-drive fan, impeller on the motor shaft, double inlet, to save space." You check it against FanPedia:

  1. Arrangement 4 is direct drive with the "impeller mounted to motor shaft" and appears on the SWSI arrangement pages (FanPedia PDF p. 20).
  2. A double inlet impeller takes air from both sides, so a shaft cannot end inside it with a motor on one side without blocking one inlet. FanPedia's double width, double inlet arrangement page lists only Arrangement 3 and 7 variants (3, 3DI, 3F, 7, and 7DI) (FanPedia PDF p. 23), and its orientation page shows those arrangements with the impeller between two bearings (FanPedia PDF p. 30).
  3. The request is inconsistent. You go back to the contractor with two options: an Arrangement 4 SWSI fan, or a double width fan in Arrangement 3 or 7.

The words "single width single inlet" carry a real constraint on arrangement, so they belong on every centrifugal order.

docs.title: Impeller Orientation
docs.text:
Impeller orientation describes where the impeller sits on the shaft relative to the bearings. FanPedia names two orientations for centrifugal fans (FanPedia PDF p. 30):

  • Overhung impeller: the impeller is mounted on the end of the shaft, outboard of the bearings. FanPedia lists Arrangements 1, 8, 9, and 10, and Arrangement 4, where the impeller hangs on the motor shaft.
  • Center hung impeller: the impeller is mounted between the bearings. FanPedia lists Arrangement 3 and Arrangement 7, single and double width.

Orientation matters for the order because it fixes which arrangements are possible and where the bearings sit relative to the airstream. Chapter 11 develops the arrangements in full.

docs.title: Backward Inclined Impeller
docs.text:
A backward inclined impeller has flat, single-thickness blades tilted backward, so each blade's outer end trails behind its inner end as the impeller turns. FanPedia's caption reads "impeller with flat, single thickness, backward inclined blades" (FanPedia PDF p. 31). Its close relatives are the backward curved impeller, whose single-thickness blades are curved backward, and the airfoil impeller, whose backward inclined blades have a hollow airfoil section; both are in Chapter 9.

Backward inclined impellers are widely used for general ventilation and clean or lightly dusty air because they combine good efficiency with a useful property called a non-overloading power curve. On a fan curve, which Chapter 10 covers in detail, the brake horsepower of a backward inclined fan at a fixed speed rises to a peak and then falls as airflow keeps increasing. A motor sized for that peak cannot be overloaded at that speed, wherever the fan ends up operating on its curve.

docs.title: Worked Example: Will the Motor Overload?
docs.text:
A rooftop filtered supply unit is being selected for a building whose duct system is still being designed. The engineer worries that the real duct resistance may be lower than calculated, which would push the fan to more airflow than planned. FanPedia notes that filtered units use either forward curved or backward inclined impellers (FanPedia PDF p. 4). Which is safer here?

  1. Lower system resistance moves the operating point to the right on the fan curve, toward more airflow.
  2. With a backward inclined impeller, power peaks and then falls toward higher airflow, so a motor sized for the peak power at the selected speed covers this case.
  3. With a forward curved impeller, power keeps rising with airflow (next section), so the same shift can overload a motor that was sized only for the design point.
  4. When the system resistance is uncertain, the backward inclined unit, or a forward curved unit with a motor sized for the highest airflow it could reach, protects the motor.

docs.title: Forward Curved Impeller
docs.text: A forward curved impeller has many short, shallow blades that curve forward, so their tips point in the direction of rotation. FanPedia's caption is "impeller with single thickness, forward curved blades," and its drawing shows the end ring and tie rods that hold the narrow blades in place (FanPedia PDF p. 31). The forward curve throws air off the tips at high velocity, so a forward curved impeller moves a given airflow at a lower speed and in a smaller size than a backward inclined impeller, which suits compact, low-pressure equipment. The trade-offs are lower efficiency, a power curve that keeps rising with airflow (an overloading curve), and shallow blade pockets that collect dust, so forward curved impellers belong in clean air.

docs.title: Mixed Flow Impeller
docs.text:
A mixed flow impeller is a hybrid of axial and centrifugal designs: air leaves it partly along the shaft and partly outward. FanPedia calls it a "hybrid axial-centrifugal impeller design" used in mixed flow fans with tubular housings (FanPedia PDF p. 6), and describes its shape: "airfoil blades taper from impeller front plate to hub end resulting in a larger tip width" (FanPedia PDF p. 32). Because the air turns only partway, a mixed flow fan can sit in a straight duct like an axial fan while developing more pressure than a comparable axial impeller.

Now that the centrifugal family and the mixed flow hybrid have been described, the comparison below summarizes them.

Impeller Blade shape (FanPedia caption) Air leaves Power curve Best airstream Backward inclined Flat, single thickness, tilted backward Outward, at a right angle to the shaft Non-overloading Clean to lightly dusty Forward curved Single thickness, curved forward; many short blades Outward, at a right angle to the shaft Overloading Clean Mixed flow Airfoil blades tapering from front plate to hub, larger tip width Partly along the shaft, partly outward Depends on design; see the catalog Clean

Do Not Judge a Wheel by Its Width

A common trap is calling any wheel with many narrow blades "forward curved" without checking which way the blades curve against the rotation. Before you write the impeller type on an order, find the rotation arrow and confirm the blade tips point with it (forward curved) or trail it (backward inclined).

docs.title: Axial Impellers
docs.text:
An axial impeller moves air parallel to the shaft. Its blades are attached to a central hub and, as the impeller turns, the concave side of each blade "cups the air and pushes it away from the impeller" (FanPedia PDF p. 37). Air enters at the blades' leading edges and leaves straight through, so an axial fan can sit in a duct with no change of direction. Axial impellers are used in tubeaxial and vaneaxial fans, roof mounted axial fans, and panel fans; FanPedia notes that inline centrifugal fans can share the same arrangements but use different impellers (FanPedia PDF p. 28).

FanPedia lays out three steps for configuring an axial fan (FanPedia PDF p. 36):

  1. Select the model and impeller type, for example "Model TCTA with 'TCTA' impeller."
  2. Choose the airflow direction: air through the impeller then over the motor (airflow = PM), or air over the motor then through the impeller (airflow = MP).
  3. Determine the rotation the impeller needs to produce that airflow direction.

FanPedia adds two notes to every axial airflow page: airflow direction and rotation "must be correct for the fan to operate at 100% performance," and if the impeller rotates in the wrong direction, "you will not get any airflow in the proper direction" (FanPedia PDF pp. 37–40). For axial fans, rotation is determined by viewing the impeller from the discharge side of the fan.

docs.title: Fixed Pitch and Adjustable Pitch Impellers
docs.text:
The pitch of an axial blade is its angle relative to the plane of rotation. A steeper pitch takes a bigger bite of air per revolution.

A fixed pitch impeller has its blades set at one angle that cannot be changed. FanPedia shows fixed pitch impellers as cast or fabricated (FanPedia PDF p. 35); its axial type pages mark the "TCTS," "TCTA," "Z Series," and "L Series" impellers as fixed (FanPedia PDF p. 34).

An adjustable pitch impeller has separate blades whose shanks are clamped into the hub, so the blade angle can be reset to a different pitch. Resetting the pitch moves the fan to a different performance curve without changing the impeller diameter or speed. FanPedia marks the "B Series," "E Series," "TCVX," "A," and "AXIAD" impellers as adjustable and the "C Series" as adjustable only (FanPedia PDF p. 33). Blade count and pitch angle are covered in more depth in Chapter 9.

docs.title: Fiberglass Axial Impeller
docs.text: A fiberglass axial impeller has blades, and sometimes a hub, molded from fiberglass-reinforced plastic instead of metal, which suits corrosive airstreams that would attack steel or aluminum. FanPedia shows a fiberglass group (FanPedia PDF p. 34): the "TF" and "FG7" impellers, marked fixed, and the adjustable "F4/F6" impellers with an aluminum hub and "FG4/FG6" impellers with a fiberglass hub. Whether the hub is aluminum or fiberglass is part of the impeller designation, so it has to be stated on the order.

docs.title: Worked Example: Configuring an Axial Fan
docs.text:
A customer needs a direct-drive tubeaxial fan to exhaust warm air from a process area, and asks how the order should describe the impeller. Following FanPedia's three steps:

  1. Model and impeller. Suppose the selection, made from the current catalog, is a fan with a fixed pitch cast impeller. (The model is not the point of this example.)
  2. Airflow direction. With airflow = PM, air passes through the impeller and then over the motor. With airflow = MP, air passes over the motor first. In a direct-drive axial fan the motor is in the airstream either way; when that is a problem, a belt-driven arrangement is the answer, which Chapter 11 covers. Here the customer chooses MP to match an existing duct layout.
  3. Rotation. Rotation is read from the discharge side. The rotation must match the impeller hand (left hand or right hand), because FanPedia shows both left hand and right hand fixed and adjustable impellers (FanPedia PDF pp. 42–43). A right hand impeller is ordered with right hand rotation.

The finished line on the order states the impeller, the airflow direction (MP), and the rotation, and the next section shows how MP also fixes the hub position.

docs.title: Hub on Intake Side and Hub on Discharge Side
docs.text:
FanPedia gives each airflow direction an alternative name based on where the hub's boss faces (FanPedia PDF pp. 36–40):

  • Hub on intake side: airflow = PM, air through the impeller then over the motor. The hub faces the incoming air.
  • Hub on discharge side: airflow = MP, air over the motor then through the impeller. The hub faces the leaving air.

The hub bore follows the same choice. On FanPedia's left hand and right hand pages, a standard bore hub goes with MP airflow and a reverse bore hub goes with PM airflow, for both adjustable and fixed cast impellers (FanPedia PDF pp. 42–43). In other words, "MP," "hub on discharge," and "standard bore hub" all describe the same build, and "PM," "hub on intake," and "reverse bore hub" describe the other.

Airflow code Air path Also called Hub bore (FanPedia pp. 42–43) PM Through impeller, then over motor Hub on intake Reverse bore hub MP Over motor, then through impeller Hub on discharge Standard bore hub

One Letter Order, Three Answers

Read the airflow code left to right as the air's path; FanPedia capitalizes the P in "imPeller" to make the point, so PM means impeller first, then motor. If the impeller comes first, the hub faces the intake and the bore is reversed; if the motor comes first, the hub faces the discharge and the bore is standard.

docs.title: Reversible Impeller
docs.text: A reversible impeller is an axial impeller designed to move air in either direction along the shaft. FanPedia shows one reversible impeller in two modes (FanPedia PDF p. 41): standard flow, with airflow = MP and the hub on the discharge side, and reverse flow, with airflow = PM and the hub on the intake side. In both modes, air is drawn in at the blades' leading edge for that flow direction. FanPedia labels the rotation the same in both modes; since rotation is always viewed from the discharge side and the discharge switches ends when the flow reverses, the motor's actual direction of turning reverses with the flow. Reversible impellers are used where a single fan must both supply and exhaust, such as a space that is ventilated in one direction during some operations and the other direction at other times.

docs.title: Diagram: Axial Airflow and Hub Position Configurator
docs.text:
Axial Airflow and Hub Position Configurator

Type: microsim sim-id: ch08-axial-airflow-hub-configurator Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Apply Bloom Verb: apply Learning Objective: The learner will apply FanPedia's axial airflow rules to state the hub position and hub bore for an axial fan order, given its airflow code or air path, with at least 7 of 8 orders correct.

Prerequisites: axial impeller, blade leading edge, airflow = PM, airflow = MP, hub on intake side, hub on discharge side, standard bore hub, reverse bore hub, reversible impeller, rotation viewed from the discharge side (all defined in the section "Axial Impellers" above).

Evidence of Mastery: For each of 8 orders the learner commits two answers before the fan is animated: hub position (intake side or discharge side) and hub bore (standard bore or reverse bore). An order is correct when both answers match the answer table. Mastery is 7 of 8 orders correct on the first attempt. Running the free model is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) "Hub on intake" means the motor is on the intake side. (2) PM and MP are rotation codes rather than airflow codes. (3) A reversible impeller has a fixed hub position. (4) Running an axial impeller backward simply gives less airflow in the same direction.

Instructional Rationale: Applying a rule set to new orders, with a committed answer checked against the rule, is the Apply-level evidence; animating the air path only after the answer lets the learner see why the rule holds.

Content:

A side view of a direct-drive axial fan: tubular housing, motor, impeller with hub and blades, and labels "Intake" and "Discharge" that move with the airflow direction. The free model has two settings: airflow code (PM or MP) and rotation (correct for the impeller, or reversed).

The 8 orders, in this fixed order:

# Order text shown Hub position Hub bore Why (feedback) 1 Airflow = PM, adjustable pitch Intake side Reverse bore PM is air through the impeller then over the motor, also called hub on intake, built with a reverse bore hub. 2 Airflow = MP, fixed pitch cast Discharge side Standard bore MP is air over the motor then through the impeller, also called hub on discharge, built with a standard bore hub. 3 Air passes over the motor first, then through the impeller Discharge side Standard bore Motor first is MP, which is hub on discharge with a standard bore hub. 4 Air passes through the impeller first, then over the motor Intake side Reverse bore Impeller first is PM, which is hub on intake with a reverse bore hub. 5 Reversible impeller, standard flow Discharge side Standard bore FanPedia shows standard flow as MP, hub on discharge. 6 Reversible impeller, reverse flow Intake side Reverse bore FanPedia shows reverse flow as PM, hub on intake. 7 Right hand adjustable pitch impeller, airflow = MP Discharge side Standard bore Impeller hand does not change the rule: MP is a standard bore hub on the discharge side. 8 Left hand fixed cast impeller, airflow = PM Intake side Reverse bore Impeller hand does not change the rule: PM is a reverse bore hub on the intake side.

Provenance: Airflow codes, "aka" names, leading-edge statement and rotation viewing side from FanPedia PDF pp. 36–40; reversible impeller modes from FanPedia PDF p. 41; standard bore with MP and reverse bore with PM for left hand and right hand, adjustable and fixed cast impellers from FanPedia PDF pp. 42–43; wrong-rotation note from FanPedia PDF pp. 37–40.

Rules: PM gives hub on intake side and reverse bore hub. MP gives hub on discharge side and standard bore hub. Impeller hand (left or right) and pitch type (fixed or adjustable) do not change hub position or bore. Reversible impeller: standard flow = MP, reverse flow = PM. In the free model, correct rotation shows air entering at the leading edges and leaving at the discharge; reversed rotation shows no airflow in the intended direction, with the message "Wrong rotation: no airflow in the proper direction (FanPedia note 2)." The rotation is always labeled as viewed from the discharge side.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner reads an order and chooses a hub position and a hub bore, then presses Check.
  2. The fan is drawn with the hub on the correct side and animated with air moving in the order's direction, intake to discharge.
  3. Feedback appears; the learner moves to the next order.
  4. After order 8, the free model unlocks. The learner switches between PM and MP and watches the hub and the intake and discharge labels move, then reverses the rotation and sees the airflow stop in the intended direction.

Feedback: 8 orders, fixed order, one attempt each. Correct (both answers right): "Correct." followed by the Why text. Incorrect (either answer wrong): "Not quite." followed by the correct hub position and bore and the Why text. A running count "Orders correct: n of 8" is shown. No retry of scored items; the learner can restart the whole set.

Starting State: Order 1 is shown with the fan drawn without its hub, and the question "Which side does the hub face, and which hub bore does this build use?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter states that PM is hub on intake with a reverse bore hub, MP is hub on discharge with a standard bore hub, reversible standard flow is MP and reverse flow is PM, rotation is viewed from the discharge side, and wrong rotation gives no airflow in the proper direction. Mastery is 7 of 8.

Two Codes, Many Names

If PM, MP, hub on intake, hub on discharge, standard bore, and reverse bore feel like six things to memorize, most people feel the same on first pass. There are really only two builds with three names each, so learn the air path for one of them and the other is just its opposite; the configurator above lets you test that before it goes on an order.

docs.title: Hub Types
docs.text: The hub's bore has to grip the shaft tightly enough to carry full motor torque and stay put under vibration, and it must also come off when the impeller or shaft needs service. FanPedia shows two common ways to do this, for both centrifugal and axial impellers (FanPedia PDF pp. 44–45). A third, the Trantorque hub, is in Chapter 9.

docs.title: Straight Bore Hub
docs.text: In a straight bore hub, "the bore of the hub is straight through. Shafts are keyed and mounted to the hub" (FanPedia PDF p. 45). A key, a small square bar, sits half in a keyway in the shaft and half in a matching keyway in the hub, so it carries the torque. On centrifugal impellers, set screws through the hub press on the key and shaft to stop the hub sliding along the shaft. On axial impellers FanPedia shows two versions: with key and set screws, and with key, retaining washer, and bolt at the shaft end (FanPedia PDF p. 44). A straight bore has to be machined to suit one shaft diameter.

docs.title: Taper Lock Hub
docs.text: In a taper lock hub, "the hub bore is tapered with respect to the fan shaft. The hub is locked to the shaft using a tapered bushing" (FanPedia PDF p. 45). The bushing has a straight bore that fits the shaft and a tapered outside that fits the hub. Tightening the bushing's screws draws it into the tapered hub, which squeezes the bushing onto the shaft for a tight clamping fit along its whole length. Loosening the screws, and using the bushing's removal holes, releases it. FanPedia's axial version is shown "with key and hardware" (FanPedia PDF p. 44).

docs.title: Worked Example: Choosing Between Two Hubs
docs.text:
A plant engineer replaces impellers every few years because of wear and wants the change-outs to be quick. The current impeller has a straight bore hub that has seized to the shaft twice. Compare the two hub types for this customer:

Question Straight bore hub Taper lock hub How is torque carried? Key in matching keyways Clamping fit of the bushing, with a key How is it held in place along the shaft? Set screws (or washer and bolt on axial) The bushing's grip on the shaft What does removal require? Pulling the hub off a close-fitting bore Loosening the bushing screws to release the taper Does the hub bore have to match the shaft? Yes, machined to one shaft diameter The bushing's bore matches the shaft

For this customer, the taper lock hub answers the stated problem: the taper releases the grip when the screws are backed out, so change-outs do not depend on forcing a close-fitting bore off the shaft. The hub type then goes on the replacement order along with the shaft diameter. Confirm in the current catalog that the impeller is offered with that hub.

docs.title: Impeller Balancing
docs.text:
An impeller is never perfectly symmetric. Slight differences in plate thickness, weld beads, and blade position leave more mass on one side of the axis than the other. When the impeller spins, that off-center mass is pulled outward and the whole rotor is pushed around in a circle once per revolution, which the bearings, shaft, and structure feel as vibration. Impeller balancing is the process of measuring that unbalance, usually by spinning the impeller on a balancing machine, and correcting it by adding or removing small weights until what is left, the residual unbalance, is within an allowed limit. Detailed balancing procedures are outside the scope of this course; what an application or sales engineer needs is why it matters and how the limit is set.

The force from a given unbalance grows with the square of speed. For a residual unbalance \( U \) in ounce-inches turning at \( N \) rpm, the rotating force is approximately:

\[ F \approx 1.77 \, U \left( \frac{N}{1000} \right)^2 \]

where \( F \) is the force in pounds-force (lbf), \( U \) is the unbalance (the unbalance mass in ounces multiplied by its distance from the axis in inches), and \( N \) is the speed in rpm.

The allowed residual unbalance is set by a balance quality grade, \( G \), from the international balancing standard ISO 21940-11 (formerly ISO 1940-1). The grade is a speed in millimeters per second; a smaller grade is tighter balance. The fan industry standard AMCA 204 assigns balance grades by fan application category, with grades such as G6.3 and G2.5 common for industrial fans. For an impeller weighing \( W \) pounds running at a maximum service speed of \( N \) rpm, the permissible residual unbalance is:

\[ U_{per} = \frac{6.015 \, G \, W}{N} \]

where \( U_{per} \) is the permissible residual unbalance in ounce-inches, \( G \) is the balance grade in mm/s, \( W \) is the impeller weight in pounds, and \( N \) is the speed in rpm.

docs.title: Worked Example: How Much Unbalance Is Allowed?
docs.text:
A 200 lb impeller runs at 1,200 rpm and is balanced to grade G6.3 (illustrative values; the grade for a real fan comes from the specification or catalog).

  1. Permissible residual unbalance: \( U_{per} = 6.015 \times 6.3 \times 200 / 1200 = 6.32 \) oz·in.
  2. If the balancer corrects at a radius of 15 in, the largest uncorrected mass allowed there is \( 6.32 / 15 = 0.42 \) oz, less than half an ounce on a 200 lb wheel.
  3. At G2.5 the limit drops to \( 2.51 \) oz·in, or \( 0.17 \) oz at 15 in.
  4. The force from the G6.3 limit at 1,200 rpm is \( 1.77 \times 6.32 \times 1.2^2 \approx 16 \) lbf. Run the same impeller at 1,800 rpm and the force is about 36 lbf; at 2,400 rpm, twice the speed, about 65 lbf, four times as much.

That last step is the practical lesson: an impeller balanced for one speed is not automatically acceptable at a higher one, which is one more reason a speed increase is checked against the catalog before it is made.

docs.title: Diagram: Impeller Balance Calculator
docs.text:
Impeller Balance Calculator

Type: microsim sim-id: ch08-impeller-balance-calculator Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Apply Bloom Verb: calculate Learning Objective: The learner will calculate the permissible residual unbalance and the matching correction mass for an impeller from its weight, speed, balance grade and correction radius, to within 2% of the model value.

Prerequisites: impeller balancing, residual unbalance, balance quality grade G, ounce-inch, correction radius (all defined in the section "Impeller Balancing" above).

Evidence of Mastery: For three challenge impellers the learner types the permissible residual unbalance (oz·in) and the correction mass (oz) before the answer is shown. A value is correct when it is within ±2% of the model value. Mastery is 3 of 3 challenges with both values correct. Moving the free-exploration controls is not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) A heavier impeller is allowed less unbalance (it is allowed more, in proportion to weight). (2) Force from unbalance grows in proportion to speed (it grows with the square of speed). (3) A larger grade number means tighter balance (it means looser balance).

Instructional Rationale: Calculation at the Apply level needs practice with a committed, checked number; the free model afterward lets the learner see the speed-squared force growth that the misconceptions get wrong.

Content:

Adjustable quantities in free exploration:

Quantity Min Max Step Default Unit Impeller weight W 20 2000 10 200 lb Maximum service speed N 300 3600 50 1200 rpm Correction radius r 4 40 1 15 in

Balance grade G choices: G16, G6.3, G2.5, G1.0. Default G6.3.

Displayed results: permissible residual unbalance U (oz·in, two decimals), correction mass m (oz, two decimals), rotating force F at the selected speed (lbf, whole number), and a line showing F at half and at double the selected speed when those speeds lie within 300–3600 rpm.

Challenge impellers, in this order (all illustrative):

# W (lb) N (rpm) G r (in) U (oz·in) m (oz) Feedback when wrong 1 200 1200 G6.3 15 6.32 0.42 U = 6.015 × 6.3 × 200 / 1200 = 6.32 oz·in; m = 6.32 / 15 = 0.42 oz. 2 200 1200 G2.5 15 2.51 0.17 A tighter grade lowers the limit: U = 6.015 × 2.5 × 200 / 1200 = 2.51 oz·in; m = 2.51 / 15 = 0.17 oz. 3 600 1800 G6.3 20 12.63 0.63 U = 6.015 × 6.3 × 600 / 1800 = 12.63 oz·in; m = 12.63 / 20 = 0.63 oz.

Provenance: Formulas from the chapter section "Impeller Balancing": U = 6.015 G W / N (ISO 21940-11 permissible residual unbalance converted to US units) and F ≈ 1.77 U (N/1000)². Grade choices are ISO balance quality grades. All weights, speeds and radii are illustrative and the sim labels them "illustrative".

Rules: U = 6.015 × G × W / N, with G in mm/s, W in lb, N in rpm, U in oz·in. m = U / r. F = 1.77 × U × (N/1000)². Speed N is the speed used for both U and F. Values are rounded only for display. Answers are judged within ±2% of the unrounded model value.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner reads challenge 1 and types U and m.
  2. The learner presses Check. The model values and the worked calculation appear next to the learner's answers.
  3. After the three challenges, free exploration unlocks: the learner changes W, N, G and r, and U, m and F update at once.
  4. The learner doubles N from 1200 to 2400 rpm with U held by the grade, and notices that F becomes four times larger while U halves.

Feedback: Three challenges, fixed order, two attempts each. Correct (both values within ±2%): "Correct: U = oz·in, m = oz." Incorrect: the "Feedback when wrong" text for that challenge. After the second wrong attempt the model values and calculation are shown and the challenge counts as missed. A running count "Challenges correct: n of 3" is shown.

Starting State: Challenge 1 with empty answer boxes and the question "How much unbalance may this 200 lb impeller keep at 1,200 rpm and grade G6.3?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter's worked example uses W = 200 lb, N = 1,200 rpm, G6.3, r = 15 in and gets U = 6.32 oz·in and m = 0.42 oz; G2.5 gives 2.51 oz·in and 0.17 oz; F is about 16 lbf at 1,200 rpm, about 36 lbf at 1,800 rpm and about 65 lbf at 2,400 rpm.

docs.title: Identifying an Impeller Type
docs.text: You now have the vocabulary to name an impeller from what you can see. The decision runs in a fixed order: first the air path (outward, straight through, or partway), then for centrifugal impellers the blade shape against rotation and the number of inlets, and for axial impellers the pitch type, material, and hub position. The classifier below gives you practice on descriptions like the ones you will meet in field photos and catalog pages.

docs.title: Diagram: Impeller Type Classifier
docs.text:
Impeller Type Classifier

Type: microsim sim-id: ch08-impeller-type-classifier Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Understand Bloom Verb: classify Learning Objective: The learner will classify written descriptions of impellers into the impeller types named in this chapter, with at least 8 of 10 correct on the first attempt.

Prerequisites: centrifugal impeller, axial impeller, mixed flow impeller, backward inclined impeller, forward curved impeller, single width single inlet, fixed pitch impeller, adjustable pitch impeller, fiberglass axial impeller, reversible impeller (all defined in this chapter above this block).

Evidence of Mastery: The learner sorts each of 10 description cards into one of six bins before any feedback is shown for that card. A card is correct when its bin matches the answer column. Mastery is 8 of 10 on the first attempt.

Misconceptions: (1) Many narrow blades always means forward curved. (2) Any impeller in a tubular housing is axial. (3) Adjustable pitch means the blades can be changed while the fan runs. (4) Fiberglass impellers are always fixed pitch.

Instructional Rationale: Classifying new descriptions requires the learner to apply the defining features of each type rather than recall a picture, and asking for a prediction before feedback makes the learner commit to a reason.

Content:

Bins: Backward inclined (centrifugal); Forward curved (centrifugal); Mixed flow; Axial, fixed pitch; Axial, adjustable pitch; Axial, reversible.

# Card text Correct bin Why (feedback) 1 Flat, single-thickness blades whose tips trail the direction of rotation; air leaves at a right angle to the shaft Backward inclined (centrifugal) Flat blades tilted backward against rotation define backward inclined. 2 Many short, shallow blades curved so their tips point in the direction of rotation, held by an end ring and tie rods Forward curved (centrifugal) Tips pointing with rotation, plus end ring and tie rods, define forward curved. 3 Airfoil blades that taper from the front plate to the hub end, giving a larger tip width; air leaves partly along the shaft Mixed flow A tapered blade with partly axial discharge is the hybrid axial-centrifugal impeller. 4 Cast impeller with blades formed at one angle that cannot be changed Axial, fixed pitch Cast or fabricated blades at one angle are fixed pitch. 5 Separate blades whose shanks clamp into the hub so the blade angle can be reset Axial, adjustable pitch Clamped shanks allow the pitch to be reset. 6 One axial impeller shown in two modes: standard flow MP and reverse flow PM Axial, reversible An impeller built to move air either way along the shaft is reversible. 7 Fiberglass blades on an aluminum hub, sold as the "F4/F6" impeller Axial, adjustable pitch FanPedia marks F4/F6 and FG4/FG6 as adjustable; fiberglass does not mean fixed. 8 Fiberglass "TF" impeller with molded blades Axial, fixed pitch FanPedia marks the TF impeller as fixed. 9 A single width single inlet wheel with backward-tilted flat blades in an inline (tubular) centrifugal fan Backward inclined (centrifugal) Air still leaves the wheel outward; the tubular housing turns it back in line, so the impeller is centrifugal. 10 "TCTA" impeller, as listed in FanPedia's axial impeller types Axial, fixed pitch FanPedia marks the TCTA impeller as fixed.

Provenance: Centrifugal captions from FanPedia PDF p. 31; mixed flow caption from FanPedia PDF p. 32 and hybrid description from p. 6; fixed and adjustable markings from FanPedia PDF pp. 33–34; fixed pitch "cast or fabricated" from p. 35; reversible modes from p. 41.

Rules: Each card has exactly one correct bin, given in the table. Cards are judged on the first placement only for the score.

Learner Activity:

  1. A card appears; the learner drags or assigns it to one bin.
  2. The card is marked correct or incorrect and the Why text is shown.
  3. Incorrectly placed cards return to a review pile that the learner can redo after card 10.

Feedback: 10 cards in shuffled order, one scored attempt each. Correct: "Correct: ." plus the Why text. Incorrect: "This one is ." plus the Why text. Score "n of 10" shown at the end; the review pile does not change the score.

Starting State: Six empty bins and the first card, with the prompt "Where does the air go, and what do the blades look like?"

Chapter Anchors: Mastery is 8 of 10. The chapter states that TCTA, TF and FG7 are fixed, F4/F6 and FG4/FG6 are adjustable, and reversible standard flow is MP and reverse flow is PM.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• The impeller is the only part of a fan that adds energy to the air; its blades push the air, and the blade leading edge meets the incoming air first.
  • A centrifugal impeller's blades sit between a back plate and a shroud (FanPedia's impeller front plate); back plate fins on the back reduce bearing thrust and help limit leakage at the shaft hole.
  • The hub connects the impeller to the shaft. A straight bore hub is keyed and held by set screws (or a washer and bolt); a taper lock hub clamps to the shaft through a tapered bushing.
  • A centrifugal impeller throws air outward at a right angle to the shaft. A single width single inlet impeller takes air from one side and can be overhung; double width impellers are center hung in Arrangements 3 and 7.
  • Backward inclined impellers have flat blades tilted against rotation and a non-overloading power curve; forward curved impellers have many short blades curved with rotation, run slower and smaller, and have an overloading power curve.
  • A mixed flow impeller is a hybrid whose airfoil blades taper from front plate to hub, sending air partly along the shaft.
  • An axial impeller moves air parallel to the shaft, with fixed pitch (cast or fabricated) or adjustable pitch blades; fiberglass axial impellers come in both.
  • Airflow PM is hub on intake with a reverse bore hub; airflow MP is hub on discharge with a standard bore hub. A reversible impeller runs standard flow MP and reverse flow PM. Axial rotation is viewed from the discharge side, and wrong rotation gives no airflow in the proper direction.
  • Impeller balancing limits residual unbalance to \( U_{per} = 6.015\,G\,W/N \); the vibration force from unbalance grows with the square of speed.

You Can Name the Wheel

You can now name every major impeller part, tell backward inclined from forward curved by the blades alone, and turn an axial airflow code into a hub position and bore. That is exactly what an impeller line on an order needs.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: This chapter goes deeper into impeller design: airfoil and backward curved blades, double width double inlet impellers, impeller width and airflow path, end rings, gussets and tie rods, axial blade tips, blade count and pitch angle, and fiberglass and Trantorque hubs. It then covers impellers built for dirty airstreams: radial bladed, radial tip, open radial paddle, material handling, and paper handling designs. After completing it, readers can explain why a given impeller suits clean air, high efficiency, or a particulate-laden airstream.

This chapter builds on concepts from:

  • Chapter 2: Airstreams, Total Pressure and Standard Air

docs.title: Why Impeller Construction Matters
docs.text:
Chapter 8 taught you to name an impeller by its blade shape. This chapter looks at how impellers are actually built, which parts hold them together, and why Twin City Fan offers so many radial designs for airstreams that carry sawdust, paper trim, threads or grit. The question behind every section is the one a customer asks on the phone: what is in the airstream, and which wheel will survive it while still meeting the duty point?

From Wheel Shape to Wheel Survival

A selection that looks perfect on the performance curve can be wrapped in shredded paper or worn through in a few months if the impeller is wrong for the airstream. By the end of this chapter you will be able to read a job description and say which impeller belongs in it, and why. Let's follow the airflow.

docs.title: Reading an Impeller: Airflow Path and Width
Impeller Airflow Path
docs.text:
The impeller airflow path is the route air takes from the moment it reaches the blades until it leaves them. FanPedia's technical descriptions (p. 186) separate impellers by exactly this: in a centrifugal or radial impeller, air enters axially, along the shaft, is accelerated by the blades and leaves radially, at a right angle to the shaft. In an axial impeller, the blades push air along the shaft with a swirling, tangential motion. A mixed flow impeller sits between the two; FanPedia (p. 32) describes its airfoil blades tapering from the impeller front plate to the hub end, which gives a larger tip width and a diagonal path. The path matters because it decides the housing shape, where ductwork connects, and where material in the air will strike the blades.

The table below collects the three paths you have just read about.

Impeller family Air enters Air leaves Where to look on a drawing Centrifugal (radial flow) Along the shaft, through the inlet At a right angle to the shaft, into the scroll Inlet on the side, outlet on the scroll Axial Along the shaft Along the shaft, with swirl Inlet and outlet on the same centerline Mixed flow Along the shaft Diagonally, then turned back to the axis Tubular housing, tapered blades

docs.title: Impeller Width
docs.text: Impeller width is the axial distance across the blades of a centrifugal impeller, from back plate to front plate (or inlet side to inlet side on a double inlet wheel). At a fixed diameter and speed, a wider impeller passes more air, while pressure capability is set mostly by tip speed. FanPedia (p. 4) notes that pressure blowers use narrower housings and impeller widths than standard centrifugal fans, and that Arrangement 4 plenum fans "can be selected with varying impeller widths to provide desired performance at direct drive motor speeds" (p. 170). The current Twin City Fan catalog lists special width and diameter impellers as an option on its radial tip and high efficiency fans, for the same reason: width is the factory's way to fit flow to a fixed motor speed.

docs.title: Holding an Impeller Together: End Rings, Tie Rods and Gussets
docs.text:
A spinning impeller carries large centrifugal loads, so every design needs parts whose only job is to keep the blades where they belong. Three of these show up on FanPedia's impeller drawings (pp. 31–32).

An impeller end ring (FanPedia also calls it an end rim) is a flat ring that joins the ends of the blades at the face of the impeller. On a forward curved wheel, end rings at each side hold the many short, shallow blades in a drum shape. On the radial bladed paddle impeller, Twin City Fan adds front and back end rings to the open paddle design, which stiffens the blades without closing off the back of the wheel.

An impeller tie rod is a rod that runs across the width of the impeller, usually between the end rings, to tie them together and resist the blades spreading under load. FanPedia's forward curved drawing calls out both the end ring and the tie rod; a long, narrow-bladed drum is exactly the shape that needs one.

An impeller gusset is a triangular or trapezoidal plate welded where a blade meets the hub or back plate, bracing the blade against bending. The open radial paddle impeller uses support gussets at the hub, and the paper handling impeller uses trapezoidal gussets on its full back plate "for extra rugged durability" (FanPedia p. 32).

Part Joins Where FanPedia shows it End ring (end rim) Blade ends at the impeller face Forward curved; radial paddle impeller Tie rod One end ring to the other, across the width Forward curved Gusset Blade to hub or back plate Open radial paddle (support gussets); paper handling (trapezoidal gussets)

docs.title: Backward Curved and Airfoil Impellers
docs.text:
Both designs below are refinements of the backward inclined impeller from Chapter 8: the blades lean away from the direction of rotation, which keeps the power curve from rising without limit as flow increases.

A backward curved impeller has single thickness blades that are curved, rather than flat, with the curve leaning back from the direction of rotation (FanPedia p. 31). The curve gives smoother air passage than a flat blade, while the single thickness plate stays simple, solid and tolerant of some dust.

An airfoil impeller has backward inclined blades with an airfoil cross section: a hollow, wing-shaped blade with a rounded leading edge and a tapered trailing edge (FanPedia p. 31). The airfoil shape lets air follow the blade surface with less separation, which is why airfoil wheels reach the highest static efficiency of the centrifugal family. The trade-off is that a hollow, formed blade is less forgiving of abrasive or sticky material than a solid plate.

Efficiency and Ruggedness Pull in Opposite Directions

Notice the pattern that runs through this whole chapter: the shapes that guide air most smoothly are the shapes that dust can erode, coat or fill. Every step from airfoil to backward curved to radial tip to radial bladed trades some efficiency for the ability to survive a dirtier airstream.

docs.title: High Efficiency Centrifugal Fans
docs.text:
A high efficiency centrifugal fan is a housed industrial centrifugal fan built around an airfoil or backward curved impeller and meant for high airflow at moderate to high pressure where power cost matters. Twin City Fan's current catalog groups two such models under "Radial Tip & High Efficiency Fans," describing the design as non-overloading:

  • HAF High Efficiency Airfoil Fan: a heavy-gauge, all-welded, non-overloading airfoil impeller for clean air and high pressure; typical uses include forced draft on fluid boilers, dryers, solvent recovery, moisture blow-off, product cooling and recirculation.
  • HIB High Efficiency Industrial Backward Curved Fan: a backward curved impeller for clean air or air with light dust loading; widely used on the clean side of baghouses, in high efficiency filtration, forced draft and high-pressure process supply.

The split between the two is the efficiency-ruggedness trade in miniature: choose the airfoil when the air is truly clean, and the backward curved wheel when some dust will get through.

docs.title: What DWDI Means
docs.text:
A double width double inlet (DWDI) fan uses an impeller that is, in effect, two single width impellers placed back to back on one hub, inside a housing about twice as wide, with an inlet on each side. Air enters from both sides, turns, and leaves through a single scroll outlet. FanPedia's housed centrifugal page (p. 4) shows both forms side by side, and its discharge charts (pp. 48–49) list DWDI fans with forward curved, backward inclined and airfoil impellers.

Because both sides of the wheel work at once, a DWDI fan moves roughly twice the air of a single width single inlet (SWSI) fan of the same diameter and speed, at about the same pressure. That is why DWDI fans are common in air handlers and duct fans, where a lot of air must move through a limited footprint.

docs.title: DWDI Flow Approximation
docs.text:
\[ Q_{\text{DWDI}} \approx 2\,Q_{\text{SWSI}} \]

where:

  • \( Q_{\text{DWDI}} \) is the airflow of the double width double inlet fan, in CFM
  • \( Q_{\text{SWSI}} \) is the airflow of a single width single inlet fan with the same impeller diameter, the same width per side and the same speed, at the same pressure, in CFM

This is a sizing rule of thumb for comparing families, not a rating. Real selections always come from the catalog's performance tables, because the inlet conditions on each side are never perfectly identical.

docs.title: Bearings, Supports and the Outlet Flange
docs.text:
Two parts on a DWDI housing exist because of the double inlet. FanPedia's technical description of Arrangement 3 DWDI (p. 167) explains that the impeller is mounted between the bearings and supported by the fan housing, and since both bearings are located in the airstream, standard DWDI fans should be used for clean air applications with air temperatures limited to 130°F.

The bearing structural support is the welded steel frame that carries each bearing in front of an inlet and transfers the rotor's weight into the housing. FanPedia's DWDI housing drawing (p. 61) shows one at each inlet, outboard of the inlet funnel. Because the support crosses the inlet opening, it sits in the incoming airstream; that is part of why the inlet conditions matter.

The setback outlet flange is the bolted flange frame around the DWDI discharge opening, labeled separately on FanPedia's DWDI housing drawing (p. 61). The duct connection is made to this flange, so its position and bolt pattern come from the certified dimensional drawing, not from an assumption that it matches an SWSI housing.

The drawing also repeats parts you met in Chapter 7: the housing side and housing scroll (the curved wrapper that collects air from the impeller), the cutoff (the tongue of the scroll at the outlet that separates discharging air from air that would recirculate), a wiper bar at each inlet funnel (FanPedia p. 59: it helps direct air through the housing in the inlet funnel area to prevent turbulence and increase efficiency), the two inlet funnels that direct air into the impeller, and the framing that stiffens the housing.

Evidence of Mastery: In the check phase the learner reads eight function descriptions, one at a time, and clicks the part on the exploded DWDI housing that matches. A click is correct when it lands on the part named in the Content table's "Correct part" column. Mastery is 7 of 8 correct on the first attempt. Opening infoboxes in the explore phase is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) The bearing structural support is part of the motor base. (2) The cutoff and the wiper bar are the same part. (3) A DWDI fan has one inlet funnel, like an SWSI fan.

Instructional Rationale: Remember-level recognition of parts is built by pairing each label with its job and then retrieving the label from the job alone. Click-to-identify on the real exploded view ties the vocabulary to the picture a learner will see on a submittal drawing.

# Part Infobox text (explore phase) 1 Housing side One of the two flat side sheets of the housing; on a DWDI fan each side carries an inlet. 2 Housing scroll The curved wrapper that collects air leaving the impeller and guides it to the outlet. 3 Cutoff The tongue of the scroll at the outlet that separates air leaving the fan from air that would recirculate around the housing. 4 Wiper bar (one at each inlet) Helps direct air through the housing in the inlet funnel area to prevent turbulence and increase efficiency. 5 Inlet funnel (one at each inlet) Aerodynamically shaped piece that directs air into the impeller. 6 Bearing structural support (one at each inlet) Steel frame that carries a bearing in front of an inlet and transfers rotor weight into the housing; it sits in the airstream. 7 Setback outlet flange Bolted flange frame around the discharge opening; the duct connects here, and its location comes from the dimensional drawing. 8 Framing Structural members that stiffen the housing and carry it to its mounting.
