motor on a slide base on the side of the bearing pedestal Overhung All out of airstream Arrangement 9 is in the overhung group with Arrangements 1, 8 and 10 (FanPedia p. 30). 12 Arrangement 10 SWSI: belt driven; motor on an adjustable base inside the bearing pedestal Overhung All out of airstream Arrangement 10 is in the overhung group, with its bearings on the pedestal (FanPedia pp. 30, 167).

Provenance: FanPedia p. 30 (impeller orientation: overhung for Arrangements 1, 8, 9, 10 and 4; center hung for Arrangements 3 and 7, single and double width), p. 79 (shaft overview), and pp. 162–168 (technical descriptions cited per card).

Rules: Each card has two answer fields; both must be chosen before Check is enabled. A card is correct only when both fields match. There is no partial credit in the score, but feedback states which field was wrong.

Learner Activity:

  1. A card appears with its text. The learner predicts the impeller position, then the bearing location.
  2. The learner presses Check. A simple side-view schematic of that arrangement appears, showing the impeller, the shaft, the bearings and the edge of the airstream, with the correct answers.
  3. The learner moves to the next card. Cards already answered cannot be re-answered in the same round.
  4. After 12 cards, the learner sees the score and the list of missed cards and may start a new shuffled round.

Feedback: 12 cards, shuffled, one attempt each per round. Correct: "Correct: , ." Incorrect: names the wrong field and shows the "Why" text. If card 6 or card 10 is marked center hung, the feedback adds: "Direct drive does not decide impeller position; Arrangements 4 and 8 are direct drive and overhung." The schematic and answer appear after each check. A running count "Correct: n of 12" is shown.

Starting State: Card 1 of a shuffled deck is shown with both answer fields empty and the question "Where is the impeller, and where are the bearings?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter states that FanPedia p. 30 lists Arrangements 1, 8, 9, 10 and 4 as overhung and Arrangements 3 and 7 as center hung; that Arrangement 3 SWSI has one bearing in the airstream; that standard DWDI fans have both bearings in the airstream and are limited to 130°F clean air; and that Arrangement 4's only bearings are in the motor frame.

docs.title: The Fan Arrangement
docs.text:
A fan arrangement is a standard numbered description of how a fan's drive, impeller, bearings and motor are put together. The number tells the reader, in one or two characters, whether the fan is direct or belt driven, whether the impeller is overhung or center hung, what carries the bearings, and where the motor is mounted. The numbering comes from the Air Movement and Control Association (AMCA) arrangement standard, and Twin City Fan, like other manufacturers, uses those base numbers on its drawings and catalogs. Suffix letters then mark variants: SI for a single inlet fan with an integral inlet box, DI for a double inlet fan with integral inlet boxes, F for an extended frame that carries the motor, P for a pedestal (grade mounted) plug fan, and so on (FanPedia pp. 20–29).

Arrangements are always defined for a fan type. FanPedia groups its arrangement drawings by family: centrifugal fans (SWSI on pp. 20–22 and DWDI on p. 23), plenum fans (pp. 24–25), plug fans (pp. 26–27), axial and inline centrifugal fans (p. 28), and fume exhaust fans (p. 29). The same base number can look different from one family to the next. An Arrangement 4 centrifugal fan has its motor on a pedestal beside the housing, while an Arrangement 4 axial fan has its motor inside the tube; both are "impeller mounted to motor shaft."

The table below collects the base arrangements this chapter covers and the defining features of each; the sections that follow explain each one. The table reinforces what you already know about drives and impeller positions.

Arrangement Drive Impeller position Bearings carried by Motor mounted 1 Belt (direct drive possible) Overhung Pedestal, out of airstream On floor or fan base, separate from fan 2 Belt or direct Overhung Bracket on the fan housing Separate from fan 3 Usually belt Center hung Housing; one bearing on each side of impeller On floor or fan base 4 Direct Overhung on motor shaft No fan bearings (motor bearings only) On a pedestal; impeller on motor shaft 7 Direct, coupled Center hung Housing and a pedestal that also carries the motor On the pedestal, coupled to fan shaft 8 Direct, coupled Overhung Extended Arrangement 1 pedestal On the extended pedestal, coupled 9 Belt only Overhung Pedestal On the side of the pedestal 10 Belt only Overhung Pedestal Inside the pedestal

Arrangements 8, 9 and 10, and the many lettered variants, are developed in Chapter 24. They appear here so you can see the whole numbering pattern.

Worked example: naming an arrangement from a drawing. An outline drawing shows a single inlet centrifugal fan. Working through it systematically:

  1. Find the drive. There is a belt guard and two sheaves, so the fan is belt driven. That rules out 4, 7 and 8.
  2. Find the impeller relative to the bearings. Both bearings sit together on a pedestal on the drive side; nothing is on the inlet side. The impeller is overhung. That rules out 3 (and 7).
  3. Find the motor. The motor is bolted to a slide base on the side of the bearing pedestal, so the fan ships as one assembly with motor and drive mounted.

Overhung, belt driven, motor on the side of the pedestal: Arrangement 9. Had the motor stood on its own base on the floor beside the fan, it would be Arrangement 1; had it been tucked inside the pedestal, Arrangement 10 (FanPedia pp. 165–167).

Three Questions Make the Number

Think of an arrangement number as a compressed answer to three questions: how is it driven, where is the impeller relative to the bearings, and what carries the motor? Once you can answer those from a drawing, the number almost names itself.

docs.title: Arrangement 1
docs.text:
Arrangement 1 is an overhung impeller fan with both bearings on a pedestal and the motor mounted separately on the floor or fan base. FanPedia's drawing caption reads "Direct Drive or Belt Driven; Motor Mounted on Floor or Fan Base" (FanPedia p. 20), and the technical description adds that it "is usually belt driven" and that its pedestal bearings sit "out of the airstream, which makes them ideal for high temperature or contaminated air applications" (FanPedia p. 162). With belt drive, "the motor can be mounted in any of the four AMCA standard motor positions: W, X, Y or Z"; motor positions are defined in Chapter 12.

Arrangement 1 is also the parent of other arrangements. Arrangement 8 is "a modified version of Arrangement 1 used for direct drive," with the pedestal extended to carry a coupled motor (FanPedia p. 165), and Arrangement 9F extends the frame to carry a motor "similar to an Arrangement 1 fan" (FanPedia p. 166).

Worked example: checking a motor position. A customer orders an Arrangement 1 fan with clockwise (CW) rotation and a bottom horizontal discharge (BHD), and asks for the motor in position Z. FanPedia lists these motor position restrictions for Arrangement 1, all because the motor would interfere with the housing outlet or not fit (FanPedia p. 162):

  • BHD discharge: CW rotation, position Z not allowed; CCW rotation, position W not allowed.
  • TAD (top angular down) discharge: CW rotation, position W not allowed; CCW rotation, position Z not allowed.
  • THD (top horizontal) discharge: CW rotation, position W, and CCW rotation, position Z, face a height restriction because the motor may not fit below the discharge.

The requested combination, BHD with CW rotation and motor position Z, is on the list. The application engineer offers W, X or Y instead, or a different discharge. The same check applies to Arrangements 3 and 3F, which carry the identical restriction list (FanPedia p. 163). For the THD cases, FanPedia adds that "on Arrangement 1 fan the motor will fit if pedestal is lengthened to accommodate motor" (FanPedia p. 162).

docs.title: Arrangement 2
docs.text: Arrangement 2 is defined in the AMCA arrangement standard as an overhung impeller fan, belt or direct driven, whose bearings are mounted in a bracket supported by the fan housing rather than on a separate pedestal. It is essentially Arrangement 1 with the pedestal replaced by a bracket on the housing. FanPedia's arrangement drawings (pp. 20–29) do not include an Arrangement 2, so treat it as a code you may meet on older drawings or other manufacturers' equipment. If a customer asks for one, check what the current Twin City Fan catalog offers before quoting; an Arrangement 1 or 9 usually meets the same need.

docs.title: Arrangement 3
docs.text:
Arrangement 3 is a center hung impeller fan with one bearing on each side of the impeller, the bearings supported by the fan housing, and the motor mounted separately on the floor or fan base. FanPedia shows it for single width fans as "Belt Driven; Motor Mounted on Floor or Fan Base" (FanPedia p. 20) and for double width fans as "Direct Drive or Belt Driven" (FanPedia p. 23). The description calls it "structurally sound and compact" and notes that the single width version "has one bearing located in the airstream" (FanPedia p. 163). Double width fans "are generally supplied in Arrangement 3 for V-belt drive" (FanPedia p. 167), and Arrangement 3 is also "the most common plenum fan arrangement," frequently used in OEM and site-built air handlers (FanPedia p. 168).

Worked example: matching Arrangement 3 to the air. Two DWDI fan requests arrive on the same day. The first is a supply fan for an office air handler moving filtered outdoor air. The second exhausts 200°F air from a dryer. For the first, a standard Arrangement 3 DWDI is a natural choice: it is compact, belt driven for easy speed adjustment, and the air is clean and well under 130°F. For the second, the same arrangement fails on FanPedia's own limit: both bearings sit in the airstream, and standard DWDI fans are for clean air "limited to 130°F" (FanPedia p. 167). The engineer looks instead at Arrangement 3DI, which uses integrated inlet boxes to move the bearings out of the airstream (next section), or at an overhung arrangement.

Arrangement 3 Is Not Automatically Hot-Air Ready

A common trap is assuming that because Arrangement 3 is common and robust, it suits any temperature. Its inlet-side bearing (both bearings on a DWDI) sits in the air; check the air temperature and cleanliness first, and move to an SI/DI or overhung arrangement when the air is hot or dirty.

docs.title: Arrangement 3 SI and DI
docs.text: Arrangement 3SI and Arrangement 3DI are center hung arrangements that add integral inlet boxes so that the bearings can stand outside the airstream. In 3SI (single inlet), a single width fan "utilizes an attached inlet box to locate the bearing outside of the airstream on independent bearing pedestals that allows for elevated operating temperatures and relatively clean air" (FanPedia p. 164). In 3DI (double inlet), a double width fan uses "integrated inlet boxes to locate the bearings outside of the airstream on independent bearing pedestals" (FanPedia p. 167). Both are usually direct drive: "the motor is located by the customer off the fan assembly and direct-coupled to the shaft," and both include a pie split housing for easy impeller removal (FanPedia pp. 164, 167). The inlet box turns the incoming air through a right angle, which is what clears a path for the shaft to pass out of the box to a bearing that the air never touches.

docs.title: Arrangement 4
docs.text:
Arrangement 4 is a direct drive fan with the impeller mounted on the motor shaft and the motor mounted on a pedestal. FanPedia's caption: "Direct Drive; Impeller Mounted to Motor Shaft" (FanPedia p. 20). It has no fan shaft and no fan bearings, which gives it the lowest maintenance of any arrangement: "there are no fan bearings, fan shaft or drive parts to maintain" (FanPedia p. 164). It is also compact. The limits come from the same simplicity. The motor's bearings carry the whole impeller, which limits size: FanPedia notes that "Arrangement 4 fans are typically limited up to size 365" (FanPedia p. 164). And the motor sits close to the air, so "high airstream temperatures may limit the use of this arrangement" (FanPedia p. 171). Arrangement 4 is still used for hot air with special construction: FanPedia's high temperature page for Arrangement 4 centrifugal fans adds a shaft seal, a shaft cooler, a cooler guard and a hub, for airstream temperatures from 181°F to 1,000+°F (FanPedia p. 111).

Several variants build on it (FanPedia pp. 20–21):

  • 4S: swingout construction for easy access to the impeller and housing interior.
  • 4VI and 4HI: mounted directly on the fan inlet, vertical or horizontal; "the entire fan is supported by the inlet flange only."
  • Plenum, plug, axial, inline and lab exhaust Arrangement 4: covered later in this chapter.

Worked example: when Arrangement 4 fits. A small exhaust fan serves a clean, room-temperature process with no one available for belt maintenance. Direct drive at a standard motor speed meets the duty, and the selected fan size is well under the size where Arrangement 4 is typically limited. Arrangement 4 is the natural choice: no belts, no fan bearings to grease, compact footprint. Now raise the air temperature to 600°F. Arrangement 4 is still possible, but only with the high temperature package (shaft cooler, shaft seal) and an engineering review; an overhung Arrangement 1, 8, 9 or 10 with the bearings and motor well away from the heat may be the simpler answer (FanPedia pp. 110–111).

docs.title: Arrangement 7
docs.text: Arrangement 7 is a direct drive, center hung fan whose motor is coupled to the fan shaft and mounted on a pedestal. FanPedia captions it "similar to Arr. 3 but with motor pedestal" (FanPedia p. 21) and describes it as an arrangement in which "the impeller is mounted between the bearings, but the Arrangement 7 incorporates a pedestal designed to accommodate the motor, flexible coupling and one bearing" (FanPedia p. 168). The SI and DI versions, 7SI and 7DI, add integrated inlet boxes to move the bearings out of the airstream and are mounted on a unitary base as standard, with an inertia base available as an option (FanPedia pp. 165, 168). Choose Arrangement 7 over 3 when the duty suits a direct drive motor speed and you want the motor carried on the fan's own pedestal instead of driving through belts.

docs.title: Bearings Out of the Airstream
docs.text:
You have now seen one idea several times: some arrangements are chosen because they keep the bearings out of the airstream. Bearings are lubricated precision parts. Hot air thins and breaks down their grease; dusty, corrosive or wet air attacks their seals; and in spark-resistant construction, a bearing in the airstream is a potential ignition source. FanPedia's spark-resistant construction pages state flatly: "Bearings not allowed in airstream" (FanPedia p. 104). Keeping the bearings outside the housing also makes them easier to reach for lubrication and inspection.

An arrangement keeps its bearings out of the airstream in one of three ways:

  1. Overhang the impeller so both bearings sit on a pedestal outside the housing: Arrangements 1, 8, 9 and 10 (FanPedia pp. 30, 162).
  2. Add inlet boxes to a center hung fan so the inlet-side bearing stands outside the box: Arrangements 3SI, 3DI, 7SI and 7DI (FanPedia pp. 164–168).
  3. Put the whole rotating assembly outside the air path, as plug fans do: in Arrangement 9 plug fans, "motor, shaft and bearings are outside of the process airstream" (FanPedia p. 172), and belt driven axial and inline Arrangement 9 fans are "the perfect choice for applications that require the motor to be out of the airstream" (FanPedia p. 173).

Worked example: screening arrangements for a hot, dirty exhaust. A foundry needs a belt driven centrifugal exhaust fan for 350°F air carrying dust. The application engineer screens the arrangements:

Candidate Bearings in the airstream? Verdict Arrangement 3 SWSI Yes, one (FanPedia p. 163) Reject: hot, dusty air at a bearing Arrangement 3 DWDI Yes, both; limited to 130°F clean air (FanPedia p. 167) Reject Arrangement 4 No fan bearings, but the motor is close to the air (FanPedia p. 171) Possible only with high temperature construction; not belt driven anyway Arrangement 1 No; both on the pedestal (FanPedia p. 162) Keep Arrangement 9 or 10 No; overhung, bearings on the pedestal (FanPedia p. 30) Keep; choose by where the motor should go

The shortlist is Arrangements 1, 9 and 10, which also appear in FanPedia's high temperature centrifugal construction list, for 276°F to 1,000+°F (FanPedia p. 110). The final choice comes down to motor location and footprint, the subject of Chapter 24.

The Code Alphabet Takes a Few Passes

If 3SI, 7DI, 4VI and 9SS are starting to blur together, that's normal; most people need a few drawings before the suffixes stick. Anchor each one to its base number first (overhung or center hung, belt or direct), then read the letters as modifications, and keep FanPedia pp. 20–29 open beside you while you practice.

The microsim below lets you practice naming the base arrangement from the features a drawing shows.

docs.title: Diagram: Arrangement Identifier
docs.text:
Run Arrangement Identifier Fullscreen

Arrangement Identifier

Type: microsim sim-id: ch11-arrangement-identifier Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Analyze Bloom Verb: distinguish Learning Objective: The learner will distinguish ten centrifugal fan arrangements (1, 2, 3, 3SI, 3DI, 4, 7, 8, 9 and 10) from schematic side-view drawings by identifying the drive type, the impeller position relative to the bearings, and what carries the bearings and the motor.

Prerequisites: direct drive, belt drive, shaft coupling, sheave, overhung impeller, center hung impeller, bearing pedestal, inlet box, SWSI, DWDI, fan arrangement, Arrangements 1, 2, 3, 3SI, 3DI, 4, 7, 8, 9 and 10 (defined in this chapter).

Evidence of Mastery: For each of 10 drawings, the learner first answers three feature questions (drive: Belt / Direct with coupling / Direct on motor shaft; impeller: Overhung / Center hung; bearings carried by: Pedestal / Fan housing (at least one bearing) / Independent pedestals outside inlet boxes / Motor only), then names the arrangement from a list of the ten. The arrangement answer is correct when it matches the "Arrangement" column. Mastery is 8 of 10 arrangements correct on the first attempt. Feature answers are scaffolding and are scored separately.

Misconceptions: (1) Every direct drive fan is Arrangement 4. (2) Any fan with a coupling is Arrangement 7, whatever the impeller position. (3) Arrangement 1 and Arrangement 9 differ in impeller position (they differ only in motor location). (4) Arrangement 2 and Arrangement 1 are the same (Arrangement 2's bearings are on a bracket carried by the housing).

Instructional Rationale: Distinguishing arrangements is an Analyze task: the learner must break each drawing into its defining features before naming the whole. Asking for the features first, and committing them before the name, makes the learner perform that decomposition rather than pattern-match a picture.

Content:

Each drawing is a simple schematic side view (viewed from the side of the shaft) showing only the parts listed for it. The parts drawn are the content being taught.

# Parts shown in the drawing Drive Impeller Bearings carried by Arrangement Why (feedback) 1 SWSI housing; two bearings together on a pedestal beside the drive side of the housing; impeller at the shaft end; motor on its own base on the floor, belts to the fan sheave Belt Overhung Pedestal 1 Overhung on a pedestal with a separately mounted motor is Arrangement 1 (FanPedia pp. 20, 162). 2 SWSI housing; two bearings in a bracket bolted to the drive side of the housing; impeller at the shaft end; separate motor with belts Belt Overhung Fan housing (at least one bearing) 2 Overhung with bearings in a bracket on the housing is AMCA Arrangement 2. 3 SWSI housing; one bearing on the drive side and one on a bracket across the inlet; impeller between them; motor on the floor beside the fan, belts to the fan sheave Belt Center hung Fan housing (at least one bearing) 3 Center hung with bearings carried by the housing and a separate motor is Arrangement 3 (FanPedia pp. 20, 163). 4 SWSI housing with an attached inlet box; impeller between two bearings, each on its own pedestal outside the housing and inlet box; a coupled motor off the fan assembly Direct with coupling Center hung Independent pedestals outside inlet boxes 3SI The attached inlet box puts the bearing outside the air on independent pedestals (FanPedia p. 164). 5 DWDI housing with an inlet box on each side; impeller between two bearings on independent pedestals; a coupled motor off the fan assembly Direct with coupling Center hung Independent pedestals outside inlet boxes 3DI Double width with integrated inlet boxes and independent bearing pedestals is Arrangement 3DI (FanPedia p. 167). 6 SWSI housing; motor on a pedestal; impeller hub on the motor shaft; no separate shaft, no fan bearings Direct on motor shaft Overhung Motor only 4 Impeller mounted to the motor shaft is Arrangement 4 (FanPedia pp. 20, 164). 7 DWDI housing; impeller between two bearings; a pedestal on the drive side carrying one bearing, a flexible coupling and the motor Direct with coupling Center hung Fan housing (at least one bearing) 7 Center hung with a pedestal for motor, coupling and one bearing is Arrangement 7 (FanPedia pp. 21, 168). 8 SWSI housing; two bearings on a long pedestal; impeller at the shaft end; a flexible coupling and the motor on the far end of the same pedestal Direct with coupling Overhung Pedestal 8 An Arrangement 1 pedestal extended for a coupled motor is Arrangement 8 (FanPedia p. 165). 9 SWSI housing; two bearings on a pedestal; impeller at the shaft end; motor on a slide base on the side of the pedestal, belts to the fan sheave Belt Overhung Pedestal 9 Overhung with the motor on the side of the bearing pedestal is Arrangement 9 (FanPedia p. 165). 10 SWSI housing; two bearings on a pedestal; impeller at the shaft end; motor on an adjustable base inside the pedestal, belts to the fan sheave Belt Overhung Pedestal 10 Overhung with the motor inside the bearing pedestal is Arrangement 10 (FanPedia p. 167).

Answer list for the arrangement question, in this order: 1, 2, 3, 3SI, 3DI, 4, 7, 8, 9, 10.

A note on screen reads: "Schematics are simplified. Twin City Fan arrangement drawings: FanPedia pp. 20–23. Arrangement 2 is from the AMCA standard and is not shown in FanPedia."

Provenance: FanPedia pp. 20–23 (arrangement drawings and captions), p. 30 (impeller orientation), pp. 162–168 (technical descriptions cited per row). Arrangement 2: AMCA arrangement standard definition, as stated in this chapter's "Arrangement 2" section.

Rules: Drawings are shown in shuffled order. The arrangement question unlocks only after all three feature questions are answered. Feature answers are scored but do not block the arrangement answer. If the three committed features match the drawing's columns, the arrangement list highlights the arrangements consistent with those features (for drawing 1, features Belt / Overhung / Pedestal highlight 1, 9 and 10). If any feature is wrong, no highlighting is shown.

Learner Activity:

  1. A drawing appears. The learner answers the drive question, the impeller question and the bearings question.
  2. The learner presses Check Features. Each feature is marked correct or incorrect, with the correct answer shown.
  3. The learner selects an arrangement from the list and presses Check Arrangement. The drawing's parts are labeled and the "Why" text appears.
  4. After 10 drawings the learner sees separate scores for features and arrangements and may start a new shuffled round.

Feedback: 10 drawings, shuffled, one attempt per question per round. Correct arrangement: "Correct: Arrangement ." Incorrect: "This is Arrangement . ." Added messages for likely confusions: choosing 4 for drawings 4, 5, 7 or 8: "There is a coupling and a separate fan shaft, so this is not Arrangement 4." Choosing 7 for drawing 8: "The impeller is overhung, not between the bearings; a coupled overhung fan is Arrangement 8." Choosing 1 for drawing 9 or 10, or 9 for 10: "Look at where the motor is mounted; Arrangements 1, 9 and 10 differ only in motor location." Choosing 1 for drawing 2: "The bearings are on a bracket carried by the housing, not on a pedestal." The answer is revealed after each check. Running counts "Features correct: n of 30" and "Arrangements correct: n of 10" are shown.

Starting State: The first drawing of a shuffled set is shown with all questions unanswered and the prompt "How is this fan driven, where is the impeller, and what carries the bearings?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter's worked example names an Arrangement 9 from a drawing with a belt guard, an overhung impeller with both bearings on a pedestal, and the motor on a slide base on the side of the pedestal, and states that Arrangements 1, 9 and 10 differ in motor location. The chapter states that Arrangement 2 is not shown in FanPedia's arrangement drawings (pp. 20–29).

Read a Drawing in Three Glances

Want to name an arrangement in ten seconds? Glance once for a belt guard or a coupling, once to see whether anything stands on the inlet side of the impeller, and once to find the motor; check it from the drive side, and the number follows.

docs.title: Arrangement Families Beyond the Housed Centrifugal
docs.text: The numbers above were defined for housed centrifugal fans. The other fan families from Chapters 4 through 6 reuse many of the same base numbers, with letters that describe how each family is mounted. This section introduces the families; Chapter 24 covers each lettered variant in detail.

docs.title: Plug Fan Arrangements
docs.text:
A plug fan is an unhoused centrifugal fan whose impeller and inlet funnel sit inside the customer's enclosure, while the shaft, bearings and motor stay outside it, mounted through a wall panel; "the system plenum acts as the fan housing" (Chapter 7; FanPedia p. 172). Plug fan arrangements describe how that fan is supported and driven. FanPedia shows six (FanPedia pp. 26–27):

  • Arrangement 9: belt driven, "fully supported by the customer's wall"; FanPedia calls it "the most common plug fan arrangement" (FanPedia p. 172).
  • Arrangement 4: direct drive, impeller on the motor shaft, wall mounted; compact and low maintenance, though "high airstream temperatures may limit the use of this arrangement" (FanPedia p. 171).
  • Arrangement 8: direct drive, motor coupled to the fan shaft, wall mounted; "the least common plug fan arrangement due to the length of the assembly" (FanPedia p. 171).
  • Arrangements 1P, 4P, 8P and 9P: the "P" (pedestal plug) versions are floor mounted. FanPedia explains why: they are "typically used on larger fans and/or larger HP motors where the customer's wall may not be sufficient by itself," and "mounting to the foundation also makes it better for meeting lower vibration requirements" (FanPedia pp. 170–172).

Worked example: wall or floor? An oven builder wants a large belt driven plug fan to recirculate hot air, and the oven wall is light-gauge insulated panel. The default plug fan choice is Arrangement 9, which hangs the whole fan on the wall. Here the wall may not carry a large fan and motor, and an oven line usually cares about vibration. Arrangement 9P mounts the same belt driven fan on its own pedestal at grade, so the wall only seals around the fan, with the mounting panel optional (FanPedia p. 172). Because the bearings and motor are outside the oven in both versions, the hot air never reaches them.

docs.title: Plenum Fan Arrangements
docs.text: A plenum fan is an unhoused centrifugal fan that sits inside an air plenum and pressurizes it, with its motor and drive inside the plenum too, unlike a plug fan (FanPedia pp. 5, 172). Plenum fan arrangements describe how the motor and drive are mounted on the fan frame. FanPedia shows belt driven Arrangements 1 and 3, the top-mounted motor versions 3HS and 3HA, the side-mounted 3SM, the vertical 3VA and 3VS, and direct drive Arrangements 4 and 4V (FanPedia pp. 24–25). Arrangement 3 is "the most common plenum fan arrangement" in OEM and site-built air handlers, and direct drive Arrangement 4 plenum fans serve cleanroom and pharmaceutical work (FanPedia pp. 168, 170).

docs.title: Vertical Arrangement
docs.text: A vertical arrangement is one in which the fan shaft is vertical, so air enters or leaves the impeller vertically. FanPedia's vertical arrangements include Arrangement 4VI, a centrifugal fan "designed to mount directly on the inlet of the fan" with "a vertical airflow into the fan (vertical motor shaft)" (FanPedia p. 164); the vertical plenum arrangements 3VA and 3VS (FanPedia pp. 169–170); and plenum Arrangement 4V, available "with either vertical up airflow (inlet under the motor) or vertical down airflow (inlet above the motor)" (FanPedia p. 170). Vertical fans need bearing and shaft details suited to a vertical shaft, covered in Chapter 16.

docs.title: Axial and Inline Arrangements
docs.text:
Axial and inline arrangements apply the same numbering to tubular fans: axial fans and inline centrifugal fans. FanPedia shows two base arrangements with access variants, and notes that "inline centrifugal fans are available with the same arrangements but use different impellers" (FanPedia p. 28):

  • Arrangement 4 (direct drive): "the impeller is mounted directly on the fan motor shaft," making it "the logical choice when space is at a premium or a simple, dependable fan with minimum maintenance is required." Exact performance is reached by adjusting the blade angle (FanPedia p. 172). The motor sits inside the tube on its support.
  • Arrangement 9 (belt driven): "the perfect choice for applications that require the motor to be out of the airstream," with "either a fixed or adjustable V-belt drive system," so a rating change is "a simple sheave change or blade angle adjustment" (FanPedia p. 173). The motor sits outside the tube and the belts run through a belt tube.
  • CS and SO variants (4CS, 4SO, 9CS, 9SO) add a clamshell door or a swingout rotor for maintenance access (FanPedia pp. 172–173).

Worked example: an inline fan for oily, moist exhaust. A designer specifies a tubeaxial exhaust fan for air that carries oil mist and moisture. A direct drive Arrangement 4 would put the motor inside the tube, in that air. Arrangement 9 keeps the motor outside the tube with the belts shielded by the belt tube, so the motor stays clean and cool, and if the system turns out to need a little more air after balancing, a sheave change handles it without replacing the motor. If cleaning access matters, the 9CS (clamshell) or 9SO (swingout) variant adds a door to reach the rotor (FanPedia p. 173).

docs.title: Lab Exhaust Arrangements
docs.text:
Lab exhaust arrangements are the arrangements offered on laboratory fume exhaust fans, the high-plume fans that dilute and discharge hazardous fumes above a building (Chapter 5 and Chapter 6). FanPedia's fume exhaust arrangement page (FanPedia p. 29) and descriptions (FanPedia pp. 174–175) show five, each tied to particular models. The table below gathers them; the models were introduced in Chapter 4.

Arrangement Drive Models shown (FanPedia p. 29) Notes from FanPedia pp. 174–175 1 Belt BAIFE, BCIFE Overhung; two bearings on the pedestal, out of the airstream 4 Direct BAIFE, BCIFE, TVIFE Impeller on motor shaft; motor on a pedestal (BAIFE, BCIFE) or motor drive plate (TVIFE) 8 Direct (coupled) BAIFE, BCIFE Arrangement 1 pedestal extended for the motor; flexible coupling 9 Belt BAIFE, BCIFE, TFE, QFE, QIFE Motor slide base on the pedestal (BAIFE, BCIFE) or adjustable motor base on the housing exterior (inline models, excluding TVIFE) 10 Belt BAIFE, BCIFE Scroll-type centrifugal only; motor base inside the pedestal; weather cover option for roof or outdoor use

Worked example: matching a lab exhaust model to an arrangement. A lab project calls for an induced-flow mixed flow fan and asks for "belt drive with the motor out of the exhaust." Of the two induced-flow mixed flow models, FanPedia shows TVIFE only in direct drive Arrangement 4 (on a motor drive plate) and QIFE in belt driven Arrangement 9 (FanPedia pp. 29, 174–175). So the request points to a QIFE in Arrangement 9, with its adjustable motor base on the outside of the housing. If the project had specified a scroll housed BCIFE with a compact rooftop footprint, Arrangement 10, with the motor inside the pedestal and the optional weather cover, would be worth offering.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Direct drive turns the impeller at motor speed, either with the impeller on the motor shaft (Arrangement 4) or through a shaft coupling to a fan shaft (Arrangements 7 and 8). It is simple and low maintenance, but fan speed is fixed unless a VFD is added. A direct drive tubular fan carries its motor on a motor support base inside the tube.
  • Belt drive sets fan speed through the sheave ratio, \( N_{fan} = N_{motor} \times D_{motor} / D_{fan} \). A larger fan sheave slows the fan. V-belts wedge into sheave grooves; belt count is design horsepower divided by per-belt rating, rounded up.
  • The drive service factor multiplies motor horsepower to give design horsepower for belts and sheaves. It is not the motor nameplate's service factor.
  • An overhung impeller sits at the end of the shaft with both bearings on one side (Arrangements 1, 8, 9, 10 and 4); a center hung impeller sits between the bearings (Arrangements 3 and 7).
  • A fan arrangement number answers three questions: how the fan is driven, where the impeller sits relative to the bearings, and what carries the bearings and motor. Arrangement 1 is overhung with a separate motor; Arrangement 2 (AMCA, not in FanPedia) carries its bearings on a housing bracket; Arrangement 3 is center hung with one bearing (SWSI) or both (DWDI) in the airstream; Arrangement 4 puts the impeller on the motor shaft; Arrangement 7 is a coupled, center hung fan with a motor pedestal.
  • Arrangements 3SI and 3DI (and 7SI, 7DI) use inlet boxes to move center hung bearings out of the air.
  • Keeping the bearings out of the airstream matters for hot, dirty, corrosive and spark-resistant duty; overhung arrangements, inlet-box arrangements and plug fans all achieve it.
  • The same numbers reappear in the plug, plenum, vertical, axial and inline, and lab exhaust families, with letters that describe the mounting.

You Can Name the Arrangement

You can now size a belt drive from its sheaves, tell an overhung rotor from a center hung one, and turn a drawing into an arrangement number by asking three questions. That's the vocabulary every order, outline drawing and field service call in the rest of this book will use.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: This chapter introduces the conventions used to describe a fan's orientation. It establishes the rule that a fan is viewed from the drive side, then covers discharge positions and angles (up blast, top horizontal, bottom horizontal, down blast, and the angular discharges), inlet box position, rotation, inline configurations, and the standard W, X, Y, Z and axial motor positions. After completing it, readers can describe which way a fan discharges and where its motor sits.
