docs.title: Why Orientation Needs a Shared Language
docs.text:
A fan that arrives on a job site with its outlet pointing the wrong way is not a small problem. The housing of a centrifugal fan is cast or welded around a fixed scroll, so the outlet cannot simply be turned to meet the duct. The installing contractor either rebuilds the ductwork, returns the fan, or waits for a replacement, and all three cost time and money. Almost every one of these mistakes traces back to two people describing the same fan from opposite sides.

This chapter gives you the vocabulary that prevents that mistake. You will learn the single viewing rule the industry uses, then the names for which way the impeller turns, which way the outlet points, where an inlet box sits, and where the motor goes. Chapter 13 turns these names into the compact codes written on orders; this chapter makes sure you can see what each code means before you write one.

Point It the Right Way the First Time

Every order you write, quote you check, or drawing you approve carries a rotation, a discharge and a motor position. Get them right and the fan bolts straight onto the duct; get one wrong and a crane sits idle while the outlet points at the wrong wall. By the end of this chapter you will read any fan's orientation as easily as reading a clock. Let's follow the airflow.

docs.title: Viewed From the Drive Side
docs.text:
Before you can name a fan's rotation or discharge, you must agree where the observer is standing. A fan housing seen from one side is the mirror image of the same housing seen from the other side: the outlet that points right from one side points left from the other, and a wheel that turns clockwise from one side turns counterclockwise from the other. Without a fixed viewpoint, every orientation word is ambiguous.

The convention that resolves this is to describe a centrifugal fan viewed from the drive side. The drive side is the side of the fan where the drive is located: the sheave and belts on a belt-driven fan, the coupling on a coupled fan, or the motor on a direct-drive fan. FanPedia's discharge pages show a person standing beside the bearing pedestal and looking at the housing, under the heading "Rotation View From Drive Side" (FanPedia pp. 46-49). Rotation, discharge position, inlet box position and the centrifugal motor positions are all read from that spot.

Two practical consequences follow. First, on a single-inlet fan with the drive on the pedestal, the drive side is the side opposite the inlet, so an installer standing at the inlet sees everything mirrored. Second, on a double-width, double-inlet (DWDI) fan, both faces of the housing have inlets, so "the inlet side" means nothing; only the end of the shaft carrying the drive identifies the viewpoint.

Worked example. A field technician sends a photo taken from the inlet of an Arrangement 1 single-inlet fan. In the photo the outlet is at the top of the housing and points to the technician's left, and the rotation arrow on the housing appears counterclockwise. The order says CW, Top Horizontal. Is the fan wrong?

  1. The photo was taken from the inlet side, which on this fan is opposite the drive side.
  2. Mirror the photo left to right. The outlet now points right, and the rotation arrow now reads clockwise.
  3. From the drive side, the fan is clockwise with a top horizontal outlet pointing right, which is exactly what was ordered.

The fan is correct. The only error was the viewpoint, which is the most common cause of a false "wrong fan" report.

Ask Where the Photo Was Taken

A common trap is comparing a job-site photo or sketch with the order without asking which side it was taken from. Before you agree that a fan is wrong, find the sheave, coupling or motor in the picture; if it is on the far side of the housing, mirror the image before you compare. Check it from the drive side.

docs.title: Rotation
docs.text:
Rotation is the direction in which the impeller turns. For centrifugal fans it is stated as clockwise (CW) or counterclockwise (CCW), judged from the drive side. Rotation is not a free choice once the housing is built: a centrifugal impeller must turn toward the outlet, so that the air spinning off the blades travels around the scroll and leaves through the outlet. A backward-inclined or airfoil wheel turned the wrong way still moves some air, but at a fraction of its rated performance, while drawing power and making noise.

Axial impellers use a different reference. FanPedia's airflow and rotation pages state that axial rotation "is determined by viewing the impeller from the discharge side of the fan," and name the result left-hand (LH) or right-hand (RH) rotation (FanPedia pp. 37-41). The same pages warn that airflow direction and rotation must both be correct for the fan to deliver full performance, and that an impeller turning the wrong way will not move air in the proper direction. Chapter 13 develops the axial convention fully; for now, remember that the viewing rule depends on the fan family.

The following list summarizes the two viewpoints just described:

  • Centrifugal fans: view from the drive side; rotation is CW or CCW.
  • Axial impellers: view from the discharge side; rotation is LH or RH.

Worked example. After a motor replacement on a belt-driven SWSI fan, a facilities technician bumps the motor to check rotation. Standing at the sheave guard (the drive side), they see the wheel turning counterclockwise. The nameplate and order say CW.

  1. The observer is on the drive side, so no mirroring is needed: the wheel really is turning CCW.
  2. The required rotation is CW, so the wheel is turning backward.
  3. On a three-phase motor, interchanging any two of the three supply leads reverses the motor. The electrician swaps two leads, and the next bump shows clockwise rotation.

Had the technician stood at the inlet, the wheel would have appeared clockwise and the backward wheel would have been missed. That fan would then have run at reduced airflow with no obvious fault, which is the expensive version of this mistake.

docs.title: Discharge Position
docs.text:
The discharge position of a centrifugal fan is the direction in which air leaves the housing outlet, described from the drive side. Because the housing scroll wraps around the impeller in the direction of rotation, the outlet always sits where the spinning air naturally leaves the wheel. That ties discharge position to rotation: a given outlet direction can be built on a clockwise housing or on a counterclockwise housing, and the two are mirror images that are not interchangeable.

FanPedia defines eight standard discharge positions for single-width, single-inlet (SWSI) centrifugal fans, each 45 degrees apart (FanPedia pp. 46-47). Each has a full name and a three-letter abbreviation:

  • UBD, Upblast: the outlet points straight up.
  • TAU, Top Angular Up: the outlet is near the top and points upward at 45 degrees.
  • THD, Top Horizontal: the outlet is at the top and points horizontally.
  • TAD, Top Angular Down: the outlet is near the top and points downward at 45 degrees.
  • DBD, Downblast: the outlet points straight down.
  • BAD, Bottom Angular Down: the outlet is near the bottom and points downward at 45 degrees.
  • BHD, Bottom Horizontal: the outlet is at the bottom and points horizontally.
  • BAU, Bottom Angular Up: the outlet is near the bottom and points upward at 45 degrees.

The name alone does not tell you whether a horizontal outlet points left or right. That comes from the rotation. On a clockwise fan, air at the top of the wheel is moving to the right, so a CW top horizontal outlet points right; on a counterclockwise fan, the same outlet points left. A complete discharge description therefore always pairs a rotation with a position.

docs.title: Discharge Angle
docs.text:
The discharge angle is the number of degrees from the upblast position to the actual outlet direction, measured in the direction of rotation. Upblast is both 0 and 360 degrees, and FanPedia writes it as 360. Each step of 45 degrees moves the outlet one position around the housing, so the angle and the name carry the same information: FanPedia lists "CW 90" as also known as "Clockwise 90°" for Top Horizontal, and so on around the circle (FanPedia pp. 46-47).

Measuring in the direction of rotation is what makes the system work for both hands. A CW 90 outlet and a CCW 90 outlet are both top horizontal, one pointing right and the other pointing left. If you want the outlet direction as a single compass-style angle, measured clockwise from straight up as seen from the drive side, it is:

\[ \theta = \begin{cases} N & \text{for clockwise rotation} \\ 360^\circ - N & \text{for counterclockwise rotation} \end{cases} \]

where \( N \) is the discharge angle in degrees (45 to 360) and \( \theta \) is the direction the air leaves, with 0 degrees straight up, 90 degrees to the right, 180 degrees straight down, and 270 degrees to the left (360 is treated as 0).

Worked example. A submittal lists a fan as CCW 135. Which way does the air leave?

  1. The angle is \( N = 135^\circ \) and the rotation is counterclockwise.
  2. \( \theta = 360^\circ - 135^\circ = 225^\circ \), which is down and to the left as seen from the drive side.
  3. An outlet that points downward at 45 degrees from near the top of the housing is Top Angular Down, so CCW 135 is TAD with the air heading down and to the left.

A CW 135 fan is also TAD, but with \( \theta = 135^\circ \) the air heads down and to the right. The two housings are mirror images.

The table below gathers the eight positions with their angles and the outlet direction for each rotation, using the rule you just applied.

Abbreviation Name Discharge angle Air leaves toward (CW) Air leaves toward (CCW) UBD Upblast 360 Straight up Straight up TAU Top Angular Up 45 Up and right Up and left THD Top Horizontal 90 Right Left TAD Top Angular Down 135 Down and right Down and left DBD Downblast 180 Straight down Straight down BAD Bottom Angular Down 225 Down and left Down and right BHD Bottom Horizontal 270 Left Right BAU Bottom Angular Up 315 Up and left Up and right

The Angle Follows the Wheel

Notice that the discharge angle is not a compass bearing; it counts degrees in whichever direction the wheel turns, starting from upblast. That is why one table of names serves both rotations, and why "CW 90" and "CCW 90" are the same name with mirror-image housings.

Even upblast and downblast, which point the same way for both rotations, are not interchangeable between hands. On a CW upblast fan the outlet sits on the left side of the housing top, because that is where air on a clockwise wheel is moving upward; on a CCW upblast fan it sits on the right. Duct centerlines on a drawing reveal the difference immediately.

Before working through the interactive explorer below, make sure the three ideas it uses are clear: rotation is read from the drive side, the discharge angle counts from upblast in the direction of rotation, and a view from the opposite side is a mirror image.

docs.title: Diagram: Discharge Position Explorer
docs.text:
Discharge Position Explorer

Type: microsim sim-id: ch12-discharge-position-explorer Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Apply Bloom Verb: apply Learning Objective: The learner will apply the drive-side viewing rule and the discharge-angle convention to name the rotation and discharge position of ten SWSI centrifugal housing drawings, with at least 8 of 10 correct on the first attempt.

Prerequisites: drive side, viewed from the drive side, rotation (CW and CCW), discharge position, discharge angle, the eight position names and abbreviations, mirror image of an opposite-side view (all defined in the sections "Viewed From the Drive Side", "Rotation", "Discharge Position" and "Discharge Angle" above).

Evidence of Mastery: For each of the ten challenge drawings, the learner commits one rotation (CW or CCW) and one of the eight discharge abbreviations before pressing Check. An answer is correct only when both the rotation and the abbreviation match the answer column in Content. Mastery is 8 of 10 correct on the first attempt. Exploration mode (changing rotation, angle and viewpoint and watching the housing redraw) is not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) The rotation seen from the inlet side is the fan's rotation. (2) The discharge angle is a fixed compass bearing that ignores rotation, so CW 90 and CCW 90 point the same way. (3) Upblast and downblast housings are the same for both rotations because the air points the same way. (4) "Top Horizontal" alone tells you which way the air goes.

Instructional Rationale: Naming an orientation from a drawing is an Apply-level skill that needs practice with a judged answer, so the learner commits rotation and position before feedback. Exploration mode first lets the learner see each angle step move the outlet around the housing and see the mirror flip when the viewpoint changes, which confronts misconceptions 2 and 3 with the drawing itself; the inlet-side challenge items confront misconception 1.

Content:

Exploration mode. The learner can set three things, and the sim draws an SWSI centrifugal housing with a rotation arrow, the outlet, and a label stating the viewpoint:

Quantity Values Default Rotation CW, CCW CW Discharge angle 45 to 360 in steps of 45 degrees (eight values) 360 Viewpoint Drive side, Inlet side (opposite drive) Drive side

For the current setting the sim shows: the abbreviation and full name; the designation in the form "CW 90"; the FanPedia "also known as" form ("Clockwise 90°"); and the direction the air leaves as seen from the drive side, from the "Air leaves toward" columns of the chapter's discharge table. When the viewpoint is Inlet side, the drawing is mirrored left to right and a note reads: "You are looking from the inlet side. The fan's rotation and discharge are still named as seen from the drive side."

The eight positions (abbreviation, name, discharge angle): UBD Upblast 360; TAU Top Angular Up 45; THD Top Horizontal 90; TAD Top Angular Down 135; DBD Downblast 180; BAD Bottom Angular Down 225; BHD Bottom Horizontal 270; BAU Bottom Angular Up 315.

Challenge mode. Ten drawings in this fixed order. "Viewpoint" is what the drawing shows; the arrow and outlet are described as they appear in that drawing.

# Viewpoint shown Rotation arrow as drawn Outlet as drawn Correct answer Why (shown as feedback) 1 Drive side Clockwise At the top, pointing right CW THD (CW 90) From upblast, 90 degrees clockwise is top horizontal, and a CW wheel throws air to the right at the top. 2 Drive side Counterclockwise On the right side of the top, pointing straight up CCW UBD (CCW 360) Straight up is upblast; it sits on the right because air on the right of a CCW wheel moves upward. 3 Drive side Clockwise At the bottom, pointing left CW BHD (CW 270) 270 degrees clockwise from upblast is bottom horizontal; a CW wheel moves air to the left at the bottom. 4 Drive side Counterclockwise On the left side, pointing straight down CCW DBD (CCW 180) Straight down is downblast; it sits on the left because air on the left of a CCW wheel moves downward. 5 Drive side Clockwise Near the top on the left, pointing up and to the right at 45 degrees CW TAU (CW 45) One 45-degree step clockwise from upblast is top angular up. 6 Drive side Counterclockwise Near the top on the left, pointing down and to the left at 45 degrees CCW TAD (CCW 135) Three 45-degree steps counterclockwise from upblast is top angular down; the air heads down and left. 7 Drive side Clockwise Near the bottom on the left, pointing up and to the left at 45 degrees CW BAU (CW 315) Seven 45-degree steps clockwise from upblast is bottom angular up. 8 Inlet side Counterclockwise At the top, pointing left CW THD (CW 90) From the inlet side everything is mirrored; from the drive side the wheel is CW and the top outlet points right. 9 Inlet side Clockwise On the left side of the top, pointing straight up CCW UBD (CCW 360) Mirror the inlet-side view: from the drive side the wheel is CCW and the upblast outlet is on the right. 10 Drive side Counterclockwise At the bottom, pointing right CCW BHD (CCW 270) 270 degrees counterclockwise from upblast is bottom horizontal; a CCW wheel moves air to the right at the bottom.

Provenance: Position names, abbreviations, angles and the "also known as" forms come from FanPedia pp. 46-47 (SWSI Centrifugal Fans, Clockwise and Counterclockwise, "Rotation View From Drive Side"), local copy fanpedia.pdf in the course source folder. The outlet-location rule follows the housing drawings on those pages. Challenge items are constructed for this chapter from those rules.

Rules: Let N be the discharge angle (45, 90, ..., 360) and let all directions be measured clockwise from straight up, as seen from the drive side, with 360 treated as 0. Air direction: theta = N for CW; theta = (360 - N) mod 360 for CCW. Outlet location on the housing: for CW, location = (theta - 90) mod 360; for CCW, location = (theta + 90) mod 360. Inlet-side view: draw the mirror image, so every direction d becomes (360 - d) mod 360 and the drawn rotation arrow reverses; the correct name does not change. Position names map from N exactly as in Content. A challenge answer is correct when rotation equals the answer's rotation AND abbreviation equals the answer's abbreviation; there is no partial credit.

Learner Activity:

  1. In exploration mode the learner steps the discharge angle from 360 through 45, 90 and on to 315 with CW selected, and watches the outlet move clockwise around the housing one position per step while the name and designation update.
  2. The learner switches rotation to CCW at the same angle. The housing redraws as a mirror image and the "Air leaves toward" text changes side; the learner should notice that the name and angle stayed the same.
  3. The learner sets the viewpoint to Inlet side. The drawing mirrors and the arrow appears reversed, while the name and designation do not change; the learner should notice that only the picture changed.
  4. The learner starts the challenge. For each drawing they choose a rotation and an abbreviation, then press Check.
  5. After the tenth item a summary shows the score and lists any missed items with their feedback.

Feedback: Ten items, fixed order, two attempts each. Correct: "Correct: ( )." Incorrect on the first attempt: if the rotation is wrong on an inlet-side item, "Check the viewpoint: this drawing is from the inlet side, so mirror it before naming the rotation."; if the rotation is wrong on a drive-side item, "Read the arrow as drawn: this view is from the drive side."; if only the abbreviation is wrong, "Count 45-degree steps from upblast in the direction of rotation." After a second wrong attempt the correct answer and the Why text are shown and the item counts as missed. Only first-attempt answers count toward the score. A running count "Correct on first attempt: n of 10" is shown.

Starting State: Exploration mode, CW, discharge angle 360, viewpoint Drive side. The housing shows a CW upblast outlet on the left side of the top. The prompt reads: "Step the angle and predict where the outlet will go before it moves."

Chapter Anchors: Eight positions, 45 degrees apart; upblast written as 360; the discharge angle is measured from upblast in the direction of rotation; theta = N for CW and 360 - N for CCW; CCW 135 is TAD with the air heading down and to the left; a CW upblast outlet sits on the left of the housing top and a CCW upblast outlet on the right; the challenge has ten items with mastery at 8 of 10.

docs.title: Up Blast Discharge Position
docs.text:
The up blast discharge position (UBD, 360 degrees) points the outlet straight up. It is the natural choice when a fan exhausts vertically through a roof or into a stack, because the air leaves the housing already moving in the direction it must travel and no elbow is needed at the outlet. Avoiding an elbow close to the outlet matters because a fan's outlet velocity profile is uneven for several duct diameters downstream, and an elbow placed in that region costs pressure that the fan rating does not account for. Chapter 25 treats this loss, called system effect, in detail.

Worked example. A dust collector exhaust fan sits on a pad beside a building and must discharge into a vertical stack directly above it.

  1. The air must leave going up, so the discharge position is UBD.
  2. The stack foundation was poured before the fan was selected, and from the drive side its centerline sits to the left of the fan shaft.
  3. For UBD the outlet sits on the left side of the housing top for CW and on the right side for CCW, so only the CW housing puts the outlet over the existing foundation. The order reads CW 360.
  4. Had the order been written as "upblast" with no rotation, the factory could have built either hand, and half the time the outlet would miss the stack.

docs.title: Top Horizontal Discharge
docs.text:
Top horizontal discharge (THD, 90 degrees) puts the outlet at the top of the housing, pointing sideways. It suits a fan that feeds an overhead horizontal duct, a common layout in mechanical rooms and plants where ducts run near the ceiling. Because the air leaves at the top of the housing and travels horizontally, the duct can start at roughly the height of the housing top without an elbow.

THD also has a practical interaction with the motor. FanPedia's technical descriptions for Arrangements 1, 3 and 3F note a height restriction for THD: the motor "may not fit below the discharge" in one of the four standard motor positions, a limit described later in this chapter and in detail in Chapter 13 (FanPedia pp. 162-163).

Worked example. A supply fan in a penthouse must feed a duct running to the east at the ceiling. The fan will be set so that, standing on the drive side, the observer faces north.

  1. Facing north, east is on the observer's right.
  2. The air must leave horizontally at the top, toward the right: THD.
  3. From the discharge table, a CW top horizontal outlet throws air to the right. The order reads CW 90 (CW THD).
  4. Had the fan been set with the drive side facing south, east would be on the observer's left, and the same duct would need CCW 90.

The same duct can need either hand, depending on which way the fan is set on its base, which is why layout drawings must show the drive side.

docs.title: Bottom Horizontal Discharge
docs.text:
Bottom horizontal discharge (BHD, 270 degrees) puts the outlet at the bottom of the housing, pointing sideways. It suits fans that feed a duct running at floor level or below grade, a tunnel, or an under-floor plenum. A bottom horizontal outlet keeps the duct low, which helps when headroom is limited or when the discharge feeds equipment at grade.

BHD has its own interaction with the motor. FanPedia notes that on Arrangements 1, 3 and 3F a BHD outlet can collide with the motor in one standard position, because the motor "interferes with outlet opening of housing" (FanPedia pp. 162-163).

Worked example. A boiler forced-draft fan must deliver air into a windbox inlet located low on the boiler front, to the observer's left when they stand on the fan's drive side.

  1. The air must leave horizontally at the bottom of the housing: BHD.
  2. From the discharge table, a CW bottom horizontal outlet throws air to the left.
  3. The order reads CW 270 (CW BHD).
  4. Because a CW BHD outlet projects to the left at floor level, the motor cannot be placed on the left side of the fan in the position the outlet occupies. The motor position must be chosen with the outlet in mind, as the motor position section below shows.

docs.title: Down Blast Discharge Position
docs.text:
The down blast discharge position (DBD, 180 degrees) points the outlet straight down. It suits a fan mounted above the space it serves: a fan on a platform or mezzanine discharging down into a duct or chamber below it, or a fan supported on structural steel above a process. A downblast fan's outlet usually connects through a floor opening or into a plenum, so the support frame must leave room around the outlet flange.

Like upblast, downblast points the same direction for both rotations, but the housings differ: a CW downblast outlet sits on the right side of the housing bottom, and a CCW downblast outlet on the left, because those are the sides where the wheel moves air downward.

Worked example. A fan on a mezzanine must discharge through a floor sleeve into a supply chamber below. The sleeve is already cast in the slab, and the architect's drawing shows the sleeve centerline offset to the right of the fan shaft when viewed from the drive side.

  1. Air must leave straight down: DBD.
  2. The outlet must sit to the right of the shaft.
  3. A CW downblast outlet sits on the right of the housing bottom, so the order reads CW 180.
  4. Ordering CCW 180 would put the outlet on the left, off the sleeve, and the slab would need a new opening.

docs.title: Angular Discharge
docs.text: An angular discharge is any of the four positions that point the outlet at 45 degrees rather than straight up, straight down or horizontally: TAU (45), TAD (135), BAD (225) and BAU (315). Angular discharges let the outlet meet a duct that rises or falls at an angle, or clear an obstruction without a full elbow. They are named by where the outlet is (top or bottom of the housing) and which way the air heads (up or down). Not every fan type offers all four: FanPedia's DWDI discharge pages list seven positions and omit Bottom Angular Down, a limit covered in Chapter 13 (FanPedia pp. 48-49).

docs.title: Top Angular Up Discharge
docs.text: Top angular up discharge (TAU, 45 degrees) places the outlet near the top of the housing with the air heading upward at 45 degrees, one step past upblast in the direction of rotation. For a CW fan the air heads up and to the right; for a CCW fan, up and to the left. A TAU outlet is a good fit when an exhaust duct must climb toward a roof penetration that is offset from the fan, because it replaces an elbow with the housing's own geometry.

docs.title: Top Angular Down Discharge
docs.text: Top angular down discharge (TAD, 135 degrees) places the outlet near the top of the housing with the air heading downward at 45 degrees. For a CW fan the air heads down and to the right; for a CCW fan, down and to the left. Because the outlet projects down beside the housing, it can collide with a motor placed on that side; FanPedia lists TAD among the discharges that restrict motor position on Arrangements 1, 3 and 3F (FanPedia pp. 162-163).

docs.title: Bottom Angular Up Discharge
docs.text: Bottom angular up discharge (BAU, 315 degrees) places the outlet near the bottom of the housing with the air heading upward at 45 degrees. For a CW fan the air heads up and to the left; for a CCW fan, up and to the right. BAU is one step short of upblast in the direction of rotation, and it suits a duct that leaves low and climbs away from the fan at an angle, for instance to rise over a walkway beside the unit.

docs.title: Inlet Box Position
docs.text:
Some centrifugal fans are fitted with an inlet box, a sheet-metal box attached to the fan inlet that turns the incoming air 90 degrees so the inlet duct can approach from the side, top or bottom instead of along the shaft. An inlet box also lets the bearing on an Arrangement 3 fan sit outside the airstream; Chapter 18 covers inlet boxes as accessories. The inlet box position states where the box's opening faces.

FanPedia defines inlet box position by an angle measured around the fan as viewed from the drive side, in 45-degree steps from 45 to 360, with 360 at the top and the angle increasing clockwise (FanPedia p. 144). Unlike the discharge angle, this angle does not change direction with rotation: it is a fixed clock around the housing. Each position also has a description of how the air enters:

  • 45 — Angular Down Intake (box at the upper right)
  • 90 — Horizontal Right Intake (box on the right)
  • 135 — Angular Up Intake (box at the lower right)
  • 180 — Bottom Up Intake (box at the bottom)
  • 225 — Angular Up Intake (box at the lower left)
  • 270 — Horizontal Left Intake (box on the left)
  • 315 — Angular Down Intake (box at the upper left)
  • 360 — Top Down Intake (box at the top)

The descriptions repeat for the angular positions: 45 and 315 are both Angular Down Intake, and 135 and 225 are both Angular Up Intake. The number, not the description, is what pins down the side.

Worked example. A fan with an inlet box must take air from a horizontal duct that arrives from the observer's left when standing on the drive side, and the fan's outlet is CW top horizontal, pointing right.

  1. The box opening must face left to meet the duct: Horizontal Left Intake.
  2. Horizontal Left Intake is position 270.
  3. Check for conflicts: the outlet is at the top pointing right, and the box is on the left, so the two connections do not compete for the same space.
  4. The order specifies CW 90 discharge with the inlet box at 270.

If the duct instead arrived from above at an angle on the left, the position would be 315, Angular Down Intake.

Two Angles, Two Rules

Watch out for treating the inlet box angle like the discharge angle. The discharge angle counts from upblast in the direction of rotation, but the inlet box angle is always counted clockwise from the top as seen from the drive side, so a CCW fan's inlet box at 90 is still on the right. Write each angle with its own label on the order so no one converts one into the other.

Before working through the next interactive element, recall that the inlet box angle runs clockwise from the top in 45-degree steps and that two pairs of positions share a description.

docs.title: Diagram: Inlet Box Position Dial
docs.text:
Inlet Box Position Dial

Type: microsim sim-id: ch12-inlet-box-position-dial Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Apply Bloom Verb: use Learning Objective: The learner will use the drive-side inlet box angle convention to set the correct inlet box position for eight duct-approach descriptions, with at least 7 of 8 correct on the first attempt.

Prerequisites: inlet box, inlet box position, viewed from the drive side, the eight inlet box position numbers and their descriptions, the difference between the inlet box angle and the discharge angle (all defined in the sections "Viewed From the Drive Side", "Discharge Angle" and "Inlet Box Position" above).

Evidence of Mastery: For each of eight challenge items, the learner sets the inlet box to one of the eight positions on a drive-side view of the fan and presses Check. An answer is correct when the position number equals the answer column in Content. Mastery is 7 of 8 correct on the first attempt. Rotating the box freely in exploration mode is not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) The inlet box angle counts in the direction of rotation, like the discharge angle. (2) The description alone ("Angular Down Intake") identifies one position. (3) The inlet box angle is read from the inlet side.

Instructional Rationale: Setting a position from a described duct approach makes the learner perform the conversion an order writer performs, and judging each setting gives immediate correction. Items 5 to 8 share descriptions in pairs so that the learner must use the location, not the words, which confronts misconception 2; item 8 is shown on a CCW fan to confront misconception 1.

Content:

Exploration mode. A drive-side view of a centrifugal housing with an inlet box that the learner can move to any of eight positions. For the current position the sim shows the number and its FanPedia description:

Position Description Box location seen from the drive side 45 Angular Down Intake Upper right 90 Horizontal Right Intake Right 135 Angular Up Intake Lower right 180 Bottom Up Intake Bottom 225 Angular Up Intake Lower left 270 Horizontal Left Intake Left 315 Angular Down Intake Upper left 360 Top Down Intake Top

The learner can also switch the fan's drawn rotation between CW and CCW; the position numbers do not move.

Challenge mode. Eight items in this fixed order:

# Fan rotation shown Duct approach described to the learner Correct position Why (shown as feedback) 1 CW The inlet duct runs horizontally and arrives from the right of the drive-side observer. 90 A box opening facing right is Horizontal Right Intake, position 90. 2 CW The inlet duct drops vertically from the roof directly above the fan. 360 Air entering downward from the top is Top Down Intake, position 360. 3 CW The inlet duct rises from a trench directly below the fan. 180 Air entering upward from the bottom is Bottom Up Intake, position 180. 4 CW The inlet duct runs horizontally and arrives from the left of the drive-side observer. 270 A box opening facing left is Horizontal Left Intake, position 270. 5 CW The inlet duct comes down at 45 degrees from the upper right. 45 Angular Down Intake on the upper right is 45; the upper-left one is 315. 6 CW The inlet duct comes down at 45 degrees from the upper left. 315 Angular Down Intake on the upper left is 315, counted clockwise from the top. 7 CW The inlet duct rises at 45 degrees from the lower left. 225 Angular Up Intake on the lower left is 225; the lower-right one is 135. 8 CCW The inlet duct rises at 45 degrees from the lower right. 135 The inlet box angle always runs clockwise from the top, whatever the rotation, so lower right is 135.

Provenance: Position numbers, descriptions and the drive-side viewing rule come from FanPedia p. 144 (Inlet Boxes: Positions, "Inlet Box Positions Determined From Drive Side"), local copy fanpedia.pdf in the course source folder. Challenge items are constructed for this chapter.

Rules: Positions are 45, 90, 135, 180, 225, 270, 315 and 360 degrees, measured clockwise from the top as seen from the drive side; 360 is the top. The position does not depend on the fan's rotation. An answer is correct only when the selected number equals the answer; there is no partial credit.

Learner Activity:

  1. In exploration mode the learner moves the box around the housing one position at a time and reads each number and description.
  2. The learner switches the drawn rotation from CW to CCW; the box and its number stay where they were. The learner should notice that rotation does not change the inlet box angle.
  3. The learner starts the challenge, reads each duct description, moves the box to a position and presses Check.
  4. After item 8 a summary shows the score and lists missed items with their feedback.

Feedback: Eight items, fixed order, two attempts each. Correct: "Correct: position , ." Incorrect on the first attempt: if the learner chose the mirror position (for example 315 instead of 45), "Same description, other side: the angle counts clockwise from the top as seen from the drive side."; if the learner's answer equals the correct position counted counterclockwise on item 8, "The inlet box angle does not follow rotation; count clockwise from the top."; otherwise "Find where the duct arrives, then read that position's number." After the second wrong attempt the correct answer and the Why text are shown and the item counts as missed. Only first-attempt answers count. A running count "Correct on first attempt: n of 8" is shown.

Starting State: Exploration mode, CW fan, inlet box at 360 (Top Down Intake). The prompt reads: "Move the box. Which positions share a description?"

Chapter Anchors: Eight positions in 45-degree steps from 45 to 360; 360 is the top and the angle increases clockwise; positions are read from the drive side; 45 and 315 are both Angular Down Intake; 135 and 225 are both Angular Up Intake; the inlet box angle does not change with rotation; the worked example sets a left-hand horizontal approach at 270.

docs.title: Inline Configuration
docs.text: Inline, mixed flow and axial fans move air straight through a cylindrical housing, so they have no scroll outlet to point. Their orientation is instead described by an inline configuration: whether the fan's axis runs horizontally or vertically, which way the air flows, and how the fan is supported. FanPedia lists three horizontal configurations, HOR (Horizontal, No Brackets), HCH (Horizontal, Ceiling Hung) and HBM (Horizontal, Base Mount), and ten vertical configurations whose codes begin VU (vertical up), VD (vertical down) or VR (vertical reversible), such as VUI (Vertical Up, Floor Mount Brackets on Inlet) and VDH (Vertical Down with Hood) (FanPedia pp. 50-51). For example, an inline fan hung from roof joists in a horizontal duct run is HCH. Chapter 13 covers the full horizontal and vertical lists.

docs.title: Motor Position
docs.text:
The motor position states where a belt-drive motor sits relative to the fan. On a direct-drive fan the motor is on the shaft and has no separate position, but on a belt-driven fan the motor can be placed on several sides of the fan, and the choice affects floor space, access for belt changes, and whether the motor collides with the outlet or the inlet duct. Like rotation and discharge, the motor position of a centrifugal fan is read from the drive side.

Different fan families use different naming systems for motor position, and FanPedia's motor position pages show each one (FanPedia pp. 52-57):

  • Arrangements 1, 3 and 3F use the four AMCA standard positions W, X, Y and Z.
  • Arrangements 9 and 9F use L and R; FanPedia lists the standard as CW (L) / CCW (R).
  • "K" mount motors, also called piggyback or scroll-mounted motors, sit directly on the housing scroll and are located by clock positions such as 12 o'clock or 1:30.
  • Plenum fans and swingout fans have their own position sets; Chapter 13 covers the plenum positions.
  • Axial and inline Arrangement 9 fans use the letters A through H.

Worked example. A distributor receives two quotes for "the same" belt-driven SWSI fan. One lists "Arr. 9, CW, motor position L"; the other lists "Arr. 1, CW, motor position W". Are they the same?

  1. The arrangement differs. In Arrangement 9 the motor hangs on the side of the fan's own bearing pedestal; in Arrangement 1 the motor sits on the floor or a base beside the pedestal (Chapter 11).
  2. The motor position systems differ because the arrangements differ: L and R describe the two sides of a pedestal-mounted motor, and W, X, Y and Z describe four floor positions around an Arrangement 1 or 3 fan.
  3. The quotes are therefore for different assemblies with different footprints and different base requirements. The distributor should ask which arrangement the job needs before comparing prices.

Read the Arrangement Before the Letter

Here's a shortcut: a motor position letter means nothing until you know the arrangement, because each arrangement family has its own letters. Find the arrangement on the order first, then look up that arrangement's motor position page.

docs.title: Motor Positions W X Y Z
docs.text:
The motor positions W, X, Y and Z are the four standard belt-drive motor locations that AMCA defines for centrifugal fans, and FanPedia states that the motor on an Arrangement 1 or Arrangement 3 SWSI fan "can be mounted in any of the four AMCA standard motor positions: W, X, Y or Z" (FanPedia pp. 162-163). The positions are read facing the drive side. FanPedia's illustration for Arrangements 1 and 3 places W and X on the right-hand side of the fan and Y and Z on the left-hand side; on an Arrangement 3F, whose extended frame carries the motor, the illustration shows two positions, Z and W, also known as L and R (FanPedia p. 52).

Not every position works with every discharge. The technical descriptions list restrictions for Arrangements 1, 3 and 3F where the outlet and the motor would collide or the motor would not fit under the outlet. For example, with a BHD discharge the motor "interferes with outlet opening of housing," so on a CW fan motor position Z is not allowed and on a CCW fan motor position W is not allowed (FanPedia pp. 162-163). Chapter 13 sets out the complete restriction list.

Worked example. Return to the boiler forced-draft fan from the bottom horizontal section: an Arrangement 1 fan, CW 270 (CW BHD), with the outlet projecting to the left at floor level. Maintenance wants the motor on the left side of the fan for belt access from an aisle.

  1. Facing the drive side, the left-hand positions are Y and Z.
  2. FanPedia's restriction for a CW BHD discharge rules out Z, because the motor would interfere with the housing outlet.
  3. That leaves Y on the left side, or W and X on the right side.
  4. The engineer checks Y against the drawing and confirms it clears the outlet, and the order reads CW 270, motor position Y. If it did not clear, the motor would move to the right side and the aisle access would be rearranged instead.

Every Orientation Choice Is Linked

Think of rotation, discharge, inlet box and motor position as four hands on one clock face: moving one can push another out of a legal position. That is why experienced application engineers sketch the drive-side view with all four before they write any of them on the order.

docs.title: Axial Motor Positions
docs.text: Axial motor positions locate the belt-drive motor on an Arrangement 9 axial, mixed flow or inline fan in a horizontal configuration. FanPedia labels eight positions A through H around the fan as seen in the discharge view: A at the top, then B, C, D, E, F, G and H in turn around the housing, with E at the bottom (FanPedia p. 56). A duct- or ceiling-mounted fan can take any of the eight; FanPedia's floor-mounted illustration shows only the upper five, G, H, A, B and C, since the floor supports sit below the fan. For vertical configurations FanPedia specifies no motor position for roof- and duct-mounted fans: the motor is centered on the curb cap or between the support brackets (FanPedia p. 57).

docs.title: Putting It Together: Reading a Full Orientation
docs.text:
A complete orientation for a belt-driven centrifugal fan pairs the arrangement with four facts, each read from the drive side. The table below summarizes the conventions covered in this chapter.

Item What it states How it is read Rotation Direction the impeller turns CW or CCW from the drive side (axial: LH or RH from the discharge side) Discharge position Direction the air leaves the outlet One of eight names, 45 degrees apart Discharge angle Degrees from upblast to the outlet Counted from 360 in the direction of rotation Inlet box position Where the inlet box opening faces 45 to 360, clockwise from the top, from the drive side Motor position Where the belt-drive motor sits Letters set by the arrangement family

Worked example. A specifying engineer's schedule reads: "Arr. 3 SWSI, CCW, discharge THD, inlet box 90, motor position X." Sketch it from the drive side.

  1. CCW rotation with THD: the outlet is at the top and the air leaves to the left (\( \theta = 360^\circ - 90^\circ = 270^\circ \)).
  2. Inlet box 90 is Horizontal Right Intake, so the inlet duct arrives from the right.
  3. Motor position X is on the right-hand side of the fan.
  4. Check conflicts: the outlet is at the top heading left, so it neither collides with the right-hand motor nor competes with the right-hand inlet box duct. THD on a CCW fan restricts position Z, which is not the one chosen.

The sketch confirms the schedule is buildable, and it is the drawing the installer will compare against when the fan arrives.

You Can Read a Fan From Across the Room

You just learned to fix the viewpoint at the drive side, name all eight discharge positions with their angles, place an inlet box, and locate a motor in each arrangement family's system. That is the orientation half of every fan order handled, and Chapter 13 turns it into codes.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Centrifugal fan orientation is read viewed from the drive side, the side where the sheave, coupling or motor is. A view from the inlet side is a mirror image.
  • Rotation is CW or CCW from the drive side for centrifugal fans; axial impeller rotation is LH or RH viewed from the discharge side. A wheel turning the wrong way delivers only a fraction of its rated performance.
  • The discharge position is one of eight directions 45 degrees apart: UBD, TAU, THD, TAD, DBD, BAD, BHD and BAU. Each name is valid for both rotations, with mirror-image housings.
  • The discharge angle counts from upblast (360) in the direction of rotation, so CW 90 and CCW 90 are both top horizontal, pointing right and left respectively.
  • Up blast, top horizontal, bottom horizontal and down blast suit vertical stacks, overhead ducts, low ducts and downward discharges; the four angular discharges point the outlet at 45 degrees.
  • Inlet box position runs from 45 to 360 clockwise from the top, from the drive side, and does not change with rotation.
  • Inline configuration describes axis orientation, flow direction and support for inline, mixed flow and axial fans.
  • Motor position depends on the arrangement: W, X, Y, Z for Arrangements 1, 3 and 3F, L and R for Arrangement 9, clock positions for K-mount motors, and A through H for axial Arrangement 9 fans. Some discharges rule out some motor positions.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: This chapter turns the orientation conventions into the codes used on orders. It covers clockwise and counterclockwise rotation and rotation arrows, the combined rotation and discharge code, the limits on double width double inlet discharges, motor position restrictions that depend on discharge, conduit box position, plenum motor positions, and the conventions for axial and inline fans in horizontal and vertical configurations. After completing it, readers can write a correct rotation and discharge designation for a fan.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
This chapter builds on concepts from:

  • Chapter 3: Basic Fan Anatomy
  • Chapter 4: Centrifugal, Axial and Mixed Flow Fans
  • Chapter 5: Roof, Wall and Specialty Exhaust Fans
  • Chapter 8: Centrifugal and Axial Impeller Types
  • Chapter 9: Impeller Construction and Material Handling
  • Chapter 12: Discharge Positions and Rotation

Welcome to Rotation and Discharge Codes

A fan that arrives with its outlet pointing the wrong way, or its motor sitting where the ductwork needs to go, costs days on a job site and a fresh order at the factory. This chapter gives you the short codes that prevent that: a rotation, a discharge, a motor position, and a conduit box location that the plant, the drafter, and the installer all read the same way. By the end you will write a complete designation for a centrifugal, plenum, or inline fan without guessing. Let's follow the airflow.

docs.title: From Orientation to Order Codes
docs.text:
Chapter 12 set up the vocabulary for describing which way a fan faces: the eight discharge positions, the discharge angle, the rule that a centrifugal fan is viewed from the drive side, and the AMCA motor positions W, X, Y and Z. This chapter turns that vocabulary into the codes that go on a quote, a submittal drawing, and a factory order. Each code answers one question the factory cannot answer for you:

  1. Which way does the impeller turn? (rotation)
  2. Which way does the air leave the housing? (discharge)
  3. Where does the motor sit relative to the fan? (motor position)
  4. Which side of the motor carries the electrical connection? (conduit box position)

The sections below take these in order for housed centrifugal fans, then cover plenum fans, and finish with the different conventions used for axial and inline fans.

docs.title: Clockwise and Counterclockwise Rotation
docs.text: Every centrifugal fan turns in one of two directions, and the direction is fixed by the housing: a scroll housing is built to collect air that moves around it one way only. The direction is always judged from a stated viewpoint, because the same impeller looks clockwise from one side and counterclockwise from the other. For housed centrifugal fans, FanPedia states that viewpoint on every discharge page: rotation is viewed from the drive side (FanPedia PDF pp. 46–49). The drive side is the side of the fan where the drive is: the sheave and belts on a belt-driven fan, or the motor on a direct-drive fan.

docs.title: Clockwise Rotation
docs.text: Clockwise rotation (CW) means that an observer standing on the drive side and looking toward the fan sees the impeller turn the same way as the hands of a clock. FanPedia's CW page shows a person standing beside the bearing pedestal, looking at the drive end of the shaft, with the rotation arrow sweeping over the top of the housing from left to right (FanPedia PDF p. 46). The same page draws each centrifugal impeller type with its blades oriented for clockwise rotation, because blade shape and rotation must agree.

docs.title: Worked Example: Confirming CW on an Existing Arrangement 1 Fan
docs.text:
A plant engineer wants a duplicate of an existing Arrangement 1 SWSI exhaust fan whose nameplate is painted over.

  1. Find the drive side. The belt guard and motor are on the east side of the fan, so the east side is the drive side.
  2. Stand on the drive side. The engineer stands east of the fan, facing west toward the shaft end and sheave.
  3. Watch the shaft or a blade. With the fan coasting down after a stop, the shaft turns the way clock hands turn.
  4. Record it. The rotation is CW. Write it down before the discharge, because the discharge code means something different for CW and CCW fans.

If the engineer had stood on the inlet side instead, the shaft would have appeared to turn counterclockwise, and an order written from that view would have produced a mirror-image housing.

docs.title: Counterclockwise Rotation
docs.text: Counterclockwise rotation (CCW) means that the observer on the drive side sees the impeller turn opposite to the hands of a clock. A CCW housing is the mirror image of a CW housing: the scroll expands in the opposite direction and every discharge comes out on the opposite side (FanPedia PDF p. 47). Neither direction is better aerodynamically; the choice comes from the duct connection, service access, and how paired fans are laid out.

docs.title: Worked Example: Choosing CCW for a Mirror-Image Pair
docs.text:
Two supply fans stand side by side in a mechanical room with a service aisle between them, and both must blow north into a common plenum through Top Horizontal outlets. The west fan has its drive on its east side, facing the aisle; the east fan has its drive on its west side, also facing the aisle.

  1. West fan. Its observer stands in the aisle looking west. North is on that observer's right, so the top outlet blows right, which makes the top of the impeller move right: the fan is CW, ordered CW THD.
  2. East fan. Its observer also stands in the aisle but looks east. North is now on the observer's left, so the top outlet blows left and the top of the impeller moves left: the fan is CCW.
  3. Write both lines. West fan CW THD, east fan CCW THD. The discharge code is the same; only the rotation differs.

The pair looks like a reflection in a mirror placed in the aisle, which is exactly what CW and CCW housings are.

One Fan, Two Answers

Rotation is not a property you can read without a viewpoint: the same spinning wheel is clockwise from one side and counterclockwise from the other. That is why every rotation code silently carries the phrase "viewed from the drive side," and why the first question to ask about any sketch is "Check it from the drive side."

docs.title: Rotation Arrow
docs.text:
A rotation arrow is the curved arrow that shows the required direction of rotation. It appears on FanPedia's discharge and impeller drawings, where it sweeps around the housing or the impeller in the direction the wheel must turn (FanPedia PDF pp. 37–49), and in common practice it is also marked on the fan housing so that whoever wires the motor can check the direction at startup.

A centrifugal impeller turning backward still moves some air, but far less than its rating, so a reversed fan often "runs but does not move much air" rather than failing outright. FanPedia is blunter about axial fans: if the impeller rotates in the wrong direction, "you will not get any airflow in the proper direction" (FanPedia PDF pp. 37–40).

docs.title: Worked Example: The Startup Bump Check
docs.text:
An electrician has just wired a new belt-driven centrifugal fan with a three-phase motor, and the startup checklist calls for a bump test.

  1. Clear the fan. Guards are in place and nobody is inside the housing or ductwork.
  2. Bump the motor. Energize it just long enough for the shaft to start turning, then de-energize it.
  3. Compare with the arrow. While the shaft coasts, compare its direction with the rotation arrow on the housing. Read both from the same side.
  4. Correct if needed. On a three-phase motor, interchanging any two of the three supply leads reverses rotation. Bump again to confirm, and record the result on the startup sheet.

If the fan was ordered CW but the housing arrow shows CCW from the drive side, the housing was built to the wrong hand, and no rewiring will fix it.

docs.title: Rotation and Discharge Code
docs.text:
A rotation and discharge code is the short designation that states both which way a centrifugal fan turns and which way its outlet points. FanPedia gives two equivalent ways to write it (FanPedia PDF pp. 46–49):

  • Letter form: the rotation (CW or CCW) followed by a three-letter discharge abbreviation, such as CW THD.
  • Angle form: the rotation followed by the discharge angle in degrees, such as CW 90, also written "Clockwise 90°".

The discharge angle steps around the housing in 45° increments. A practical way to read it from FanPedia's drawings is to start with the outlet pointing straight up (360°) and turn the outlet in the direction of rotation, as seen from the drive side: a quarter turn gives 90°, a half turn 180°, and three quarters 270°. That is why the same number means opposite outlet directions for CW and CCW fans: CW 90 blows toward the right of an observer on the drive side, and CCW 90 blows toward the left.

The following table lists the eight discharges from Chapter 12 in both code forms.

Discharge Letter code CW angle form CCW angle form SWSI DWDI Upblast UBD CW 360 CCW 360 Yes Yes Top Angular Up TAU CW 45 CCW 45 Yes Yes Top Horizontal THD CW 90 CCW 90 Yes Yes Top Angular Down TAD CW 135 CCW 135 Yes Yes Downblast DBD CW 180 CCW 180 Yes Yes Bottom Angular Down BAD CW 225 CCW 225 Yes No Bottom Horizontal BHD CW 270 CCW 270 Yes Yes Bottom Angular Up BAU CW 315 CCW 315 Yes Yes

Source: FanPedia PDF pp. 46–49.

docs.title: Worked Example: Writing the Code from a Duct Layout
docs.text:
A contractor's sketch shows a single-width, single-inlet (SWSI) fan whose outlet connects to a duct running horizontally along the floor, leaving toward the right of an observer on the drive side. The fan turns counterclockwise from that side.

  1. Rotation. CCW, from the drive side.
  2. Discharge position. The outlet is at the bottom of the housing and blows horizontally, so it is Bottom Horizontal, BHD.
  3. Check the direction. For a CCW fan, start with the outlet pointing up and turn it counterclockwise: 90° points left, 180° points down, 270° points right. A right-pointing bottom outlet on a CCW fan is 270°, which agrees with BHD in the table.
  4. Write the code. CCW BHD, or in angle form CCW 270.

Had the contractor's fan been CW, a right-pointing outlet at the bottom would be impossible: on a CW fan the bottom horizontal outlet blows left. Rotation and discharge must be chosen together.

Write Both Forms Once

When a customer's drawing uses one form and your order entry uses the other, write both on your worksheet, "CCW BHD (CCW 270)," and check that they name the same row of the table. One alias on FanPedia's CCW pages prints Downblast as "Counterclockwise 80°"; it is a misprint, and the code is CCW 180 (FanPedia PDF pp. 47 and 49).

docs.title: Bottom Angular Down Discharge
docs.text: Bottom Angular Down discharge (BAD) is the discharge whose outlet sits at the bottom of the housing and points downward at 45° between Downblast and Bottom Horizontal. Its angle form is CW 225 or CCW 225 (FanPedia PDF pp. 46–47). On a CW fan seen from the drive side it points down and to the left; on a CCW fan it points down and to the right. FanPedia lists BAD for single-width, single-inlet fans only.

docs.title: DWDI Discharge Limits
docs.text:
A double width, double inlet (DWDI) fan takes air into both sides of its impeller, which you met in Chapter 8. The DWDI discharge limits are the restriction that a DWDI centrifugal fan is offered in seven discharges, not eight: FanPedia's DWDI discharge pages list UBD, TAU, THD, TAD, DBD, BHD and BAU in both rotations, and omit Bottom Angular Down (FanPedia PDF pp. 48–49). The same pages show only three DWDI impeller types: forward curved, backward inclined and airfoil. When a layout calls for a DWDI fan blowing bottom angular down, the fix belongs in the ductwork (a Downblast or Bottom Horizontal outlet with a duct elbow) or in the fan type, and the current catalog for the product line should be checked before promising anything else.

The interactive below lets you practice writing codes, including a request that cannot be filled.

docs.text:
Run Rotation and Discharge Code Builder Fullscreen

Rotation and Discharge Code Builder

Type: microsim sim-id: ch13-rotation-discharge-code-builder Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Apply Bloom Verb: apply Learning Objective: The learner will apply the drive-side rotation and discharge-angle conventions to write the correct rotation and discharge code, in letter form and angle form, for a described centrifugal fan.

Prerequisites: drive side, clockwise rotation (CW), counterclockwise rotation (CCW), discharge position, discharge angle, SWSI, DWDI, Bottom Angular Down discharge, DWDI discharge limits (all defined in the sections above).

Evidence of Mastery: For each of 8 job cards, the learner selects a rotation (CW or CCW) and one of the 8 discharge letter codes, or selects "Not offered", and submits. A submission is correct when it matches the Answer column in Content. Mastery is 7 of 8 correct on the first attempt. Rotating the free-practice housing is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) The same angle number points the same way for CW and CCW fans. (2) Rotation can be judged from the inlet side. (3) Every discharge is available on every centrifugal fan, including DWDI.

Instructional Rationale: Apply-level skill needs repeated use of the rule on varied cases with a check after each one. Each card describes the outlet direction in words as seen from the drive side, so the learner must convert direction plus rotation into a code rather than match a picture to a label.

Content:

Job cards, in this fixed order. Directions are as seen by an observer on the drive side.

# Fan Rotation stated on card Outlet description on card Answer Why (shown as feedback) 1 SWSI CW Outlet blows straight up CW UBD (CW 360) Straight up is Upblast, 360°, for either rotation. 2 SWSI CCW Outlet at the top blows horizontally to the left CCW THD (CCW 90) For CCW, a quarter turn counterclockwise from straight up points left: 90°, Top Horizontal. 3 SWSI CW Outlet blows straight down CW DBD (CW 180) A half turn from straight up is 180°, Downblast, for either rotation. 4 SWSI CCW Outlet at the bottom blows horizontally to the right CCW BHD (CCW 270) For CCW, three quarter turns counterclockwise from up points right: 270°, Bottom Horizontal. 5 SWSI CW Outlet at the bottom points down and to the left at 45° CW BAD (CW 225) 225° clockwise from up is down-left, Bottom Angular Down, which SWSI fans offer. 6 DWDI CW Outlet at the bottom points down and to the left at 45° Not offered DWDI fans are offered in seven discharges; Bottom Angular Down is not one of them. 7 SWSI CCW Outlet at the top points up and to the left at 45° CCW TAU (CCW 45) 45° counterclockwise from up is up-left, Top Angular Up. 8 DWDI CCW Outlet at the bottom points up and to the right at 45° CCW BAU (CCW 315) 315° counterclockwise from up is up-right, Bottom Angular Up, which DWDI fans offer.

Discharge choices shown to the learner: UBD Upblast, TAU Top Angular Up, THD Top Horizontal, TAD Top Angular Down, DBD Downblast, BAD Bottom Angular Down, BHD Bottom Horizontal, BAU Bottom Angular Up, and Not offered.

After each submission the sim shows a drive-side outline of the housing with its outlet drawn in the answer's direction and a rotation arrow in the answer's rotation, labeled with both code forms.

Provenance: Discharge names, letter codes, angle forms and the DWDI list are from FanPedia PDF pp. 46–49 and this chapter's section "Rotation and Discharge Code." The outlet direction for each angle follows the chapter's reading rule. Job cards are illustrative scenarios and are labeled "illustrative".

Rules: Outlet direction, seen from the drive side, is the direction "straight up" turned through the discharge angle in the direction of rotation: clockwise for CW, counterclockwise for CCW. Angles: UBD 360, TAU 45, THD 90, TAD 135, DBD 180, BAD 225, BHD 270, BAU 315. A DWDI card whose only matching discharge is BAD has the answer "Not offered". In free practice, the rotation is CW or CCW (default CW) and the discharge angle runs from 45 to 360 in steps of 45 (default 360, unit degrees); the sim shows the matching letter code, and when the fan type is DWDI and the angle is 225 it shows "Not offered on DWDI".

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner reads job card 1 and predicts the code by choosing a rotation and a discharge, then submits.
  2. The sim checks the answer, shows the feedback, and draws the housing outline with the correct outlet and rotation arrow.
  3. The learner moves to the next card; previous cards cannot be re-answered for score.
  4. After card 8, free practice unlocks: the learner chooses SWSI or DWDI, a rotation, and an angle, and the outline and code update at once. The learner should notice that switching rotation at a fixed angle mirrors the outlet left to right.

Feedback: 8 cards, fixed order, one scored attempt each, then a second unscored attempt is allowed. Correct: "Correct: ." Incorrect: the "Why" text for that card, followed by the correct answer. The correct answer is revealed after the first submission. A running score "Codes correct: n of 8" is shown.

Starting State: Card 1 is shown with no rotation or discharge selected and the question "What code goes on the order?"

Chapter Anchors: Eight discharges for SWSI fans; seven for DWDI, without BAD. CW 90 blows to the right and CCW 90 to the left of an observer on the drive side. The worked example's answer is CCW BHD (CCW 270).

docs.title: Motor Position Restrictions
docs.text:
For SWSI Arrangements 1 and 3, FanPedia states that the motor can be mounted in any of the four AMCA motor positions W, X, Y and Z from Chapter 12 (FanPedia PDF pp. 162–163). Motor position restrictions are the combinations of rotation, discharge and motor position that cannot be built, or that need a check, because the motor would block the outlet or would not fit under it.

FanPedia lists the same restrictions for SWSI Arrangements 1, 3 and 3F (FanPedia PDF pp. 162–163):

  • BHD discharge, because the motor interferes with the outlet opening: CW rotation, position Z is not allowed; CCW rotation, position W is not allowed.
  • TAD discharge, for the same reason: CW rotation, position W is not allowed; CCW rotation, position Z is not allowed.
  • THD discharge, a height restriction, because the motor may not fit below the discharge: CW rotation, position W; CCW rotation, position Z. On an Arrangement 1 fan, the motor will fit if the pedestal is lengthened to accommodate it.

Notice the mirror pattern: every CW restriction on W becomes a CCW restriction on Z, and the reverse, because a CCW housing is the mirror image of a CW housing.

Other arrangements carry their own rules. Swingout fans (Arrangements 9SS and 9ST) open the housing for impeller access, and a K mount motor, also called piggyback or scroll mounted, sits directly on the housing scroll on an adjustable motor base, so the outlet decides where there is room for it (FanPedia PDF pp. 53–54). The table summarizes these rules.

Arrangement Motor position rule Source 9 and 9F (SWSI) Standard: CW fans use (L), CCW fans use (R) FanPedia PDF p. 52 9SS swingout Fixed: CW with (L) only (right swing); CCW with (R) only (left swing) FanPedia PDF pp. 53, 166 9ST swingout Standard (R) on right swing, (L) on left swing; motor on slide base above the pedestal FanPedia PDF pp. 53, 166 10 (SWSI) Motor position unique to the pedestal design, no options FanPedia PDF p. 52 3F (DWDI) W and Z standard; consult factory for X and Y FanPedia PDF p. 167 K mount, SWSI and DWDI Arrangement 3 Clock positions depend on discharge: UBD 9 and 3 o'clock; THD 9, 10:30 and 12; DBD 9, 10:30, 12, 1:30 and 3; BHD 12, 1:30 and 3 FanPedia PDF p. 54

docs.title: Worked Example: Rejecting a Motor Position Before It Ships
docs.text:
A specifying engineer sends a schedule line: "SWSI Arrangement 3 fan, CW, BHD, motor position Z, belt drive."

  1. Look up the discharge. BHD is one of the three discharges with a restriction.
  2. Apply the rotation. For CW rotation with BHD, position Z is not allowed: the motor would interfere with the outlet opening.
  3. Offer the alternatives. Positions W, X and Y carry no restriction for CW BHD, and the engineer picks W.
  4. Write the corrected line: "Arrangement 3, CW BHD, motor position W."

Rotation Changes Which Letter Is Forbidden

A common trap is to remember "BHD means no Z" and forget that it only holds for CW fans; for CCW BHD the forbidden position is W. Always look up the restriction with the rotation and the discharge together, and recheck it whenever either one changes late in the job.

The checker below drills exactly that habit across the three restricted discharges and a few arrangements with their own rules.

docs.title: Diagram: Motor Position Restriction Checker
docs.text:
Motor Position Restriction Checker

Type: diagram sim-id: ch13-motor-position-restriction-checker Library: html Status: Specified Bloom Level: Evaluate Bloom Verb: judge Learning Objective: The learner will judge whether each proposed combination of arrangement, rotation, discharge and motor position can be ordered as written, using the FanPedia restriction rules.

Prerequisites: arrangement, CW and CCW rotation, discharge letter codes, motor positions W, X, Y and Z, motor positions (L) and (R), swingout arrangement 9SS, motor position restrictions (all defined in the chapter above this block).

Evidence of Mastery: For each of 10 order lines, the learner selects one verdict, "Allowed", "Not allowed" or "Height check needed", and submits. A verdict is correct when it matches the Verdict column in Content. Mastery is 9 of 10 correct on the first attempt. Opening the reference rule card is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) A restriction on a position holds for both rotations. (2) The THD restriction forbids the position outright instead of calling for a height check. (3) Arrangement 9SS lets the buyer choose either side for the motor.

Instructional Rationale: Evaluate-level judgment requires the learner to weigh a proposal against stated criteria and commit to a verdict before seeing the answer. Mixing allowed lines with restricted ones forces a real check on every line instead of pattern guessing.

Content:

Order lines, in this fixed order:

# Order line shown Verdict Why (shown as feedback) 1 SWSI Arrangement 3, CW, BHD, motor position Z Not allowed For CW BHD the motor in Z interferes with the outlet opening. 2 SWSI Arrangement 3, CW, BHD, motor position W Allowed For CW BHD only Z is restricted; W is available. 3 SWSI Arrangement 1, CCW, BHD, motor position W Not allowed The mirror rule: for CCW BHD the restricted position is W. 4 SWSI Arrangement 1, CW, TAD, motor position W Not allowed For CW TAD the motor in W interferes with the outlet opening. 5 SWSI Arrangement 3F, CCW, TAD, motor position Z Not allowed For CCW TAD the restricted position is Z, on Arrangement 3F as on 1 and 3. 6 SWSI Arrangement 3, CCW, TAD, motor position W Allowed For CCW TAD only Z is restricted. 7 SWSI Arrangement 1, CW, THD, motor position W Height check needed The motor may not fit below a CW THD outlet in W; on Arrangement 1 a lengthened pedestal makes it fit. 8 SWSI Arrangement 3, CCW, THD, motor position Z Height check needed For CCW THD the height restriction applies to Z. 9 SWSI Arrangement 3, CW, UBD, motor position Y Allowed FanPedia lists no motor position restriction for UBD. 10 Arrangement 9SS swingout, CCW, UBD, motor position (L) Not allowed Arrangement 9SS is built CW with (L) or CCW with (R) only.

Reference rule card the learner can open at any time:

Discharge CW restriction CCW restriction Reason BHD Z not allowed W not allowed Motor interferes with outlet opening TAD W not allowed Z not allowed Motor interferes with outlet opening THD W, height check Z, height check Motor may not fit below the discharge; Arrangement 1 pedestal can be lengthened

Provenance: Restrictions for Arrangements 1, 3 and 3F from FanPedia PDF pp. 162–163; Arrangement 9SS rule from FanPedia PDF pp. 53 and 166. Order lines are illustrative and are labeled "illustrative".

Rules: A line is "Not allowed" when its rotation, discharge and position appear as NOT ALLOWED in the rule card, or when it breaks the Arrangement 9SS pairing (CW with L, CCW with R). A line is "Height check needed" when it is CW THD with W or CCW THD with Z. Every other line is "Allowed".

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner reads order line 1, predicts a verdict, and submits it.
  2. The sim marks the verdict, shows the "Why" text, and highlights the matching row of the rule card.
  3. The learner continues through all 10 lines in order.
  4. At the end the sim shows each line with the learner's verdict and the correct verdict side by side, and the learner should notice that every restriction flips between W and Z when the rotation flips.

Feedback: 10 lines, fixed order, one scored attempt each. Correct: "Correct: ." Incorrect: "Not quite: ." followed by the "Why" text. The correct verdict is revealed after each submission. A running score "Verdicts correct: n of 10" is shown.

Starting State: Order line 1 is shown with three verdict choices and the question "Can this line be ordered as written?" The rule card is closed.

Chapter Anchors: Restrictions apply to BHD, TAD and THD on SWSI Arrangements 1, 3 and 3F. The worked example's line, Arrangement 3, CW, BHD, Z, is not allowed and is corrected to W.

docs.title: Conduit Box Position
docs.text:
The conduit box is the motor's power connection point, the box where the supply wiring enters and joins the motor leads (FanPedia PDF p. 75). Its conduit box position is the side of the motor it is mounted on, coded F1 or F2 and always viewed from the drive side of the motor, looking at the motor shaft (FanPedia PDF pp. 52–57). FanPedia marks F1 as the standard position on its motor position pages. Its motor modification page adds that F1 or F3 is standard, and that F2 is standard on IEC frames but a special modification for NEMA motors (FanPedia PDF p. 75).

The conduit box position matters because the box can end up facing a wall, the fan housing, or the belt guard, where an electrician cannot reach it. FanPedia gives two rules tied to motor position:

  • For Arrangement 9 and for plenum Arrangement 3SM, motor position (L) is normally ordered with an F1 conduit box; select F2 if there are clearance issues (FanPedia PDF pp. 52 and 55).
  • For Arrangement 9SS in the left swing, CCW rotation and (R) motor position, the fan must have an F2 conduit box (FanPedia PDF p. 53).

docs.title: Worked Example: Choosing F1 or F2 for an Arrangement 9 Fan
docs.text:
A distributor orders an SWSI Arrangement 9 fan, CW rotation, for a tight equipment room. The fan's left side, seen from the drive side, sits 18 inches from a block wall (an illustrative site dimension).

  1. Motor position. Arrangement 9 standard is (L) for CW, so the motor hangs on the left side of the pedestal, on the wall side.
  2. Default conduit box. Position (L) is normally ordered with F1.
  3. Check clearance. Ask which side of the motor F1 puts toward the wall. If the electrician cannot reach or route conduit to the box in that space, FanPedia's note applies: select F2.
  4. Write the line: "Arrangement 9, CW, motor position (L), conduit box F2 (clearance)."

Had the fan been an Arrangement 9SS in left swing, there would be no choice to make: CCW and (R) require F2.

docs.title: Plenum Motor Positions
docs.text:
A plenum fan has no scroll housing, so its motor positions are named differently from a housed fan's. Plenum motor positions are the motor locations FanPedia defines for belt-driven plenum fan arrangements (FanPedia PDF p. 55):

  • Arrangement 3 (horizontal): motor on the floor or fan base, in AMCA positions W, X, Y or Z.
  • Arrangement 3HS (horizontal, top-mounted motor on a slide base): Standard (S), also known as "R", or Optional (O), also known as "L".
  • Arrangement 3HA (horizontal, top-mounted motor on an adjustable motor base): Top Center (TC).
  • Arrangement 3SM (horizontal, side-mounted motor on a slide base): (L) or (R), with (R) standard.
  • Arrangement 3VA (vertical, adjustable motor base): Top Center (TC).
  • Arrangement 3VS (vertical, slide base): Standard (S), also known as "R", or Optional (O), also known as "L".

The arrangement code tells you which set of positions applies: H or V for horizontal or vertical, then S, A or M for slide base, adjustable base or side mounting.

docs.title: Axial and Inline Conventions
docs.text: Axial, mixed flow and inline fans have no scroll, so the eight centrifugal discharge codes do not apply to them. They use their own rotation rule and a configuration code instead.

docs.title: Axial Rotation Convention
docs.text:
The axial rotation convention is the rule that an axial fan's rotation is determined by viewing the impeller from the discharge side of the fan, not from the drive side (FanPedia PDF pp. 37–42). Axial rotation is written as left hand (LH) or right hand (RH), and it must match the impeller's hand and the airflow direction (PM, air through the impeller then over the motor, or MP, air over the motor then through the impeller) that Chapter 8 covered. Do not convert an axial LH or RH into CW or CCW for an order; each family keeps its own viewpoint.

Two Families, Two Viewpoints

Notice the pattern: a centrifugal fan is judged from where the drive is, and an axial fan from where the air leaves. Before you read any rotation on a drawing, ask which family the fan belongs to, and the viewpoint follows from that one answer.

docs.title: Axial Fan Configuration
docs.text: An axial fan configuration is the code that states how an inline, mixed flow or axial fan is oriented and supported: horizontal or vertical, which way the air goes, and what brackets, cap or hood it carries (FanPedia PDF pp. 50–51). It replaces the centrifugal discharge code, because a duct-shaped fan always discharges along its own axis.

docs.title: Inline Horizontal Configuration
docs.text: An inline horizontal configuration is a configuration in which the fan's axis is horizontal. FanPedia defines three codes: HOR, horizontal with no brackets; HCH, horizontal ceiling hung; and HBM, horizontal base mount (FanPedia PDF p. 50). For a belt-driven Arrangement 9 horizontal fan, the motor positions are lettered A through H around the casing as seen from the discharge, with A at the top. A floor-mounted fan shows positions A, B, C, G and H, the five not blocked by its base; a duct or ceiling mount shows all eight (FanPedia PDF p. 56).

docs.title: Inline Vertical Configuration
docs.text:
An inline vertical configuration is a configuration in which the fan's axis is vertical and the air moves up or down. FanPedia defines ten codes (FanPedia PDF p. 51):

Code Airflow Support or top VUN Vertical up No brackets VUI Vertical up Floor mount brackets on inlet VUO Vertical up Ceiling hung brackets on outlet VUS Vertical up Stack cap VUH Vertical up Hood VDN Vertical down No brackets VDI Vertical down Ceiling hung brackets on inlet VDO Vertical down Floor mount brackets on outlet VDH Vertical down Hood VRH Vertical reversible Hood

The letters read left to right: V for vertical, then U, D or R for up, down or reversible, then the support or top.

docs.title: Vertical Inline Motor Location
docs.text:
The vertical inline motor location is the place the motor occupies on a belt-driven Arrangement 9 vertical inline fan. FanPedia states that there is no specified motor position for these configurations (FanPedia PDF p. 57): on a roof-mounted fan the motor is centered on the curb cap, and on floor, ceiling and duct mounted fans it is centered between the support brackets. The order needs the configuration code and the conduit box position, but no motor position letter.

Designations You Can Defend

You can now turn a layout sketch into a rotation and discharge code, check the motor position against the discharge, pick the conduit box side, and switch to the axial and inline conventions when the fan has no scroll. That is the full orientation line on a centrifugal fan order, written so the factory, the drafter and the installer all build the same fan.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Centrifugal rotation, CW or CCW, is viewed from the drive side; a CCW housing is the mirror image of a CW housing, and the housing's rotation arrow is the startup check.
  • A rotation and discharge code is written in letter form (CW THD) or angle form (CW 90); the angle turns from straight up in the direction of rotation.
  • DWDI fans are offered in seven discharges; Bottom Angular Down (BAD, 225°) is SWSI only.
  • On SWSI Arrangements 1, 3 and 3F, BHD and TAD each forbid one motor position and THD needs a height check; the letter flips between W and Z with rotation.
  • Conduit box position is F1 or F2, viewed from the drive side of the motor; F2 is the clearance fix and is required on 9SS left swing.
  • Plenum, axial and inline fans use their own codes: plenum position letters, LH or RH from the discharge side, and configuration codes such as HOR or VUH.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: This chapter introduces the motors that drive fans: induction and electronically commutated (EC) motors, NEMA frame sizes, C-face and foot mounting, the motor nameplate, service factor, insulation class, and efficiency class. It explains the motor enclosures (open drip proof, totally enclosed fan cooled, totally enclosed air over, totally enclosed non-ventilated, and explosion proof) and when each is used. It also covers conduit boxes, shaft grounding rings, motor bases, and K mount motors. After completing it, readers can read a motor nameplate and choose a suitable enclosure.

docs.title: Concepts Covered
docs.text:
This chapter covers the following 20 concepts from the learning graph:

Concept Concept Impact Score Induction Motor 71 EC Motor 24 NEMA Frame Size 5 Motor Enclosure 154 Motor Service Factor 51 Insulation Class 5 Motor Efficiency Class 26 Conduit Box 1 Motor Base 43 Motor Nameplate 3 ODP Motor 25 TEFC Motor 25 TEAO Motor 1 TENV Motor 1 Explosion Proof Motor 26 C-Face Motor Mount 2 Foot Mounted Motor 1 Shaft Grounding Ring 27 Motor Base Saddle 1 K Mount Motor 1

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
This chapter builds on concepts from:
