  • Chapter 1: Air, Pressure and the Fan
  • Chapter 2: Airstreams, Total Pressure and Standard Air
  • Chapter 3: Basic Fan Anatomy
  • Chapter 4: Centrifugal, Axial and Mixed Flow Fans
  • Chapter 11: Drives and Standard Fan Arrangements
  • Chapter 12: Discharge Positions and Rotation

The Motor Line on the Order

Every fan order carries one dense line about the motor, and a wrong word in it can mean a motor that overheats on a dusty roof or one that is not allowed in a paint booth at all. By the end of this chapter you will read that line field by field and pick the enclosure the job site really needs. Let's follow the airflow.

Chapter 3 introduced the fan motor as the machine that turns electrical energy into the rotation of the impeller, named its main parts, and showed how a service factor is checked against the fan's brake horsepower. This chapter goes one level deeper. FanPedia (page 71) gives a typical motor specification exactly as it appears on a Twin City Fan order:

50 HP, 1800 RPM, IN, P, 3 Phase, 60 Frequency, 460 Volt, SD, TEFC, 326T

Each comma-separated field answers a different question: how much power, how fast, what technology, how efficient, what electrical supply, what duty, what enclosure, and what frame. The sections below take those questions in the order you will need them on a real job: first the motor technology, then the frame and how the motor is mounted, then the ratings on the nameplate, then the enclosure, and finally the accessories and bases that tie the motor to the fan. The chapter ends by decoding the whole line.

docs.title: Two Motor Technologies
docs.text: FanPedia (page 68) says the electric motor is by far the most common way to power a ventilating fan, and that two technologies are used: induction and electronically commutated. The "IN" in the motor line above is the technology field; the other value it can take is "EC".

docs.title: Induction Motor
docs.text:
An induction motor is an alternating-current (AC) motor in which the current in the rotor, needed to produce torque, is obtained by electromagnetic induction from the magnetic field of the stator winding (FanPedia page 68). Because the rotor current is induced rather than supplied, an induction motor needs no electrical connection to the rotor: no brushes and no slip rings, which is why it is rugged and why it powers most fans in the industry.

The AC supply makes the stator's magnetic field rotate. The speed of that rotating field is the synchronous speed, and it depends only on the supply frequency and the number of magnetic poles wound into the stator. The rotor always turns slightly slower than the field, because if it ever caught up, no current would be induced and no torque produced. The difference is called slip. That is why FanPedia (page 71) lists "typical synchronous speeds" of 3600, 1800, 1200 and 900 RPM at 60 Hz, and 3000, 1500, 1000 and 750 RPM at 50 Hz, then adds that actual nominal motor speeds vary by horsepower and manufacturer.

docs.title: Synchronous Speed
docs.text:
\[ N_s = \frac{120 \, f}{p} \]

where:

  • \( N_s \) is the synchronous speed in RPM
  • \( f \) is the supply frequency in hertz (Hz)
  • \( p \) is the number of stator poles (2, 4, 6 or 8 for the speeds listed above)

docs.title: Worked Example: The 1800 RPM Motor at 60 Hz and 50 Hz
docs.text:
The motor line above says 1800 RPM and 60 Hz.

  1. Find the poles: \( p = 120 \times 60 / 1800 = 4 \). It is a four-pole motor.
  2. Estimate slip. Suppose the nameplate shows a full-load speed of 1,770 RPM (an illustrative value; the real figure depends on the motor). Slip is \( (1800 - 1770)/1800 = 0.017 \), or about 1.7 percent.
  3. Now suppose the same fan design is quoted for a plant on a 50 Hz grid. A four-pole motor there has a synchronous speed of \( 120 \times 50 / 4 = 1500 \) RPM, which is \( 1500/1800 = 0.83 \) of the 60 Hz speed.
  4. On a direct-drive fan the impeller turns at motor speed, so the fan runs about 17 percent slower. The fan laws in Chapter 25 show that airflow falls in proportion to speed and pressure with the square of speed, so this fan would deliver roughly 83 percent of the airflow at about 69 percent of the pressure.

Result: frequency is not a detail to fill in later. A 50 Hz job needs its own selection, or a belt drive resized to restore the fan speed.

docs.title: EC Motor
docs.text:
An electronically commutated (EC) motor uses on-board electronics to control motor speed (FanPedia page 68). It has two main electronic parts: a rectifier, which converts the AC supply to direct current (DC), and a controller, which sends the right amount of current, in the right direction, at the right time, through each winding. That switching builds magnetic poles in the stator, which interact with permanent magnets in the rotor. Because the electronics, not the grid frequency, decide how fast the field turns, speed can be set by a speed controller or by a 0-10 V signal from an outside source such as a building automation system.

FanPedia makes two performance claims for EC motors: they run very efficiently even at reduced speeds, and they have a larger usable turndown range than a traditional speed-controllable motor. Turndown is how far below full speed a motor can usefully run. On page 70, FanPedia also describes Twin City Fan's GridPoint EC motor controller, a plug-and-play device that works with TCF's second-generation EC motors. It switches the motor between constant-speed mode and 0-10 V mode and lets a user view and set the operating speed and maximum speed. One controller can be carried from fan to fan, so a technician can commission several EC packages with the same unit.

docs.title: Worked Example: Setting an EC Fan from a 0-10 V Signal
docs.text:
An illustrative EC fan has its maximum speed set to 1,700 RPM with the GridPoint controller, and for this example the motor is assumed to scale speed linearly with the control signal, so that 10 V means maximum speed. (Check the installation manual for the actual signal mapping of any real motor.)

  1. The building controller sends 6.0 V. Speed is \( 1700 \times 6.0/10 = 1{,}020 \) RPM.
  2. The balancer wants 10 percent more air. Airflow is proportional to speed, so the target speed is \( 1020 \times 1.10 = 1{,}122 \) RPM, which needs \( 10 \times 1122/1700 = 6.6 \) V.
  3. Compare the belt-driven alternative from Chapter 3: there the same 10 percent change means buying and fitting a new sheave. Here it is a change to a number in the controller.
Question Induction motor EC motor What sets its speed? Supply frequency and number of poles, less slip On-board electronics, set by a controller or a 0-10 V signal What is in the rotor? Conductors in which current is induced Permanent magnets How is speed varied? An external drive or a sheave change Built in Code in the motor line IN EC

Who Decides the Speed?

Here is the mental model that sorts every speed question: in an induction motor, the power grid decides the speed and the motor follows it with a little slip; in an EC motor, the electronics decide. Once you ask "who decides the speed?", it is clear why a 50 Hz job changes an induction fan's performance and why an EC fan can be rebalanced from a controller.

docs.title: The Motor Nameplate
docs.text:
The motor nameplate is the metal plate fixed to the motor frame that identifies the motor: its manufacturer, serial number and technical characteristics (FanPedia page 69). It is the authority in the field. When a drawing, a submittal and the installed motor disagree, the nameplate tells you what was actually shipped, and a service call almost always starts with a photo of it.

A nameplate carries the same kinds of information as the motor line on the order: power, speed, electrical supply (phase, frequency and voltage), frame, enclosure, insulation class, service factor and efficiency. FanPedia (page 75) notes that a nameplate with extra information beyond the standard plate can be ordered as a motor modification. The sections that follow explain the frame, insulation, service factor, efficiency and enclosure entries, so that by the end of the chapter every field on the plate has a meaning.

docs.title: NEMA Frame Size
docs.text:
A frame size is a standardized code for a motor's mounting dimensions: shaft height, shaft diameter and length, and the bolt pattern of the feet or face. Two motors of the same frame size from different manufacturers bolt into the same place. In imperial units, frames are standardized by NEMA (the National Electrical Manufacturers Association); metric motors use IEC (International Electrotechnical Commission) frames (FanPedia page 74). Typical NEMA sizes run from 42, 48 and 56 through 143, 145, 182, 184, and on up to 444, 445, 447 and 449, with special large-horsepower sizes such as 5011B beyond that.

Letters after the number describe the frame type. The ones you will see most are listed below.

  • T: the standard post-1964 "T-frame" foot-mount motor (143T, 326T, 444T).
  • C: a face-mounted motor (56C, 184TC); you also need to know whether it has feet.
  • S: a short shaft (284TS, 326TS).
  • U: the older 1952-1964 "U-frame", still seen on some orders.
  • TC: a motor with both feet and a C-face.

FanPedia also lists D (flange mount), Y (special mounting) and Z (special shaft), all rarely seen on fans. So "326T" in the motor line is a 326 frame of the standard T-frame foot-mount type.

Shaft Height Is Hiding in the Frame Number

Here's a shortcut for checking a drawing: on NEMA foot-mounted frames from 143T up, the first two digits divided by 4 give the shaft height in inches, measured from the bottom of the feet. A 326T motor has a shaft height of \( 32/4 = 8 \) inches, and a 184T has \( 18/4 = 4.5 \) inches.

docs.title: Foot Mounted Motor and C-Face Motor Mount
docs.text:
A foot mounted motor is supported by feet cast or welded to the bottom of its frame, which bolt down to a motor base, a slide base or a pedestal. It is the default for belt-driven fans and for most direct-drive arrangements, because the feet can sit on any flat, adjustable surface.

A C-face motor mount uses a machined face on the drive end of the motor, with a pilot and a ring of tapped bolt holes, to bolt the motor directly to a matching face on the fan. The face locates the shaft accurately without shims, so it suits compact direct-drive designs where the motor hangs from the fan. A TC frame has both feet and a C-face.

FanPedia (page 21) shows all three options on the inlet-mounted direct-drive centrifugal fans, Arrangements 4VI and 4HI: a foot mounted motor, a C-face mounted motor, or a foot/C-face combination motor. When you take an order for one of these arrangements, confirm which mounting the fan is drawn for, because a C-face motor without feet cannot be swapped for a foot-mount motor in the field.

docs.title: Insulation Class
docs.text:
The stator windings are copper wires coated with insulation; FanPedia (page 69) describes it as a coat of baked-on varnish around the winding wires. Insulation class is a letter that rates how hot that insulation may run continuously. The classes are A, B, F and H, and the later the letter in the alphabet, the higher the temperature capability. Class A is no longer used by motor manufacturers.

The commonly published NEMA limits for the hottest spot in the winding are Class B 130 °C, Class F 155 °C and Class H 180 °C (Class A was 105 °C). FanPedia notes that the typical fan motor is rated for Class F insulation but is designed for a Class B temperature rise (the climb from ambient temperature to steady running temperature). The gap between the two is thermal margin that extends winding life. Class H insulation is available as an upgrade from the usual Class F (FanPedia page 75); Chapter 15 covers temperature rise and thermal protection in more detail.

docs.title: Motor Service Factor
docs.text:
The service factor (S.F.) is the multiplier above rated horsepower at which a motor may be used (FanPedia page 69). A 100 HP motor with a 1.15 service factor may be run at 115 HP. Other common values are 1.25 and 1.0, and 1.0 applies when the motor is operated on a variable frequency drive (VFD).

Chapter 3 showed the basic check: the fan's brake horsepower (BHP) at the design point should be at or below the nameplate horsepower, and the service factor is a margin, not extra capacity to plan around. Running in the service factor means running hotter, which spends the insulation's thermal margin. The case where engineers get caught is not the design point at all but a condition the fan passes through, such as a cold start on a hot-gas fan.

docs.title: Worked Example: The Cold Start That Overloads the Motor
docs.text:
An illustrative fan exhausts air at 200 °F. At that temperature its selection shows 7.0 BHP, and the submittal proposes a 7-1/2 HP motor with a 1.15 service factor.

  1. At operating temperature, \( 7.0 \le 7.5 \) HP. The motor looks right.
  2. At startup the fan is full of 70 °F air. From Chapter 2, density varies inversely with absolute temperature, so the cold air is denser by \( (200 + 460)/(70 + 460) = 660/530 = 1.245 \).
  3. Fan power is proportional to density at the same speed and airflow, so cold BHP is \( 7.0 \times 1.245 = 8.7 \) BHP.
  4. The most the motor may carry is \( 7.5 \times 1.15 = 8.6 \) HP. The cold-start load is above even the service-factor limit, and on a VFD (service factor 1.0) the limit is only 7.5 HP.

Result: choose a 10 HP motor, or reduce the load during warm-up, for example with a damper. The motor must be sized for the worst condition the fan will see, not the design temperature alone.

docs.title: Motor Efficiency Class
docs.text:
Motor efficiency is the ratio of the useful work a motor delivers to the electrical energy it takes in (FanPedia page 71). The rest becomes heat in the windings, core and bearings. An efficiency class is a named band of minimum efficiencies that a motor must meet.

FanPedia (page 72) gives two families of names. Twin City Fan designates motors Standard Efficiency (comparable to NEMA High Efficiency) or Premium Efficiency (comparable to NEMA Premium Efficiency). Worldwide, IEC classes are IE1 (standard), IE2 (high, comparable to TCF Standard), IE3 (premium, comparable to TCF Premium) and IE4 (super premium, listed by FanPedia as a future designation). The "P" in the motor line is this field: Premium Efficiency.

TCF designation NEMA equivalent IEC equivalent Standard Efficiency NEMA High Efficiency IE2 Premium Efficiency NEMA Premium Efficiency IE3 (not used) (not used) IE4, super premium

Load matters as much as class. FanPedia notes that most motors are designed to run at 50 to 100 percent of rated load, with peak efficiency near 75 percent; a 10 HP motor therefore has an acceptable load range of 5 to 10 HP and peaks around 7.5 HP. Efficiency drops sharply below about half load, so a badly oversized motor wastes energy even if its class is premium.

docs.title: Worked Example: What Two Points of Efficiency Are Worth
docs.text:
A fan draws 40 BHP and runs 6,000 hours a year. Compare two illustrative full-load efficiencies, 93.0 percent and 95.0 percent, at an illustrative electricity price of $0.10 per kWh.

  1. Shaft power: \( 40 \times 0.7457 = 29.8 \) kW (FanPedia's conversion, kW = HP × 0.7457).
  2. Electrical input: \( 29.8/0.930 = 32.1 \) kW versus \( 29.8/0.950 = 31.4 \) kW, a difference of about 0.67 kW.
  3. Annual energy: \( 0.67 \times 6000 = 4{,}020 \) kWh, or about $400 a year.

Over a motor life of many years, that difference usually pays for the more efficient motor, which is why specifications often require premium efficiency. Use the real efficiencies from the motor data sheet when you run this for a customer.

docs.title: Motor Enclosures
docs.text:
A motor enclosure is the casing style around the internal rotating parts of the motor (FanPedia page 71). It decides two things at once: how the motor gets rid of its heat, and how well the windings are protected from whatever is in the surrounding air. FanPedia (page 73) lists five enclosures used by Twin City Fan: ODP, TEFC, explosion proof, TEAO and TENV. The enclosure field in the motor line above is "TEFC".

Two ideas tie the enclosure to its neighbors on the order. Intended duty describes the operating environment the motor is built for: GD (general duty) for normal, clean and cool air; SD (severe duty) and IEEE 841 for process industries; and DFG for explosion-proof motors in hazardous locations (FanPedia page 73; Chapter 15 covers duty in depth). The IP rating is the international (IEC) code for protection against solids and water; the higher the two digits, the better sealed the motor. FanPedia maps each NEMA enclosure to the IP ratings and duties that go with it, which matters when a specification is written in metric terms.

docs.title: ODP Motor
docs.text: An open drip proof (ODP) motor has an internal fan that pulls air in, blows it across the windings inside the motor, and lets it exit opposite the drive end (FanPedia page 73). The surrounding air passes directly over the windings, which makes ODP motors cool well and cost less. The openings face downward or are shielded so that water dripping from above at a modest angle does not fall in, which is where the name comes from. The same openings let in anything carried by the air, so FanPedia states plainly that ODP motors should not be used in dirty or wet atmospheres. The metric equivalent is IP22, and the duty is general duty.

docs.title: Worked Example: Is ODP Acceptable Here?
docs.text:
A contractor asks for ODP motors on two belt-driven Arrangement 9 fans to save money.

  1. Fan A is a supply fan in a clean, dry, indoor mechanical room. The air around the motor is the clean, cool air that general duty assumes. ODP is acceptable.
  2. Fan B is a rooftop exhaust fan whose motor sits outside under the weather, exposed to rain and blowing dust. That is both a wet and a dirty atmosphere, and the ODP motor would draw both through its windings. ODP is not acceptable; Fan B needs a totally enclosed motor.
  3. Record the reason on the quote, so that the substitution is not made later on Fan B to match Fan A.

docs.title: TEFC Motor
docs.text:
A totally enclosed fan cooled (TEFC) motor keeps the windings sealed inside the frame. An external fan on the back of the shaft pulls air in through the fan cover and blows it over the outside surface of the motor only (FanPedia page 73); the ribs on a TEFC frame give that air more surface to carry heat away. Because outside air never touches the windings, TEFC is the usual choice for dirty, damp or outdoor locations, and it is the most common enclosure on industrial fans.

TEFC covers a wide range of protection. FanPedia's table maps TEFC to IP44, IP54, IP55 and IP56, and to general duty, severe duty, IEEE 45 (marine) and IEEE 841 duty at the higher ratings.

docs.title: Worked Example: A Specification Written in IP Ratings
docs.text:
A European consultant's specification calls for "IP55 motors, general purpose, non-hazardous area" on a TCF fan.

  1. Find IP55 in the FanPedia table: it maps to TEFC with general or severe duty, and also to the explosion-proof enclosure.
  2. The area is non-hazardous, so the explosion-proof enclosure is not needed and would add cost.
  3. The motor line becomes "... GD, TEFC ...". If a later revision raises the requirement to IP56 for a marine installation, the table points to TEFC with IEEE 45 duty instead.

docs.title: TEAO Motor
docs.text: A totally enclosed air over (TEAO) motor is sealed like a TEFC motor but has no cooling fan of its own. It relies on the fan's own airstream for cooling: FanPedia (page 73) describes it as a motor in the air stream of the fan, either with the impeller mounted on the motor shaft or placed in the air stream of a belt-driven fan or blower. Direct-drive axial and inline fans, where the motor sits inside the housing, are the typical case. The catch is that a TEAO motor is only cooled while air is moving over it, so it suits fans that always run with airflow, not ones that may run against a closed damper.

docs.title: TENV Motor
docs.text: A totally enclosed non-ventilated (TENV) motor has no cooling fan at all, inside or outside. It dissipates its heat through the frame and body of the motor only (FanPedia page 73). Without forced cooling, a TENV motor runs hotter and usually needs a larger frame than a standard motor of the same horsepower. It is chosen when an external fan or fan cover would be a problem, for example where lint or fibers would clog a fan cover, and the larger frame is acceptable. FanPedia maps TENV to IP56 with general or severe duty.

docs.title: Explosion Proof Motor
docs.text: An explosion proof (EXPL) motor has an external fan that helps cool it, like a TEFC motor, but its internal parts are engineered so that an arc or explosion inside the motor cannot ignite a dangerous surrounding atmosphere containing flammable dust or gas (FanPedia page 73). Its intended duty code is DFG, and the hazardous location it is built for is specified under the National Electrical Code (NEC) by group number. FanPedia lists the groups TCF commonly sees as Group D (gases), Group F and Group G (dusts, with Group G covering food-industry dusts), and refers to the NEC for full definitions along with class and division ratings. FanPedia also notes that ATEX applications, the European system for explosive atmospheres, require a special motor.

docs.title: Worked Example: Exhaust from a Paint Spray Room
docs.text:
A customer needs an exhaust fan for a room where solvent-based paint is sprayed. The plant's engineer has classified the area around the fan as a hazardous location for flammable vapors.

  1. The motor sits inside the classified area, so it needs an explosion-proof enclosure with DFG duty for the stated gas group. Ask the customer for the class, division and group in writing; the classification is theirs to make, not the fan supplier's.
  2. Ask what is in the airstream. Solvent vapor passes through the fan itself, so the fan also needs spark resistant construction (Chapter 20), and a belt-driven arrangement such as Arrangement 9 keeps the motor and bearings out of the airstream.
  3. If the job is in Europe under ATEX, flag that a special motor is required and do not substitute a standard EXPL motor.

An Explosion Proof Motor Does Not Make a Spark Resistant Fan

A common trap is to order an EXPL motor and assume the whole fan is now safe for flammable air. The motor enclosure only protects against ignition from inside the motor; a rubbing impeller or a dropped tool can still strike a spark in the housing. Whenever the motor needs EXPL, check the airstream separately and add spark resistant construction when the gas or dust passes through the fan.

docs.title: Comparing the Five Enclosures
docs.text:
The table below summarizes the five enclosures just described, using the cooling method and protection each one offers.

Enclosure How it is cooled Windings exposed to outside air? IP ratings per FanPedia Typical use ODP Internal fan blows room air across the windings Yes IP22 Clean, dry, indoor locations TEFC External fan blows air over the frame No IP44, IP54, IP55, IP56 Dirty, damp or outdoor locations; most industrial fans TEAO The fan's own airstream flows over the frame No (not listed) Motors inside the airstream of direct-drive axial and inline fans TENV Heat leaves through the frame only No IP56 Where a cooling fan is a problem; larger frame accepted EXPL External fan; interior built to contain ignition No IP55 NEC-classified hazardous locations (DFG duty)

Two Questions Settle Most Enclosure Choices

If five enclosures, several IP codes and a handful of duty codes feel like a lot to hold at once, that is normal; most people need a few real orders before it sticks. Reduce it to two questions you already know how to ask: is the area classified as hazardous, and what is in the air around the motor? Then try the sorter below and see how many jobs those two questions decide.

The interactive sorter below lets you practice the choice on ten job descriptions drawn from the cases in this section.

docs.title: Diagram: Motor Enclosure Selector
docs.text:
Motor Enclosure Selector

Type: microsim sim-id: ch14-motor-enclosure-selector Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Evaluate Bloom Verb: recommend Learning Objective: The learner will recommend a motor enclosure (ODP, TEFC, TEAO, TENV or EXPL) for each of ten described fan jobs, with at least 8 of 10 first-attempt choices falling in the accepted set.

Prerequisites: motor enclosure, ODP, TEFC, TEAO, TENV and explosion proof motors, intended duty (GD, SD, IEEE 841, IEEE 45, DFG), IP rating, hazardous location (all defined in the "Motor Enclosures" section above).

Evidence of Mastery: For each of the ten jobs, the learner commits one enclosure choice before any feedback is shown. A choice is correct when it is in the item's Accepted set in the Content table. Mastery is 8 or more of 10 correct on the first attempt. Reading the enclosure reference cards is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) ODP is fine anywhere indoors, even in dirty or wet air. (2) An explosion-proof motor is needed whenever the air is dirty. (3) A TEAO motor cools itself the way a TEFC motor does. (4) IP55 always means explosion proof. (5) TENV is simply a better TEFC with no downside.

Instructional Rationale: Evaluate-level judgment needs the learner to weigh job conditions against criteria and commit to a recommendation, then see the reason; a sorter with committed choices and reasoned feedback produces that evidence, where a reference table alone would only support recall.

Content:

Five enclosure reference cards the learner may open at any time:

  • ODP: internal fan blows surrounding air across the windings; not for dirty or wet atmospheres; IP22; general duty.
  • TEFC: sealed windings; external fan blows air over the frame; IP44, IP54, IP55, IP56; general duty, severe duty, IEEE 45, IEEE 841.
  • TEAO: sealed, no fan of its own; cooled by the fan's airstream, with the motor in the air stream.
  • TENV: sealed, no fan; heat leaves through the frame only; runs hotter; usually a larger frame; IP56.
  • EXPL: external fan; interior built so an internal arc or explosion cannot ignite a flammable surrounding atmosphere; DFG duty; NEC group; IP55.

Ten jobs, shown in this order:

# Job description shown to the learner Accepted Why (shown as feedback) 1 Belt-driven Arrangement 9 supply fan; motor in a clean, dry, indoor mechanical room. ODP, TEFC The air around the motor is clean and dry, so ODP is acceptable; TEFC also works but is not required. 2 Belt-driven exhaust fan on a roof; motor exposed to rain and blowing dust. TEFC Wet and dirty air would pass through an ODP motor's windings; TEFC keeps the windings sealed. 3 Direct-drive vaneaxial fan; motor inside the housing, cooled by the air the fan moves. TEAO A motor in the fan's own airstream is cooled by that air, which is what TEAO is built for. 4 Belt-driven fan whose motor is mounted in the fan's air stream. TEAO FanPedia lists the air stream of a belt-driven fan or blower as a TEAO location. 5 Textile plant where lint would clog an external fan cover; the customer accepts a larger frame. TENV TENV has no fan or fan cover to clog; the cost is a hotter motor in a larger frame. 6 Exhaust from a solvent paint spray room; the area around the motor is classified for flammable gases and vapors. EXPL A classified hazardous location for gases needs an explosion-proof (DFG) motor for its NEC group. 7 Grain-handling area classified as a hazardous location for combustible dust. EXPL Combustible dust locations are NEC hazardous locations; the motor must be explosion proof for the dust group. 8 Paper mill process fan; the specification calls for IEEE 841 motors. TEFC FanPedia maps IEEE 841 duty to the TEFC enclosure (IP56). 9 Metric specification: IP55, general purpose, non-hazardous area. TEFC IP55 maps to TEFC or EXPL; with no hazardous location, TEFC is the right choice and EXPL adds needless cost. 10 Metric specification: IP22, clean indoor location. ODP IP22 is the metric equivalent of ODP in FanPedia's table.

Provenance: Enclosure descriptions, IP ratings and duty mappings from FanPedia, page 73 (Motor Specifications: Enclosure and Intended Duty). Jobs 1, 2, 6 and 9 match the worked examples in this chapter's "Motor Enclosures" section. Jobs are illustrative scenarios and must be labeled "illustrative jobs".

Rules: One choice per job from the five enclosures. A first-attempt choice is correct when it is in the Accepted set. Job 1 accepts two answers; when the learner picks TEFC on job 1, the sim marks it correct and adds "ODP would also have been acceptable here." The score counts first-attempt correct choices only; 8 or more of 10 is mastery.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner reads job 1 and may open any enclosure reference card.
  2. The learner commits an enclosure. Feedback appears and the job is marked correct or incorrect.
  3. If incorrect, the learner chooses again until correct; later attempts do not change the score.
  4. The learner advances to the next job; jobs cannot be revisited once answered.
  5. After job 10, a summary lists each job, the learner's first choice, and the accepted answer.

Feedback: Ten jobs, fixed order, unlimited attempts per job, only the first attempt scored. Correct: "Correct: " followed by that job's Why text. Incorrect: "Not this one. Reread the job and the card for the enclosure you chose, then try again." The Why text is shown only once the learner reaches the correct choice. The accepted answer is revealed after the learner's correct choice. A running count "First-try correct: n of 10" is shown, and the summary states whether mastery (8 of 10) was reached.

Starting State: Job 1 is shown with the five enclosure choices and all reference cards closed. The prompt reads "Which motor enclosure would you recommend for this job?"

Chapter Anchors: Five enclosures (ODP, TEFC, TEAO, TENV, EXPL); ten jobs; mastery 8 of 10; ODP equals IP22; IEEE 841 and IEEE 45 map to TEFC; IP55 maps to TEFC or EXPL; ATEX requires a special motor (prose only, not a sim job).

docs.title: Conduit Box
docs.text:
The conduit box is the motor's power connection point: a small enclosure on the side or top of the frame where the supply wiring, run in conduit, connects to the motor leads (FanPedia page 69). Its location is named looking from the drive side of the motor, at the shaft: F1 and F2 are the two side locations and F3 is on top. FanPedia (page 75) gives F1 or F3 as standard on NEMA motors; F2 is standard on IEC frames but is a special modification for NEMA.

The conduit box location matters because it has to clear the fan. On centrifugal fans with motor position L, FanPedia (page 52) says the motor is normally ordered with an F1 conduit box, and F2 is selected if there are clearance issues; some swingout arrangements must have F2 (page 53). Chapter 13 covers conduit box positions with the motor position codes. Related options include extended leads (48 inches is standard) and an externally mounted conduit box at the cable opening outside the fan (FanPedia page 75), which is useful when the motor sits inside the housing.

docs.title: Shaft Grounding Ring
docs.text:
A variable frequency drive (VFD) varies motor speed by switching the supply voltage on and off very rapidly. That fast switching can induce a voltage on the motor shaft. The charge builds until it discharges to ground through the easiest path, which is usually across the thin film of grease in the motor bearings. Each discharge burns a tiny pit in the bearing race; over months, millions of them leave a washboard pattern called fluting, and the bearing becomes noisy and fails early. FanPedia (page 72) notes that precautions may be needed against these shaft currents, citing NEMA MG-1 Part 31.

A shaft grounding ring is a ring of conductive fibers mounted around the motor shaft that gives those charges a low-resistance path to ground, so they bypass the bearings. FanPedia (page 75) lists it as a motor modification designed to protect motor bearings from electrical charges induced by a VFD, available in internal and external versions. The related option is insulated bearings, whose outer race is coated with insulating material to block the current path through the bearing.

docs.title: Worked Example: Adding a VFD to an Existing Fan
docs.text:
A plant wants to add a VFD to a 40 HP fan that has run across the line for years. The order review goes like this.

  1. Check the load against the new service factor. On a VFD the service factor is 1.0 (FanPedia page 69), so the fan's maximum BHP must now be at or below 40, not 46.
  2. Protect the bearings. The existing motor has no shaft grounding ring, so quote one, internal or external depending on the motor, and ask the motor supplier whether insulated bearings are recommended for this frame.
  3. Check the motor's suitability for inverter use; Chapter 15 covers inverter-duty motors.
  4. Record that the VFD was added, so a later bearing failure is investigated for shaft current rather than blamed on lubrication alone.

Electricity Takes the Easy Path

Notice that a shaft grounding ring does not stop shaft voltage; it gives the charge an easier way home than through the bearing. Insulated bearings work from the other side by making the bearing a harder path. Think of the two as "open a better path" and "close the bad one".

docs.title: Motor Bases and Mounting on the Fan
Motor Base
docs.text:
A motor base is the structure that supports the motor on the fan or its base and, on a belt drive, lets the motor move to set belt tension and alignment. The base type depends on the fan type and on the motor's frame size. FanPedia (pages 76 to 78) groups them as follows; Chapter 15 covers their adjustment hardware in detail.

  • NEMA type slide base: for motors from 48 to 445 frame, on Arrangements 1, 3, 9, 9F, 9H and 9ST, plenum fans and pedestal plug fans.
  • Heavy-duty slide rails: two rails per motor, for very large 440, 500 and 5000 series frames.
  • Automotive pivot base: used mostly in automotive applications, on Arrangement 9H, 9SS swingout and specially mounted Arrangement 3 fans.
  • Adjustable bases, standard post mount: 48 to 215 frame; on tubular centrifugal and axial fans (Arrangement 9) and plenum and plug fans; saddle or flat mount.
  • Adjustable bases, pivot/bolted design: 254 to 445 frame; saddle or flat mount.
  • Bolt-on mount: 48 to 286 frame; saddle mount; on tubeaxial, vaneaxial and centaxial fans in Arrangement 9.

docs.title: Worked Example: Matching the Base to the Motor
docs.text:
Three belt-driven fans on one job each need a motor base.

  1. An Arrangement 1 centrifugal fan with a 326T motor: the NEMA slide base covers 48 to 445 frame on Arrangement 1, so 326T fits.
  2. An Arrangement 9 tubular centrifugal fan with a 256T motor: the standard post-mount adjustable base stops at 215 frame, so use the pivot/bolted design, which covers 254 to 445.
  3. An Arrangement 9 vaneaxial fan with a 184T motor: the bolt-on mount covers 48 to 286 frame on vaneaxial fans and uses a saddle to sit on the round housing.

If the motor size changes during submittal review, for example from 215T to 254T, recheck the base: the change crosses the line between the post-mount and pivot/bolted designs.

docs.title: Motor Base Saddle
docs.text: A motor base saddle is the curved support that lets a motor base sit on a round fan housing. Tubeaxial, vaneaxial and inline fans have cylindrical housings, so a flat base cannot bolt directly to them; the saddle is shaped to the housing's curve on one side and carries the flat motor base on the other. FanPedia's exploded views of belt-driven tubeaxial, vaneaxial and inline centrifugal and mixed flow fans label it on each (pages 15 to 17), and the adjustable bases on page 78 are offered as either "saddle mount" or "flat mount", the flat version being for fans with flat mounting surfaces.

docs.title: K Mount Motor
docs.text: A K mount motor, also known as a piggyback or scroll mounted motor, is mounted directly on the scroll of a centrifugal fan's housing rather than on the floor or a separate base (FanPedia page 54). It uses an adjustable motor base (post mount or pivot/bolted design) and is used on SWSI and DWDI Arrangement 3 fans. Because the motor rides on the curved scroll, its location is described by a clock position around the housing; FanPedia shows positions such as 9, 10:30, 12, 1:30 and 3 o'clock for upblast (UBD), top horizontal (THD), downblast (DBD) and bottom horizontal (BHD) discharges. A K mount keeps the motor and fan together as one compact assembly instead of placing the motor on the floor beside the fan.

docs.title: Reading the Whole Motor Line
docs.text:
Every field of the motor line from the start of the chapter now has a meaning. The table below decodes it in order.

Field Meaning Section 50 HP Rated power: 50 horsepower (about 37 kW) Motor Service Factor 1800 RPM Synchronous speed; a four-pole motor at 60 Hz Induction Motor IN Technology: induction (the alternative is EC) Two Motor Technologies P Efficiency: TCF Premium Efficiency, comparable to NEMA Premium and IE3 Motor Efficiency Class 3 Phase, 60 Frequency, 460 Volt Electrical supply Motor Nameplate SD Intended duty: severe duty Motor Enclosures TEFC Enclosure: totally enclosed fan cooled TEFC Motor 326T NEMA 326 frame, standard T-frame foot mount; 8-inch shaft height NEMA Frame Size

The interactive decoder below asks you to predict each field's meaning before it is revealed.

docs.title: Diagram: Motor Line Decoder
docs.text:
Motor Line Decoder

Type: infographic sim-id: ch14-motor-line-decoder Library: html Status: Specified Bloom Level: Understand Bloom Verb: interpret Learning Objective: The learner will interpret each of the ten fields of a Twin City Fan motor specification line, choosing the correct meaning for at least 8 of 10 fields on the first attempt.

Prerequisites: horsepower, synchronous speed, poles, induction and EC technology, efficiency class, phase, frequency, voltage, intended duty, motor enclosure, NEMA frame size and frame letters (all defined in this chapter above this block).

Evidence of Mastery: For each of the ten fields, the learner picks one of four meanings before the field's explanation is revealed. A pick is correct when it matches the Correct meaning column. Mastery is 8 or more of 10 correct on the first attempt. Opening a field's explanation after answering is exploration.

Misconceptions: (1) "1800 RPM" is the exact running speed (it is the synchronous speed; the motor runs slightly slower). (2) "P" means phase. (3) "SD" means standard duty. (4) "T" in 326T means TEFC. (5) "60 Frequency" is a speed.

Instructional Rationale: Interpreting a coded line is an Understand task; asking the learner to predict each field's meaning before it is revealed makes them retrieve the definition rather than read it, and the field-by-field structure keeps the concrete string visible at every step.

Content: The motor line shown in full: "50 HP, 1800 RPM, IN, P, 3 Phase, 60 Frequency, 460 Volt, SD, TEFC, 326T". Ten fields, in order:

# Field Four choices (correct first here; shuffle when shown) Correct meaning Explanation revealed 1 50 HP Rated power 50 horsepower / Fan brake horsepower at design / Service-factor limit / Motor weight class Rated power 50 horsepower Rated output power; about 37 kW using kW = HP × 0.7457. 2 1800 RPM Synchronous speed of a 4-pole 60 Hz motor / Exact full-load speed / Fan speed on a belt drive / Maximum safe speed Synchronous speed of a 4-pole 60 Hz motor \( 120 \times 60 / 4 = 1800 \); the motor runs slightly slower because of slip. 3 IN Induction technology / Insulated bearings / Indoor use only / Inverter duty Induction technology The technology field is IN (induction) or EC (electronically commutated). 4 P Premium Efficiency / Phase / Pivot base / Piggyback mount Premium Efficiency TCF Premium Efficiency is comparable to NEMA Premium and IEC IE3. 5 3 Phase Three-phase AC supply / Three poles / Three-speed motor / Third efficiency tier Three-phase AC supply Part of the electric power field: phase. 6 60 Frequency 60 Hz supply frequency / 60 percent load / 60 °C rise / 60-minute rating 60 Hz supply frequency Part of the electric power field: frequency (cycles per second). 7 460 Volt 460 V supply voltage / 460 W input / 460 RPM / 460 frame 460 V supply voltage Part of the electric power field: voltage. 8 SD Severe Duty / Standard Duty / Single Drive / Slide base Severe Duty Intended duty; GD is general duty, DFG is explosion proof. 9 TEFC Totally enclosed fan cooled / Totally enclosed, fan cover removed / Temperature-rated, fully certified / Thermally protected Totally enclosed fan cooled Sealed windings; an external fan blows air over the frame. 10 326T NEMA 326 frame, T-frame foot mount / 326 lb motor / TEFC frame 326 / 32.6 kW rating NEMA 326 frame, T-frame foot mount Shaft height is 32/4 = 8 inches from the bottom of the feet.

Provenance: The motor line and the field categories are from FanPedia, page 71 (Typical Motor Specifications). Efficiency mapping from page 72; enclosure and duty from page 73; frame letters from page 74. The shaft-height rule is the standard NEMA relationship for foot-mounted frames from 143T up. Distractor choices are illustrative and must not be presented as real codes.

Rules: Ten fields in fixed order. Each field shows four choices in shuffled order. A first pick is correct when it equals the Correct meaning. Score counts first picks only; 8 or more of 10 is mastery.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner sees the full motor line with field 1 highlighted and its four choices.
  2. The learner picks a meaning. The explanation for that field is revealed with the correct meaning marked.
  3. The learner advances to the next field; the decoded meaning stays visible under that field of the line.
  4. After field 10, the whole line is shown decoded, with the learner's first-try score.

Feedback: Ten fields, fixed order, one scored attempt each. Correct: "Correct: " plus the Explanation revealed. Incorrect: "Not quite: " plus the Explanation revealed and, for the misconception choices, a one-line note (choice "Exact full-load speed" on field 2: "Induction motors run slightly below synchronous speed because of slip."; choice "Phase" on field 4: "Phase appears later as 3 Phase; P here is efficiency."; choice "Standard Duty" on field 8: "General duty is GD; SD is severe duty."; choice "TEFC frame 326" on field 10: "T marks the standard T-frame foot mount, not the enclosure."; choice "60 percent load" on field 6: "Frequency is the supply's cycles per second, 60 Hz."). A running count "First-try correct: n of 10" is shown.

Starting State: The motor line is shown with no meanings, field 1 highlighted, and the question "What does 50 HP tell you about this motor?"

Chapter Anchors: The line "50 HP, 1800 RPM, IN, P, 3 Phase, 60 Frequency, 460 Volt, SD, TEFC, 326T"; 50 HP is about 37 kW; 1800 RPM is a four-pole motor at 60 Hz; P is Premium Efficiency; SD is severe duty; 326T has an 8-inch shaft height; ten fields; mastery 8 of 10.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• An induction motor runs a little below its synchronous speed, \( N_s = 120f/p \), so the supply frequency sets fan speed on a direct drive; an EC motor sets its own speed electronically from a controller or a 0-10 V signal.
  • The motor nameplate is the field authority for what was shipped; the motor line on the order lists power, speed, technology, efficiency, electrical supply, duty, enclosure and frame.
  • A NEMA frame size standardizes mounting dimensions; the letters after the number (T, C, S, U, TC) describe the frame type. Motors are foot mounted, C-face mounted, or both.
  • Insulation class (B, F, H) rates winding temperature; fan motors typically have Class F insulation with a Class B rise. Service factor is margin, not capacity, and drops to 1.0 on a VFD. Check the worst operating condition, such as a cold start.
  • TCF efficiency classes are Standard (NEMA High, IE2) and Premium (NEMA Premium, IE3); efficiency peaks near 75 percent load.
  • The motor enclosure sets cooling and protection: ODP for clean, dry air; TEFC for dirty, damp or outdoor locations; TEAO in the fan's airstream; TENV with no fan; explosion proof for NEC-classified hazardous locations, which still requires a separate check of the fan's own spark resistance.
  • The conduit box location (F1, F2, F3) must clear the fan; a shaft grounding ring protects motor bearings from VFD-induced shaft currents.
  • A motor base is chosen by fan type and frame size; a motor base saddle seats it on a round housing; a K mount motor rides on the scroll of an Arrangement 3 centrifugal fan.

You Can Read the Motor Line

You can now take a line like "50 HP, 1800 RPM, IN, P, 3 Phase, 60 Frequency, 460 Volt, SD, TEFC, 326T", say what every field means, and decide whether that enclosure belongs on the job site in front of you. That is the skill behind every motor question on a quote.

docs.title: Motor Ratings, Speed Control and Positioners
Summary
docs.text: This chapter covers motor ratings and features beyond the basics: intended duty, premium efficiency, voltage and phase, synchronous speed, temperature rise, thermal protection, and winding RTDs; severe duty, hazardous location, and inverter-duty motors; and variable frequency drives for speed control. It then covers how motors are mounted and adjusted: slide bases, pivot bases, post mount bases, and bi-directional, tri-directional, and jack-screw motor positioners. After completing it, readers can specify a motor's ratings and mounting for a belt-driven fan.

docs.title: Concepts Covered
docs.text:
This chapter covers the following 18 concepts from the learning graph:

Concept Concept Impact Score Motor Winding RTD 2 Variable Frequency Drive 69 Motor Positioner 5 Motor Intended Duty 51 Premium Efficiency Motor 25 Motor Voltage and Phase 2 Motor Temperature Rise 2 Bi-Directional Positioner 1 Tri-Directional Positioner 1 Vertical Jack Screws 1 Severe Duty Motor 25 Hazardous Location Motor 25 Synchronous Motor Speed 1 Motor Thermal Protection 1 Inverter-Duty Motor 25 Post Mount Motor Base 1 Slide Base 6 Pivot Motor Base 3

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
This chapter builds on concepts from:

  • Chapter 1: Air, Pressure and the Fan
  • Chapter 2: Airstreams, Total Pressure and Standard Air
  • Chapter 3: Basic Fan Anatomy
  • Chapter 5: Roof, Wall and Specialty Exhaust Fans
  • Chapter 11: Drives and Standard Fan Arrangements
  • Chapter 14: Fan Motors and Enclosures

The Rest of the Motor Line

A motor line on an order is short, but every field on it decides whether the fan starts, survives its environment and stays aligned. By the end of this chapter you will be able to write that line for a belt-driven fan, choose how the motor is mounted and adjusted, and explain each choice to a customer or a plant electrician. Let's follow the airflow.

Chapter 14 introduced the motor itself: induction and EC technology, horsepower, enclosure, frame size, service factor, insulation class and efficiency class. This chapter finishes the job. FanPedia gives a typical motor specification as a single line (FanPedia p. 71):

50 HP, 1800 RPM, IN, P, 3 Phase, 60 Frequency, 460 Volt, SD, TEFC, 326T

You already know how to read the horsepower, the technology code (IN for induction), the enclosure (TEFC) and the frame (326T). The remaining fields are the subject of the first half of this chapter: the speed (1800 RPM), the efficiency designation (P for premium), the electric power (phase, frequency and voltage), and the intended duty (SD for severe duty). Along the way we add the ratings and protective devices that keep a motor from overheating, and the variable frequency drive that lets a fixed-speed motor run at other speeds. The second half turns to the hardware that holds the motor on a belt-driven fan: slide bases, pivot bases, post mounts and positioners.

The table below lines up each field of the FanPedia example with the section of this book that explains it, so you can see where the gaps are before we fill them.

Field in the example Meaning Where it is covered 50 HP Rated power Chapter 14 1800 RPM Synchronous speed This chapter IN Induction technology Chapter 14 P Premium efficiency This chapter 3 Phase, 60 Frequency, 460 Volt Electric power This chapter SD Intended duty: severe duty This chapter TEFC Enclosure Chapter 14 326T NEMA frame size Chapter 14

docs.title: Synchronous Motor Speed
docs.text:
An induction motor's stator windings create a magnetic field that rotates around the motor. The speed of that rotating field is the synchronous motor speed, and it depends on only two things: the frequency of the power supply in hertz (Hz, cycles per second) and the number of magnetic poles wound into the stator. Poles always come in pairs, so a motor has 2, 4, 6 or 8 poles, and so on.

\[ n_s = \frac{120 \times f}{p} \]

where:

  • \( n_s \) is the synchronous speed in revolutions per minute (RPM)
  • \( f \) is the supply frequency in Hz
  • \( p \) is the number of poles

A 4-pole motor on 60 Hz power runs its field at \( 120 \times 60 / 4 = 1800 \) RPM, which is the "1800 RPM" in the FanPedia example. The same motor on 50 Hz power would run at 1500 RPM. FanPedia lists the typical synchronous speeds by frequency (FanPedia p. 71):

Poles 60 Hz 50 Hz 2 3600 RPM 3000 RPM 4 1800 RPM 1500 RPM 6 1200 RPM 1000 RPM 8 900 RPM 750 RPM

The rotor of an induction motor always turns a little slower than its field. That small difference, called slip, is what induces current in the rotor and produces torque. This is why a motor ordered as "1800 RPM" shows a somewhat lower full-load speed on its nameplate, and FanPedia notes that actual nominal motor speeds vary by motor horsepower and manufacturer. On an order, the motor speed is stated as the synchronous speed; the fan selection uses the actual operating speed.

docs.title: Motor Voltage and Phase
docs.text:
The electric power line of a motor specification has three parts. Phase is single phase (one alternating voltage, common in small commercial equipment) or three phase (three alternating voltages offset in time, the standard for industrial motors). Frequency is 60 Hz in North America and 50 Hz in much of the rest of the world. Voltage is the nominal supply voltage at the motor terminals. The fan industry generally uses AC power for induction motors, and DC power for EC motors and some light commercial accessories and damper motors (FanPedia p. 72).

FanPedia lists the common combinations (FanPedia p. 72):

Power Phase Frequency Voltages AC Single 60 Hz 115, 230 or 277 AC Single 50 Hz 220 or 240 AC Three 60 Hz 200, 208, 230, 400, 440, 460, 575, 2300, 4160 or 4300 AC Three 50 Hz 190, 380, 415 or 4000 DC – – 12, 24, 28, 36, 48, 72, 90, 150, 180, 240, 300 or 500

Many motors are dual voltage, such as 115/230, 208/230 or 230/460, and can be wired for either. That flexibility creates a trap on orders with electrical add-ons, which the next note explains.

A Dual-Voltage Motor Still Needs One Voltage

It is tempting to write "230/460 V" on an order and let the field decide, but a disconnect switch or speed controller supplied with the fan is built for one voltage. FanPedia says the customer needs to state the actual voltage the fan will use whenever the motor has add-ons (FanPedia p. 72). Ask for the site voltage before you release the order, not after the equipment arrives.

docs.title: Premium Efficiency Motor
docs.text:
Motor efficiency is the ratio of the useful shaft power a motor delivers to the electrical power it draws; the difference leaves the motor as heat. Chapter 14 introduced efficiency classes in general. Twin City Fan uses two designations based on the NEMA classifications (FanPedia p. 72):

  • Standard Efficiency, which compares to NEMA High Efficiency (and to IEC IE2)
  • Premium Efficiency, which compares to NEMA Premium Efficiency (and to IEC IE3)

A premium efficiency motor is therefore the "P" in the example line: a motor built with more and better active material (copper, electrical steel) so that less of its input becomes heat. FanPedia also notes that IE1 is the IEC standard-efficiency level and that IE4 (super premium) is a future designation not currently used.

Efficiency also depends on how heavily the motor is loaded. FanPedia states that most motors are designed to run at 50% to 100% of rated load, that maximum efficiency is usually near 75% of rated load, and that efficiency drops sharply below about 50% load. A 10 HP motor therefore has an acceptable load range of 5 to 10 HP, with peak efficiency near 7.5 HP (FanPedia p. 72). An oversized premium motor running at 30% load can waste more energy than a correctly sized standard motor.

Worked example: what does "P" buy? A belt-driven fan needs 20 brake horsepower (bhp) at its duty point and runs 6,000 hours a year. The selection uses a 25 HP motor, so the motor runs at \( 20 / 25 = 80\% \) load, inside the 50% to 100% band and close to the peak-efficiency point. For this illustration, assume the standard efficiency motor is 92.4% efficient at this load and the premium motor is 93.6% (illustrative values; real values come from the motor data sheet).

  1. Convert the shaft power to kilowatts: \( 20 \times 0.7457 = 14.91 \) kW.
  2. Electrical input, standard motor: \( 14.91 / 0.924 = 16.14 \) kW.
  3. Electrical input, premium motor: \( 14.91 / 0.936 = 15.93 \) kW.
  4. Difference: \( 16.14 - 15.93 = 0.21 \) kW.
  5. Annual energy saved: \( 0.21 \times 6000 \approx 1{,}240 \) kWh per year.

At an illustrative $0.10 per kWh, that is about $124 a year for one fan. The number is small per fan but recurs every year of the motor's life, and it scales with horsepower and run hours. That is why premium efficiency is the usual request on continuously running fans and why many specifications require it outright.

docs.title: Heat: Temperature Rise, Thermal Protection and Winding RTDs
docs.text: Every watt a motor loses becomes heat in its windings, and heat is what ages motor insulation. Three related ideas describe and control that heat.

docs.title: Motor Temperature Rise
docs.text: Motor temperature rise is the change in temperature from the ambient air around the motor to the motor's steady-state operating temperature (FanPedia p. 69). The rise is a property of the motor design and its load; the ambient is a property of the site. Add them and you get the winding temperature, which must stay within the limit of the insulation class from Chapter 14. FanPedia notes that the typical fan motor is built with Class F insulation but rated for a Class B temperature rise. The motor therefore runs cooler than its insulation could tolerate, and that margin is what lets it survive a hot day, a dirty cooling fan, or a period on the service factor. When a motor sits in a hot location, the ambient temperature rating (the maximum allowable temperature around the motor) has to be checked along with the rise.

docs.title: Motor Thermal Protection
docs.text: Motor thermal protection is a device built into the motor that responds to winding temperature. FanPedia lists thermistors and thermostats as the common choices and says they protect the motor against locked-rotor conditions, continuous overload and high ambient temperature (FanPedia p. 75). A thermostat is a switch that opens at a set temperature; a thermistor is a resistor whose resistance changes sharply at a set temperature and is read by a relay. Either one gives the control circuit a signal to shut the motor down before the insulation is damaged. Do not confuse thermal protection with a space heater (also called a strip heater), which warms an idle motor to prevent condensation.

docs.title: Motor Winding RTD
docs.text:
A motor winding RTD is a resistance temperature detector embedded in the motor windings to sense their heat rise (FanPedia p. 75). Where a thermostat or thermistor answers a yes-or-no question (too hot or not), an RTD reports a continuous temperature, because its electrical resistance changes in a known way with temperature. Plants with monitoring systems use winding RTDs to trend motor temperature, alarm at one value and trip at a higher one. RTDs are also available for motor bearings, and Chapter 16 covers bearing RTDs on the fan itself. Winding RTDs are a motor modification, so they must be called out on the order; they are more common on large induction motors in process plants.

Match the Device to the Plant's Control System

Before choosing between thermostats, thermistors and winding RTDs, ask one question: "What will this signal be wired to?" A plant with a monitoring system wants RTDs it can trend; a simple starter circuit only needs a switch that opens.

docs.title: Motor Intended Duty
docs.text:
Motor intended duty describes the operating conditions a motor is built for, based on its surrounding environment (FanPedia p. 71). It is the "SD" in the example line, and it is separate from the enclosure: the enclosure says how the motor is sealed and cooled, while the intended duty says how well the whole motor (paint, seals, hardware, bearings, conduit box) stands up to its surroundings. FanPedia lists these duty designations (FanPedia p. 73):

  • GD (General Duty): general purpose motors used where the air around the motor is normal, clean and cool.
  • SD (Severe Duty): used where a severe duty motor is needed but IEEE 841 motors are not specified. Also called Mil/Chem duty or chemical duty.
  • IEEE 841: an industry standard for severe duty motors begun in 1986, used in process industries.
  • DFG: explosion proof enclosure motors used in hazardous locations.
  • Special basis: IEEE 45 motors for marine applications and washdown duty motors for food applications.

Enclosure and duty have to agree. The motor specifications page pairs them (FanPedia p. 73); the NEMA side of that table is summarized below.

Enclosure Intended duties offered ODP GD TEFC GD or SD; IEEE 841 and IEEE 45 in the IP56 version EXPL (explosion proof) DFG TENV GD or SD

Worked example: choosing the duty. Three inquiries arrive in one week.

  1. A school's air handler fan; the motor sits in a clean, cool mechanical room. Normal, clean, cool air is the definition of general duty, so the motor is GD, and an ODP or TEFC enclosure both fit.
  2. A chemical plant asks for a "chem duty" motor on a scrubber exhaust fan; its specification does not mention IEEE 841. Chemical duty is one of the names FanPedia gives for SD, so the motor is TEFC, SD.
  3. A refinery specification calls for "IEEE 841 motors on all rotating equipment." The duty is IEEE 841, which forces a TEFC (IP56) enclosure. Quoting a plain SD motor here would not meet the specification, even though both are severe duty.

The next two sections look more closely at the two duties in this list that carry the most weight on industrial orders.

docs.title: Severe Duty Motor
docs.text:
A severe duty motor is built to keep running where a general duty motor would corrode, wear or overheat early: around moisture, chemical fumes, dust, washdown or outdoor exposure. FanPedia uses "SD" for the general severe duty motor and lists Mil/Chem duty, chemical duty and IEEE 45 as names you will see for it (FanPedia p. 73). IEEE 841 is a stricter, published standard for severe duty motors in process industries; FanPedia names automotive, mining, paper and wood mills, and refining as typical users.

The rule for choosing between them comes straight from FanPedia's definition: SD is used where a severe duty motor is required but IEEE 841 is not specified. That makes the decision a reading exercise, not an engineering judgment.

Worked example: SD or IEEE 841? An automotive paint shop needs an exhaust fan. The motor will sit near the fan in air that carries paint mist and dirt, so general duty is out. Read the customer's specification:

  1. If it says "IEEE 841" anywhere in the motor section, quote an IEEE 841 motor (TEFC, IP56).
  2. If it says "severe duty," "mill and chemical duty" or describes the environment without naming IEEE 841, quote an SD motor (TEFC).
  3. If the specification is silent and the motor is in the dirty air, recommend SD and say why on the quotation.

In this case the specification reads "TEFC, severe duty, premium efficiency," so the motor line is: TEFC, SD, P. Had the same plant's corporate standard required IEEE 841, the answer would change even though the air did not.

docs.title: Hazardous Location Motor
docs.text:
A hazardous location is an area where flammable gases or vapors, or combustible dusts, may be present in amounts that can ignite. The U.S. National Electrical Code (NEC) classifies these areas by class (Class I for gases and vapors, Class II for dusts), by division (whether the hazard is present in normal operation or only under abnormal conditions) and by group (the specific family of gas or dust). The plant owner, not the fan supplier, determines the classification of each area.

A hazardous location motor is a motor built and labeled for one of those classifications. In FanPedia's terms it is a DFG motor with an explosion proof (EXPL) enclosure: the internal portion of the motor is engineered to keep a motor arc or explosion from igniting a surrounding atmosphere that contains flammable dust or gas, while an external fan cools it (FanPedia p. 73). FanPedia names Groups D (gases), F and G (dusts) as the groups commonly used at Twin City Fan, and directs readers to the NEC for the full list of gases and dusts and their class and division ratings. Applications under the European ATEX directive require a special motor.

Worked example: reading the classification onto the order. A food plant requests a fan for a room the owner's drawings mark as Class II, Division 1, Group G (combustible food dust).

  1. The area is hazardous, so the motor must be a hazardous location motor: enclosure EXPL, duty DFG.
  2. The motor nameplate must carry the same class, division and group the owner gave: Class II, Division 1, Group G. Copy those values from the owner's documents onto the order; do not choose them yourself.
  3. The motor is only part of the answer. The fan also needs a review for spark-resistant construction, covered in Chapter 20.

An Explosion Proof Motor Does Not Make a Spark-Proof Fan

A common mistake is to order a DFG motor and assume the fan is now safe for the hazardous area. The motor rating covers the motor's own arcs and heat; a rubbing impeller or a dragging belt can still strike a spark. Treat the motor classification and the fan's spark-resistant construction as two separate lines that both need an answer.

The sorter below gives you practice with all of the duty designations from the last three sections. Each case states only what an application engineer would learn from the inquiry.

docs.title: Diagram: Motor Intended Duty Sorter
docs.text:
Motor Intended Duty Sorter

Type: microsim sim-id: ch15-motor-intended-duty-sorter Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Evaluate Bloom Verb: judge Learning Objective: The learner will judge which motor intended duty (GD, SD, IEEE 841, DFG or Washdown) an application requires, given a short description of the motor's environment and the customer's specification, with at least 7 of 8 cases correct on the first attempt.

Prerequisites: motor intended duty, general duty, severe duty motor, IEEE 841, hazardous location motor, DFG, washdown duty (all defined in the sections "Motor Intended Duty", "Severe Duty Motor" and "Hazardous Location Motor" above).

Evidence of Mastery: The learner assigns each of the 8 cases to one of five duty bins and commits each assignment with a Check action. An assignment is correct when it matches the "Correct duty" column in Content. Mastery is 7 of 8 correct on the first attempt. Reading the bin definitions is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) Any severe environment calls for IEEE 841, when IEEE 841 is used only when it is specified. (2) A dusty or dirty environment is automatically a hazardous location, when only the owner's area classification makes it one. (3) General duty is acceptable anywhere the motor has a TEFC enclosure.

Instructional Rationale: Choosing a duty is a judgment against stated criteria, so a classification sorter with one committed answer per case and criterion-based feedback makes the learner apply FanPedia's rules rather than recall a list.

Content:

The five bins, each with the definition shown when the learner opens it:

Bin Definition shown GD (General Duty) General purpose motor for normal, clean and cool air around the motor. SD (Severe Duty) Used where a severe duty motor is needed but IEEE 841 is not specified; also called Mil/Chem duty or chemical duty. IEEE 841 Industry standard for severe duty motors begun in 1986, used in process industries when specified. DFG Explosion proof enclosure motor for a hazardous location classified under the NEC. Washdown Special-basis motor for food applications that are washed down.

The eight cases, in this order:

# Case shown to the learner Correct duty Why (shown as feedback) 1 Office building supply fan. The motor is in a clean, cool mechanical room. GD Normal, clean and cool air around the motor is the definition of general duty. 2 Paper mill process fan. The mill's motor standard requires IEEE 841 motors. IEEE 841 IEEE 841 is chosen when the customer specifies it, and paper mills are a typical user. 3 Chemical plant scrubber exhaust fan. The specification asks for a "chemical duty" motor and does not mention IEEE 841. SD Chemical duty is another name for severe duty, and IEEE 841 was not specified. 4 Exhaust fan for a room the owner classifies as Class I, Division 1, Group D (flammable gas). DFG A classified hazardous location needs an explosion proof DFG motor rated for that class and group. 5 Food plant fan that is hosed down with the rest of the line during cleaning. Washdown FanPedia lists washdown duty motors, ordered on a special basis, for food applications. 6 Grain handling room the owner classifies as Class II, Division 1, Group G (combustible dust). DFG Group G dust in a classified area needs an explosion proof DFG motor. 7 Automotive plant exhaust fan. The motor sits in air with oil mist and dirt; the specification says "severe duty" and does not mention IEEE 841. SD The environment is severe, but IEEE 841 was not specified, so FanPedia's rule gives SD. 8 Mining process fan. The specification says "IEEE 841 TEFC motors." IEEE 841 IEEE 841 is specified, and mining is one of the process industries that use it.

Provenance: Bin definitions and the rules behind each answer: FanPedia p. 73 (Motor Specifications, Intended Duty and Enclosure), as presented in this chapter's sections "Motor Intended Duty", "Severe Duty Motor" and "Hazardous Location Motor". The NEC class, division and group labels in cases 4 and 6 are standard NEC terms; the cases themselves are illustrative and must be labeled "Illustrative cases".

Rules: Each case has exactly one correct bin. A case that is both severe and hazardous does not occur in this set. A case that names IEEE 841 is always IEEE 841; a severe case that does not name IEEE 841 is always SD.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner reads case 1 and opens any bin definitions they want.
  2. The learner places the case in one bin and presses Check. The case is marked correct or incorrect and the feedback text appears.
  3. The learner moves to the next case. Cases already checked stay marked and cannot be changed.
  4. After case 8, a summary lists all eight cases with the learner's bin, the correct bin and the reason.

Feedback: Eight cases, fixed order, one attempt each. Correct: "Correct: . ". Incorrect: "Not quite. The correct duty is . ". The correct answer is revealed immediately after each Check. A running score "Correct: n of 8" is shown, and the summary states whether the 7-of-8 mastery level was reached.

Starting State: Case 1 is shown with all five bins closed and no score. The prompt reads "Which intended duty does this motor need?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter names five duty bins: GD, SD, IEEE 841, DFG and Washdown. IEEE 841 began in 1986. SD is used where IEEE 841 is not specified. FanPedia lists Groups D, F and G as common at Twin City Fan.

docs.title: Variable Frequency Drive
docs.text:
A variable frequency drive (VFD) is an electronic controller placed between the power supply and an induction motor. It converts fixed-frequency AC power into AC power at a frequency it can adjust, typically from a small fraction of line frequency up to line frequency. Because synchronous speed is set by frequency, changing the frequency changes the motor speed in direct proportion, and with it the fan speed. On a belt-driven fan the sheaves still set the ratio between motor and fan speed; the VFD changes both together.

FanPedia treats the VFD as one of the two usual ways to change fan performance in the field, alongside variable inlet vanes (FanPedia p. 170). Chapter 18 covers the mechanical flow-control devices; this section covers what the VFD does to the fan.

Frequency Is the Speed Knob

Notice that nothing about the motor's poles or the fan's sheaves changes on a VFD. The drive moves the one variable in \( n_s = 120 f / p \) that the plant normally treats as fixed, and the fan laws do the rest.

The fan laws (developed fully in Chapter 25) say how a fan's performance changes with speed on a fixed system. With \( N \) the fan speed and the subscripts 1 and 2 for the old and new conditions:

\[ \frac{Q_2}{Q_1} = \frac{N_2}{N_1} \qquad \frac{P_2}{P_1} = \left(\frac{N_2}{N_1}\right)^2 \qquad \frac{H_2}{H_1} = \left(\frac{N_2}{N_1}\right)^3 \]

where \( Q \) is airflow (CFM), \( P \) is pressure (in. wg) and \( H \) is brake horsepower. On a VFD, the speed ratio equals the frequency ratio, \( N_2 / N_1 = f_2 / f_1 \).

Worked example: turning a fan down to 45 Hz. A belt-driven fan is selected for 10,000 CFM at 2.00 in. wg static pressure, needing 8.0 bhp at full speed on 60 Hz power (illustrative values). The owner wants to run it at reduced airflow overnight, and the VFD is set to 45 Hz.

  1. Speed ratio: \( 45 / 60 = 0.75 \). A 4-pole motor's synchronous speed drops from 1800 to 1350 RPM, and the fan speed drops by the same 25%.
  2. Airflow: \( 10{,}000 \times 0.75 = 7{,}500 \) CFM.
  3. Static pressure: \( 2.00 \times 0.75^2 = 2.00 \times 0.5625 = 1.13 \) in. wg.
  4. Brake horsepower: \( 8.0 \times 0.75^3 = 8.0 \times 0.4219 = 3.38 \) bhp.

A 25% cut in airflow cuts the fan's power by more than half. That cube relationship is the reason VFDs are so common on fans that spend long hours below full flow. Two limits keep the example honest. The fan laws assume the system resistance follows the fan along a system curve that passes through zero, so a system with a fixed pressure requirement will not fall off this steeply. And a VFD can drive a motor above 60 Hz, but the fan must never be run above the maximum safe speed listed in the current catalog; any speed increase starts with that check.

The calculator below lets you test these relationships at other frequencies before you see the answers.

docs.title: Diagram: VFD Frequency and Fan Law Calculator
docs.text:
VFD Frequency and Fan Law Calculator

Type: microsim sim-id: ch15-vfd-fan-law-calculator Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Apply Bloom Verb: calculate Learning Objective: The learner will calculate the airflow, static pressure and brake horsepower of a belt-driven fan at a reduced VFD frequency, using the fan laws with the frequency ratio as the speed ratio, to within 2% of the model values.

Prerequisites: variable frequency drive, synchronous motor speed, poles, frequency, airflow (CFM), static pressure (in. wg), brake horsepower, fan laws (defined in the sections "Synchronous Motor Speed" and "Variable Frequency Drive" above and in Chapter 25).

Evidence of Mastery: For each of three challenge frequencies, the learner types predicted airflow, static pressure and brake horsepower before the sim reveals the model values. A prediction is correct when it is within ±2% of the model value. Mastery is all nine values correct (three per challenge) within two attempts. Moving the frequency control in free exploration is not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) Power falls in the same proportion as frequency (a 25% cut in frequency giving a 25% cut in power). (2) Pressure is unchanged by a speed change. (3) The VFD changes the motor's number of poles or the sheave ratio.

Instructional Rationale: Apply-level calculation needs practice with a check, so each challenge requires a committed prediction before the answer appears; free exploration afterward lets the learner see the square and cube curves across the whole frequency range.

Content:

Base duty, fixed and labeled "Illustrative values": 10,000 CFM, 2.00 in. wg static pressure, 8.0 bhp at 60 Hz. Motor: 4 poles.

The adjustable quantity:

Quantity Min Max Step Default Unit Drive frequency f 20 60 1 60 Hz

Displayed at every frequency: frequency ratio f/60, synchronous speed 120 × f / 4 in RPM, airflow, static pressure, brake horsepower, and each as a percent of its 60 Hz value.

Challenge frequencies, in this order:

# Frequency (Hz) Airflow (CFM) Static pressure (in. wg) Brake horsepower Feedback when wrong 1 45 7,500 1.13 3.38 Ratio 45/60 = 0.75. Airflow × 0.75; pressure × 0.75² = 0.5625; power × 0.75³ = 0.4219. 2 30 5,000 0.50 1.00 Ratio 0.5. Pressure × 0.25 and power × 0.125: half the speed needs one eighth of the power. 3 50 8,333 1.39 4.63 Ratio 50/60 = 0.8333. Pressure × 0.6944; power × 0.5787.

Provenance: Base duty values are illustrative (this chapter, "Variable Frequency Drive" worked example).
