docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
This chapter builds on concepts from:

  • Chapter 2: Airstreams, Total Pressure and Standard Air
  • Chapter 3: Basic Fan Anatomy
  • Chapter 4: Centrifugal, Axial and Mixed Flow Fans
  • Chapter 6: Industrial Fans and Application Product Lines
  • Chapter 15: Motor Ratings, Speed Control and Positioners
  • Chapter 16: Bearings, Shafts and Shaft Seals
  • Chapter 17: Bearing Details, Lubrication and Pedestals
  • Chapter 20: Construction Classes, Materials and Spark Resistance

When the Airstream Fights Back

Some jobs hand you an airstream that is hot enough to cook a bearing, dirty enough that no gas may escape, or both at once. This chapter shows you how to read those jobs and turn them into a construction list a factory reviewer will sign off on. Let's follow the airflow, and the heat that rides along with it.

Most fans in this book could be built from a standard catalog configuration. The fans in this chapter cannot. A kiln recirculation fan, a fan pulling solvent-laden air out of an automotive paint booth, and a fan feeding a regenerative thermal oxidizer all start from a catalog model, but each one needs special construction that changes the housing, the pedestal, the bearings and the seals. Chapter 20 introduced maximum operating temperature, shaft coolers, high temperature grease and spark-resistant Type C. This chapter finishes those threads and adds two new duties: keeping gas inside the fan, and serving an RTO.

All Twin City Fan construction details in this chapter come from the Fan Construction section of FanPedia (pp. 103-121). FanPedia notes on nearly every page that construction varies by model, so treat each list here as the starting point for a conversation with the factory, not a substitute for the current catalog or an engineering review.

docs.title: How Heat Moves Through a Fan
docs.text: A high temperature fan has one structural problem and one bearing problem. The structural problem is that hot steel grows. The bearing problem is that heat travels from the airstream into the shaft and the pedestal, and the bearings sit at the end of both paths. Every high temperature feature in this chapter does one of three jobs: it lets parts grow without binding, it sheds heat before it reaches the bearings, or it blocks the path the heat would take.

docs.title: Thermal Expansion
docs.text: Thermal expansion is the increase in a part's length (and every other dimension) as its temperature rises. For a straight part such as a fan shaft, the growth is proportional to its length and to its temperature rise.

docs.title: Linear Thermal Expansion
docs.text:
\[ \Delta L = \alpha \, L \, \Delta T \]

where:

  • \( \Delta L \) is the change in length (in.)
  • \( \alpha \) is the material's coefficient of linear expansion (in./in./°F); for carbon steel a typical textbook value is about \( 6.5 \times 10^{-6} \)
  • \( L \) is the original length (in.)
  • \( \Delta T \) is the temperature rise (°F)

Example (illustrative). A steel shaft has 60 in. between bearing centers and warms by 300°F in service. Its growth is \( 6.5 \times 10^{-6} \times 60 \times 300 \approx 0.12 \) in. That is about one-eighth of an inch, and two bearings that both clamp the shaft axially would have to absorb it as thrust. This is why FanPedia's high temperature packages for pedestal-mounted fans, plug fans, air kits and axial fans call for fixed and floating bearings: the fixed bearing locates the shaft and the floating bearing lets it grow, as Chapter 17 explains.

The housing grows too. That is one reason flanged joints, split housings and pedestal attachments on hot fans get special treatment later in this chapter.

docs.title: The High Expansion Bearing
docs.text: Some fans need more axial freedom than a standard floating bearing allows. FanPedia's bearing modifications page (p. 101) shows a high expansion bearing and shaft modification, offered for air kits only, and the air kit high temperature page (p. 115) lists "high heat modified bearings" as an option. Read the name literally: it is a bearing arrangement modified to accept more thermal growth of the shaft than the standard bearing does. FanPedia's before-and-after drawing shows the change includes the shaft and its locking hardware (a socket head screw ground flat to fit the keyway), so plan it at order time. A likely reason it is limited to air kits: their enclosure and insulation are built by others in the field (p. 115), so the factory cannot control how hot the surroundings get, and extra expansion margin covers that uncertainty.

docs.title: Shedding and Blocking Heat at the Shaft
docs.text:
Heat reaches the bearings two ways: along the shaft, and through the housing into the pedestal. The shaft path is handled first, with a short family of parts that appear on almost every high temperature drawing in FanPedia.

The shaft cooler (also called a heat flinger, heat slinger or cooling impeller) is a cast aluminum wheel clamped on the shaft between the housing and the inboard bearing. FanPedia's technical description (p. 192) says it dissipates the heat transferred to the shaft from the airstream, protecting the bearings, and recommends it for applications over 300°F. The cooler only works if it has air to throw heat into, and it only stays safe if nobody can touch it. Three parts look after that:

  • A cooler guard is the guard that encloses the spinning shaft cooler so that hands and tools cannot reach it, while still letting air move across the cooler's fins. FanPedia shows a cooler guard on Arrangement 4 fans, plug fans, air kits and insulated fans (pp. 111-119), and lists the shaft cooler and cooler guard together as a common accessory (p. 127).
  • A cooler box is an uninsulated open area built around the shaft cooler so it can dissipate heat. FanPedia (p. 110) makes it standard on fans with aluminum clad insulation and on housings with insulation pins, because without it the insulation would bury the cooler and the cooler would have no cool air to work with. On insulated jackets, the jacket wraps around the cooler box (p. 119).
  • Insulation pins are pins attached to the outside of the housing that hold field- or vendor-applied insulation in place. They are optional on high temperature centrifugal fans (p. 110) and are installed by the insulating vendor on aluminum clad fans (p. 117).

Block, Shed or Allow

Every hot-fan part you will meet in this chapter answers one question: does it block heat, shed heat, or allow growth? A shaft cooler sheds, a separated pedestal blocks, and a floating bearing allows. When a drawing shows a part you don't recognize, ask which of the three it does and you will usually know why it is there.

docs.title: Aluminum Clad Construction
docs.text: Aluminum clad construction is an insulated fan in which an outside vendor insulates the housing and builds an aluminum skin around it. FanPedia (p. 117) gives its purpose as insulating the fan surface from high temperature, condensation or sound. The cladding is stucco-embossed aluminum at least 0.040 in. thick over 3-lb-density fiberglass or mineral wool unless another type is specified, and the fan ships from the vendor or back to TCF. Because the insulation adds thickness, the access door is raised (usually 2 in. above the insulation), split bars protrude 2 in. past it, the drain is extended, and inlet, outlet and centerline height are increased if required. On high temperature applications it gets a cooler box. Chapter 20 compares it with steel double wall construction and insulated jackets.

docs.title: Recess Cone
docs.text: A plug fan or air kit mounts its bearings and drive on the outside of an insulated wall, so the shaft cooler has to sit somewhere inside the wall's thickness. A recess cone (also called a drive cone) is, as FanPedia draws it, a cone-shaped pocket formed into the insulated plug or wall that gives the shaft cooler and shaft seal a recessed space with access to outside air. FanPedia shows it as "Design #2" for Arrangement 9 plug fans, where "Design #1" leaves a plain gap for the shaft cooler instead (p. 113), and on Arrangement 3 air kits (p. 115). Arrangement 4 plug fans use a recess cavity for the same purpose (p. 114). The wall opening around a plug fan is filled by an insulated plug; on Arrangement 9 high temperature plug fans it is optional up to 500°F where the plug or wall is less than 4 in. thick, and required at 301°F and above where it is 4 in. or more (p. 113).

docs.title: Diagram: High Temperature Fan Heat Path
docs.text:
High Temperature Fan Heat Path

Type: infographic sim-id: ch21-high-temp-heat-path Library: html Status: Specified Bloom Level: Understand Bloom Verb: classify Learning Objective: The learner will classify ten high temperature fan parts by whether each one blocks heat, sheds heat, or allows thermal growth, with at least 8 of 10 correct on the first attempt.

Prerequisites: thermal expansion, fixed and floating bearings, shaft cooler, cooler box, insulation pins, recess cone, insulated plug, high temperature pedestal, separated pedestal, heat shield (all defined in this chapter or Chapter 17 before this block).

Evidence of Mastery: For each of the 10 labeled parts on a side view of a high temperature fan, the learner commits a job (Block, Shed or Allow) before the part's description is revealed. A choice is correct when it matches the "Job" column. Mastery is 8 of 10 correct on the first attempt. Opening a description after answering is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) A cooler box is an insulated enclosure (it is deliberately left uninsulated so the cooler can shed heat). (2) Insulation pins are themselves insulation. (3) Every high temperature part is about keeping heat out; the floating bearing instead lets the shaft grow.

Instructional Rationale: Classifying each part by its job forces the learner to explain why it is on the drawing, which is the Understand-level skill a reviewer needs; committing before the reveal turns each label into a prediction rather than a lookup.

Content: Two side views, labeled with the ten parts below: a belt-driven centrifugal fan on a high temperature style pedestal (parts 1 and 3-8, 10) and an Arrangement 9 plug fan through an insulated wall (parts 2 and 9). Three job choices are offered for every part: "Blocks heat from reaching the bearings", "Sheds heat that has already reached the shaft", "Allows parts to grow without binding".

# Part label Job Description shown after answering (feedback) 1 Shaft cooler Shed A cast aluminum wheel on the shaft that throws off heat conducted from the airstream; recommended over 300°F. 2 Recess cone Shed A cone-shaped pocket in the insulated plug or wall that gives the shaft cooler room and outside air. 3 Cooler box Shed An uninsulated open area around the shaft cooler, so insulation does not smother it. 4 Insulation pins Block Pins that hold the housing insulation, which blocks heat leaving the housing surface. 5 Floating bearing Allow The non-locating bearing, which lets the shaft grow axially as it heats. 6 Separated pedestal Block A gap of up to 3 in. between housing and pedestal reduces heat conducted into the pedestal and bearings. 7 High temp angle Block An angle (also called heat angle, inverted angle or spacer angle) that spaces the pedestal from the housing on a high temperature style pedestal. 8 Motor heat shield Block A shield on the pedestal between the hot housing and the motor. 9 Insulated plug Block Insulation in the plug or wall that limits heat passing from the hot side to the drive side. 10 Fixed bearing Allow The locating bearing; it fixes one end so all growth goes toward the floating bearing.

Provenance: Part names and jobs from FanPedia pp. 85, 90, 110-113 and 192, and Chapter 17 of this book (fixed and floating bearings). The fan drawing is a generic illustration and must be labeled "illustrative".

Rules: Each part takes one answer. Correctness is an exact match with the Job column. Part 10 is scored Allow because fixing one end is what lets all growth go to the floating bearing; its feedback says so.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner selects a labeled part; the three job choices appear.
  2. The learner commits a choice. The part is marked correct or incorrect and its description is shown.
  3. The learner continues until all 10 parts are answered; the parts may be answered in any order.
  4. After all 10, the learner can filter the drawings to show only Block, only Shed or only Allow parts, and should notice that 5 parts block, 3 shed, and only the 2 bearings allow.

Feedback: 10 items, any order, one attempt each, no re-answering. Correct: "Correct: ." Incorrect: "Not quite. ." A running score "n of 10 correct" is shown; at the end, 8 or more shows "Mastery reached".

Starting State: The full drawing with all ten labels unanswered and the question "What job does each part do: block, shed or allow?"

Chapter Anchors: Shaft cooler recommended over 300°F; separated pedestal gap up to 3 in.; ten parts (5 Block, 3 Shed, 2 Allow); three jobs named Block, Shed and Allow.

docs.title: High Temperature Pedestals and Heat Shields
docs.text:
The second heat path runs from the hot housing, through the pedestal, into the bearings and motor. The answer is to change the pedestal itself.

A high temperature pedestal is a fan pedestal built to limit the heat conducted from the housing into the bearings and motor. FanPedia shows three forms. The high temperature style pedestal adds a high temp angle (also called a heat angle, inverted angle or spacer angle) between housing and pedestal, with a standard shaft seal and shaft cooler (p. 90). The pedestal with insulated panel adds an insulated panel on the pedestal facing the housing. The separated pedestal design leaves a gap of up to 3 in. between housing and pedestal, which reduces conducted heat and makes room for insulation (pp. 86, 112). FanPedia ties each form to arrangements and temperatures:

Pedestal form (p. 112) Arrangements Temperature limit shown Pedestal with motor heat shield 10 Up to 600°F Pedestal with insulated panel 10 Up to 600°F Pedestal with motor heat shield 9 (multiple variations) Up to 600°F Separated pedestal design 1, 8 and 9F 601°F and above

One dimension note comes with the separated design: for Arrangements 1 and 9F, the overall pedestal length is shortened by the short leg of the angle (or the width of the channel) that forms the gap.

A heat shield is a plate mounted between a hot surface and a component it protects, so radiant and convected heat from the housing does not reach that component directly. FanPedia lists it as a pedestal feature "used on high temperature applications" (p. 85). The most common form is the motor heat shield on Arrangement 9 and 10 pedestals (p. 112), where the motor sits on the pedestal close to the housing. Axial fans use one too: the Arrangement 9 axial high temperature package shows a heat shield next to the belt tube (p. 116).

Worked example: choosing a pedestal (illustrative job). An oven builder needs an Arrangement 10 recirculation fan for 550°F air.

  1. Temperature band. 550°F falls in the 501°F-600°F centrifugal package band, covered in the next section.
  2. Pedestal. Arrangement 10 puts the motor inside the pedestal envelope, so heat reaching the motor is the concern. FanPedia offers two Arrangement 10 forms up to 600°F: the pedestal with motor heat shield and the pedestal with insulated panel. Either is in range.
  3. Bearings. At 301°F and above, one fixed and one floating bearing, with high temperature grease.

Now the builder raises the setpoint to 700°F. Both Arrangement 10 pedestal forms stop at 600°F, and FanPedia's separated pedestal design is drawn for Arrangements 1, 8 and 9F at 601°F and above. The right response is not to quote Arrangement 10 anyway; it is to propose an Arrangement 1, 8 or 9F fan with a separated pedestal, or to send the Arrangement 10 request for engineering review.

The Limit Lives on the Pedestal, Too

It is easy to check the airstream temperature against the housing and impeller materials and stop there. The pedestal form, the arrangement and any aluminum rotating parts each carry their own temperature limit, so check all of them and quote the lowest one as the fan's limit.

docs.title: High Temperature Packages
docs.text:
A high temperature package is a set of construction details that FanPedia groups by an airstream temperature band. The band, not the exact temperature, decides the materials, the pedestal, the shaft cooling and the bearing requirements. Industrial uses listed on every package page are recirculating air in kilns, dryers, industrial ovens and furnaces; exhausting gases and fumes from industrial processes; and supplying air for heating and drying systems. Every page refers to Twin City Fan's Fan Engineering Letter FE-3200 for details.

The bands differ by fan family, which is why a salesperson needs to know the family before the temperature means anything:

Fan family (FanPedia page) Package bands Notes Centrifugal, Arr. 1, 8, 9, 9F, 10 (p. 110) 301-500°F, 501-600°F, 601-800°F, 801-1,000°F, 1,001°F and over Over 1,000°F requires engineering review; mild steel, Corten or stainless steel Centrifugal, Arr. 4 (p. 111) 181-300°F; 301°F and over 301°F and over requires engineering review; aluminum rotating parts only up to 250°F Arr. 9 plug fans (p. 113) Same five bands as Arr. 1, 8, 9, 9F, 10 Insulated plug and recess cone or gap for the cooler Arr. 4 plug fans (p. 114) 181-300°F (select models); 301°F and over 301°F and over requires engineering review Air kits, Arr. 3 (p. 115) Same five bands, 301°F to 1,001°F and over Enclosure and insulation by others in the field; high heat modified bearings optional Axial fans (p. 116) See below Separate axial package

The axial high temperature package is narrower because axial fans keep the motor or bearings inside the airstream's housing and typically use aluminum impellers. FanPedia (p. 116) describes axial high temperature service from 106°F to 600°F, but the bands it lists stop at 300°F: Arrangement 4 axial bands of 106-150°F, 151-195°F and 196-240°F (the upper two requiring engineering review), and Arrangement 9 bands of 201-250°F and 201-300°F (select models). The standard aluminum impeller is good to 275°F; the impeller must be on the outlet end of the housing, a fixed impeller is required over 250°F, high temperature grease is used over 275°F, lube lines are metal, and flange bearings need scalloped bearing plates. On Arrangement 9 axial fans, cool air is pulled into the bearing housing through the belt tube, and a heat shield, retaining washer and safety wire hardware appear on select models.

docs.title: Diagram: High Temperature Package Finder
docs.text:
High Temperature Package Finder

Type: microsim sim-id: ch21-high-temp-package-finder Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Apply Bloom Verb: determine Learning Objective: The learner will determine the FanPedia high temperature package band, and whether engineering review is required, for a stated fan family and airstream temperature, with at least 7 of 8 jobs correct.

Prerequisites: high temperature package, axial high temperature package, fan arrangement, plug fan, air kit (defined in this chapter and Chapters 4 and 11).

Evidence of Mastery: For 8 job tickets, the learner selects a band from the list for that ticket's fan family and marks "Engineering review required: yes/no" before checking. A ticket is correct when both the band and the yes/no match the answer table. Mastery is 7 of 8 correct.

Misconceptions: (1) All fans share one set of temperature bands. (2) An Arrangement 4 centrifugal at 400°F has a standard package (it requires engineering review). (3) Axial packages reach the same temperatures as centrifugal packages.

Instructional Rationale: Applying a lookup rule to new tickets, with the family chosen first, builds the habit of reading the family before the temperature; immediate checking with the rule shown corrects the "one table for all fans" misconception.

Content:

Band lists by family (shown once the learner opens a ticket):

Family Bands offered Engineering review Centrifugal Arr. 1, 8, 9, 9F, 10 301-500°F; 501-600°F; 601-800°F; 801-1,000°F; 1,001°F and over 1,001°F and over Centrifugal Arr. 4 181-300°F; 301°F and over 301°F and over Arr. 9 plug fan 301-500°F; 501-600°F; 601-800°F; 801-1,000°F; 1,001°F and over 1,001°F and over Arr. 4 plug fan 181-300°F (select models); 301°F and over 301°F and over Air kit, Arr. 3 301-500°F; 501-600°F; 601-800°F; 801-1,000°F; 1,001°F and over 1,001°F and over Axial Arr. 4 106-150°F; 151-195°F; 196-240°F 151-195°F and 196-240°F Axial Arr. 9 201-250°F; 201-300°F (select models) none stated

Job tickets, in this order:

# Ticket Correct band Review? Feedback reason 1 Arr. 1 centrifugal, kiln exhaust, 450°F 301-500°F No 450°F falls in the first Arr. 1 band. 2 Arr. 4 centrifugal, dryer, 250°F 181-300°F No Arr. 4 has its own lower band; aluminum rotating parts are limited to 250°F. 3 Arr. 4 centrifugal, oven, 400°F 301°F and over Yes Arr. 4 above 300°F always goes to engineering review. 4 Arr. 9 plug fan, oven, 650°F 601-800°F No Plug fans use the same five bands as Arr. 1, 8, 9, 9F, 10. 5 Air kit Arr. 3, furnace, 1,100°F 1,001°F and over Yes The top band on every centrifugal and air kit page requires engineering review. 6 Axial Arr. 4, warm exhaust, 180°F 151-195°F Yes FanPedia marks the 151-195°F axial band as requiring engineering review. 7 Axial Arr. 9, 240°F 201-250°F No 240°F is inside the 201-250°F band offered on Arr. 9 axial fans. 8 Arr. 10 centrifugal, 520°F 501-600°F No 520°F is above 500°F, so it moves up to the second band.

Provenance: FanPedia pp. 110, 111, 113, 114, 115 and 116 (2021 edition). Job tickets are illustrative and must be labeled "illustrative jobs".

Rules: A temperature belongs to a band when lower bound <= temperature <= upper bound. "And over" bands have no upper bound. For ticket 7, 240°F lies in both Arr. 9 axial bands; the correct answer is 201-250°F because the 201-300°F band is limited to select models, and the sim accepts 201-300°F as incorrect with the reason "select models only; start from the general band". Review is "Yes" exactly when the band is listed in the Engineering review column.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner reads a ticket showing family, application and temperature.
  2. The learner opens the band list for that family and selects one band.
  3. The learner marks review yes or no and presses Check.
  4. The sim shows correct or incorrect for each half and the reason; the next ticket unlocks.
  5. After ticket 8, the learner can enter any family and temperature from 100°F to 1,200°F in 10°F steps (default 300°F) and see the band and review flag, and should notice that the listed axial bands stop at 300°F.

Feedback: 8 tickets, fixed order, two attempts each. Correct: "Correct: , review . ." Incorrect first attempt: "Check the band list for again." After a second wrong attempt the answer and reason are shown and the ticket counts as missed. Score "n of 8 correct" is shown.

Starting State: Ticket 1 shown with the band list closed and the question "Which package band covers this job?"

Chapter Anchors: All bands, review requirements and the 250°F aluminum limit as stated in the chapter's package table and axial paragraph; 8 tickets; mastery 7 of 8.

docs.title: Spark-Resistant Construction, Types A and B
docs.text: Spark-resistant construction keeps a fan from striking a spark when a rotating part rubs a stationary one, which matters when the airstream can carry flammable vapor or dust. The A/B/C letters follow AMCA Standard 99-0401, and FanPedia illustrates Twin City Fan's construction for each. Chapter 20 covered Type C, the minimal level, which only reduces the chance of contact (typically with an aluminum inlet cone and an aluminum rub plate). Types A and B go further by changing what the parts are made of. In all three types, bearings are not allowed in the airstream. The non-ferrous materials FanPedia lists are aluminum, aluminum/nickel/bronze, Monel, copper, brass and bronze.

docs.title: Type A
docs.text:
Spark Resistant Type A provides the highest degree of spark resistance. It requires that all fan components in the airstream be made of non-ferrous material, and that they be assembled to reduce the chance of contact between any stationary and rotating component (p. 104). On a centrifugal fan that means a non-ferrous housing or frame, impeller with welded hub, inlet funnel, shaft sleeve, interior fasteners (hub set screws in stainless steel, flush with the hub) and hub cap with a non-ferrous bolt. Parts outside the airstream stay steel: a bolted-on pedestal, the shaft and the shaft locking collars. Type A also restrains the bearings with bearing dowel pins (the first choice) or bearing stop blocks, so a bearing cannot shift and bring the wheel into the housing. On axial fans (p. 109) the housing, impeller, fasteners and sleeve are non-ferrous, the shaft is stainless steel, and the motor mount plate, weather cover and belt guard are mild steel, with restrained bearings (slotted steel spring pins or stop blocks).

Worked example (illustrative job). A specification for a solvent recovery exhaust calls for "AMCA Type A spark-resistant construction" on an Arrangement 1 centrifugal fan. Walk the airstream from inlet to outlet:

  1. Inlet funnel, impeller and housing: all non-ferrous; aluminum is the usual choice.
  2. Where the shaft enters the airstream: a non-ferrous sleeve covers it, and the hub cap uses a non-ferrous bolt.
  3. Hardware inside the housing: non-ferrous, with stainless set screws ground flush in the hub.
  4. Outside the airstream: steel shaft and collars, and a steel pedestal bolted on, since aluminum and steel are not welded together.
  5. Bearings: restrained with dowel pins, and outside the airstream.

docs.title: Type B
docs.text:
Spark Resistant Type B requires that the impeller be non-ferrous and that the airstream parts be assembled to reduce the chance of stationary-to-rotating contact (p. 105). In practice that is an aluminum impeller (welded hub) and an aluminum rub plate, the plate at the housing's shaft opening that FanPedia also calls a shaft seal, enclosure plate, striker plate, spark plate or ash tray. The housing, frame, fasteners, pedestal, inlet funnel, shaft and collars stay steel. If the fan has an outside protruding hub, no rub plate is needed. FanPedia states the residual risk honestly: after a mechanical failure, the aluminum impeller will contact a steel inlet cone. Axial Type B makes the impeller non-ferrous and restrains the bearings (p. 109), and for radial bladed fans and pressure blowers FanPedia adds a rule: if the fan already has a non-ferrous impeller as standard, use Type B (pp. 107-108).

Worked example (illustrative job). A grain-handling customer asks for "spark-resistant" without a type, on a pressure blower that already has a cast aluminum impeller as standard. FanPedia's rule points straight to Type B, which the standard impeller nearly satisfies already. Add the rub plate at the shaft opening, keep bearings outside the airstream, and confirm the type in writing on the order, because "spark-resistant" alone does not tell the factory which type to build.

The three types compare as follows:

Type A Type B Type C Non-ferrous parts Everything in the airstream Impeller (plus rub plate) Inlet cone or rub ring, rub plate Housing Non-ferrous Steel Steel Remaining risk Lowest Aluminum wheel can strike the steel inlet cone Steel wheel; aluminum inlet cone and rub plate are the first contact points Bearings Restrained; not in airstream Not in airstream (restrained on axials) Not in airstream

Ask Two Questions Before Quoting Spark Resistance

Ask "which type?" and "how hot?" in the same breath. Types A and B lean on aluminum, and FanPedia limits aluminum rotating parts to 250°F on Arrangement 4 fans and the standard aluminum axial impeller to 275°F, so a hot spark-resistant job needs the factory's review before you quote it.

docs.title: Nominally Leak-Tight Fans
docs.text: The next two duties have nothing to do with sparks and everything to do with where the gas goes.

docs.title: Fan Leakage
docs.text: Fan leakage is air or another gas mixture leaking into the fan housing or out of it. Which way it moves depends on pressure: where the housing is above atmospheric pressure, gas leaks out; where it is below, room air leaks in. FanPedia (p. 120) names the consequences. When the gas carries hazardous contaminants, leakage can be dangerous; excessive leakage can also waste energy, create an environmental or safety hazard, damage the fan bearings, or make excessive noise.

docs.title: What "Nominally Leak-Tight" Means
docs.text:
FanPedia is direct about the limits: a fan generally cannot be built totally leak-tight. A nominally leak-tight fan is one built to reduce leakage to a level agreed with the customer, verified by shop testing, and recorded on the inspection form (p. 120). The word nominally is a promise about the method and the agreed level, not a promise of zero leakage.

You Are Selling a Leakage Level, Not a Seal

Notice that the customer, not the catalog, sets the acceptable leakage. That makes the first question on a leak-tight job "how much leakage is acceptable, and of what gas?" rather than "which seal?"

FanPedia's construction list for nominally leak-tight fans is short, and every line closes a leak path:

  • Arrangements 1, 8 and 9 only, with a solid drive side on the housing (no drive plates to leak around).
  • Not recommended over 600°F, and split housings not recommended.
  • Close bolt spacing. Bolted connections use close-centered hole patterns on 3 in. to 4 in. centers: inlet and outlet flanges, access doors, cover plates, inlet funnels and split housings. An ANSI flange hole pattern is sufficient if it is standard for the fan.
  • Gasketing on all connections, with double gaskets.
  • Continuous welds instead of intermittent welds (locations vary by model).
  • Shaft seal of the lip type, Graphoil stuffing box type, or double ring mechanical (double carbon ring) type, sealing on the fan shaft itself; do not use a shaft sleeve and cap.
  • Drain of the pipe coupling type with a plug.

FanPedia refers to Fan Engineering Letter FE-700 for details.

Worked example (illustrative job). A chemical plant requests a fan for a process vent containing a toxic vapor, at 350°F, and suggests an Arrangement 4 fan with a split housing to make maintenance easier. Check the request against the list:

  1. Arrangement 4 is not one of the allowed arrangements (1, 8 or 9). Propose an Arrangement 1 or 8 fan; Arrangement 8 keeps the direct-drive feel of Arrangement 4.
  2. A split housing is not recommended. If maintenance access truly requires one, it will need centering plates and double gaskets, and the customer should know it adds leak paths.
  3. 350°F is under the 600°F limit, so leak-tight construction is possible. The high temperature package for the band still applies, so the order carries both.
  4. Choose a seal from the three allowed types, and ask the customer to state the acceptable leakage that the soap bubble test will be judged against.

docs.title: Gasketing
docs.text:
Gasketing is the compressible sealing material placed in a bolted joint so the joint seals when the bolts are tightened. On a leak-tight fan, FanPedia requires gasketing on all connections, including inlet and outlet flanges, the funnel, inlet plate, access doors and split housing, and requires double gaskets (p. 120). RTO fans call for silicone sponge gasket and silicone caulk, with an alternative to silicone on automotive jobs (p. 121). A gasket only seals as well as the clamping force on it, which is why gasketing comes paired with close-centered bolt patterns: widely spaced bolts let the flange bow open between them.

Worked example (illustrative). A leak-tight fan has an access door, a two-flange connection (inlet and outlet), and a bolted inlet funnel. Count the gasketed joints: inlet flange, outlet flange, inlet funnel and access door make four joints, each with a double gasket, so the bill of materials carries eight gasket pieces before any cover plates are added. Then confirm each joint's bolt pattern is on 3 in. to 4 in. centers, or that the flange uses the fan's standard ANSI pattern; a joint that fails that check will leak whatever gasket it uses.

docs.title: Continuous Seal Welds, Centering Plates and the Soap Bubble Test
docs.text:
Three smaller items complete a leak-tight fan.

A continuous seal weld is a weld run without gaps along the full length of a seam, so the joint itself is gas-tight. Standard housings may use intermittent (stitch) welds, which are strong but leave gaps between beads. FanPedia's leak-tight and RTO drawings call out continuous welds, and the RTO drawing adds seal welds, with locations that vary by model (pp. 120-121).

A centering plate is a plate fitted where a split housing's joint line crosses an opening, sealing the open areas around the shaft seal and around the inlet funnel or inlet plate. A split line through a round opening leaves small gaps that a flat gasket cannot close; the centering plate closes them. FanPedia requires centering plates on any leak-tight or RTO fan built with a split housing.

The soap bubble test is the shop leak check. In the usual method the housing is put under pressure, a soap solution is applied to seams, joints and seals, and bubbles mark any leak. FanPedia (pp. 120-121) says leak-tight and RTO fans are tested this way at the shop, leaks are fixed if needed, and the result is recorded on the inspection form.

docs.title: Regenerative Thermal Oxidizer (RTO) Service
docs.text:
A regenerative thermal oxidizer (RTO) is an industrial air pollution control process that destroys pollutants in process exhaust by oxidizing them at high temperature. FanPedia (p. 121) lists typical sources: industrial process ventilation such as automotive paint booths, printing, and paper mills. In general terms, an RTO passes the exhaust through beds of ceramic media that store heat, burns the organic pollutants in a combustion chamber, and periodically reverses the flow so the outgoing hot gas reheats the media for the next cycle. The fan that pushes or pulls the exhaust through that system sees contaminated gas, pressure swings when the flow switches, and occasional high temperature, which is why RTO duty has its own construction.

Much of RTO construction matches the leak-tight list: a solid drive side, close-centered bolt patterns on 3 in. to 4 in. centers, a 600°F recommended limit, gasketing on all connections, centering plates on split housings, continuous and seal welds, and the soap bubble test. The differences are what make it its own option:

  • Gasketing material: silicone sponge and silicone caulk, but automotive jobs require an alternative to silicone. (Silicone contamination is a known cause of paint finish defects, which is the practical reason a paint shop forbids it.)
  • Shaft seals: friction type, single carbon ring type, or a commercially available carbon ring or other seal.
  • Dampers, if required, must have stuffing boxes on their shafts.
  • Structure: FanPedia's drawing shows pedestal foot gussets and a vane section.

Two Lists That Look Alike

If leak-tight and RTO construction blur together, that is normal; FanPedia's two pages share most of their lines. Learn the shared core once, then memorize only the differences: arrangements and drain for leak-tight, silicone rules, seal types and dampers for RTO.

docs.title: RTO Service Conditions
docs.text:
RTO service conditions are the operating facts the fan must survive that only the customer or the RTO builder knows. FanPedia lists them as special requirements that sales must specify (p. 121):

Item sales must specify Why the factory needs it Pedestal: concrete requirements Whether the pedestal is filled or set on concrete changes its construction Fan base: how the fan will be mounted in the field The base is built to suit that mounting Fan operation: VFD, cycling, bake-out conditions Speed range, repeated starts and temperature excursions change the fan's mechanical design

A bake-out is a periodic high temperature cycle that burns accumulated organic deposits out of the RTO's media; for the fan, it is an excursion above normal operating temperature that must be known in advance.

Worked example (illustrative job). An RTO builder sends an inquiry for an automotive paint shop: a fan on a VFD, mounted on a structural steel skid, with normal gas at 300°F and a weekly bake-out that raises the fan inlet to 650°F for several hours. Read it against FanPedia:

  1. Temperature. RTO construction is not recommended over 600°F. The 650°F bake-out exceeds that, so the job needs engineering review before it is quoted, even though normal operation is well inside the limit. The high temperature package must be chosen for the bake-out temperature, not the normal one.
  2. Gasketing. Automotive job: no silicone. The order must name the alternative gasket and caulk.
  3. Operation. VFD and cycling go on the order as service conditions.
  4. Base and pedestal. Skid mounting goes on the order as the field mounting; ask whether the pedestal needs concrete.
  5. Seals and testing. Choose a friction or carbon ring seal; the fan will be soap bubble tested at the shop.

docs.title: Diagram: Leak-Tight Versus RTO Requirement Sorter
docs.text:
Leak-Tight Versus RTO Requirement Sorter

Type: microsim sim-id: ch21-leak-tight-rto-sorter Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Analyze Bloom Verb: differentiate Learning Objective: The learner will differentiate FanPedia's nominally leak-tight and RTO construction requirements by sorting 12 requirements into Leak-Tight Only, RTO Only, or Both, with at least 10 of 12 correct on the first attempt.

Prerequisites: fan leakage, nominally leak-tight fan, gasketing, continuous seal weld, centering plate, soap bubble test, regenerative thermal oxidizer, RTO service conditions (all defined in this chapter above this block).

Evidence of Mastery: The learner places each of 12 requirement cards in one of three bins and locks each placement. A placement is correct when it matches the "Bin" column. Mastery is 10 of 12 correct on the first attempt.

Misconceptions: (1) RTO construction is just leak-tight construction under another name. (2) Leak-tight fans may be any arrangement. (3) Silicone gasketing is acceptable on every RTO job.

Instructional Rationale: Sorting near-identical requirement lists into shared and distinct bins makes the learner analyze the structure of the two options, which is the comparison a salesperson performs when a customer says "RTO" or "leak-tight".

Content:

# Requirement card Bin Why (feedback) 1 Solid drive side on housing (no drive plates) Both Both pages list it; drive plates are a leak path. 2 Not recommended for applications over 600°F Both Both pages state the same 600°F limit. 3 Bolted connections on 3 in. to 4 in. centers Both Close bolt spacing keeps gaskets clamped on both options. 4 Centering plates if the housing is split Both Both pages require them to seal the open areas at seals and inlet. 5 Soap bubble test at the shop, recorded on the inspection form Both Both pages describe the same shop test. 6 Arrangements 1, 8 and 9 only Leak-Tight Only The arrangement limit appears only on the leak-tight page. 7 Shaft seal: lip, Graphoil stuffing box, or double carbon ring Leak-Tight Only These three seal types are the leak-tight list. 8 Drain: pipe coupling type with plug Leak-Tight Only The plugged pipe-coupling drain is called out on the leak-tight page. 9 Silicone sponge gasket and silicone caulk, with an alternative on automotive jobs RTO Only The silicone rule belongs to RTO duty. 10 Dampers, if required, must have stuffing boxes RTO Only Only the RTO page sets a damper requirement. 11 Sales must specify VFD, cycling and bake-out conditions RTO Only These are the RTO service conditions. 12 Shaft seal: friction, single carbon ring, or commercial carbon ring RTO Only These are the RTO seal types.

Provenance: FanPedia p. 120 (nominally leak-tight) and p. 121 (RTO), 2021 edition.

Rules: One bin per card. Correctness is an exact match with the Bin column. Cards are dealt in a shuffled order seeded by 21 so every learner sees the same order.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner reads a card and predicts its bin by placing it.
  2. The learner locks the placement; the card shows correct or incorrect with the reason.
  3. After all 12 are locked, the learner can view the two FanPedia lists side by side with shared lines linked, and should notice that 5 of the 12 requirements are shared.

Feedback: 12 cards, shuffled with seed 21, one attempt each, no re-placement after locking. Correct: "Correct: ." Incorrect: "This one belongs in . ." Score "n of 12 correct" is shown, with "Mastery reached" at 10 or more.

Starting State: Three empty bins labeled Leak-Tight Only, Both, and RTO Only, the first card face up, and the question "Which construction calls for this?"

Chapter Anchors: 600°F limit; 3 in. to 4 in. bolt centers; Arrangements 1, 8 and 9; three leak-tight seal types; silicone alternative on automotive jobs; 12 cards; 5 shared requirements.

docs.title: Buffer Strips
docs.text: One last pedestal item often travels with hot, corrosive or leak-tight jobs because those jobs tend to use stainless steel housings. A buffer strip is a strip placed between a corrosion-resistant housing and a mild steel pedestal when the customer specifies that the two may not be welded together (p. 85). It lets a stainless steel housing sit on a less expensive mild steel pedestal without a dissimilar-metal weld; the alternative FanPedia offers is a non-rotatable bolt-on pedestal, described in Chapter 17. When a specification forbids welding stainless to carbon steel, one of the two must appear on the order.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Hot fans need parts that allow growth (fixed and floating bearings, the air kit high expansion bearing), shed heat (shaft cooler, cooler box) or block it (separated pedestal, high temp angle, heat shield, insulation).
  • \( \Delta L = \alpha L \Delta T \): a steel shaft can grow about an eighth of an inch over a few hundred degrees, which a single floating bearing absorbs.
  • High temperature packages are temperature bands that depend on the fan family. Centrifugal Arr. 1, 8, 9, 9F, 10, Arr. 9 plug fans and air kits share five bands up to 1,001°F and over; Arrangement 4 is reviewed above 300°F; the listed axial bands stop at 300°F.
  • High temperature pedestal forms carry their own limits: Arr. 9 and 10 heat shield and insulated panel pedestals are shown up to 600°F; the separated pedestal (up to 3 in. gap) is for Arr. 1, 8 and 9F at 601°F and above.
  • Spark Resistant Type A makes everything in the airstream non-ferrous and restrains the bearings; Type B makes the impeller non-ferrous and adds a rub plate. Check aluminum temperature limits on hot spark-resistant jobs.
  • A nominally leak-tight fan reduces leakage to a level agreed with the customer: Arr. 1, 8 or 9, solid drive side, double gaskets, 3-4 in. bolt centers, continuous welds, an approved shaft seal, centering plates on split housings, and a soap bubble test, up to 600°F.
  • RTO fans share that core and add silicone rules (none on automotive jobs), their own seal types, stuffing boxes on dampers, and service conditions that sales must specify: concrete, field mounting, VFD, cycling and bake-out.

Hot, Tight and Ready to Quote

You can now take a hot, hazardous or RTO inquiry and turn it into a construction list where every line traces to a reason: a package band, a pedestal limit, a spark-resistant type, a leak path closed. That is the hardest construction reading in the book, and you just did it.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: This chapter covers how fans are installed and isolated from the building. It introduces fan installation, unitary, isolation, and concrete inertia bases, vibration and vibration isolation, isolator deflection, neoprene pads, rubber-in-shear isolators, isolator mounting methods, internally isolated fans, and seismic restraint. It also covers weather covers, zero speed switches, inlet box mounting planes, and piezometer rings for measuring airflow. After completing it, readers can choose a base and isolation approach for a fan installation.

docs.title: Concepts Covered
docs.text:
This chapter covers the following 17 concepts from the learning graph:

Concept Concept Impact Score Fan Installation 91 Fan Base 25 Vibration 43 Zero Speed Switch 1 Weather Cover 2 Unitary Base 1 Isolation Base 19 Vibration Isolation 39 Inertia Base 16 Isolator Deflection 11 Neoprene Isolation Pad 2 Rubber-in-Shear Isolator 2 Seismic Restraint 3 Piezometer Ring 3 Isolator Mounting Method 4 Internally Isolated Fan 1 Inlet Box Mounting Planes 1

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
This chapter builds on concepts from:

  • Chapter 1: Air, Pressure and the Fan
  • Chapter 2: Airstreams, Total Pressure and Standard Air
  • Chapter 3: Basic Fan Anatomy
  • Chapter 4: Centrifugal, Axial and Mixed Flow Fans
  • Chapter 8: Centrifugal and Axial Impeller Types
  • Chapter 14: Fan Motors and Enclosures
  • Chapter 18: Inlets, Outlets and Flow Control
  • Chapter 19: Damper Details and Duct Connections

The Fan Has to Sit on Something

A perfectly selected fan can still hum through an office ceiling, walk off its alignment, or shake a mezzanine. The difference is usually the base and the isolators, which are a few lines on the order that nobody notices until they are wrong. By the end of this chapter you will be able to pick the base and isolation for a job and defend the choice. Let's follow the airflow.

Up to now this book has treated the fan as a machine on its own: its impeller, housing, arrangement, motor and accessories. A fan in service is also a load on a building, and a source of force that the building has to carry. This chapter covers the parts of an order that connect the fan to that building. The product statements below come from the FanPedia accessory pages on base types and vibration isolation (pp. 131–135), inlet boxes (p. 143), shaft accessories (p. 129) and piezometer rings (pp. 158–160), and from the matching technical descriptions (pp. 163–197).

docs.title: Fan Installation
docs.text:
Fan installation is everything that puts a selected fan into service in a particular place: the structure that carries it, the base under it, any isolation between the base and the structure, the connections to ductwork, protection from weather, and the devices that let operators monitor it. The fan selection answers "what fan?"; the installation answers "how does this fan live in this building?"

Installation choices appear on the order as accessories and options, so they have to be decided before the order is entered, not on the job site. The questions an application engineer works through are always the same, even when the answers change:

  1. Support. What carries the fan: a slab on grade, a steel mezzanine, a roof curb, an overhead structure? FanPedia notes that not every fan needs isolators, but every fan needs adequate support from its mounting structure (p. 133).
  2. Base. Is the fan mounted by itself, or with its motor and drive on a common base? If a base is used, which kind?
  3. Isolation. Is vibration a problem for the people, process or structure near the fan? If so, which isolators, at what deflection, mounted how?
  4. Connections. Do the inlet and outlet need flexible connectors? (They do on any isolated fan.)
  5. Environment. Is the fan outdoors, in a seismic area, or next to a detached inlet box?
  6. Monitoring. Does the control system need to know the fan's speed or airflow?

docs.title: Worked Example: Reading an Installation From a Job Description
docs.text:
A contractor asks for a belt-driven Arrangement 10 centrifugal fan to exhaust a print shop. The fan will sit on the roof of a two-story building, directly above a conference room. The building automation system must raise an alarm if the fan stops. (This job is illustrative.)

Question What the job says Line on the order Support Roof structure over an occupied room Confirm the roof structure and curb with the contractor Base Arrangement 10 has an adjustable motor base inside the bearing pedestal (FanPedia p. 167) No separate motor base needed Isolation Conference room directly below; vibration and hum are a nuisance there Vibration isolators, sized later in this chapter Connections Isolated fan Flexible connectors at inlet and outlet Environment Outdoors on a roof Optional weather cover: FanPedia rates Arrangement 10 suitable for roof or outdoor installations when supplied with it (p. 167) Monitoring Alarm if the fan stops Zero speed switch on the fan shaft

Six questions produced five order lines. Every one of them is missed regularly, because none of them shows up on the fan's performance curve.

docs.title: Vibration
docs.text:
Vibration is the repeated back-and-forth motion of a machine or structure about its resting position. Every operating fan vibrates a little. The main source is unbalance: no impeller is perfectly balanced, so the rotating mass pulls outward slightly harder on one side, and that pull swings around once per revolution. Misaligned shafts and couplings, worn belts and bearings, and aerodynamic forces in the airstream add to it.

The force that drives vibration repeats at a definite rate called the forcing frequency (or disturbing frequency). For unbalance it is simply the rotating speed expressed in cycles per second, or hertz (Hz):

\[ f = \frac{N}{60} \]

where:

  • \( f \) is the forcing frequency in hertz (cycles per second)
  • \( N \) is the rotating speed in revolutions per minute (RPM)

A machine can have several forcing frequencies. A belt-driven fan has one at the fan shaft speed and another at the motor speed, and the lowest one is the hardest to isolate, as the next sections show.

Vibration matters for three reasons that FanPedia spells out (p. 133). It can be a nuisance, as in an office where it is distracting. It can upset a process, as in electronics manufacturing. And in an extreme case it can be destructive enough to damage the supporting structure. Inside the fan, the same vibration wears bearings and loosens fasteners, which is why bearing vibration sensors exist (FanPedia p. 177).

docs.title: Worked Example: Forcing Frequencies of a Belt-Driven Fan
docs.text:
A belt-driven fan runs at 1170 RPM, driven by a motor that runs at 1770 RPM. What forcing frequencies does the installation have to deal with?

  1. Fan shaft: \( f = 1170 / 60 = 19.5 \) Hz.
  2. Motor shaft: \( f = 1770 / 60 = 29.5 \) Hz.
  3. The lower of the two, 19.5 Hz, sets the requirement for isolation. An isolator that handles 19.5 Hz handles 29.5 Hz even better.

Had the same duty been met by a slower, larger fan at 600 RPM, the fan's forcing frequency would drop to 10 Hz. Slower fans are quieter in many ways, but they are harder to isolate, and you will see why in the section on isolator deflection.

docs.title: Fan Bases
docs.text: A fan base is a structural frame that supports the fan, and usually its motor and drive, as one assembly. A base does three jobs. It gives the fan and motor a common, rigid support so the belt drive or coupling stays aligned; it spreads the load onto the floor or structure; and it gives the installer one assembly to set, level and anchor instead of several loose pieces. FanPedia describes three base types for centrifugal fans: unitary, isolation and inertia (pp. 131–132). They differ in one respect above all: whether the base is meant to sit on isolators.

docs.title: Unitary Base
docs.text: A unitary base, also known as a channel base, uses structural channel to support the fan assembly and is designed for use without isolators (FanPedia pp. 131, 176). It is bolted or anchored directly to the floor or foundation. A unitary base is the right choice when the fan is on a solid slab or foundation and nothing nearby is bothered by vibration, as in many industrial plants. Some arrangements ship on one as standard: FanPedia states that an Arrangement 7SI assembly is mounted on a unitary base as standard, with an inertia base available as an option (p. 165).

docs.title: Isolation Base
docs.text:
An isolation base provides a common support for the fan, motor and drive, including guards, and uses heavy-duty structural channel. It is built to sit on spring or rubber-in-shear isolators, which limit the forces an operating fan transmits to the support structure, and it requires flexible connectors at the inlet and outlet (FanPedia pp. 131, 176). The heavier channel matters: once the base sits on soft isolators at its corners, the base itself, not the floor, has to keep the motor and fan in line.

Some arrangements cannot take isolators directly under the fan, and the isolation base is FanPedia's stated fix:

  • Arrangement 3F SWSI (extended angle frame for the motor) is typically not suitable for mounting vibration isolators directly under the fan (p. 163).
  • Arrangement 9F SWSI (extended structural frame for a motor too large for the pedestal) is not suitable for mounting vibration isolators directly under the fan. If isolators are required, FanPedia says to use an Arrangement 1 fan with a separate isolation base (p. 166).
  • Arrangement 3F DWDI is the contrast case: its integral extended base has brackets to accept vibration isolators (p. 167).

docs.title: Worked Example: A Spec That Asks for Springs Under an Arrangement 9F
docs.text:
A specification reads: "Arrangement 9F, SWSI, belt driven, spring isolators mounted under the fan." The fan serves a mechanical room on a steel mezzanine.

  1. Check the arrangement against the isolation request. FanPedia states that Arrangement 9F is not suitable for mounting isolators directly under the fan (p. 166). The spec as written cannot be built.
  2. Apply FanPedia's stated alternative: an Arrangement 1 fan with a separate isolation base, motor mounted on the base (p. 166).
  3. Put the isolators under the isolation base's mounting brackets, not under the fan (p. 133).
  4. Add flexible connectors at the inlet and outlet, which every isolation base requires (p. 131).
  5. Send the revised arrangement back to the specifier with the reason, rather than quietly substituting it. The arrangement change moves the motor, so the drawings change too.

docs.title: Inertia Base
docs.text:
An inertia base is an isolation base with reinforcing rods (rebar), filled with concrete by the customer. Like the isolation base, it supports the fan, motor and drive including guards on heavy-duty structural channel, and it sits on spring isolators with flexible connectors required at the inlet and outlet. FanPedia notes that inertia bases are typically used on longer, direct-drive fans to mitigate assembly deflection, keeping the motor, coupling, shaft and bearings in alignment, and that an optional bottom pan makes the concrete easier to pour in the field (pp. 132, 175).

The concrete does two things. It stiffens the base, so a long coupled assembly does not sag or twist between its motor and its bearings. And it adds mass. For the same unbalance force, a heavier assembly moves less on its isolators, roughly in proportion to the total mass once the fan runs well above the isolators' natural frequency (defined in the next section). The concrete also lowers the center of gravity, which steadies the assembly on its springs.

docs.title: Worked Example: How Much Does the Concrete Add?
docs.text:
An inertia base for a direct-drive fan has a pour cavity 8 ft long, 4 ft wide and 6 in deep. The fan, motor and steel base weigh 3,000 lb. Normal-weight concrete weighs about 150 lb per cubic foot. (Dimensions and weights are illustrative.)

\[ W_c = \rho_c \times L \times B \times D \]

where:

  • \( W_c \) is the weight of the concrete fill in pounds
  • \( \rho_c \) is the unit weight of concrete, about 150 lb/ft³ for normal-weight concrete

  • \( L \), \( B \) and \( D \) are the pour cavity's length, width and depth in feet

  • Volume: \( 8 \times 4 \times 0.5 = 16 \) ft³.

  • Concrete weight: \( 150 \times 16 = 2{,}400 \) lb.
  • Total supported weight: \( 3{,}000 + 2{,}400 = 5{,}400 \) lb.
  • Effect on motion: with the same unbalance force, motion on the isolators scales roughly with \( 3{,}000 / 5{,}400 \approx 0.56 \), so the assembly moves a little more than half as much.
  • Consequence for the order: the spring isolators must be selected for 5,400 lb, not 3,000 lb. Springs sized for the bare fan would bottom out once the customer pours the concrete.

The following table summarizes the three base types described above.

Base Construction Sits on isolators? Flex connectors Typical use Unitary (channel) Structural channel No, designed for use without isolators Not required by the base Fan on a solid floor where vibration is not a concern Isolation Heavy-duty structural channel, common support for fan, motor, drive and guards Yes, spring or rubber-in-shear Required at inlet and outlet Isolated fan and motor that must stay aligned Inertia Isolation base with rebar, concrete filled by the customer Yes, spring Required at inlet and outlet Longer direct-drive fans, where stiffness and mass hold alignment

Ask Who Pours the Concrete

An inertia base ships as steel and rebar; the concrete is customer supplied. Put that sentence in the quote and the submittal, and offer the optional bottom pan if the base will be filled in place. It saves a phone call from a contractor staring at an empty frame.

docs.title: Vibration Isolation
docs.text:
Vibration isolation prevents or limits the force that an operating fan transfers to its supporting structure (FanPedia p. 133). It does not reduce the fan's own vibration; it stops that vibration from travelling into the building. The working parts are vibration isolators, resilient mounts placed between the fan or its base and the structure. FanPedia's isolator families are neoprene pads, rubber-in-shear mounts and springs, each covered below.

Not every fan needs isolation. A fan bolted to a heavy slab in a plant, far from people and sensitive equipment, usually needs only adequate support. Isolation earns its cost when the fan sits on a light or flexible structure such as a roof or mezzanine, near occupied space, or near a vibration-sensitive process. Two FanPedia rules come with it (p. 133): when isolation is used, rigid duct connections are not allowed and flex connectors are required, and some fans, such as commercial roof ventilators, are internally isolated and need no other isolation. Chapter 19 covers the flex connectors themselves.

How well an isolator works depends on how its own bounce compares with the fan's forcing frequency. Any mass resting on a spring has a natural frequency, the rate at which it bounces if you push it once and let go. The ratio of the forcing frequency to that natural frequency decides the outcome. Transmissibility is the fraction of the fan's force that gets through the isolator to the structure. For an undamped isolator it is:

\[ T = \frac{1}{\left| r^2 - 1 \right|}, \qquad r = \frac{f}{f_n} \]

where:

  • \( T \) is the transmissibility (1.0 means all of the force gets through)
  • \( r \) is the frequency ratio
  • \( f \) is the forcing frequency in hertz
  • \( f_n \) is the isolated assembly's natural frequency in hertz

Engineers usually quote the result as percent isolation, \( (1 - T) \times 100 \). The formula says three things, and the table below lists them.

Frequency ratio \( r \) What happens Result Below about 1.4 (\( \sqrt{2} \)) T is greater than 1: the isolator passes more force than a rigid mount would Amplification Exactly 1 The fan drives the assembly at its own bounce rate Resonance: large motion, possible damage Above about 1.4 T falls below 1 and keeps falling as r rises Isolation

Soft Enough Is Relative to Speed

Notice that the formula never asks how soft an isolator is in absolute terms. It asks how far apart the fan's speed and the mount's bounce are. A pad that isolates a fast fan well can make a slow fan worse than no isolator at all.

docs.title: Worked Example: Percent Isolation for a Spring Under a 1170 RPM Fan
docs.text:
The fan from the earlier example runs at 1170 RPM (19.5 Hz). It sits on springs whose natural frequency, loaded, is 3.13 Hz (the next section shows where that number comes from).

  1. Frequency ratio: \( r = 19.5 / 3.13 = 6.23 \).
  2. Transmissibility: \( T = 1 / (6.23^2 - 1) = 1 / 37.8 = 0.026 \).
  3. Percent isolation: \( (1 - 0.026) \times 100 = 97.4\% \).

About 97% of the fan's unbalance force never reaches the roof. These are idealized numbers: real isolators have some damping, and a flexible roof is not the rigid floor the formula assumes. They are good enough to compare isolator choices, which is how they are used here.

docs.title: Isolator Deflection
docs.text:
Isolator deflection is how far an isolator compresses under the weight it carries. FanPedia puts it this way: vibration isolators normally compress to dampen the vibration during normal operation, and that compression is known as deflection (p. 134). Most isolators Twin City Fan uses have deflections under 1 in, 1 in or 2 in; higher deflection is available at additional cost, after engineering review (p. 134).

Deflection is the number that matters because it sets the natural frequency directly. A mass that sags a distance \( \delta \) on its springs bounces at:

\[ f_n = \frac{1}{2\pi}\sqrt{\frac{g}{\delta}} \approx \frac{3.13}{\sqrt{\delta}} \]

where:

  • \( f_n \) is the natural frequency in hertz
  • \( g \) is the acceleration of gravity, 386.1 in/s²
  • \( \delta \) is the static deflection in inches under the actual load

Doubling the deflection does not halve the natural frequency; it divides it by \( \sqrt{2} \). And the deflection only counts if the isolator is loaded to it: an isolator rated for 1 in but carrying a fraction of its rated load deflects less and isolates less.

docs.title: Worked Example: Choosing a Deflection for a Slow Fan
docs.text:
A large fan runs at 600 RPM, so \( f = 10 \) Hz. Compare a neoprene pad (about 0.0625 in), a rubber-in-shear mount at 0.3 in, and springs at 1 in and 2 in.

Isolator (deflection) \( f_n \) (Hz) \( r \) \( T \) Percent isolation Neoprene pad (0.0625 in) 12.52 0.80 2.76 none: force is amplified about 2.8 times Rubber-in-shear (0.3 in) 5.71 1.75 0.49 51.5% Spring (1 in) 3.13 3.19 0.11 89.1% Spring (2 in) 2.21 4.52 0.05 94.8%

The pad sits below resonance, so it makes the installation worse. Rubber-in-shear helps a little. The 1 in spring is the first choice that does real work, and 2 in buys the last few percent. Run the same pad under the 1170 RPM fan from the last example and it gives about 30% isolation, which matches FanPedia's description of pads as minimal isolation at low cost (p. 134).

Pads Under a Slow Fan

A common trap is adding neoprene pads to a slow fan "for a little isolation." A 0.0625 in pad resonates near 750 RPM and amplifies the force at any speed below about 1,060 RPM. Check the frequency ratio first, and move to rubber-in-shear or springs when it comes out under about 1.4.

The explorer below lets you repeat these calculations for any combination of fan speed and deflection before committing to an answer.

docs.title: Diagram: Isolator Transmissibility Explorer
docs.text:
Isolator Transmissibility Explorer

Type: chart sim-id: ch22-isolator-transmissibility-explorer Library: Plotly Status: Specified Bloom Level: Apply Bloom Verb: calculate Learning Objective: The learner will calculate the transmissibility of an undamped isolator from the fan speed and the isolator's static deflection, to within 5% of the model value.

Prerequisites: forcing frequency, natural frequency, frequency ratio, transmissibility, percent isolation, static deflection, resonance (all defined in "Vibration", "Vibration Isolation" and "Isolator Deflection" above).

Evidence of Mastery: For three challenges, the learner types a transmissibility before the curve and answer are revealed. An answer is correct when it is within ±5% of the model value. Mastery is 3 of 3. Changing speed and deflection in exploration mode is not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) Any isolator reduces transmitted force; in fact T > 1 when r < 1.414. (2) An isolator that works on one fan works on any fan; the result depends on the fan's speed. (3) Doubling deflection halves the natural frequency; it divides it by √2.

Instructional Rationale: Apply-level calculation needs practice with a check, so the learner commits a number before the curve shows it. The plotted curve afterwards connects each calculation to the amplification, resonance and isolation regions, which confronts misconceptions 1 and 2.

Content:

Adjustable quantities:

Quantity Min Max Step Default Unit Fan speed N 300 3600 30 1170 RPM

Static deflection δ is chosen from six values, default 1.0 in: 0.0625, 0.2, 0.3, 0.5, 1.0, 2.0 in.

Labels for the deflection options: 0.0625 in "Neoprene pad"; 0.2, 0.3 and 0.5 in "Rubber-in-shear"; 1.0 and 2.0 in "Spring".

The chart plots T against frequency ratio r from 0 to 10, marks the current operating point, shades r < 1.414 as "amplification" and r >= 1.414 as "isolation", and marks r = 1 as "resonance". Readouts: f (Hz), f_n (Hz), r, T, percent isolation.

Challenges, fixed order:

# Fan speed Deflection Model T Feedback when wrong 1 1170 RPM 1.0 in 0.026 f = 19.5 Hz, f_n = 3.13 Hz, r = 6.23, T = 1/(6.23² − 1) = 0.026, about 97.4% isolation. 2 1170 RPM 0.0625 in 0.70 A pad's f_n is 12.52 Hz, so r = 1.56 and T = 1/(1.56² − 1) = 0.70: only about 30% isolation. 3 600 RPM 0.0625 in 2.76 r = 10/12.52 = 0.80 is below 1.414, so T = 1/|0.80² − 1| = 2.76: the pad amplifies the force.

Provenance: Deflection options from FanPedia p. 134 (pads about 0.0625 in; rubber-in-shear 0.2 to 0.5 in; springs 1 in or 2 in). Formulas are the standard undamped single-degree-of-freedom model. Fan speeds are illustrative; the sim labels them "illustrative".

Rules: f = N/60. f_n = 3.13/√δ (from (1/2π)√(386.1/δ)). r = f/f_n. T = 1/|r² − 1|. Percent isolation = (1 − T) × 100; when T > 1 the readout shows "amplified ×T" instead of a negative percentage. When |r − 1| < 0.05 the readout shows "at or near resonance" and the plotted T is capped at 10. Values rounded to 3 significant figures for display; answers judged against the unrounded model.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner reads challenge 1 and types a transmissibility.
  2. The learner presses Check. The operating point appears on the curve with the model value and the learner's answer side by side.
  3. After the three challenges, exploration unlocks: the learner changes speed and deflection, and the point, readouts and region label update at once.
  4. The learner should notice that at 420 RPM with 0.2 in the readout shows resonance, and that every pad setting below about 1,060 RPM lands in the amplification region.

Feedback: Three challenges, fixed order, two attempts each. Correct: "Correct: T = , ." Incorrect: the "Feedback when wrong" text. After the second wrong attempt the worked calculation is shown and the challenge counts as missed. Running count "Challenges correct: n of 3".

Starting State: Challenge 1 shown with an empty answer box and the curve hidden. The prompt reads "What fraction of the fan's force gets through a 1 in spring at 1170 RPM?"

Chapter Anchors: 1170 RPM → 19.5 Hz; 600 RPM → 10 Hz; f_n = 3.13 Hz at 1 in; T = 0.026 and 97.4% isolation at 1170 RPM on 1 in springs; the four-row table at 600 RPM (pad T 2.76; RIS 0.3 in 51.5%; 1 in 89.1%; 2 in 94.8%); pad at 1170 RPM about 30%; amplification below r ≈ 1.4; pads resonate near 750 RPM and amplify below about 1,060 RPM.

docs.title: Neoprene Isolation Pads
docs.text: A neoprene isolation pad is the simplest isolator FanPedia lists: molded, ribbed neoprene pads with a metal plate mounted between two of them, and a neoprene washer between the pad and the fan structure (pp. 134, 195). Typical deflection is about 0.0625 in. FanPedia's own verdict is that pads offer minimal vibration isolation and are low cost. As the worked example showed, they suit fast fans on solid floors, where they mostly stop noise and fretting at the mounting feet, and they should not be used where real isolation is required.

docs.title: Rubber-in-Shear Isolators
docs.text:
A rubber-in-shear (RIS) isolator carries its load through a rubber element loaded in shear rather than straight compression, which makes it softer than a pad of similar size. FanPedia's floor-mounted RIS pads consist of two steel load plates embedded in a rubber pad; ceiling-hung RIS mounts sit in a formed metal surround (pp. 134, 196). Typical deflection is 0.2 to 0.5 in for both. RIS is the middle step between pads and springs: enough deflection for a fast fan, not enough for a slow one, and it is one of the two isolator types an isolation base accepts.

Springs are the third family and the subject of Chapter 23. For now, the summary below sets the three side by side.

Isolator Construction (FanPedia p. 134) Typical deflection Isolation Neoprene pad Metal plate between two ribbed neoprene pads, neoprene washer About 0.0625 in Minimal, low cost Rubber-in-shear Steel load plates in rubber (floor); formed metal surround (ceiling hung) 0.2 to 0.5 in Moderate Spring (open, housed, restrained, seismic) Steel spring, with or without housing 1 in or 2 in (ceiling-hung open: 1 in) High

docs.title: Isolator Mounting Methods
docs.text:
An isolator mounting method is where the isolators go between the fan and the structure. FanPedia lists five (p. 133):

  • Directly under the fan: isolators under the foundation holes in the fan structure, using springs, RIS or neoprene pads. This is usually limited to fans with impellers 36.5 in in diameter or less; swingout housed centrifugal fans of any impeller size are an exception, with flat pads only.
  • Isolation rails: isolators between two flat bars, the top bar bolted to the fan's foundation holes and the bottom bar to the floor. Springs or RIS.
  • Mounting angle: an angle between the fan and the isolators, usually used when the fan inlet lacks a structural support. Springs or RIS.
  • Isolation base: the fan, possibly the motor and other components, on a structural base with isolators under the base's mounting brackets. Springs, RIS or pads.
  • Isolation hangers: the fan suspended from an overhead structure with spring or RIS hangers between it and the structure.

Chapter 23 works through each method's hardware.

docs.title: Internally Isolated Fans
docs.text: An internally isolated fan carries its own isolators inside the unit, between the rotating assembly and the fan's outer structure, so no other isolation is required. FanPedia gives commercial roof ventilators as the example (p. 133). On an order, that means the isolation question is already answered by the product. Check the current catalog to confirm a model is internally isolated before leaving external isolators off.

docs.title: Seismic Restraint
docs.text:
A seismic restraint is a device that holds an isolated fan in place during an earthquake, when ground motion would otherwise throw it off its soft mounts. Isolators are deliberately free to move; a restraint limits how far. FanPedia shows two forms (pp. 134–135). Seismic springs are like restrained springs, except that the housing nearly surrounds the entire spring so it can withstand the loads of a seismic event. Snubbers work alongside the isolators on a fan or base as shock absorbers that prevent excessive movement in any direction, and are often used when a fan must withstand seismic loading. Whether a job needs seismic restraint is set by the building's location and code, so ask for it at the quotation stage. Chapter 23 covers both devices.

Lots of Mounts, One Decision

Bases, isolator families, deflections and mounting methods can feel like a pile of unrelated parts. They are really one decision taken in order: does this fan need isolation, how much deflection does its speed demand, and what does the arrangement allow underneath it. Work the selector below one scenario at a time and the pattern shows itself.

The selector below gives you seven installations and asks you to recommend the base or mounting for each, using only the FanPedia rules covered so far.

docs.title: Diagram: Fan Base and Isolation Selector
docs.text:

  3. Feedback appears; the learner moves to the next scenario.

Which FanPedia rule decides this case?" After the second wrong attempt the answer and justification are shown and the scenario counts as missed. Score "n of 7 first-attempt correct".

docs.title: Inlet Box Mounting Planes
docs.text:
An inlet box (Chapter 18) can be attached to the fan or detached from it and supported separately. When it is detached, the installer has to know whether the fan and the box share one mounting surface. Inlet box mounting planes describes that relationship. FanPedia shows two cases (p. 143):

  • Same plane: the fan and inlet box both stand on grade (legs to grade), or both stand on one base, unitary or isolation (legs to base). They move together.
  • Different planes: the fan sits on an isolation base or a unitary base while the inlet box stands on grade. Now the fan and box can move relative to each other, and FanPedia requires a flex connector (slip connection) between the fan and the inlet box.

The practical rule follows from the isolation section: if the fan floats on isolators and the inlet box does not, the joint between them must be flexible, exactly as at the duct connections.

docs.title: Installation Accessories: Weather Cover, Zero Speed Switch, Piezometer Ring
docs.text:
Three smaller accessories complete most installations.

A weather cover (FanPedia lists it with the motor cover, p. 126) is a cover that protects the motor from rain, snow and sun when the fan is installed outdoors. It is an option that makes some arrangements suitable for outdoor use: FanPedia describes Arrangement 10 fans, including the lab exhaust version, as suitable for roof or outdoor installations when supplied with the optional weather cover (pp. 167, 175). On spark-resistant construction, the weather cover is one of the mild-steel parts FanPedia lists (p. 109).

A zero speed switch, also called a speed sensor, detects slowing or stopping of the fan shaft (FanPedia p. 129). Other designs are provided when the customer requests them. Its usual job is to tell a control or alarm system that a fan has stopped even though its motor starter is still energized, as when a belt breaks.

A piezometer ring is part of an airflow measuring system based on the principle of a flow nozzle, with the fan's own inlet funnel serving as the nozzle (FanPedia pp. 158, 191). Tubing around the throat of the funnel forms the ring, and a tap on the face of the funnel provides the second pressure. The pressure drop between them is measured by a differential pressure transducer: the face tap goes to the high-pressure side and the ring to the low-pressure side. The tubing is nylon for temperatures up to 180°F and copper above. Piezometer rings are available on plenum fans and on SWSI and DWDI housed centrifugal fans (p. 158), and FanPedia also shows inline centrifugal and mixed flow mountings (p. 160). Turning that pressure reading into airflow is covered in Chapter 23.

Accessory What it does Order note Weather cover Protects the motor outdoors Makes some arrangements, such as Arrangement 10, suitable for roof or outdoor use Zero speed switch Detects slowing or stopping of the fan shaft Other designs on customer request Piezometer ring Measures inlet funnel pressure drop for airflow Plenum, SWSI and DWDI centrifugal fans; transducer optional

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Fan installation is a set of order decisions (support, base, isolation, connections, environment, monitoring) that must be made before the order, because none of them appear on the fan curve.
  • Vibration is driven mainly by unbalance at the forcing frequency \( f = N/60 \); the lowest forcing frequency sets the isolation requirement.
  • A unitary base is for use without isolators; an isolation base sits on spring or RIS isolators with flex connectors; an inertia base is an isolation base with rebar and customer-poured concrete for longer direct-drive fans.
  • Vibration isolation works only when the frequency ratio exceeds about 1.4; below that an isolator amplifies the force, and at 1 it resonates.
  • Isolator deflection sets the natural frequency, \( f_n \approx 3.13/\sqrt{\delta} \): pads (about 0.0625 in) give minimal isolation, rubber-in-shear (0.2 to 0.5 in) moderate, springs (1 or 2 in) high.
  • The five isolator mounting methods are directly under the fan, isolation rails, mounting angle, isolation base and isolation hangers; some arrangements, such as 9F, cannot take isolators directly under the fan.
  • Internally isolated fans, such as commercial roof ventilators, need no other isolation; seismic restraints keep isolated fans in place during an earthquake.
  • When a fan and a detached inlet box sit on different mounting planes, a flex connector is required between them.
  • Weather covers, zero speed switches and piezometer rings finish the installation: outdoor protection, stop detection and airflow measurement.

You Can Put a Fan in a Building

You can now read a job, pick a unitary, isolation or inertia base, and check a deflection against a fan speed with the frequency ratio. That last calculation is the one that separates an isolator that works from one that makes things worse.

docs.title: Spring Isolators, Restraints and Field Measurement
Summary
docs.text: This chapter completes installation. It covers spring isolators (open, housed, restrained, and seismic), floor mounted and ceiling hung isolation, direct mounted isolators, isolation rails, mounting angles, snubbers, and thrust restraints that resist the fan's pressure thrust. It also covers shaft and coupling alignment, anti-backspin devices, and measuring airflow in the field with piezometer rings and pressure transmitters. After completing it, readers can specify isolation hardware and explain how installed airflow is verified.

docs.title: Concepts Covered
docs.text:
This chapter covers the following 16 concepts from the learning graph:
