docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
This chapter builds on concepts from:

  • Chapter 1: Air, Pressure and the Fan
  • Chapter 2: Airstreams, Total Pressure and Standard Air
  • Chapter 3: Basic Fan Anatomy
  • Chapter 11: Drives and Standard Fan Arrangements
  • Chapter 12: Discharge Positions and Rotation
  • Chapter 15: Motor Ratings, Speed Control and Positioners
  • Chapter 16: Bearings, Shafts and Shaft Seals
  • Chapter 22: Fan Bases and Vibration Isolation

The Last Few Feet of the Job

A well-selected fan can still disappoint if it rocks on the wrong springs, walks away from its duct at start-up, or spins backward on a windy night. This chapter covers the hardware and checks that make an installation quiet, stable and verifiable. By the end you can read an isolation line on a specification and tell the customer how their airflow will be proven. Let's follow the airflow.

Chapter 22 explained why fans are isolated, what deflection means, and how unitary, isolation and inertia bases support a fan. This chapter turns to the specific hardware on the order: the four kinds of spring isolator, the ways isolators attach to a fan, the snubbers and thrust restraints that limit motion, and three field topics that decide whether the installed fan runs as rated: shaft and coupling alignment, anti-backspin devices, and airflow measurement. The product statements come from the FanPedia vibration isolation pages (pp. 133–135), the piezometer ring pages (pp. 158–160) and the technical descriptions (pp. 162–197).

docs.title: Spring Isolators
docs.text:
A spring isolator is a steel coil spring, with its top and bottom load plates, placed between a fan (or its base) and the supporting structure. Under the fan's weight the spring compresses; that compression is the isolator's static deflection. A soft spring that compresses a lot lets the fan bounce at a low natural frequency, and a fan that runs well above that frequency passes very little of its vibrating force into the floor. Springs reach much larger deflections than rubber-in-shear mounts or neoprene pads, which is why they are the usual choice when isolation really matters.

FanPedia (p. 134) states that most isolators Twin City Fan uses have deflections under 1 inch (25.4 mm), 1 inch, or 2 inches (50.8 mm). Higher deflection is available at additional cost after engineering review. Those three values are the vocabulary of a spring isolator line item: a specification that asks for "2-inch deflection springs" is asking for the high end of the standard range.

Two relationships connect a spring to the fan it carries. The first converts load into deflection.

docs.title: Static Deflection of a Spring
docs.text:
\[ \delta = \frac{W / n}{k} \]

where:

  • \( \delta \) is the static deflection of each isolator, in inches
  • \( W \) is the total weight carried by the isolators (fan, motor, drive and base), in pounds
  • \( n \) is the number of isolators, assuming the load is shared equally
  • \( k \) is the spring rate of one isolator, in pounds per inch of compression

The second, a standard result for an undamped spring and mass, gives the natural frequency of the fan bouncing on its springs.

docs.title: Natural Frequency of a Spring-Mounted Fan
docs.text:
\[ f_n = \frac{3.13}{\sqrt{\delta}} \]

where:

  • \( f_n \) is the natural frequency of the mounted assembly, in hertz (cycles per second)
  • \( \delta \) is the static deflection, in inches
  • 3.13 comes from \( \frac{1}{2\pi}\sqrt{g} \) with \( g = 386 \) in/s²

Isolation begins only when the fan's running frequency is more than \( \sqrt{2} \), about 1.41, times the natural frequency. Below that ratio the springs amplify vibration instead of blocking it.

Softer Is Lower, Lower Is Better

Notice that deflection sits under a square root: doubling deflection lowers the natural frequency only by a factor of 1.41. That is why the jump from 1-inch to 2-inch springs matters most on slower fans, whose running frequency sits closest to the springs' bounce.

Worked example (illustrative numbers). A fan, motor and isolation base weigh 2,400 lb and sit on four spring isolators, each with a spring rate of 600 lb/in. The fan runs at 1,180 rpm.

  1. Load per isolator: \( 2{,}400 / 4 = 600 \) lb.
  2. Static deflection: \( \delta = 600 / 600 = 1.00 \) in, a standard 1-inch spring.
  3. Natural frequency: \( f_n = 3.13 / \sqrt{1.00} = 3.13 \) Hz.
  4. Running frequency: \( 1{,}180 / 60 = 19.67 \) Hz.
  5. Frequency ratio: \( r = 19.67 / 3.13 = 6.28 \), far above 1.41, so the springs isolate. The undamped transmissibility \( T = 1/(r^2 - 1) = 0.026 \): about 2.6% of the vibrating force reaches the floor, an isolation efficiency of about 97.4%.

Real bases rarely load four corners equally, because the motor side is heavier. Isolator suppliers then choose a different spring for each corner so that every corner deflects the same amount; the calculation per corner is the same.

docs.title: Diagram: Spring Isolator Deflection Calculator
docs.text:
Spring Isolator Deflection Calculator

Type: microsim sim-id: ch23-spring-isolator-deflection-calculator Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Apply Bloom Verb: calculate Learning Objective: The learner will calculate the static deflection of equally loaded spring isolators from total weight, isolator count and spring rate, to within 0.02 in.

Prerequisites: spring isolator, static deflection, spring rate, natural frequency, running frequency, frequency ratio, transmissibility (all defined in the section "Spring Isolators" above).

Evidence of Mastery: For three challenge cases, the learner types the deflection in inches before the sim shows it. An answer is correct when it is within ±0.02 in of the model value. Mastery is 3 of 3 correct. Free exploration of the controls afterward is not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) Doubling deflection halves the natural frequency (it divides it by 1.41). (2) Any spring isolates, whatever the fan speed (below a ratio of 1.41 the springs amplify). (3) Adding isolators adds deflection (more isolators share the load, so each deflects less).

Instructional Rationale: Calculation at the Apply level needs practice with a check, so the learner commits a number before the answer appears. The exploration mode then shows how deflection, natural frequency and isolation respond to each input, which confronts the three misconceptions with computed values.

Content:

Adjustable quantities:

Quantity Min Max Step Default Unit Total supported weight W 400 8000 100 2400 lb Number of isolators n 4 8 2 4 count Spring rate k (each) 100 3000 50 600 lb/in Fan speed 300 3600 10 1180 rpm

Displayed results: load per isolator (lb), static deflection (in, 2 decimals), natural frequency (Hz, 2 decimals), running frequency (Hz, 2 decimals), frequency ratio (2 decimals), transmissibility (3 decimals), isolation efficiency (%, 1 decimal), and a status line.

Challenge cases, in this order:

# W (lb) n k (lb/in) Model deflection (in) Feedback when wrong 1 2400 4 600 1.00 Divide the weight among the isolators first: 2,400 / 4 = 600 lb, then 600 / 600 = 1.00 in. 2 3600 6 300 2.00 Six isolators share 3,600 lb, so each carries 600 lb; 600 / 300 = 2.00 in. 3 1600 4 1600 0.25 Each isolator carries 400 lb; a stiff 1,600 lb/in spring compresses only 400 / 1,600 = 0.25 in.

All values are labeled "illustrative" on screen.

Provenance: Equations and the 1.41 threshold are standard vibration-isolation results stated in the chapter section "Spring Isolators". The typical deflections (under 1 in, 1 in, 2 in; higher by engineering review) are from FanPedia p. 134. Challenge values are illustrative.

Rules:

  • Load per isolator = W / n. Deflection δ = (W / n) / k.
  • f_n = 3.13 / √δ (Hz). Running frequency f = rpm / 60. Ratio r = f / f_n.
  • If r > 1.41: T = 1 / (r² − 1), efficiency = (1 − T) × 100%, status "Isolating".
  • If r <= 1.41 and r is not within ±0.02 of 1.00: T = 1 / |1 − r²|, efficiency is shown as "none", status "Amplifying: springs too stiff for this speed".
  • If |r − 1.00| <= 0.02: status "Resonance", T shown as "very large".
  • If δ > 2.00 in: add the note "Above the typical 2-inch deflection; higher deflection requires engineering review (FanPedia p. 134)."

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner reads challenge 1 (W, n, k) and types a deflection.
  2. The learner presses Check. The sim shows the model deflection, the spring compressed to scale beside an uncompressed spring, and the derived natural frequency.
  3. After all three challenges, exploration unlocks with the default values. Changing any input updates every result at once.
  4. The learner should notice that raising n lowers deflection, that raising fan speed raises the ratio, and that a 0.25-in spring on a 300-rpm fan reaches the Amplifying status.

Feedback: Three challenges, fixed order, two attempts each. Correct: "Correct: δ = in." Incorrect: the "Feedback when wrong" text. After the second wrong attempt the model value and its calculation are shown and the challenge counts as missed. A running count "Challenges correct: n of 3" is shown.

Starting State: Challenge 1 with an empty answer box, an uncompressed spring drawing, and the question "How far will each spring compress?"

Chapter Anchors: Worked example: 2,400 lb on four isolators at 600 lb/in gives 600 lb each, 1.00 in deflection, 3.13 Hz natural frequency; 1,180 rpm is 19.67 Hz; ratio 6.28; transmissibility 0.026; efficiency about 97.4%. Isolation begins above a ratio of 1.41. Typical deflections under 1 in, 1 in or 2 in.

docs.title: Open, Housed, Restrained and Seismic Springs
docs.text:
FanPedia (pp. 134, 196) names four spring isolator types. They share the same coil spring; what differs is how much of the spring is enclosed and how much motion the enclosure allows.

An open spring isolator is the simplest spring mount: a bare coil between two load plates. It does not offer any restriction of the motion caused by aerodynamic forces, so a fan on open springs is free to shift when its airstream pushes on it. Twin City Fan typically does not use floor mounted open springs. Ceiling hung open springs are mounted in a formed metal surround, and the typical deflection is 1 inch.

A housed spring isolator works the same way as an open spring but sits inside an enclosed housing. The housing can hold one or more springs, depending on the load and application. Typical deflection is 1 or 2 inches.

A restrained spring isolator is the same design as an open spring with a housing or frame added to restrain the vertical and/or horizontal motion of the spring. The restraint matters when a fan must not drift, rock or lift as its load and aerodynamic forces change. Typical deflection is 1 or 2 inches.

A seismic spring isolator is similar to a restrained spring, except that the housing nearly surrounds the entire spring so that it can withstand the loads generated during a seismic event such as an earthquake. Typical deflection is 1 or 2 inches. Seismic springs are the isolator-level answer to the seismic restraint requirement introduced in Chapter 22.

The table below lines the four types up against each other.

Spring type Enclosure Limits motion? Typical deflection (FanPedia p. 134) Open None (ceiling hung: formed metal surround) No 1 in Housed Enclosed housing, one or more springs No more than an open spring 1 or 2 in Restrained Housing or frame Yes, vertical and/or horizontal 1 or 2 in Seismic Housing nearly surrounds the spring Yes, built for seismic loads 1 or 2 in

docs.title: Where the Isolators Go
docs.text:
The second half of an isolation specification says how the isolators meet the fan and the structure. FanPedia (p. 133) groups the choices into five mounting styles. Two of them describe which way the load hangs: from the floor up or from the structure down.

Floor mounted isolation places isolators beneath the fan or its base, bearing on the floor, a housekeeping pad or a support frame. It can use springs, rubber-in-shear (RIS) mounts or neoprene pads, and it includes three of the styles below: directly under the fan, isolation rails and mounting angles, plus the isolation base from Chapter 22.

Ceiling hung isolation suspends the fan from an overhead structure, such as a ceiling or roof steel, with the isolators between that structure and the fan. FanPedia calls these isolation hangers, and they can be spring or RIS hangers. The threaded rod that carries them is supplied by others, and ceiling hung springs and RIS mounts sit in a formed metal surround.

Direct mounted isolators sit directly under the foundation holes in the fan's own structure, with no base between. They can be springs, RIS pads or neoprene pads. FanPedia limits this style, usually, to fans with impellers of 36.5 inches in diameter or less. The exception is swingout housed centrifugal fans of any impeller size, with flat pads only. Some arrangements cannot take isolators directly under the fan at all: Arrangement 3F is typically not suitable (p. 163), and Arrangement 9F is not suitable; FanPedia's remedy for 9F is an Arrangement 1 fan on a separate isolation base (p. 166).

Isolation rails put the isolators between two pieces of flat bar. The top bar bolts to the fan's foundation holes and the bottom bar attaches to the floor or other mounting structure. Springs or RIS pads can be used. Rails spread the fan's foundation pattern onto a pair of bars, which gives the isolators a clean place to sit.

An isolator mounting angle is a structural angle mounted between the fan and its isolators. It is usually used when the fan's inlet side has no structural support of its own for an isolator to bear on. Springs or RIS pads can be used.

The list below restates the choices as questions to ask when you read a drawing.

  • Does the fan hang from structure? Use isolation hangers (ceiling hung).
  • Does the fan structure have usable foundation holes and an impeller of 36.5 in or less? Isolators can mount directly under the fan.
  • Do the foundation holes need a continuous member to bolt to? Use isolation rails.
  • Is one side of the fan, usually the inlet side, without structural support? Add a mounting angle.
  • Must fan, motor and drive move together? Use an isolation base (Chapter 22).

docs.text:
Isolation Hardware Sorter

Type: microsim sim-id: ch23-isolation-hardware-sorter Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Understand Bloom Verb: classify Learning Objective: The learner will classify eleven job-site descriptions by the isolation hardware FanPedia calls for, with at least 9 of 11 correct on the first attempt.

Prerequisites: open, housed, restrained and seismic spring isolators; ceiling hung isolation; direct mounted isolators; isolation rails; isolator mounting angle; snubber; thrust restraint (all defined in the chapter above this block, the last two in "Snubbers and Thrust Restraints").

Evidence of Mastery: The learner assigns each of the 11 descriptions to one of 10 bins. An assignment is correct when it matches the Correct bin column. Mastery is 9 of 11 correct on the first attempt.

Misconceptions: (1) A snubber and a seismic spring are the same device. (2) Any spring restrains a fan against airflow forces (open springs do not). (3) Every fan can sit on isolators bolted directly under it.

Instructional Rationale: Classifying realistic descriptions makes the learner map features (enclosure, direction of support, where brackets attach) onto hardware names, which is the Understand-level skill used when reading a specification.

Content:

Bins (10): Open spring isolator; Housed spring isolator; Restrained spring isolator; Seismic spring isolator; Snubber; Thrust restraint; Isolation hangers (ceiling hung); Isolators directly under fan; Isolation rails; Isolator mounting angle.

# Description shown to the learner Correct bin Why (shown as feedback) 1 The fan hangs from roof steel; the isolators go between the overhead structure and the fan on threaded rod by others. Isolation hangers (ceiling hung) A fan suspended from structure with isolators between structure and fan uses isolation hangers. 2 A horizontal-discharge fan on springs slides back at every start; the spec asks for two devices, 180° apart, tying the fan discharge to the discharge duct with threaded rod. Thrust restraint Thrust restraints are ceiling hung type isolators attached to fan discharge and duct, two per fan, 180° apart. 3 The inlet side of the fan has no structural member for an isolator to bear on. Isolator mounting angle A mounting angle is used when the fan inlet does not have a structural support. 4 Isolators sit between two flat bars; the top bar bolts to the fan's foundation holes and the bottom bar anchors to the floor. Isolation rails That is FanPedia's definition of isolation rails. 5 A fan with a 30-inch impeller (illustrative) gets springs bolted straight under the foundation holes in its own structure, with no base. Isolators directly under fan Direct mounting is usually limited to impellers of 36.5 in or less; 30 in qualifies. 6 A swingout housed centrifugal fan with a large impeller sits on flat pads bolted directly under its own structure. Isolators directly under fan Swingout housed centrifugal fans are the exception: any impeller size, flat pads only. 7 The spec calls for spring mounts whose housings nearly surround the entire spring so they withstand earthquake loads. Seismic spring isolator A housing that nearly surrounds the spring for seismic loads defines a seismic spring. 8 A separate device, one bracket on the base and one on the floor with elastomeric material between them, limits movement in any direction; it is used along with the isolators. Snubber A snubber works with isolators as a shock absorber; the elastomer prevents metal-to-metal contact. 9 Springs with a frame added to limit vertical and horizontal travel; no seismic requirement is stated. Restrained spring isolator A housing or frame that restrains vertical and/or horizontal motion defines a restrained spring. 10 A bare coil spring in a formed metal surround on a ceiling hung fan; it does nothing to resist aerodynamic forces. Open spring isolator Open springs offer no restriction of aerodynamic motion; ceiling hung types sit in a formed metal surround. 11 An enclosed housing holds two springs that act exactly like open springs. Housed spring isolator Housed springs work like open springs inside an enclosed housing that can hold one or more springs.

Provenance: FanPedia pp. 133–135 and 196–197 (all definitions, the 36.5-inch limit, the swingout exception, thrust restraint details). The 30-inch impeller in item 5 is illustrative and is labeled so on screen.

Rules: Each description has exactly one correct bin. Bins can receive more than one description (item 5 and item 6 share a bin). No partial credit.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner reads one description and places it in a bin.
  2. The sim marks the placement correct or incorrect at once and shows the "Why" text.
  3. An incorrect placement returns the card for a second try; the first-attempt result is what counts toward mastery.
  4. After all 11, the sim shows the first-attempt score and lists the descriptions missed with their reasons.

Feedback: 11 items in shuffled order, two attempts each. Correct: "Correct. ." Incorrect: "Not quite. Look for ." After the second wrong attempt the card moves to its correct bin and the Why text is shown. Score shown: "First-attempt correct: n of 11; mastery at 9."

Starting State: Ten empty labeled bins and the first card face up, with the prompt "Which hardware does this job call for?"

Chapter Anchors: Four spring types; five mounting styles; direct mounting usually limited to impellers of 36.5 in or less; swingout housed centrifugal fans excepted with flat pads only; two thrust restraints per fan, 180° apart.

docs.title: Snubbers and Thrust Restraints
docs.text:
Springs let a fan move. Two devices limit how far.

A snubber is a stop used together with the isolators on a fan or base. It serves as a shock absorber that prevents excessive movement of the fan or base in any direction, and it is often used when the fan must withstand seismic loading (FanPedia p. 135). A snubber is two brackets, one attached to the fan or base and one attached to the floor, with elastomeric (rubberized) material between them that prevents metal-to-metal contact. In normal running the fan floats on its springs; the snubber engages only when an unusual load, such as an earthquake, tries to move the fan too far.

A thrust restraint prevents excessive motion caused by aerodynamic force. Any fan that pushes air feels a reaction force, roughly its pressure rise times its outlet area, in the direction opposite the flow. For an illustrative outlet of 4 ft² at 4 in. wg, with 1 in. wg equal to 5.2 lb/ft², that is about \( 4 \times 5.2 \times 4 = 83 \) lb pushing the fan backward each time it starts. On stiff mounts the force is lost in friction; on soft springs the fan moves, and the flex connector takes the strain.

FanPedia (p. 197) describes the standard thrust restraint: ceiling hung type isolators (springs or spring/RIS pad combinations) attached to both the fan discharge and the discharge duct with threaded rod, adjusted to prevent horizontal motion. Two restraints are used per fan, mounted 180° apart, and FanPedia's drawing shows them for horizontal airflow in either direction.

Open Springs Do Not Hold a Fan in Place

A common trap is quoting open springs on a high-pressure fan and assuming the flex connector will keep it in place. Open springs offer no restriction of aerodynamic motion, so the fan shifts at every start and the connector tears over time. When pressure is high and discharge is horizontal, add thrust restraints or use restrained springs.

docs.title: Shaft and Coupling Alignment
docs.text:
A coupling connects the fan shaft to the motor shaft, or one fan shaft to another in a twin fan assembly (FanPedia p. 129). Shaft and coupling alignment is the process of positioning the motor and the fan bearings so that the two shaft centerlines run as one straight line through the coupling. Misalignment comes in two forms: offset, where the centerlines are parallel but displaced, and angular, where they meet at an angle. Either form loads the coupling and the bearings on every revolution and shows up as vibration at running speed or twice running speed.

FanPedia hardware exists to make alignment repeatable. Motor positioners, also called motor alignment jacking screws, move the motor in small steps (p. 148). Bearing dowel pins hold a bearing's position once it is aligned (p. 176). A machined pedestal top gives the bearings and motor a flat reference surface (p. 130). Inertia bases are used on longer direct drive fans because their mass and stiffness keep the motor, coupling, shaft and bearings aligned (p. 175).

Align Last, Then Check Again

Do the final alignment after the isolators are adjusted to their working deflection and the duct and flex connectors are attached. Then recheck it after the first run, because a base that settles on its springs can carry the motor out of line.

docs.title: Anti-Backspin Devices
docs.text:
An anti-backspin device, also called an anti-rotation device or anti-rotation clutch (FanPedia p. 125), prevents the rotor from freewheeling in reverse when the fan is not running (p. 162). It is a one-way clutch on the shaft: the fan turns freely in its correct rotation, and the device locks against rotation the other way.

Reverse freewheeling happens when air flows backward through an idle fan. The common causes are a second fan in parallel pushing air back through the stopped one, stack draft in a tall exhaust system, and wind on a roof or wall discharge. A fan spinning backward causes two problems. First, when its motor starts it must stop the rotor and then accelerate it the other way, which lengthens the high-current start and loads belts, couplings and shafts. Second, a rotor that can turn on its own is a hazard for anyone working on a fan that is supposed to be stopped. A zero speed switch, from Chapter 22, can report the motion; an anti-backspin device prevents it.

Where the device mounts depends on how the impeller is supported (p. 162):

  • Overhung impeller designs, where the impeller sits at the end of the shaft (Arrangements 1 and 9, for example): mounted between the bearings.
  • Center hung impeller designs, where the impeller sits between the bearings (Arrangement 3, for example): mounted on a shaft extension on the non-drive end.

Worked example. A plant runs two identical exhaust fans in parallel into one stack. Fan A is an Arrangement 9 SWSI belt drive; Fan B, the standby, is an Arrangement 3 SWSI belt drive. The operator wants to run one fan at a time.

  1. Is reverse flow possible? Yes. When Fan A runs, the shared stack connection is at a higher pressure than Fan B's inlet, so air flows backward through idle Fan B. The same happens to Fan A when Fan B runs.
  2. Which fans need the device? Both, because each will be the idle fan at some point.
  3. Fan A, Arrangement 9: the impeller is overhung, so the device mounts between the two bearings on the pedestal.
  4. Fan B, Arrangement 3: the impeller is center hung, so the shaft must have an extension on the non-drive end to carry the device. That extension is a shaft detail, so it belongs on the order, not as a field add-on.
  5. Line items: anti-backspin device on both fans, plus the non-drive-end shaft extension on Fan B. If the customer also wants a start interlock, add a zero speed switch.

docs.title: Measuring Airflow in the Field
docs.text:
Airflow measurement is the determination of the volume of air a fan actually delivers in its installed system, in cfm. A catalog rating describes the fan on a test stand; a field measurement tells the owner what the system is getting, which is how system effect and duct errors are found. A traditional method is a pitot tube traverse across a duct. The method FanPedia describes uses the fan itself.

The piezometer ring, introduced in Chapter 22, uses the fan's inlet funnel as a flow nozzle (FanPedia p. 158). A tap on the face of the funnel connects to the high-pressure side of a pressure-measuring device; tubing around the throat of the funnel, the ring, connects to the low-pressure side. The air speeds up as it enters the throat, so the throat pressure falls, and that pressure difference rises with the square of the airflow.

docs.title: Flow Through the Inlet Funnel
docs.text:
\[ Q = K \sqrt{\Delta p} \]

where:

  • \( Q \) is the airflow, in cfm
  • \( K \) is the flow coefficient for that fan's inlet funnel, supplied by the fan manufacturer, in cfm per \( \sqrt{\text{in. wg}} \)
  • \( \Delta p \) is the pressure difference between the funnel face tap and the throat ring, in in. wg

With an illustrative \( K = 10{,}000 \), a reading of 1.44 in. wg gives \( 10{,}000 \times 1.2 = 12{,}000 \) cfm. If the reading falls to 1.00 in. wg, the flow is 10,000 cfm: a 31% drop in the reading is only a 17% drop in airflow. Twin City Fan's installation manual IM-105 carries the detailed piezometer information for each fan type (p. 160).

A pressure transmitter is the device that turns that pressure difference into a signal a controls system can use, typically an electrical output for the building automation system, with or without a local display. FanPedia (p. 160) lists two optional versions a customer can buy from Twin City Fan: a pressure transmitter without display, and a pressure transmitter/transducer with display, shown in regular and NEMA 4 enclosures. Either can be mounted on the fan or remotely by others. Transmitters must be sized based on the application and fan performance: the transmitter's range has to cover the pressure difference the fan will produce at its highest expected airflow, without being so wide that normal readings sit at the bottom of the scale.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• A spring isolator compresses under load; deflection = load per isolator divided by spring rate, and natural frequency = 3.13 / √deflection (Hz, inches). Isolation needs a running-to-natural frequency ratio above 1.41. Twin City Fan's typical deflections are under 1 in, 1 in and 2 in.
  • Open springs restrain nothing; housed springs enclose one or more springs; restrained springs add a housing or frame to limit vertical and/or horizontal motion; seismic springs have a housing that nearly surrounds the spring for earthquake loads.
  • Floor mounted isolation supports the fan from below; ceiling hung isolation suspends it on isolation hangers. Direct mounted isolators sit under the fan's foundation holes (usually impellers of 36.5 in or less; swingout housed centrifugal fans excepted with flat pads). Isolation rails and isolator mounting angles give isolators a place to bear.
  • Snubbers limit motion in any direction, often for seismic loading; thrust restraints are paired ceiling hung isolators, 180° apart, between fan discharge and duct that resist aerodynamic thrust.
  • Shaft and coupling alignment makes the motor and fan shaft centerlines one line; positioners, dowel pins, machined tops and inertia bases help hold it.
  • An anti-backspin device stops an idle fan from freewheeling in reverse: between the bearings on overhung designs, on a non-drive-end shaft extension on center hung designs.
  • Airflow measurement with a piezometer ring reads the pressure drop across the inlet funnel; airflow varies with its square root. A pressure transmitter, sized to the application, sends that reading to the controls.

Isolation Specified, Airflow Proven

You can now calculate spring deflection, name the right spring and mounting style for a job, explain why thrust restraints and anti-backspin devices go on the order, and describe how a piezometer ring proves installed airflow. That completes the path from a selected fan to a running, verified installation.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: This chapter returns to fan arrangements with the variants that build on motors, bases, and installation: Arrangements 8, 9, and 10; plug arrangements 1P, 4P, 8P, and 9P; plenum arrangements 3HS, 3HA, 3SM, 3VA, 3VS, and 4V; Arrangements 3F, 9F, 9H, and 9ST/9SS; vertical and horizontal inline variants; and swingout and clamshell fans and their door assemblies. It closes with motor positions L and R, the standard and swingout motor position rules, inline motor positions A to H, and ventilating sets. After completing it, readers can identify any arrangement code in a FanPedia or catalog drawing.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
This chapter builds on concepts from:

  • Chapter 3: Basic Fan Anatomy
  • Chapter 11: Drives and Standard Fan Arrangements
  • Chapter 12: Discharge Positions and Rotation
  • Chapter 13: Rotation and Discharge Codes
  • Chapter 14: Fan Motors and Enclosures
  • Chapter 15: Motor Ratings, Speed Control and Positioners
  • Chapter 17: Bearing Details, Lubrication and Pedestals
  • Chapter 22: Fan Bases and Vibration Isolation
  • Chapter 23: Spring Isolators, Restraints and Field Measurement

Every Letter on the Drawing Means Something

A customer's drawing says "Arr. 9SS, CCW, R" and the order desk wants to know if it can ship. By the end of this chapter you will read that code, picture the fan, and know whether the motor and conduit box can go where the customer wants them. Let's follow the airflow.

docs.title: From Base Numbers to Variants
docs.text:
Chapter 11 introduced the base arrangement numbers: 1, 3, 4 and 7 for housed centrifugal fans, plus the plug, plenum, axial and lab exhaust families. Real orders rarely stop at the base number. A drawing title block is just as likely to read 9H, 3SM, 8P or 4CS, and each suffix changes what the factory builds: where the motor sits, what holds the fan up, and how a mechanic gets to the impeller.

This chapter takes the variants in groups: the overhung pedestal arrangements 8, 9 and 10; frame and inlet variants of 3, 4 and 7; plenum and plug variants; and swingout and clamshell construction. It closes with the motor position rules that go with them.

Most suffixes abbreviate a word in FanPedia's drawing captions, where the key letter is underlined (FanPedia pp. 20–28):

Suffix Stands for Seen on F Extended frame that carries the motor 3F, 9F H Motor mounted horizontally on the side of the pedestal 9H SI, DI Integral inlet box on a single or double width fan 3SI, 7SI, 3DI, 7DI VI, HI Fan hung from its own inlet, vertical or horizontal shaft 4VI, 4HI P Pedestal plug fan, mounted to grade 1P, 4P, 8P, 9P S, ST, SS, SO Swingout construction (ST top motor, SS side motor) 4S, 9ST, 9SS, 4SO, 9SO CS Clamshell construction 4CS, 9CS HS, HA, SM, VA, VS, V Plenum motor mounting variants 3HS, 3HA, 3SM, 3VA, 3VS, 4V

docs.title: The Overhung Pedestal Family: Arrangements 8, 9 and 10
docs.text: Arrangements 1, 8, 9 and 10 share one skeleton. The impeller is overhung, mounted on the end of the shaft, and both bearings sit on a bearing pedestal outside the housing (FanPedia p. 30). What separates the four is the drive and the motor's location.

docs.title: Arrangement 8
docs.text:
Arrangement 8 is a direct drive, overhung fan in which the Arrangement 1 bearing pedestal is extended to carry the motor, and a flexible coupling joins the motor shaft to the fan shaft. FanPedia calls it "a modified version of Arrangement 1 used for direct drive" (FanPedia p. 165). The fan keeps its own shaft and two bearings, so the impeller does not hang on the motor bearings as it does in Arrangement 4.

That is the reason to specify it. Arrangement 4 fans "are typically limited up to size 365" (FanPedia p. 164) and put the motor against the housing; Arrangement 8 lets the fan bearings carry the impeller and keeps the motor away from the airstream. The layout also appears in BAIFE and BCIFE lab exhaust fans and in wall-mounted plug fans (FanPedia pp. 26, 29, 174).

The cost is length, with motor, coupling, bearings and housing in a line. FanPedia calls the Arrangement 8 plug fan "the least common plug fan arrangement due to the length of the assembly" (FanPedia p. 171). FanPedia notes that inertia bases "are typically used on longer, direct drive fans to mitigate assembly deflection, maintaining proper alignment between the motor, coupling, shaft and bearings" (FanPedia p. 175), a base covered in Chapter 22.

Worked example: direct drive above the Arrangement 4 range. A process engineer wants a direct drive SWSI exhaust fan with no belts to maintain, and the selection lands on a fan size larger than 365.

  1. Try Arrangement 4 first. Size 365 is its typical upper limit, so this selection is outside it.
  2. Keep the overhung impeller. The engineer wants both bearings out of the airstream, which rules out the center hung Arrangement 7.
  3. Choose Arrangement 8. The Arrangement 1 pedestal is extended for the motor, and a flexible coupling transmits the power.
  4. Plan the support. The assembly is long, so the engineer asks whether an inertia base is needed to hold coupling alignment, and adds an alignment check to start-up.

The order line then adds rotation and discharge as in Chapter 13, but no motor position letter: the motor sits on the shaft centerline.

docs.title: Arrangement 9
docs.text:
Arrangement 9 is a belt driven, overhung fan with the motor mounted on the side of the fan's own bearing pedestal. FanPedia states that it "is available as belt driven only," that "a motor slide base is mounted on the side of the bearing pedestal," and that the arrangement "permits the unit to ship as a complete assembly with the motor and drive mounted" (FanPedia p. 165). Unlike Arrangement 1, whose motor stands on the floor or a fan base, Arrangement 9 is one package with one footprint.

FanPedia also uses Arrangement 9 for plug fans ("the most common plug fan arrangement", p. 172), for axial and inline fans that need "the motor to be out of the airstream" (p. 173), and for lab exhaust fans (p. 175). In every family the motor is outside the air path and a sheave change can retune the speed. The motor side follows rotation, left for CW and right for CCW (FanPedia p. 165), a rule covered at the end of this chapter.

Worked example: choosing within the 9 family. An industrial customer needs a belt driven SWSI fan for a hot process exhaust. The plant wants the fan shipped as one assembly, belt tension that a millwright can set without special tools, and spring isolators under the fan. The candidate variants are 9, 9F, 9H and 10:

  1. Arrangement 9 fits: the motor is on a slide base on the side of the pedestal, the unit ships complete, and the bearings are outside the hot airstream.
  2. The motor size check. The selection calls for a large motor. If it is too large for the pedestal, FanPedia's answer is Arrangement 9F (p. 166), but 9F "is not suitable for mounting vibration isolators directly under the fan" and FanPedia's advice when isolators are required is to "use an Arrangement 1 fan with a separate isolation base" (p. 166).
  3. The adjustment check. If the millwright prefers to move the motor horizontally to tension the belts, Arrangement 9H puts the motor on the side of an extended pedestal for horizontal adjustment (p. 166).
  4. The decision. The motor fits on the pedestal, so the engineer offers Arrangement 9, CW, with spring isolators. Had the motor been too large, the quote would have switched to Arrangement 1 with an isolation base, not 9F.

docs.title: Arrangement 9F
docs.text: Arrangement 9F is an Arrangement 9 whose fan frame is extended to carry a motor that is too large for the bearing pedestal. The motor sits horizontally on the extended structural frame, "similar to an Arrangement 1 fan" (FanPedia p. 166), and the F in the code stands for that frame (FanPedia p. 22). The frame ties the fan and motor together, but it also means the fan cannot float on isolators: FanPedia states that 9F "is not suitable for mounting vibration isolators directly under the fan," and directs the reader to Arrangement 1 with a separate isolation base when isolation is required (FanPedia p. 166). Its motor position follows the same CW (L) / CCW (R) standard as Arrangement 9 (FanPedia p. 52).

docs.title: Arrangement 9H
docs.text: Arrangement 9H is an Arrangement 9 in which the pedestal is extended on one side so the motor mounts horizontally on the side of the pedestal. FanPedia offers it "when horizontal motor adjustment is preferred" (FanPedia p. 166). The drawing shows two ways to hold the motor: a slide base or rails, and a pivot base (FanPedia p. 22). Heavy-duty slide rails mounted on a pedestal are shown for Arrangement 9H only, and the automotive pivot base is used on 9H pedestals (FanPedia pp. 76–77). As with Arrangement 9, the motor is typically on the left side for CW fans and on the right side for CCW fans (FanPedia p. 166).

docs.title: Arrangement 10
docs.text: Arrangement 10 is a belt driven, overhung fan with the motor mounted inside the bearing pedestal. FanPedia states that it is "available as belt driven only," that the motor bases are "mounted inside the bearing pedestal," and that it "offers a more compact design than the Arrangement 9 and is suitable for roof or outdoor installations when supplied with the optional weather cover" (FanPedia p. 167). The arrangement drawing shows two motor mounts: sizes 122–365 with the motor on an adjustable plate at the bottom of the pedestal, and sizes 402 and larger with the motor on a slide base on the side of the pedestal (FanPedia p. 22). FanPedia lists the Arrangement 10 motor position as "unique to pedestal design (no options)" (FanPedia p. 52).

docs.title: Ventilating Set
docs.text:
A ventilating set is the trade name for a compact Arrangement 10 centrifugal fan in the smaller sizes. FanPedia states that "for Class I and II fans, sizes 122 through 365, Arrangement 10 units are commonly referred to as Ventilating Sets," and refers the reader to TCF Catalog 600 for details (FanPedia p. 167). So a specification that asks for a "vent set" is asking for a compact Arrangement 10 package, Class I or II, with no motor position to choose.

One Skeleton, Four Motor Homes

Notice that Arrangements 1, 8, 9 and 10 share one skeleton: an overhung impeller and a two-bearing pedestal. Only the motor's home changes: on the floor (1), coupled at the end of the pedestal (8), hung on the side (9), or tucked inside (10). Picture the skeleton first, and each code becomes a question of where the motor lives.

docs.title: Frame and Inlet Variants of Arrangements 3, 4 and 7
docs.text: These variants solve mounting problems: carrying the motor on the fan, hanging the fan from its inlet, or moving bearings out of a hot airstream.

docs.title: Arrangement 3F
docs.text: Arrangement 3F is an Arrangement 3 fan with an extended frame that carries the motor. For single width fans, FanPedia describes it as "an Arrangement 3 with extended angle frame to mount the motor and horizontal slide base as an assembly," and notes that the fan is welded to the frame and "typically not suitable for mounting vibration isolators directly under the fan" (FanPedia pp. 20, 163). The double width version is built differently: FanPedia describes an "integral extended base" with "brackets to accept vibration isolators," available to size 660, with motor positions W and Z as standard and X and Y by factory consultation (FanPedia p. 167). The same code therefore carries different isolation answers for SWSI and DWDI fans, so check which width the drawing shows before promising springs.

docs.title: Arrangement 4VI and 4HI
docs.text: Arrangements 4VI and 4HI are modified Arrangement 4 fans that mount directly on their own inlet. The whole fan, motor included, "is supported by the inlet flange only" (FanPedia p. 21). In 4VI the air enters vertically and the motor shaft is vertical; in 4HI the air enters horizontally and the shaft is horizontal (FanPedia pp. 164–165). Both have reinforced inlets and a removable motor side, so "the rotating assemblies [can] be removed without removing the housing from the mounting structure" (FanPedia p. 164). Either can use a C-face mounted, foot mounted, or combination foot and C-face motor (FanPedia p. 21).

docs.title: Arrangement 7SI and 7DI
docs.text: Arrangements 7SI and 7DI are direct drive, center hung fans with integral inlet boxes that keep the bearings out of the airstream. 7SI is single width; 7DI is double width. In both, the impeller is mounted between the bearings and the pedestal carries "the motor, flexible coupling and one bearing" (FanPedia pp. 165, 168). A pie split housing allows the impeller to be removed, the assembly is mounted on a unitary base as standard, and an inertia base is optional (FanPedia pp. 165, 168). FanPedia describes the 7DI's bearing location as "allowing for elevated operating temperatures and relatively clean air" (FanPedia p. 168). They are the coupled counterparts of 3SI and 3DI, covered in Chapter 11, whose motors the customer locates off the fan assembly (FanPedia pp. 164, 167).

docs.title: Plenum Fan Variants
docs.text: A plenum fan, as Chapter 11 described, is an unhoused fan that sits inside the plenum it pressurizes, with its motor and drive in the same space. Because the fan sits inside an air handler, the plenum variants are mostly about where the motor fits: on top of the fan, beside it, or below it in a vertical unit. Two kinds of motor mount appear throughout. A slide base is a NEMA-type base whose motor slides along adjusting screws to tension the belts. An adjustable motor base carries the motor on a post mount or a pivot/bolted design and sets belt tension by moving the motor plate (FanPedia pp. 76–78; Chapter 15).

docs.title: Plenum Arrangements 3HS and 3HA
docs.text: Plenum Arrangements 3HS and 3HA are horizontal Arrangement 3 plenum fans with the motor mounted on top of the fan. FanPedia says both provide "a means for mounting the motor on top of the unit," a design "often desirable when floor space is limited" (FanPedia p. 169). They differ only in the motor base. 3HS uses a slide base, and "due to limited belt center range, NEMA 'slide base' option is available on sizes 182 and larger only." 3HA uses a heavy-duty adjustable motor base that "is available for all fan sizes" (FanPedia p. 169). So a top-mounted motor on a fan smaller than size 182 is a 3HA.

docs.title: Plenum Arrangement 3SM
docs.text: Plenum Arrangement 3SM is a horizontal Arrangement 3 plenum fan with the motor mounted on the side of the fan frame on a slide base. FanPedia calls it "an economical and space-saving means to supply plenum fans with motors mounted to the side of the fan frame," with the slide base allowing "quick and easy belt adjustments" (FanPedia p. 169). Its standard motor position is (R); position (L) is normally ordered with an F1 conduit box, with F2 selected if there are clearance issues (FanPedia p. 55).

docs.title: Plenum Arrangements 3VA and 3VS
docs.text: Plenum Arrangements 3VA and 3VS are vertical Arrangement 3 plenum fans with a side mounted motor, used where the air handler turns the airflow vertically. 3VA uses the heavy-duty adjustable motor base, available for all fan sizes; 3VS uses a slide base, available on sizes 182 and larger only because of the limited belt center range (FanPedia pp. 169–170). The A and S letters therefore mean the same thing in the vertical pair as in 3HA and 3HS. On the motor position page, 3VA shows a single Top Center (TC) position, and 3VS shows Standard (S) and Optional (O) positions (FanPedia p. 55).

docs.title: Plenum Arrangement 4V
docs.text:
Plenum Arrangement 4V is the vertical form of the direct drive Arrangement 4 plenum fan, with the impeller mounted on the motor shaft. FanPedia states that it "is available for mounting with either vertical up airflow (inlet under the motor) or vertical down airflow (inlet above the motor)" (FanPedia p. 170). It keeps the Arrangement 4 benefits, a compact unit with no belts and "less maintenance than other arrangements" (FanPedia p. 170), in an air handler whose air path runs vertically. Since there are no belts, there is no motor base and no motor position to choose.

The table below gathers the five belt driven plenum variants just described, so they can be compared on one line each.

Arrangement Orientation Motor location Motor base Size note (FanPedia p. 169–170) 3HS Horizontal Top of fan NEMA slide base Sizes 182 and larger 3HA Horizontal Top of fan Heavy-duty adjustable base All sizes 3SM Horizontal Side of fan frame Slide base None stated 3VA Vertical Side of fan Heavy-duty adjustable base All sizes 3VS Vertical Side of fan NEMA slide base Sizes 182 and larger

Spell the Code Out Loud

Here's a shortcut for plenum codes: read the letters after the 3 as "Horizontal or Vertical, then Slide or Adjustable." 3VS is "vertical, slide base," so before quoting it, check that the fan is size 182 or larger; if it is smaller, offer 3VA.

docs.title: Pedestal Plug Arrangements
docs.text: A plug fan, from Chapter 11, is an unhoused fan whose impeller sits inside the customer's enclosure while the shaft, bearings and motor stay outside, normally carried by the customer's wall through a mounting panel. The wall-hung plug arrangements are 4, 8 and 9. Each has a pedestal plug counterpart, marked with a P, in which the fan stands on its own pedestal at grade and the wall only seals around it. FanPedia gives the same reason for every P variant: it is "typically used where the customer's wall may not be sufficient by itself," and "mounting to the foundation also makes it better for meeting lower vibration requirements," with the mounting panel optional (FanPedia pp. 170–172). The belt driven Arrangement 1P has no wall-hung counterpart in FanPedia's set.

docs.title: Arrangement 1P Plug
docs.text:
Arrangement 1P is a belt driven pedestal plug fan in which the fan is mounted to grade and the motor is mounted separately on the floor or a fan base. FanPedia describes it as "a belt driven arrangement where the fan is mounted to grade and the motor is mounted separate from the fan," and notes that it is "typically used on larger fans and/or larger HP motors where the customer's wall may not be sufficient by itself" (FanPedia p. 170). Its motor mount is the NEMA type slide base listed for pedestal plug fans 1P and 9P (FanPedia p. 76). The difference from 9P is the same as the difference between Arrangements 1 and 9 on a housed fan: in 1P the motor stands apart from the fan pedestal.

Worked example: a large belt driven plug fan. An air handler builder needs a large belt driven plug fan with a high horsepower motor. The casing wall is a double-wall insulated panel.

  1. Start from the default. The most common plug arrangement is the wall-hung Arrangement 9 (FanPedia p. 172), but the builder's wall is not designed to carry a large fan and motor.
  2. Move the fan to grade. A P variant puts the fan on a pedestal on the unit floor or foundation. The choice is between 9P, with the motor on the fan pedestal, and 1P, with the motor separate.
  3. Size the motor. With a large motor, the builder prefers the motor on its own base beside the fan, where it can be reached for belt changes from the service side of the unit. That is Arrangement 1P.
  4. Write the result. "Arrangement 1P plug fan, belt driven, motor on separate base," adding a mounting panel if the builder wants one. The foundation also helps with lower vibration.

docs.title: Arrangement 4P Plug
docs.text:
Arrangement 4P is a direct drive pedestal plug fan: the impeller is mounted on the motor shaft and the fan is mounted to grade. FanPedia defines it as "same as the Arrangement 4 fan except the fan is mounted to grade" (FanPedia p. 171), where the plain Arrangement 4 plug fan is wall mounted (FanPedia p. 26).

The Arrangement 4 plug fan's own strengths and limits carry over. FanPedia notes that Arrangement 4 "is more compact and requires less maintenance due to not having fan shaft, bearings or belts," but that "high airstream temperatures may limit the use of this arrangement" (FanPedia p. 171), since the motor bearings carry the impeller and the motor sits close to the air path. 4P adds the floor support without changing those facts.

Worked example: choosing between 4 and 4P. A pharmaceutical air handler needs a direct drive plug fan at room-temperature air, driven by a VFD. The engineer first checks the temperature limit: the air is not hot, so Arrangement 4 is acceptable. Next comes the wall. The unit casing is a lightweight panel, and the owner's specification sets a strict vibration limit for the supply fans. Both points match FanPedia's reasons for a P variant: a wall that may not be sufficient by itself, and lower vibration requirements. The engineer offers Arrangement 4P. Had the air been hot, the temperature limit would have pointed to a belt or coupled arrangement with the bearings outside the airstream instead, either 8P or 9P.

docs.title: Arrangement 8P and 9P Plug
docs.text:
Arrangements 8P and 9P are the grade-mounted versions of the Arrangement 8 and 9 plug fans. FanPedia defines each as "same as the Arrangement 8 [or 9] fan except the fan is mounted to grade," for larger fans or motors where the wall may not be sufficient and for lower vibration, with the mounting panel optional (FanPedia pp. 171–172). In 8P the motor is coupled to the fan shaft on the pedestal (direct drive); in 9P the motor sits on a slide base on the pedestal and drives the fan through belts (FanPedia pp. 13, 26–27, 76).

Both keep a fan shaft on two bearings outside the enclosure, so they suit hot air better than 4P: the motor bearings do not carry the impeller. Between them, the choice is Chapter 11's direct drive against belt drive trade: 8P has no belts but a fixed speed unless a VFD is used, and a long assembly; 9P is shorter and its speed is set by sheaves.

Worked example: a hot recirculation fan. A dryer manufacturer needs a plug fan to recirculate hot air in a large dryer. The dryer wall is insulated panel, and the fan and motor are large.

  1. Rule out 4 and 4P. High airstream temperatures may limit Arrangement 4 (FanPedia p. 171), and this air is hot.
  2. Rule out wall mounting. The wall may not be sufficient for a large fan and motor, so the fan goes to grade with a P variant.
  3. Compare 8P and 9P. The duty may need retuning after start-up, and the crew is used to belt drives, so 9P fits. Had the owner banned belts, 8P with a VFD would meet the duty with a longer assembly.
  4. Order: "Arrangement 9P plug fan, belt driven, motor on pedestal slide base, fan mounted to grade."
Plug arrangement Drive Fan support Motor location 4 Direct, impeller on motor shaft Customer's wall Motor shaft carries impeller 4P Direct, impeller on motor shaft Pedestal at grade Motor shaft carries impeller 8 Direct, coupled Customer's wall End of pedestal, coupled 8P Direct, coupled Pedestal at grade End of pedestal, coupled 9 Belt Customer's wall On fan pedestal 9P Belt Pedestal at grade On fan pedestal, slide base 1P Belt Pedestal at grade Separate, on floor or fan base

The P Does Not Fix a Temperature Problem

A common trap is assuming that putting a fan on a pedestal also protects it from heat. The P only changes what holds the fan up; a 4P still hangs its impeller on the motor shaft. For hot air, choose the drive first (8P, 9P or 1P) and the support second.

docs.title: Swingout and Clamshell Construction
docs.text: Some fans must be opened often, such as washdown exhausts and process fans that collect residue. Swingout and clamshell constructions build the opening into the fan, so no ductwork has to be unbolted.

docs.title: Swingout Fan
docs.text:
A swingout fan is a fan whose rotating assembly is mounted on a hinged door, so the impeller swings out of the housing for cleaning and inspection. FanPedia states that swingout fans "are designed for frequent cleaning and provide full access to the impeller and inner casing of the fan," and that "the entire impeller/shaft/bearing assembly is mounted on a large swingout door" (FanPedia p. 123). Swingout construction is available for centrifugal, inline centrifugal and axial fans (FanPedia p. 123). The housed centrifugal versions are Arrangements 4S, 9ST and 9SS; the axial and inline centrifugal versions are Arrangements 4SO and 9SO (FanPedia p. 123).

The duct connections and housing stay in place while the rotor swings clear. FanPedia also notes an isolation advantage: vibration isolators directly under a fan are "usually limited to fans with 36.5" diameter impellers or less," with "an exception … made for swingout housed centrifugal fans, any size impeller, with flat pads only" (FanPedia p. 134).

Worked example: a washdown exhaust fan. A food processor needs a belt driven SWSI exhaust fan that is cleaned every week.

  1. Housed centrifugal, belt driven. That points to the 9-family swingout arrangements, 9ST or 9SS, rather than 4S (direct drive) or 4SO/9SO (axial and inline).
  2. Swing side. FanPedia notes that the door "can swing left or right depending on the application" (FanPedia p. 22). The cleaning aisle is on the left of the fan, so the engineer asks for a left swing.
  3. Motor mount. 9ST puts the motor on a NEMA slide base above the pedestal; 9SS puts it on the side of the pedestal on an automotive pivot base (FanPedia p. 166). The plant prefers the side mount for reach, so the choice is 9SS.
  4. Check the rotation. A left swing 9SS is limited to CCW rotation with motor position (R) and requires an F2 conduit box (FanPedia p. 53). The duct layout gives CCW, so the order reads "Arrangement 9SS, left swing, CCW, motor position (R), F2 conduit box." Had the layout required CW, the engineer would switch to a right swing 9SS or to a 9ST.
  5. Isolation. If isolators are wanted directly under the fan, FanPedia allows swingout housed centrifugal fans of any impeller size on flat pads only (FanPedia p. 134).

Step 4 shows why swingout fans have their own motor position page: swing side, rotation and motor position are tied together.

docs.title: Swingout Door Assembly
docs.text: The swingout door assembly is the hinged door and reinforced framework that carry a swingout fan's rotating parts. On the housed centrifugal Arrangements 4S, 9ST and 9SS, FanPedia describes the motor and impeller assembly as "mounted to reinforced framework to support the opened housing" (FanPedia pp. 164, 166), and the general description puts the "entire impeller, shaft and bearing assembly" on "a large swingout door" (FanPedia p. 195). On the axial and inline 4SO and 9SO, "the rotor assembly is built onto a swingout door that allows maintenance personnel to easily inspect, clean or repair out of the airstream" (FanPedia p. 173). The door assembly is the structural heart of the design: it must hold bearing alignment when closed and carry the rotor's weight when open.

docs.title: Arrangement 4S Swingout
docs.text: Arrangement 4S is "a modified Arrangement 4 fan intended for easy access to the impeller and housing interior" (FanPedia p. 164). The impeller stays on the motor shaft, as in every Arrangement 4, but the motor and impeller are mounted on reinforced framework so the assembly swings out with the door (FanPedia pp. 20, 164). It is the direct drive housed centrifugal swingout choice. Because there is no fan shaft or belt, there is no motor position to choose; the motor rides on the door.

docs.title: Arrangement 9ST and 9SS
docs.text: Arrangements 9ST and 9SS are the belt driven housed centrifugal swingout fans, both modified Arrangement 9 fans "intended for easy access to the impeller and housing interior" (FanPedia p. 166). They differ in the motor mount, and the second letter says where. In 9ST the T is for top: the motor is mounted above the bearing pedestal, on a NEMA type slide base only. In 9SS the second S is for side: the motor is on the side of the bearing pedestal, on an automotive pivot base only, and "motor location is restricted based on the fan's rotation" (FanPedia pp. 22, 166). Both come in right swing and left swing versions, and both put the drive on the swinging door.

docs.title: Arrangement 4SO and 9SO
docs.text: Arrangements 4SO and 9SO are the swingout versions of the direct drive Arrangement 4 and belt driven Arrangement 9 axial and inline centrifugal fans. In both, "the rotor assembly is built onto a swingout door" so maintenance staff can "inspect, clean or repair out of the airstream" (FanPedia p. 173). 4SO keeps the compact Arrangement 4 envelope with the impeller on the motor shaft; 9SO keeps the motor out of the airstream with a fixed or adjustable V-belt drive. FanPedia's drawings show axial fans, and notes that inline centrifugal fans "are available with the same arrangements but use different impellers" (FanPedia p. 28).

docs.title: Clamshell Fan
docs.text: A clamshell fan is an axial or inline centrifugal fan whose casing opens on a hinged door to give access to the inside without removing the duct. FanPedia states that clamshell fans "are designed to provide complete access to the interior of the fan for maintenance or cleaning without removal of ductwork," that the construction "is available for inline centrifugal and axial fans," and that it "is typically used in vertical mount applications" (FanPedia p. 123). The difference from a swingout fan is what moves. In a swingout fan the rotor rides out on the door; in a clamshell fan the casing opens around a rotor that stays in place. Clamshell fans come in single door and double door versions (FanPedia p. 123).

docs.title: Double Door Clamshell
docs.text: A double door clamshell is a clamshell fan with two access doors instead of one. FanPedia notes that "for the double door configuration, one of the two access doors is wide enough for impeller removal" (FanPedia pp. 123, 180). The second door matters when the impeller must come out of the fan entirely, for a rebalance or a blade change, rather than simply be cleaned in place. Both single door and double door clamshell fans are offered in Arrangements 4CS and 9CS (FanPedia p. 123).

docs.title: Arrangement 4CS and 9CS
docs.text:
Arrangements 4CS and 9CS are the clamshell versions of the axial and inline centrifugal Arrangements 4 and 9. In 4CS the impeller is "mounted directly on the fan motor shaft … for a compact envelope"; in 9CS a fixed or adjustable V-belt drive keeps the motor "out of the airstream." In both, "a spacious clamshell door gives maintenance personnel access to the rotor assembly for ease of inspection, cleaning or repair" (FanPedia pp. 172–173). Choose between them the way you choose between Arrangements 4 and 9 for an inline fan, then add the clamshell for access.

What Moves When the Door Opens?

Think of the two constructions by asking what moves when the door opens. In a swingout fan the rotor swings out with the door; in a clamshell fan the casing opens and the rotor stays put. That one question tells you which codes (S, ST, SS, SO or CS) can answer a customer's cleaning problem.

Before the motor position rules, the interactive decoder below brings the arrangement variants in this chapter together. Every code in it, and every feature in its descriptions, was defined in the sections above.

docs.title: Diagram: Arrangement Variant Decoder
docs.text:
Arrangement Variant Decoder

Type: microsim sim-id: ch24-arrangement-variant-decoder Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Analyze Bloom Verb: differentiate Learning Objective: The learner will differentiate twelve arrangement variants by naming the arrangement code that matches a written description of a fan's drive, motor location, support and access features.

Prerequisites: overhung and center hung impellers, direct drive and belt drive, bearing pedestal, slide base, adjustable motor base, plug fan, pedestal plug, plenum fan, swingout and clamshell construction (all defined in this chapter and Chapter 11).

Evidence of Mastery: For each of the 12 descriptions the learner commits one code from the answer list. An answer is correct when it matches the Correct code column. Mastery: 10 of 12 correct on the first attempt. Revealing feature hints is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) Any direct drive fan is Arrangement 4. (2) The P suffix changes the drive. (3) Swingout and clamshell are the same construction. (4) 9F is the right fix whenever a large motor needs isolators.

Instructional Rationale: Differentiating near-identical codes forces the learner to attend to the one feature that separates them (motor location, support, or door type), which is the analysis an application engineer does on a drawing.

Content:

Answer list (shown for every item): 8, 9F, 9H, 10, 3F, 4VI, 7DI, 3HS, 3HA, 3SM, 3VS, 4V, 1P, 4P, 8P, 9P, 9ST, 9SS, 4SO, 9CS.

Each item also has a feature hint the learner may reveal before answering: drive type, impeller position, fan support, and motor location, as listed in the description.

# Description shown Correct code Why (feedback) 1 Housed SWSI fan, overhung impeller, two bearings on a long pedestal, motor coupled to the fan shaft at the end of the pedestal 8 An Arrangement 1 pedestal extended for a coupled motor is Arrangement 8. 2 Housed SWSI fan, belt driven, motor too large for the pedestal, carried on an extended structural frame 9F The F is the extended frame that carries a motor too large for the pedestal. 3 Housed SWSI fan, belt driven, motor inside the bearing pedestal, sold as a ventilating set 10 Arrangement 10 puts the motor inside the pedestal; small Class I and II sizes are vent sets. 4 Direct drive SWSI fan hung entirely from its inlet flange, vertical motor shaft 4VI VI is vertical inlet-mounted; the inlet flange carries the whole fan. 5 Direct drive DWDI fan, impeller between bearings, integral inlet boxes, motor coupled on a pedestal 7DI A coupled double width fan with integral inlet boxes is 7DI. 6 Horizontal belt driven plenum fan, motor on top on an adjustable motor base, size smaller than 182 3HA Top-mounted motor with an adjustable base is 3HA; the 3HS slide base starts at size 182. 7 Horizontal belt driven plenum fan, motor on the side of the fan frame on a slide base 3SM SM is side-mounted motor on a slide base. 8 Vertical direct drive plenum fan, impeller on the motor shaft, inlet under the motor 4V 4V is the vertical direct drive plenum fan, offered for up or down airflow. 9 Belt driven plug fan on a pedestal at grade, motor on its own base beside the fan 1P The motor is separate from the fan pedestal, so this is 1P, not 9P. 10 Direct drive plug fan, impeller on the motor shaft, fan floor mounted 4P Arrangement 4 mounted to grade is 4P; Rules: One code per item. Exact match with the Correct code column. Item order is shuffled once per session. The answer list never changes between items.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner reads a description and may reveal its feature hint.
  2. The learner selects a code and presses Check. The item is scored and the Why text appears.
  3. The learner advances to the next item. After item 12 a summary lists every missed item with its correct code.
  4. A Retry Missed option re-presents only the missed items; retries are not counted toward mastery.

Feedback: 12 items, shuffled, one scored attempt each. Correct: "Correct: Arrangement ." Incorrect: "This is Arrangement . ." Added messages: choosing 4P or 4 for item 1: "There is a coupling and a separate fan shaft, so the impeller is not on the motor shaft." Choosing 9P for item 9: "In 9P the motor sits on the fan pedestal; here it stands apart." Choosing 9F for item 3: "The motor is inside the pedestal, not on a frame." Choosing 9SO for item 12: "In a swingout fan the rotor moves; here only the casing opens." A running "Correct: n of 12" score is shown.

Starting State: Item 1 of the shuffled set, hint hidden, no code selected, score "Correct: 0 of 12." Prompt: "Which arrangement code matches this fan?"

Chapter Anchors: Arrangement 4 is typically limited to size 365; 3HS and 3VS slide bases start at size 182; 3HA and 3VA bases are available for all sizes; vent sets are Class I and II, sizes 122 through 365.

docs.title: Motor Positions for Arrangement Variants
docs.text: Chapter 12 introduced motor position as the location of a belt-drive motor relative to the fan, read from the drive side, and the four AMCA positions W, X, Y and Z used on Arrangements 1 and 3. The variants in this chapter use other systems, because their motors are tied to the fan's own pedestal, frame or casing. Four rules cover them.

docs.title: Motor Positions L and R
docs.text: Motor positions L and R name the two sides of the bearing pedestal or fan frame on which a belt-drive motor can hang, left or right as seen from the drive side. They are used where the motor is carried by the fan itself rather than standing on the floor: Arrangements 9, 9F, 9H and the swingout 9ST and 9SS, and the plenum 3SM (FanPedia pp. 52–55). On the plenum Arrangements 3HS and 3VS, FanPedia names the positions Standard (S) and Optional (O), and labels them "also known as" R and L respectively (FanPedia p. 55). Floor-standing motors on Arrangements 1 and 3 use the four AMCA letters W, X, Y and Z instead.

docs.title: Standard Motor Position Rule
docs.text:
The standard motor position rule is FanPedia's default pairing of motor side with rotation on pedestal-mounted motors: clockwise fans take position (L), counterclockwise fans take position (R). FanPedia prints it as "Standard Motor Position: CW (L) / CCW (R)" for Arrangements 9 and 9F (FanPedia p. 52), and the technical descriptions say the same for Arrangements 9 and 9H: "the motor is mounted on the left side of the pedestal for CW rotation fans and on the right side for CCW rotation fans" (FanPedia pp. 165–166). FanPedia adds on the same page that position (L) "is normally ordered with F1 conduit box. Select F2 if clearance issues" (FanPedia p. 52).

Treat any other pairing as a special request to confirm with the factory before quoting.

docs.title: Swingout Motor Position Rule
docs.text:
The swingout motor position rule ties motor position to the swing side of a 9ST and to the rotation and swing side of a 9SS (FanPedia p. 53):

  • 9SS right swing: CW rotation and (L) motor position only.
  • 9SS left swing: CCW rotation and (R) motor position only, and the fan "must have F2 conduit box for this orientation."
  • 9ST right swing: standard motor position (R).
  • 9ST left swing: standard motor position (L).

The 9SS limits are firm ("only"); FanPedia gives the same rotation-motor pairing for the automotive pivot base on 9H and 9SS fans (FanPedia p. 77). The 9ST positions are standards. On a 9SS, choosing the swing side fixes rotation and motor position.

Swing Side Is Not a Late Detail

Watch out for orders that settle rotation from the duct layout and leave the swing side "to be decided." On a 9SS the swing side fixes the rotation, so a late swing change can force a different discharge. Settle swing side, rotation and motor position together, on the same drive-side sketch.

docs.title: Inline Motor Positions A to H
docs.text:
Inline motor positions A to H are the eight motor locations around the casing of a belt driven Arrangement 9 inline, mixed flow or axial fan in a horizontal configuration, lettered as seen in the discharge view with A at the top and the letters running around the casing (FanPedia p. 56). A duct or ceiling mounted fan can take any of the eight. A floor mounted fan shows only G, H, A, B and C, the five positions not blocked by its floor supports (FanPedia p. 56). Vertical inline fans have no specified motor position: the motor is centered on the curb cap or between the support brackets (FanPedia p. 57).

The table below collects the motor position systems for the arrangements in this chapter.

Arrangement Positions Standard or limit Source 9, 9F L, R CW (L) / CCW (R) FanPedia p. 52 9H L, R Typically left for CW, right for CCW FanPedia p. 166 9SS right / left swing L / R CW (L) only / CCW (R) only, F2 required FanPedia p. 53 9ST right / left swing R / L Standard (R) / Standard (L) FanPedia p. 53 10 None Unique to pedestal, no options FanPedia p. 52 3SM plenum L, R Standard (R); (L) with F1, F2 if tight FanPedia p. 55 3HS, 3VS plenum S ("R"), O ("L") Standard (S) FanPedia p. 55 3HA, 3VA plenum TC Top Center only FanPedia p. 55 9 inline, horizontal A to H Floor mount: G, H, A, B, C FanPedia p. 56 9 inline, vertical None Centered on curb cap or between brackets FanPedia p. 57

Ten Rows Is a Lot to Hold

If this table feels like a lot to memorize, that is normal; nobody keeps it in their head. You already know the logic from Chapter 12, read from the drive side and find the arrangement first. Work through the checker below one order at a time, and keep FanPedia pp. 52–57 open as your reference.

The checker below practices these rules on orders like the ones an inside sales desk sees. Each term it uses (L and R, the standard rule, swing side, conduit box F1 and F2, and the inline letters) is defined in the sections above and in Chapter 13.

Motor Position Rule Checker

Type: microsim sim-id: ch24-motor-position-rule-checker Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Apply Bloom Verb: apply Learning Objective: The learner will apply FanPedia's motor position rules to ten order lines, judging each as standard, allowed with a condition, or not allowed, and stating the correct position or conduit box when the line is wrong.

Prerequisites: drive side, CW and CCW rotation, motor positions L and R, standard motor position rule, swing side, swingout motor position rule, conduit box F1 and F2, plenum positions S, O and TC, inline motor positions A to H (defined in this chapter and Chapters 12–13).

Evidence of Mastery: For each order line the learner commits a verdict (Standard, Allowed with condition, Not allowed) and, for Not allowed, picks the correction from a list. Correct when both match the Content table. Mastery: 8 of 10 correct on the first attempt.

Misconceptions: (1) L and R are free choices on every pedestal-mounted motor. (2) A 9SS can take either motor position on either swing. (3) Arrangement 10 has a motor position to choose. (4) A floor mounted inline fan can take any of A to H.

Instructional Rationale: Applying a rule to an order line, then correcting it, is the exact task an order desk performs; judging and correcting forces use of the rule, not recognition of it.

Verdict options: Standard; Allowed with condition; Not allowed. Correction options: change motor to (L); change motor to (R); change to F2 conduit box; change to Top Center (TC); remove motor position (none applies); choose a position from G, H, A, B or C.

Not allowed = a pairing FanPedia excludes ("only", "must", "no options", or a position not shown for that mount). The correction is scored only when the verdict is Not allowed.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner reads an order line and selects a verdict.
  2. If the verdict is Not allowed, the correction list opens and the learner selects one correction.
  3. The learner presses Check; the sim shows a sketch of the fan in its reference view (drive side, or discharge view for the inline item) with the motor in the correct position, and the Why text.
  4. The learner advances; after item 10 a summary shows misses with their rules.

Incorrect verdict: "Check the rule for Arr. : ." Correct verdict but wrong correction: "Right verdict; the fix is ." Score "Correct: n of 10" counts items with verdict and correction both right.
