Eight designations, in this order:

# Designation Offered? Class maximum RPM Why (shown as feedback) 1 RBA 913, Class 22, Arrangement 10 Offered 2,812 Arrangement 10 is in the Class 22 list for RBA 913. 2 RBA 913, Class 32, Arrangement 10 Not offered 3,337 Arrangement 10 is offered only in Class 22 for this size; Class 32 lists 1, 4, 8, 9, 4VI, 9F. 3 RBA 913, Class 45, Arrangement 4 Not offered 4,000 Class 45 lists only 1, 8, 9 and 9F; the direct-drive Arrangement 4 is not offered at Class 45. 4 RBA 913, Class 45, Arrangement 9 Offered 4,000 Arrangement 9 is in the Class 45 list. 5 RBO 905, Class 22, Arrangement 9A Offered 5,296 Size 905 offers 9A in Class 22; selections above 4,000 RPM are not recommended without consulting the factory. 6 RBO 905, Class 32, Arrangement 1 Not offered none Size 905 is built only in Class 22. 7 BC-SW 365, Class II, Arrangement 9 Offered 1,283 Arrangement 9 is offered for BC-SW, and Class II size 365 runs to 1,283 RPM. 8 BC-DW 365, Class I, Arrangement 9 Not offered 1,015 Arrangement 9 is a single width arrangement; BC-DW is offered in 3, 3F, 3DI and 7DI.

Provenance: Catalog 902 (November 2017), page 13 (RB Series Availability) and performance pages 20 and 24 (maximum RPM, diameters). Catalog 300 (April 2024), page 3 (arrangements by model) and page 16 (maximum RPM). https://tcf.com/resources/product-catalogs/

Rules: Offered when the arrangement appears in the list for that model, size and class; Not offered otherwise, including when the class is not built for that size. The class maximum RPM answer is the value in the extract for that class, or "none" when the class is not built. Both answers must match for the designation to count as correct.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner reads designation 1 and opens whichever extract they need.
  2. The learner chooses Offered or Not offered, and chooses the class maximum RPM from the values in that model's row plus "none".
  3. The learner submits; both answers are marked and the Why text appears.
  4. The learner moves to the next designation. After designation 8, the score and missed items are shown.

Feedback: Eight designations, fixed order, one attempt each for scoring, with a second try allowed for practice. Correct: "Correct: " plus the Why text. Incorrect: names which of the two answers was wrong, then the Why text. Score shown as "Designations correct: n of 8".

Starting State: Designation 1 is shown with both extracts collapsed. The prompt reads "Can the factory build this fan, and how fast can it run?"

Chapter Anchors: RBA 913 diameter 22.625 in.; RBO 905 diameter 8.75 in.; RBA 913 Class 22 arrangements 1, 4, 8, 10, 4VI, 9A, 9B, 9F; Class 32 arrangements 1, 4, 8, 9, 4VI, 9F; Class 45 arrangements 1, 8, 9, 9F; RBA 913 maximum RPM 2,812 / 3,337 / 4,000; BC-SW 365 Class II maximum 1,283 RPM; designations 1, 2 and 3 match the worked example.

docs.title: Where the Duty Point Comes From
docs.text: A performance table is entered with an airflow and a static pressure, the duty point. On many inquiries the customer supplies both. On others, especially ventilation and dust collection jobs, the airflow has to be estimated first. Twin City Fan's Engineering Resource Guide ERG-100 gives two quick methods that belong in every application engineer's toolkit.

docs.title: Air Change Method
docs.text: The air change method estimates the ventilation airflow for a space from its volume and a recommended time to replace all of its air once. ERG-100 recommends it for standard commercial applications where environmental control of hazards, heat or odors is not required, and it lists typical minutes per air change by area type, for example 3–6 minutes for a machine shop, 1–3 for a boiler room and 4–10 for a warehouse. Local code, how the space is used, and the climate also affect the choice.

docs.title: Airflow by the Air Change Method
docs.text:
\[ Q = \frac{V_{room}}{t_{change}} \]

where:

  • \( Q \) is the required airflow in CFM
  • \( V_{room} \) is the room volume in ft³
  • \( t_{change} \) is the chosen time per air change in minutes

For an illustrative machine shop 100 ft × 60 ft × 20 ft high (120,000 ft³), choosing 4 minutes per change gives \( Q = 120{,}000 / 4 = 30{,}000 \) CFM. The method gives airflow only; the static pressure still comes from the duct, louver and filter losses.

docs.title: Minimum Conveying Velocity
docs.text: The minimum conveying velocity is the lowest average duct velocity that keeps a given material suspended in the airstream so it does not settle and clog the duct. ERG-100 reprints typical values from the ACGIH Industrial Ventilation manual: 2,500–3,000 FPM for very fine light dust such as cotton lint, 3,500–4,000 FPM for average industrial dust such as grinding dust, 4,000–4,500 FPM for heavy dusts such as metal turnings, and 4,500 FPM and up for heavy or moist material. Dividing the airflow by the conveying velocity gives the largest duct area that will still convey: 4,092 CFM at 4,000 FPM needs a duct no larger than about 1.02 ft² (roughly a 13.7-inch round duct). Conveying velocity also points toward the fan family, because a fan that the material passes through must survive it.

docs.title: Fan Family Selection
docs.text:
Fan family selection is choosing the product line, and within it the impeller type, before choosing a size. It comes first because every later step happens inside one catalog. Chapter 6 described the families; here the point is that each catalog's overview tells you, in a few sentences, what the family is for:

  • Catalog 300 calls the BC "a popular choice for the efficient handling of large volumes of relatively clean air at low to moderate pressures," with BC-SW static pressure to 20 in. wg and airflow to 277,500 CFM.
  • Catalog 902 describes the radial bladed fans as "designed for applications with moderate air volumes of moderate to high pressures," built for "dirty, abrasive, sticky or bulky particulate-laden airstreams," with static pressure to 46 in. wg for RBA, RBO and RBR.
  • Within Catalog 902, the RBA is "the most efficient impeller in the RB family" but is "limited to handling relatively clean air or gases," the RBO and RBR suit "coarse, sticky, heavy and/or abrasive materials," the RBW keeps "long, stringy, fibrous" material from wrapping, and the RBP handles paper trim. The RBP is not AMCA licensed, and its Class 32 construction is limited to 22 in. wg.

docs.title: Worked Example: Three Inquiries, Three Families
docs.text:
Inquiry Deciding facts Family and impeller Catalog reason 60,000 CFM at 4 in. wg supply air for an air handler Large volume, clean air, low pressure BC (backward inclined) Large volumes of relatively clean air at low to moderate pressure 4,000 CFM at 12 in. wg, clean side of a dust collector Moderate volume, moderate-high pressure, light contaminant RBA Most efficient RB impeller, for relatively clean air 3,000 CFM at 18 in. wg conveying metal turnings through the fan Material passes through the fan; heavy dust needs 4,000–4,500 FPM RBO or RBR Paddle impellers for coarse, heavy and abrasive material

The table is the summary; the reasoning is in the second column. Notice that the second and third inquiries have similar airflow and pressure. What separates them is the airstream, which the duty point does not show. Ask what passes through the fan before you open a performance table.

docs.title: Performance Tables
docs.text: A performance table is a grid in a product catalog that lists, for one model and size at standard air, the fan speed (RPM) and brake horsepower (BHP) required to deliver each combination of airflow and static pressure. Rows are airflows; columns are static pressures; each cell holds an RPM and a BHP. A performance table is a fan curve (Chapter 10) laid out as numbers: each column is one pressure, and reading down the column follows the fan along a family of curves at increasing speed.

docs.title: The Performance Table Header
docs.text:
The performance table header is the block above and around the grid that tells you what the grid means. On a Catalog 902 page it has four parts:

  • The size block: size number, impeller diameter, tip speed factor, inlet area and diameter, outlet area and outlet dimension, as in the Fan Size section.
  • The model line: the model and size (for example RBA 913) and its Fan Efficiency Grade (FEG), an AMCA 205 rating of the fan's peak efficiency; RBA 913 is FEG80 and RBO 913 is FEG67.
  • The column heads: CFM and OV (outlet velocity in FPM) for the rows, then one static pressure per column pair, each split into RPM and BHP.
  • The footer: maximum RPM for each class, followed by the rating notes that say what the numbers include and exclude (covered under Rating Conditions below), and the legend for shading, italics and underlining.

Read the header and footer before the grid. The grid has no units printed in its cells, no class labels and no conditions; all of that is in the header and footer.

docs.title: Reading a Performance Table
docs.text:
Reading a performance table means finding the row for the required airflow and the column for the required static pressure, and taking the RPM and BHP printed where they meet. The excerpt below reproduces part of the RBA 913 table. In the printed catalog, Class 22 cells are in regular face, Class 32 cells are shaded, and Class 45 cells are in italics; here shaded cells are shown in bold, italic cells in italics, and the cells the catalog underlines (maximum static efficiency) are underlined. Each cell gives RPM / BHP.

CFM OV (FPM) 4 in. SP 8 in. SP 12 in. SP 16 in. SP 20 in. SP 24 in. SP 28 in. SP 32 in. SP 3,348 3,600 1384 / 3.59 1774 / 6.42 2093 / 9.39 2374 / 12.52 2630 / 15.84 2868 / 19.35 3088 / 22.95 3295 / 26.70 3,720 4,000 1439 / 4.20 1818 / 7.30 2128 / 10.51 2401 / 13.87 2648 / 17.34 2879 / 21.02 3095 / 24.83 3299 / 28.79 4,092 4,400 1495 / 4.86 1865 / 8.25 2167 / 11.72 2433 / 15.30 2674 / 19.00 2897 / 22.82 3108 / 26.82 3307 / 30.95 4,464 4,800 1552 / 5.58 1915 / 9.29 2210 / 13.01 2470 / 16.85 2705 / 20.77 2922 / 24.78 3126 / 28.92 3321 / 33.24 4,836 5,200 1612 / 6.38 1967 / 10.41 2256 / 14.40 2510 / 18.48 2740 / 22.64 2953 / 26.89 3152 / 31.23 3340 / 35.65

Source: Twin City Fan Catalog 902 (November 2017), page 24, RBA 913, standard air, installation type B and D. Excerpt only; the printed table runs from 1,116 to 6,696 CFM and from 1 to 46 in. SP.

docs.title: Worked Example: A Direct Reading
docs.text:
A customer needs 4,092 CFM at 12 in. wg static pressure, standard air, from an RBA 913.

  1. Row: 4,092 CFM (OV 4,400 FPM).
  2. Column: 12 in. SP.
  3. Cell: 2,167 RPM and 11.72 BHP.
  4. Class: The cell is in regular face to the left of the shaded area, so it is Class 22. Check it against the footer: 2,167 RPM is at or below the Class 22 maximum of 2,812 RPM.
  5. State the result with its conditions: RBA 913, Class 22, 2,167 RPM, 11.72 BHP at standard air, not including drive losses or accessory effects.

Step 5 is not decoration. A number quoted without its conditions will be compared with a motor nameplate or a field reading taken under different conditions, and someone will conclude the fan is wrong.

docs.title: Class Shading in Tables
docs.text: Class shading is the catalog's way of showing, inside the grid, which fan class each duty point requires. Because a class is defined by a maximum safe speed for the size (Chapter 10), the class boundary in a table is really a speed boundary. On the RBA 913 page the footer gives Class 22 = 2,812 RPM, Class 32 = 3,337 RPM and Class 45 = 4,000 RPM, and the legend says: regular face to the left of Class 32 = Class 22; regular face in light shaded area = Class 32; italic face to right of Class 32 = Class 45. Other catalogs use the same idea with their own legend, so read the legend on the page you are using.

docs.title: Class from Selection Speed
docs.text:
\[ \text{Class} = \begin{cases} 22 & N \le 2{,}812 \\ 32 & 2{,}812 < N \le 3{,}337 \\ 45 & 3{,}337 < N \le 4{,}000 \end{cases} \]

where:

  • \( N \) is the selection speed in RPM read from the RBA 913 table
  • the limits are the RBA 913 maximum RPM values for each class from Catalog 902, page 24

docs.title: Worked Example: Reading the Class from the Grid
docs.text:
Take three cells from the 4,836 CFM row of the excerpt:

  • 20 in. SP: 2,740 RPM, regular face. \( 2{,}740 \le 2{,}812 \), so Class 22.
  • 28 in. SP: 3,152 RPM, shaded. \( 2{,}812 < 3{,}152 \le 3{,}337 \), so Class 32.
  • 32 in. SP: 3,340 RPM, italic. \( 3{,}337 < 3{,}340 \le 4{,}000 \), so Class 45.

The last cell is the instructive one. At 4,464 CFM the same 32 in. column reads 3,321 RPM and is Class 32; one row lower it crosses the Class 32 limit by 3 RPM and becomes Class 45. Class boundaries do not follow straight columns or rows, which is why the catalog shades cell by cell. When a selection lands within a few RPM of a boundary, consider the heavier class or a different size, because any later correction for temperature, drive slip or system effect will push the speed up, not down.

The Shading Is a Speed Map

Notice that class shading is just the maximum safe speed for each class drawn onto the grid. Once you see it that way, you can check any cell yourself by comparing its RPM with the footer, and you can predict where the shading starts on a table you have never seen.

docs.title: Interpolation
docs.text: Duty points rarely land exactly on a printed row and column. Interpolation is estimating the RPM and BHP between printed values by assuming they change in a straight line between neighboring rows or columns. Catalog tables are spaced closely enough that straight-line interpolation is the accepted practice; ERG-100 works its density examples this way.

docs.title: Linear Interpolation
docs.text:
\[ y = y_1 + \frac{x - x_1}{x_2 - x_1}\,(y_2 - y_1) \]

where:

  • \( x \) is the required airflow (or static pressure)
  • \( x_1 \) and \( x_2 \) are the printed airflows (or pressures) on either side of \( x \)
  • \( y_1 \) and \( y_2 \) are the printed RPM (or BHP) values at \( x_1 \) and \( x_2 \)
  • \( y \) is the interpolated RPM (or BHP)

Two Directions, One Step at a Time

Double interpolation looks like a lot of arithmetic the first time, and most people lose track of which number goes where. Do it as three single interpolations: across the airflow rows in each of two pressure columns, then once between those two results. Write each intermediate RPM and BHP down before moving on.

docs.title: Worked Example: Single and Double Interpolation on RBA 913
docs.text:
Single interpolation. Find RPM and BHP for 4,000 CFM at 12 in. SP. The airflow lies between the 3,720 and 4,092 CFM rows:

\[ f = \frac{4{,}000 - 3{,}720}{4{,}092 - 3{,}720} = \frac{280}{372} = 0.753 \] \[ N = 2{,}128 + 0.753 \times (2{,}167 - 2{,}128) = 2{,}157 \text{ RPM} \] \[ BHP = 10.51 + 0.753 \times (11.72 - 10.51) = 11.42 \]

Double interpolation. Now find 4,000 CFM at 14 in. SP. The pressure lies between the 12 and 16 in. columns, so first interpolate the 16 in. column at the same fraction \( f = 0.753 \):

\[ N_{16} = 2{,}401 + 0.753 \times (2{,}433 - 2{,}401) = 2{,}425 \text{ RPM}, \quad BHP_{16} = 13.87 + 0.753 \times (15.30 - 13.87) = 14.95 \]

Then interpolate between the two columns. 14 in. is halfway between 12 and 16, so the fraction is 0.5:

\[ N = 2{,}157 + 0.5 \times (2{,}425 - 2{,}157) = 2{,}291 \text{ RPM}, \quad BHP = 11.42 + 0.5 \times (14.95 - 11.42) = 13.18 \]

The result, 2,291 RPM and 13.18 BHP, is Class 22 (\( 2{,}291 \le 2{,}812 \)). Because the pressure columns are 4 in. wg apart at this point in the table, a straight line between them is an approximation; for a quotation, confirm the final speed in Fan Selector, which computes the point directly.

The MicroSim below lets you practice reading, interpolating and classifying on the same RBA 913 excerpt, with each answer checked.

docs.title: Diagram: Performance Table Reader
docs.text:
Performance Table Reader

Type: microsim sim-id: ch26-performance-table-reader Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Apply Bloom Verb: use Learning Objective: The learner will use an excerpt of the RBA 913 performance table to find the RPM and BHP for a duty point, by direct reading or linear interpolation within ±1%, and to name the fan class the point requires.

Prerequisites: performance table, performance table header, outlet velocity, class shading, interpolation (all defined in the section "Performance Tables" above).

Evidence of Mastery: For six duty points the learner types an RPM and a BHP and picks a class (22, 32 or 45) before checking. A duty point is correct when RPM and BHP are each within the tolerance in Rules and the class matches. Mastery is 5 of 6 correct. Hovering cells and toggling the class overlay are exploration.

Misconceptions: (1) The class is decided by the static pressure column alone. (2) Interpolation can use the nearest cell instead of the two bracketing cells. (3) A duty point between two pressure columns can be interpolated in one step.

Instructional Rationale: Computing values and committing a class before feedback is the Apply-level practice a quoting engineer needs; the class overlay is shown only after the answer so the learner must use the footer speeds.

Content:

The grid is the 5-row by 8-column RBA 913 excerpt exactly as printed in the chapter section "Reading a Performance Table" (CFM 3,348, 3,720, 4,092, 4,464, 4,836 with OV 3,600, 4,000, 4,400, 4,800, 5,200 FPM; SP 4, 8, 12, 16, 20, 24, 28, 32 in. wg; all 40 RPM / BHP cells). Cells marked as Class 32 or Class 45 in that table carry that marking only when the class overlay is turned on. The underlined cells (4,836 CFM at 28 and at 32 in. SP) carry the label "maximum static efficiency".

Header shown above the grid: "RBA 913. Impeller diameter 22.625 in. Tip speed (FPM) = 5.92 × RPM. Outlet area 0.93 ft². Fan Efficiency Grade FEG80." Footer: "Maximum RPM: Class 22 = 2,812; Class 32 = 3,337; Class 45 = 4,000. Performance certified for installation type B and D. BHP does not include transmission losses. Ratings do not include the effects of appurtenances."

Six duty points, in this order:

# Duty Method RPM BHP Class Feedback when wrong 1 4,092 CFM at 12 in. Direct 2,167 11.72 22 Row 4,092, column 12 in.; 2,167 ≤ 2,812 so Class 22. 2 3,720 CFM at 24 in. Direct 2,879 21.02 32 2,879 is above 2,812 and at or below 3,337, so Class 32. 3 4,836 CFM at 32 in. Direct 3,340 35.65 45 3,340 is 3 RPM above the Class 32 limit of 3,337, so Class 45. 4 4,000 CFM at 12 in. Interpolate CFM 2,157 11.42 22 f = (4,000 − 3,720) / (4,092 − 3,720) = 0.753 between rows 3,720 and 4,092. 5 4,000 CFM at 14 in. Interpolate CFM then SP 2,291 13.18 22 Interpolate the 12 in. and 16 in. columns at f = 0.753, then halfway between them. 6 4,464 CFM at 30 in. Interpolate SP 3,224 31.08 32 Halfway between 28 in. (3,126 / 28.92) and 32 in. (3,321 / 33.24).

Provenance: Twin City Fan Catalog 902 (November 2017), page 24, RBA 913; https://tcf.com/wp-content/uploads/2018/06/RBO-RBR-RBA-RBW-RBP-Industrial-Fans-Catalog-902.pdf. Interpolated answers computed from the Rules. The sim states that values must be confirmed in Fan Selector before quoting.

Rules: Linear interpolation y = y1 + (x − x1) / (x2 − x1) × (y2 − y1). Double interpolation interpolates airflow within each bracketing pressure column first, then interpolates pressure between the two results. Tolerance: direct readings must match exactly (±1 RPM, ±0.01 BHP); interpolated answers must be within ±1% of the RPM and BHP in Content. Class: 22 when RPM ≤ 2,812; 32 when 2,812 < RPM ≤ 3,337; 45 when 3,337 < RPM ≤ 4,000.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner reads duty point 1 and finds the row and column; hovering a cell highlights its row and column heads.
  2. The learner types RPM and BHP, picks a class and presses Check. Each of the three answers is marked; then the class overlay turns on.
  3. For interpolated points, the learner can open a scratch panel that shows the bracketing cells they selected and the fraction f once they enter it; the panel does not compute the answer.
  4. The overlay turns off again when the next duty point loads. After point 6 the score is shown.

Feedback: Six points, fixed order, two attempts each; the first is scored. Correct: "Correct: " followed by the row, column and class reasoning. Incorrect: names which of RPM, BHP or class is wrong and shows the "Feedback when wrong" text. After the second attempt the answer and its calculation are revealed. Score shown as "Duty points correct: n of 6".

Starting State: The grid with the class overlay off, the header and footer visible, and duty point 1 shown. The prompt reads "What speed and power does this duty need, and which class must you order?"

Chapter Anchors: RBA 913 values in the chapter excerpt table; 4,092 CFM at 12 in. gives 2,167 RPM and 11.72 BHP, Class 22; 4,000 CFM at 12 in. gives 2,157 RPM and 11.42 BHP; 4,000 CFM at 14 in. gives 2,291 RPM and 13.18 BHP, Class 22; 4,836 CFM at 32 in. is 3,340 RPM, Class 45; class limits 2,812, 3,337 and 4,000 RPM.

docs.title: Fan Selection Range
docs.text:
A size can deliver a duty point and still be the wrong size. The fan selection range is the part of a fan's performance table, or curve, where it runs stably and near its best efficiency: to the right of the stall region (Chapter 10) and not so far right that efficiency falls away. Catalog 902's overview puts it directly: "it is important that the fan size is selected so that it will operate at or near its maximum efficiency point." Its tables mark the maximum static efficiency by underlining those figures. Catalog 300's typical specification says the BC's horsepower curve "shall reach a peak in the normal selection area," which is the same idea expressed through the power curve.

Static efficiency for any cell can be computed from the table with the equation from Chapter 10:

docs.title: Static Efficiency from a Table Cell
docs.text:
\[ \eta_s = \frac{Q \times P_s}{6356 \times BHP} \]

where:

  • \( \eta_s \) is the fan static efficiency (as a decimal)
  • \( Q \) is the airflow in CFM
  • \( P_s \) is the fan static pressure in in. wg
  • \( BHP \) is the brake horsepower from the table
  • 6,356 converts CFM × in. wg to horsepower

docs.title: Worked Example: Same Airflow, Three Pressures
docs.text:
All three cells are on the 4,836 CFM row of RBA 913:

SP (in. wg) RPM / BHP Static efficiency Position 28 3152 / 31.23 \( 4{,}836 \times 28 / (6356 \times 31.23) = 0.68 \) Underlined: maximum static efficiency 8 1967 / 10.41 \( 4{,}836 \times 8 / (6356 \times 10.41) = 0.58 \) Right of peak 4 1612 / 6.38 \( 4{,}836 \times 4 / (6356 \times 6.38) = 0.48 \) Far right of peak

At 28 in. wg the RBA 913 is working at its best. At 4 in. wg it delivers the airflow, but at less than half the static efficiency, because a fan this size is built for higher pressure than 4 in. wg needs. A low-pressure duty at this airflow belongs on a different size or a different family, not on the RBA 913, and comparing several sizes at the same duty point, in the tables or in Fan Selector, is how you find it.

Check the Neighbors

Before accepting a size, look one size smaller and one size larger at the same duty point. If a neighbor needs noticeably less BHP, your first choice is outside its selection range.

docs.title: Rating Conditions
docs.text:
Every number in a performance table is true only under the conditions the catalog states. Rating conditions are those stated conditions: the air density, the installation type, and what the BHP does and does not include. The Catalog 902 footer states all of them in three lines:

  • "Performance certified is for installation type B & D: Free or ducted inlet, ducted outlet."
  • "Power ratings (BHP) do not include transmission losses."
  • "Performance ratings do not include the effects of appurtenances (accessories)."

The density is stated elsewhere: ERG-100 says that in each fan catalog the performance tables are based on standard air density, dry air at 70°F at sea level (29.92 in. Hg), equal to 0.075 lb/ft³. The installation types are the four AMCA test setups introduced in Chapter 10: A (free inlet, free outlet), B (free inlet, ducted outlet), C (ducted inlet, free outlet) and D (ducted inlet, ducted outlet). A rating certified for B and D therefore assumes there is a duct on the fan outlet.

docs.title: Worked Example: When the Job Is Not the Rating
docs.text:
An RBA 913 will move 4,464 CFM at 16 in. wg on a job where it discharges directly into a plenum room with no outlet duct.

  1. Read the table: 2,470 RPM, 16.85 BHP, Class 22.
  2. Compare the installation: no outlet duct means installation type A or C. The rating is certified for B and D, so the table does not describe this installation.
  3. Size the energy at stake: the outlet velocity on this row is 4,800 FPM, so the outlet velocity pressure at standard air is \( (4{,}800 / 4{,}005)^2 = 1.44 \) in. wg. That is the kinetic energy leaving the fan; with a ducted outlet some of it is recovered as static pressure, and with a free outlet it is not, so the fan will not deliver the tabulated static pressure at the tabulated speed.
  4. Act: confirm the selection for the actual installation with Fan Selector or the factory, or add an outlet duct, and account for the outlet condition as a system effect (Chapter 25).

The table value was correct and the selection was still wrong, because the job broke a rating condition. Read the conditions every time.

docs.title: AMCA Certified Ratings
docs.text:
AMCA certified ratings are published performance figures that the Air Movement and Control Association has licensed the manufacturer to mark with the AMCA seal, after testing in an AMCA-accredited laboratory and check tests under the AMCA Certified Ratings Program (AMCA 211 for air, AMCA 311 for sound). The seal applies only to the models, the catalog and the performance types the certification statement names, so the statement itself is the thing to read.

The two catalogs used here word it differently:

  • Catalog 300: "Twin City Fan & Blower certifies that the Model BC-SW fans shown herein are licensed to bear the AMCA Seal. Certified performance data may be found in Twin City Fan & Blower's Fan Selector software." The overview lists certifications as AMCA Sound/Air, AMCA Air, FEI and UL 705.
  • Catalog 902: the RBO, RBR, RBA and RBW are licensed to bear the AMCA Seal, and "the ratings shown are based on tests and procedures performed in accordance with AMCA Publication 211." The overview lists certifications as AMCA Air and FEG. The RBP "is not AMCA licensed."

docs.title: Worked Example: Checking a Specification Requirement
docs.text:
A specification requires "AMCA certified ratings seal for both sound and air performance." Three candidates are on the table:

Candidate What the catalog states Meets the requirement? BC-SW AMCA Sound/Air certification listed Yes, with certified data taken from Fan Selector RBA AMCA Air (and FEG) listed; no sound certification listed No, for the sound part; raise it with the engineer before bidding RBP Not AMCA licensed No

The RBA might be the better fan for the airstream, and it may still be the right recommendation. The point is to find the gap from the certification statement before the bid, not from a submittal rejection after it.

docs.title: Transmission Losses
docs.text:
Transmission losses are the power lost between the motor shaft and the fan shaft in the drive: belt flexing and slip, and bearing friction in the drive components. Catalog BHP is the power at the fan shaft, and the Catalog 902 footer says plainly that it does not include them. On a belt-driven fan the motor must supply the fan BHP plus the drive loss. On an Arrangement 4 or 8 fan there are no belts, and coupling losses are small enough to be ignored in a catalog selection.

AMCA Publication 203 gives estimated belt drive losses as a percentage of motor power, larger for small drives and smaller for large ones. The 4 percent used below is illustrative.

docs.title: Motor Power Including Drive Loss
docs.text:
\[ HP_{motor} = \frac{BHP}{1 - L_d} \]

where:

  • \( HP_{motor} \) is the power the motor must deliver, in horsepower
  • \( BHP \) is the fan brake horsepower from the performance table
  • \( L_d \) is the drive loss as a decimal fraction of motor power

docs.title: Worked Example: Adding the Drive Loss
docs.text:
The RBA 913 at 4,092 CFM and 12 in. wg needs 11.72 BHP at the fan shaft. On a belt-driven Arrangement 9 with an illustrative 4 percent drive loss:

\[ HP_{motor} = \frac{11.72}{1 - 0.04} = 12.21 \text{ hp} \]

The difference is about half a horsepower. It decides nothing here, but it is the half horsepower that pushes a selection over a motor size when the fan BHP sits just under a standard rating, which is exactly the case where people forget it.

docs.title: Appurtenance Effects
docs.text: Appurtenance effects are the changes in fan performance caused by accessories in or at the airstream, such as inlet boxes, variable inlet vanes, outlet dampers, inlet and outlet screens, and guards over an open inlet. Catalog ratings are for the bare fan and exclude them. Each accessory adds a pressure loss or disturbs the flow into or out of the impeller, so the fan must run faster and draw more power to deliver the same duty. The catalogs describe accessories in terms of this effect: Catalog 300 calls its inlet boxes "designed to minimize pressure drop," and its typical specification uses cantilevered inlet vane blades through size 660 "to minimize air performance insertion losses and noise." Account for appurtenances with the manufacturer's data in Fan Selector or from the factory, and treat their flow disturbance as a system effect (Chapter 25).

docs.title: Actual Operating Conditions
docs.text:
Actual operating conditions are the temperature, altitude and density at which the fan will really run, as opposed to the standard air of the table. Because tables are at standard air, actual conditions must be converted before entering the table, and the results converted back. ERG-100 works this example: 17,000 CFM at 2.5 in. wg, 300°F and 3,000 ft altitude.

  1. The ERG-100 correction factor for 300°F at 3,000 ft is 0.624.
  2. Standard-air static pressure: \( 2.5 / 0.624 = 4.0 \) in. wg. Enter the table at 17,000 CFM and 4.0 in. wg. Airflow is not corrected.
  3. The table (by interpolation) gives 918 RPM and 14.36 BHP at standard air.
  4. BHP at operating conditions: \( 14.36 \times 0.624 = 8.96 \) BHP.
  5. Cold start BHP at the site (70°F, 3,000 ft, factor 0.896): \( 14.36 \times 0.896 = 12.87 \) BHP.

The fan runs at 918 RPM in every case. The motor sees 8.96 BHP when the air is hot but 12.87 BHP when the fan starts in cold air, and that difference is the subject of motor selection below.

docs.title: Catalog Operating Limits
docs.text:
Catalog operating limits are the published boundaries a selection must stay inside: maximum RPM by size and class, temperature limits by construction and arrangement, and limits stated as notes. Examples from the two catalogs:

  • Maximum RPM: BC-SW size 365 runs to 995 RPM in Class I and 1,283 RPM in Class II (Catalog 300, page 16).
  • Speed notes: "Operating speeds above 4000 RPM are not recommended. Consult factory" (Catalog 300); RBO 905 has a Class 22 maximum of 5,296 RPM but "selections above 4000 RPM not recommended" (Catalog 902).
  • Temperature: standard BC construction from –20°F to +300°F, but Arrangements 3 and 3F only to 130°F and Arrangement 4 to 180°F; standard RB Arrangement 4 fans to 200°F.
  • Derating: maximum safe speed must be reduced at high temperature; Catalog 300 directs you to Fan Selector for the derated values.

A selection that violates any one of these is not a selection, however good its efficiency.

docs.title: First Critical Speed
docs.text: The first critical speed is the lowest rotating speed at which the shaft and impeller assembly's natural bending frequency matches the speed of rotation, so that small unbalance forces are amplified into severe vibration. Fans are designed to run well below it. Both catalogs state the margin: shafts "are sized for a first critical speed of at least 1.43 times the maximum speed for the class." For a BC-SW size 365 Class II, the shaft's first critical speed is therefore at least \( 1.43 \times 1{,}283 = 1{,}835 \) RPM. That margin is calculated at the class maximum, which is one more reason a fan must never be sped up past its class limit in the field.

docs.title: AMCA 204 Balance Grade
docs.text: The AMCA 204 balance grade is the balance quality and vibration category a fan is built to under ANSI/AMCA Standard 204, Balance Quality and Vibration Levels for Fans. Each fan application category (BV-1 through BV-5) sets a balance quality grade for the impeller and vibration limits for the assembled fan. Catalog 300 states that BC impellers are statically and dynamically balanced to grade BV-3, which "corresponds to a Balance Quality Grade G6.3," that assembled fans are test run at the rated speed or maximum RPM with vibration recorded in three directions on both bearings, and that trim balancing is performed if needed to stay within BV-3 limits. When a specification asks for a stricter category, it is asking for something beyond the catalog standard and must be quoted as such.

docs.title: Material Specifications Table
docs.text: The material specifications table lists, for each size and class, the physical makeup of the fan: housing sheet gauges for the sides and scroll, shaft diameter and bearing type by arrangement, and bare fan weight by arrangement. Its columns use terms from Chapters 16 and 17, and its footnotes carry the bearing type codes. In Catalog 300 the bearing codes are B (ball bearing), R (unit roller bearings) and SR (spherical roller bearings with split pillow block housings); gauge numbers follow sheet steel practice, where a smaller number is thicker steel.

docs.title: Worked Example: Reading One Row
docs.text:
Catalog 300, BC SWSI Class I, size 365 (page 17):

Column Value What it tells you Housing sides 10 10 gauge steel sides Housing scroll 12 12 gauge steel scroll, lighter than the sides Arr. 1 and 9 shaft and bearing 1-15/16 in., B Ball bearings on a 1-15/16 in. shaft Arr. 3 shaft and bearing 1-15/16 in., B Same shaft and bearing in Arrangement 3 Bare fan weight, Arr. 1 / 3 / 9 1,009 / 948 / 1,059 lb Weight without motor and drive, for rigging and isolator selection

Two uses follow directly. The bare fan weight, plus motor and drive weight, sets the load for vibration isolators (Chapter 22). The bearing type tells the maintenance department which bearings to stock. Moving up the same table, size 490 switches from ball to unit roller bearings in Arrangement 3 (R) while Arrangements 1 and 9 stay on ball bearings, a difference a reader only finds by reading the row.

docs.title: Product Options
docs.text: Product options are the construction choices and accessories a catalog offers beyond the standard fan: optional materials and construction (aluminum, stainless steel, high temperature, spark resistant), and accessories such as belt guards, shaft and bearing guards, vibration isolation and inertia bases, drains, access doors, flanged inlets and outlets, companion flanges, shaft seals, inlet boxes, coupling guards, inlet and outlet screens, outlet dampers, variable inlet vanes and drives. The catalog states what each one does and when to use it, and those statements are the basis of a recommendation.

docs.title: Worked Example: Choosing a Capacity Control
docs.text:
A BC-SW on clean supply air must reduce airflow, and the customer expects to run at about 60 percent of full volume for most of the year. Catalog 300 describes three options:

  1. Outlet dampers add resistance and move the operating point left. They are the least expensive option, and the horsepower savings are "usually much less than other methods." Parallel blade dampers suit modulation from full open to about 75 percent open; opposed blade dampers cost about 10 percent more and suit modulation over the entire range.
  2. Variable inlet vanes pre-spin the air in the direction of rotation, giving a family of reduced curves. They cost about 50 to 80 percent more than outlet dampers but offer significant energy savings.
  3. A variable frequency drive changes fan speed and "can provide the greatest potential for energy savings"; the catalog says it should be considered for extended operation at part load, "especially below 70% of the full volume operation."

Sixty percent of full volume for most of the year is below the 70 percent the catalog names, so the VFD is the recommendation. If the owner cannot accept a VFD, the next choice is variable inlet vanes; an outlet damper would have to be opposed blade to modulate that far. Any damper or vane is an appurtenance, so its effect must be included in the selection.

docs.title: Motor Selection
docs.text: Motor selection is choosing the motor horsepower, enclosure and type for a fan from the catalog BHP and the job conditions. The catalog gives the fan BHP at standard air; the motor must also cover drive losses, the cold start of a hot fan, and the service conditions covered in Chapters 14 and 15 (enclosure, efficiency class, inverter duty, hazardous location). Catalog 300 also sets drive rules that follow from the motor: drives and belts rated for 150 percent of the required motor horsepower, and variable pitch motor sheaves on 10 HP and smaller, fixed pitch on 15 HP and larger.

docs.title: Worked Example: Two Motors from the Catalog
docs.text:
Room-temperature duty. The RBA 913 at 4,092 CFM and 12 in. wg needs 12.21 hp at the motor after the illustrative 4 percent drive loss. The next standard NEMA motor rating at or above 12.21 hp is 15 HP. A 15 HP TEFC motor is a sound choice for a dust collector exhauster; the motor is not running into its service factor, and Catalog 300's drive rule would call for a fixed pitch sheave at 15 HP.

Hot duty. For the ERG-100 fan at 300°F and 3,000 ft, the hot BHP is 8.96, but the fan starts in 70°F air at 3,000 ft and draws 12.87 BHP until the air heats up. With the same illustrative 4 percent drive loss the cold requirement is \( 12.87 / 0.96 = 13.41 \) hp, so the motor is 15 HP, not the 10 HP that the hot BHP alone would suggest. If the fan could be started with dampers closed or on a VFD, a smaller motor might be justified, but that is a deliberate design choice covered in Chapter 27, not a default.

Size the Motor for the Cold Start

A common trap on hot jobs is sizing the motor from the operating BHP, because that is the number at the design condition. Cold air is denser, so the same fan at the same speed draws more power at start-up and until the system warms. Always take the cold BHP at the site altitude, add the drive loss, and size the motor from that.

docs.title: Fan Selector Software
docs.text:
Fan Selector software is Twin City Fan's selection program, downloaded from tcf.com, that computes certified performance for a duty point and supplies the performance, drawings and accessory data the printed catalog leaves out, including maximum safe speeds derated for elevated temperature. Catalog 300 states that BC certified performance data "may be found in Twin City Fan & Blower's Fan Selector software," and Catalog 902 says that "for complete product performance, drawings and available accessories," you should download the Fan Selector program. Fan Selector does what tables cannot: it computes the exact point instead of interpolating, and it holds certified data for lines, such as the BC, whose catalogs print no tables at all.

The catalog still matters when you use the software, because the software answers "what does it take?" and the catalog answers "is that allowed, and what does it include?"

docs.title: Worked Example: Checking a Software Selection Against the Catalog
docs.text:
Fan Selector returns a BC-SW size 365 at 1,150 RPM for a customer's duty at standard air (the selection speed is illustrative). Check it against Catalog 300:

  1. Class. Engineering data (page 16) gives size 365 maximum RPM of 995 in Class I and 1,283 in Class II. Since \( 995 < 1{,}150 \le 1{,}283 \), the fan must be ordered Class II.
  2. Critical speed margin. The shaft is sized for a first critical speed of at least \( 1.43 \times 1{,}283 = 1{,}835 \) RPM, well above 1,150 RPM.
  3. Arrangement and temperature. If the customer wants Arrangement 4 on 160°F air, Table 1 limits Arrangement 4 to 180°F, so it is allowed; at 200°F it would not be.
  4. Certification. The BC-SW is listed for AMCA Sound/Air, so certified sound and air data can be taken from the same selection.
  5. What is not included. Add drive losses for a belt-driven arrangement and any appurtenance effects before choosing the motor.

The software produced a number; the catalog turned it into an order line: BC-SW 365, Class II, at 1,150 RPM, in an arrangement and temperature the catalog permits.

Software Computes, the Catalog Permits

Think of Fan Selector and the catalog as two halves of one answer. The software tells you what speed and power a duty requires; the catalog tells you whether that speed, class, arrangement and temperature are allowed and what the numbers leave out. A selection is finished only when both halves agree.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• A Twin City Fan product catalog answers three kinds of question: can it be built, how will it perform, and what will it look like. Know which one you are asking.
  • Catalog structure is consistent: overview, construction, high temperature, arrangements, options, engineering data, material specifications, dimensions, typical specifications, and in some catalogs performance data. Catalog 300 puts BC performance in Fan Selector instead of tables.
  • Technical descriptions hold restrictions that tables omit. When FanPedia and the current catalog disagree, the current catalog wins; check the edition date on tcf.com.
  • Fan size labels one impeller diameter within a model; the performance page header gives the diameter, tip speed factor and outlet area. A model code names the line and impeller; model, size, class and arrangement must be checked together against the availability table.
  • The air change method and minimum conveying velocity supply airflow and duct velocity; fan family selection comes before size and depends on the airstream.
  • A performance table lists RPM and BHP by airflow and static pressure at standard air. Read the header and footer first, read the cell, use interpolation between rows and columns, and read the class from the class shading, which is a map of the class maximum speeds.
  • Stay in the fan selection range near the underlined maximum efficiency; compute static efficiency to compare cells and sizes.
  • Rating conditions are standard air, a stated installation type (B and D in Catalog 902), BHP without transmission losses, and no appurtenance effects. AMCA certified ratings apply only to what the certification statement names.
  • Convert actual operating conditions to standard air before entering a table, and size the motor for the cold start. Motor selection adds drive loss to BHP and goes to the next standard motor rating.
  • Catalog operating limits, first critical speed (at least 1.43 times class maximum speed), the AMCA 204 balance grade (BV-3 for BC) and the material specifications table describe what the fan is built to tolerate.
  • Product options carry catalog guidance on when to use them; Fan Selector software computes the point, and the catalog decides whether it is allowed.

You Can Read the Catalog Now

You took a duty point through a real Twin City Fan performance table, interpolated in two directions, read the class from the shading, and checked it against the rating conditions and the catalog limits. That is the core skill behind every quote, and Chapter 27 builds the full selection and specification on top of it.

docs.title: Fan Selection and Writing the Specification
Summary
docs.text: This final chapter brings the book together. It starts from application requirements (airstream conditions, space constraints, noise limits, and efficiency requirements) and walks through selecting the impeller, arrangement, construction, drive, and accessories, sizing the motor for cold start, and weighing trade-offs between candidates. It then covers the complete fan description, writing a CSI-format specification with a performance clause, submittal data and certified drawings, and specification review. It ends with the capstone: a complete written fan specification for a realistic application.

docs.text:
This chapter builds on concepts from:

  • Chapter 1: Air, Pressure and the Fan
  • Chapter 2: Airstreams, Total Pressure and Standard Air
