docs.title: Duct Airflow and Velocity Calculator
docs.text: Run the Duct Airflow and Velocity Calculator MicroSim Fullscreen Edit in the p5.js Editor

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
This calculator gives practice with the airflow equation \( Q = V \times A \) on the kinds of ducts that appear on drawings. Duct sizes come in inches, but the equation needs the flow area in square feet. A rectangular duct's area is \( (W \times H) \div 144 \) ft², and a round duct's area is \( \pi D^2 \div 576 \) ft².

The sim opens with four fixed challenges. Each one asks for a single number:

# Given Asked Model answer 1 2,400 CFM in a 16 in × 12 in rectangular duct Velocity 1,800 ft/min 2 5,000 CFM in a 24 in round duct Velocity 1,592 ft/min 3 A 20 in × 10 in rectangular duct at 1,500 ft/min Airflow 2,083 CFM 4 10,000 CFM with velocity no higher than 2,000 ft/min Minimum flow area 5.00 ft²

Challenge 1 uses the machine-shop worked example from Chapter 1. Challenges 2 to 4 are illustrative values, and the sim labels them that way.

An answer within ±2% of the model value is correct. Each challenge allows two attempts. A non-numeric or empty entry gets "Enter a number" and does not use an attempt. After every check the sim shows your number beside the model value, lays out the worked calculation, and highlights the step where your number departs from it. It recognizes common slips: forgetting to divide by 144, treating a round duct as a square of side D, using π D² ÷ 144, multiplying where you should divide, and giving the area in square inches. A running count "Challenges correct: n of 4" stays on screen.

Free mode unlocks after challenge 4. You can change the duct shape, width, height or diameter, and the airflow. The flow area (3 decimals), the velocity (to the nearest 10 ft/min) and the substituted equation update immediately. The first time you enlarge the duct while the airflow stays fixed, the sim points out that the CFM did not change and only the velocity fell.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read challenge 1 and calculate the velocity on paper or a calculator.
  2. Type the number in the Your answer box and press Check (or Enter).
  3. Read the feedback and the highlighted step. If you have an attempt left, correct your work and try again.
  4. Press Next challenge to continue. After challenge 4, press Start free mode.
  5. In free mode, set 2,400 CFM in a 16 in × 12 in duct, then change it to 24 in × 16 in. Velocity falls from 1,800 to 900 ft/min while the airflow stays at 2,400 CFM.

        height="672px"

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Adult professional development: new application engineers, sales staff, representatives and facilities staff.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10-15 minutes

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: The learner will calculate air velocity, airflow volume or required flow area from the other two quantities for rectangular and round ducts, to within 2 percent of the model value (Bloom: Apply, verb: calculate).

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Airflow volume in cubic feet per minute (CFM)
  • Air velocity in feet per minute
  • Flow area in square feet and the equation \( Q = V \times A \)
  • Converting duct dimensions in inches to square feet

All are covered in the Chapter 1 sections "Airflow Volume and Cubic Feet Per Minute" and "Air Velocity".

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Challenges (8 min): Work the four challenges in order. Commit to a number before checking. Two attempts each.
  2. Free exploration (5 min): Hold the airflow at 2,400 CFM and enlarge the duct. Then switch to a round duct and find the diameter whose area is closest to a 16 in square. It is not 16 in.
  3. Discussion (2 min): Why does a bigger duct not move more air when the fan delivers the same CFM?

docs.title: Common Misconceptions Addressed
docs.text:
• Dividing CFM by the duct dimensions in inches without converting to square feet (challenge 1).
  • Believing a bigger duct moves more air at the same fan airflow. In fact the CFM is the same and only the velocity drops (free mode note).
  • Believing a round duct of diameter D has the same area as a square duct of side D (challenge 2).

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text: Mastery is 4 of 4 challenges correct within ±2%, with at most two attempts each. Free exploration is not evidence of mastery.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Chapter 1: Air, Pressure and the Fan. The "Air Velocity" section and its worked example "Velocity in a Rectangular Duct".
  2. FanPedia online, Twin City Fan. The fan and blower encyclopedia this textbook is built from.
  3. Volumetric flow rate, Wikipedia. Defines Q = V × A for flow through a cross-section.
  4. Duct (flow), Wikipedia. Background on rectangular and round ductwork.

docs.title: Exploded View of a Belt-Driven Centrifugal Fan
docs.text: Run the Exploded View of a Belt-Driven Centrifugal Fan MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
This MicroSim shows a belt-driven single-width, single-inlet (SWSI) centrifugal fan in Arrangement 9, pulled apart along its shaft line the way an exploded view in FanPedia or a submittal drawing shows it. It names 14 parts, from the inlet collar and flanged inlet through the drive train to the pedestal.

The drawing is a simplified schematic drawn in code, modeled on the FanPedia page 10 exploded view. It is not to scale and does not show a specific Twin City Fan model.

The flanged inlet sits in its own "Inlet option" box because it is the alternative to the inlet collar. A fan ships with one or the other, not both.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Explore mode (the starting mode). Select any part to open its infobox. Only one infobox is open at a time. The label of each part you have opened turns green, and the counter shows how many of the 14 you have visited.
  2. Assemble / Explode. Press Assemble to slide the parts into place. The inlet funnel and impeller disappear inside the housing, and the shaft, bearings, sheave, belts and motor drop onto the pedestal. Press Explode to pull them apart again. Labels are shown only in the exploded view.
  3. Quiz mode. Press Quiz. The labels are hidden and the drawing stays exploded. Ten prompts appear in a fixed order. Select the part that matches each one. You get two attempts per prompt:
    • Correct: you see "Correct:" with the reason, and that part's label appears.
    • First miss: you see which part you picked and the reason for the correct answer, then you try again.
    • Second miss: the correct part is highlighted in red and the prompt counts as missed.
  4. After the tenth prompt, a summary shows your score ("Correct on first attempt: n of 10") and lists the prompts you missed with their reasons. Mastery is 9 of 10 correct on the first attempt.
  5. Reset clears your visited parts and returns to explore mode.

You can also move between parts with the Tab key and select one with Enter or Space.

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: New application engineers, sales staff, manufacturer's representatives and facilities staff who will read exploded views and submittal drawings of centrifugal fans.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: Identify each of the 14 labeled parts in an exploded view of a belt-driven Arrangement 9 centrifugal fan when given the part's name or function (Bloom's Taxonomy: Remember, verb "identify").

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10 to 15 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: Read Chapter 3, Basic Fan Anatomy, through the drive-train sections. The MicroSim uses these terms: exploded view, fan housing, impeller, inlet funnel, inlet collar, inlet flange, outlet flange, shaft, bearing, sheave, V-belt, motor, slide base and pedestal.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Explore (5 min): Open all 14 infoboxes. For each part, say out loud whether it touches the air.
  2. Assemble and explode (2 min): Press Assemble and watch where the funnel, impeller and drive parts go. Note that the bearings, sheave and motor end up outside the housing.
  3. Quiz (5 min): Switch to quiz mode and answer the ten prompts without going back to explore mode.
  4. Review (3 min): Read the reasons for any missed prompts, return to explore mode for those parts, then retake the quiz.

docs.title: Common Misconceptions to Watch For
docs.text:
• The inlet funnel and the inlet collar are the same part. The funnel shapes the air into the impeller; the collar is a duct connection.
  • The pedestal is part of the housing. It is a separate support for the bearings and shaft.
  • The fan sheave and the motor sheave are the same size. Their ratio sets fan speed.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text: Mastery is 9 of 10 prompts correct on the first attempt in quiz mode. Opening infoboxes in explore mode is exploration and does not count as evidence.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Twin City Fan & Blower. FanPedia: The Fan & Blower Encyclopedia, page 10 (exploded view, belt-driven centrifugal fans, Arrangement 9). PDF
  2. Twin City Fan & Blower. FanPedia online. https://tcf.com/fanpedia/
  3. Chapter 3, Basic Fan Anatomy, sections on the housing, impeller, inlet, outlet and drive train, which cite FanPedia pages 59, 79, 90 and 188.

docs.title: Fan Family Sorter
docs.text: Run the Fan Family Sorter MicroSim Fullscreen Edit in the p5.js Editor

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
The sorter deals fifteen current Twin City Fan product lines, one card at a time, in a shuffled order. Each card shows a model designation and a short description of the fan: the wheel or impeller, the housing, the mounting and sometimes the application. The cards never name the family. You decide whether each line is Centrifugal, Axial or Mixed flow from the clues about how air passes through the impeller.

Several cards are look-alikes on purpose. A tubular inline centrifugal fan sits next to a tubeaxial in the same kind of round tube; a centrifugal roof exhauster and an axial roof ventilator both sit on a roof; two lab exhaust fans belong to two different families. The relevant clue is always the airflow path through the impeller: in along the shaft and out at a right angle (centrifugal), in and out along the shaft (axial), or out on a diagonal (mixed flow). Housing shape, roof location and application name are distractors.

Each placement is final. The card locks into the bin you chose, is marked correct or incorrect, and the reason appears beneath it. Only first placements count toward the score.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read the face-up card and press Centrifugal, Axial or Mixed flow (or the keys 1, 2 or 3).
  2. Read the feedback under the card. A correct placement reads "Correct: family." and an incorrect one reads "This one is family.", each followed by the reason.
  3. Press Next card (or Enter) to turn up the next card. The placed card stays in its bin as a chip marked with a check or a cross.
  4. After the fifteenth card, press Show summary. The summary shows the score as "Correct: n of 15", a per-family tally and every misplaced card with its correct family and reason. Use More misses to page through a long list.
  5. Press Sort again to reshuffle all fifteen cards and reset the score.

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: New application engineers, inside and outside sales staff, manufacturer's representatives, distributors and plant staff who need to identify fans by family. This is an adult professional-development activity.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: Differentiate fifteen Twin City Fan product lines into the centrifugal, axial and mixed flow families from a short description of each, correctly placing at least 13 of 15 on the first placement (Bloom's Taxonomy: Analyze).

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10 to 15 minutes for one sort, plus 5 minutes of discussion.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: From Chapter 4: fan family, centrifugal fan, axial fan, mixed flow fan, scroll housing, tubular housing, guide vanes, unhoused centrifugal fans (plenum and plug types), inline centrifugal fan, panel fan, power roof ventilator, centrifugal roof exhauster, roof ventilator, wall mounted fan and laboratory fume exhaust fan.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. First sort (5 to 8 min): Each learner sorts all fifteen cards alone, without notes. Mastery is 13 of 15 on the first placement.
  2. Diagnose the misses (3 to 5 min): For each misplaced card in the summary, the learner names the clue that misled them: housing shape, roof location or application name.
  3. Discussion (5 min): Compare the look-alike pairs. Why are TSL and TD both in a round tube but in different families? Why are DCRD and TUD both roof fans but in different families? Why do BCIFE and TVIFE, both induced flow lab exhaust fans, land in different families?
  4. Second sort (optional): Learners who scored below 13 review the chapter sections on tubular housings and power roof ventilators, then press Sort again.

docs.title: Common Misconceptions Targeted
docs.text:
• Any fan in a tubular housing is axial (TSL, QSL and QCLB are not).
  • Any roof fan, or any power roof ventilator, is centrifugal (TUD is axial).
  • Lab exhaust fans are their own family (BCIFE is centrifugal; TVIFE is mixed flow).
  • A fan without a housing cannot be centrifugal (plenum and plug fans are).

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
• Score of 13 or more of 15 on the first sort shows mastery; the summary reads "Mastery reached."
  • For each miss, the learner can state the airflow-path clue on the card that identifies the correct family.
  • Follow-up question: given a new model description that names only a "round tube" and "vanes," what extra information would you need to name the family?

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Twin City Fan, current product catalog pages on tcf.com (products: centrifugal fans, plenum fans, plug fans, inline centrifugal fans, axial fans, wall mounted fans, roof ventilators, centrifugal roof and wall exhausters, mixed flow fans, laboratory and fume exhaust fans), retrieved 2026-10-08. Source of the model designations and their family groupings.
  2. Twin City Fan, FanPedia: The Fan & Blower Encyclopedia (2021), pp. 4-8, 17 and 32. Source of the housing and impeller descriptions.
  3. Chapter 4: Centrifugal, Axial and Mixed Flow Fans in this book.

docs.title: Fan Curve Explorer
docs.text: Run the Fan Curve Explorer MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
Two illustrative centrifugal fans, labeled Curve A and Curve B, are drawn at one fixed speed each and at standard air. The top plot shows fan static pressure (FSP, in. wg) against airflow (CFM); the bottom plot shows brake horsepower (BHP) against the same airflow axis. Hovering any data point shows its airflow, fan static pressure and BHP.

Six questions, asked in a fixed order, ask the learner to decide whether four duty points sit in the stall region, which fan has a non-overloading power curve, and how large a motor Curve A needs so that it cannot be overloaded at this speed. Each answer marks the point or curve it is about (green ring for a correct answer, red ring for an incorrect one) and shows the reason. After the last question the stall region of each fan is shaded so the two can be compared, and the score is shown.

Both curves are illustrative. They are shaped after typical backward inclined (Curve A) and forward curved (Curve B) fan behavior described in standard fan engineering texts and are not Twin City Fan published ratings. Curve A is the same illustrative fan curve tabulated in Chapter 10.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Hover along both pressure curves and both BHP curves to read values. Find the airflow at which each pressure curve reaches its peak (for Curve B, the right-hand peak after the dip).
  2. Answer each question by pressing Yes / No or Curve A / Curve B. Question 6 needs a typed number of BHP; press Submit or Enter. Each question has one attempt.
  3. Read the feedback, look at the point the sim just marked, then press Next question.
  4. After question 6, press See score. The score reads "n of 6 correct", with "Mastery reached" at 5 or more. Start over clears the marks and starts again at question 1.

        height="664px"

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: New application engineers, inside and outside sales staff, manufacturer's representatives and specifying engineers who read fan curves to judge a selection.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10-15 minutes

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: Differentiate stable from stall-region operating points, and overloading from non-overloading power curves, by reading the pressure and BHP curves of two illustrative fans (Bloom: Analyze).

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: Fan curve, fan static pressure, brake horsepower, stall region, overloading power curve and non-overloading power curve, as defined in the section "The Fan Curve" of Chapter 10.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Exploration (4 min): Hover along Curve A and find the airflow of peak pressure (4,000 CFM, 4.9 in. wg). Then find Curve B's right-hand peak. Ask: which fan has more of its airflow range to the left of its peak?
  2. Committed answers (6 min): Work through the six questions without looking back at the chapter tables. Before pressing an answer, say out loud which side of the peak the point is on.
  3. Debrief (5 min): With the stall regions shaded, compare their extent. Discuss why the highest-pressure point is the edge of the stall region rather than the best place to select a fan, and why a 10 hp motor protects Curve A at this speed while Curve B's motor must be sized for the highest airflow the fan could realistically see.

docs.title: Common Misconceptions Addressed
docs.text:
• Any point the pressure curve passes through is a safe operating point, including points left of the peak (questions 1-4).
  • A fan's BHP always rises with airflow (question 5).
  • The highest-pressure point is the best place to select a fan (debrief and final summary).

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text: Mastery is 5 of 6 correct on the first attempt. Hovering to read values is exploration and does not count as evidence. Question 6 accepts any value within 0.1 of 9.5 BHP.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Chapter 10: Fan Performance, Curves and Ratings - the fan curve, stall region and power curve sections this MicroSim exercises.
  2. FanPedia: The Fan & Blower Encyclopedia (PDF) - Twin City Fan's reference on fan types, performance and selection.
  3. FanPedia online - Twin City Fan's online fan and blower encyclopedia.
  4. Plotly JavaScript Open Source Graphing Library - the charting library used to draw the curves.

docs.title: Arrangement Identifier
docs.text: Run the Arrangement Identifier MicroSim Fullscreen Edit in the p5.js Editor

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
An arrangement number is a short answer to three questions: how is the fan driven, where is the impeller relative to the bearings, and what carries the bearings and the motor? This MicroSim shows ten schematic side views of centrifugal fans, one for each of Arrangements 1, 2, 3, 3SI, 3DI, 4, 7, 8, 9 and 10, in shuffled order. For each drawing you first answer the three feature questions and commit them, and only then name the arrangement. Splitting the drawing into features before naming it is the skill the activity practices.

The parts in each drawing are left unlabeled until you check your arrangement answer, so you have to read the picture: look for belts and sheaves or a coupling, look for anything on the inlet side of the impeller, and look at what holds the bearings and the motor.

The schematics are simplified teaching drawings, not manufacturer outline drawings. Twin City Fan's arrangement drawings are on FanPedia pp. 20–23. Arrangement 2 comes from the AMCA arrangement standard and is not shown in FanPedia.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read the drawing. Answer Drive (Belt, Direct with coupling, or Direct on motor shaft), Impeller (Overhung or Center hung) and Bearings carried by (Pedestal, Fan housing, Independent pedestals outside inlet boxes, or Motor only).
  2. Press Check Features. Each feature is marked correct or incorrect, with the correct answer shown. If all three features are right, the arrangements consistent with them are highlighted in gold (for example, Belt, Overhung and Pedestal highlight 1, 9 and 10). If any feature is wrong, nothing is highlighted.
  3. Choose an arrangement and press Check Arrangement. The parts of the drawing are labeled and the reason for the answer appears, with an extra hint when your choice is a common confusion (for example, picking 4 for a coupled fan, or 1 for an Arrangement 9 or 10).
  4. Press Next Drawing. After ten drawings, See Results shows separate scores for features (out of 30) and arrangements (out of 10). New Round starts a new shuffled set.

Each question allows one attempt per drawing. Mastery is 8 of 10 arrangements correct on the first attempt; the feature answers are scaffolding and are scored separately.

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: New application engineers, inside and outside sales staff, manufacturer's representatives and others who read fan drawings and quotes.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: The learner will distinguish ten centrifugal fan arrangements (1, 2, 3, 3SI, 3DI, 4, 7, 8, 9 and 10) from schematic side-view drawings by identifying the drive type, the impeller position relative to the bearings, and what carries the bearings and the motor (Bloom level: Analyze; verb: distinguish).

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10–15 minutes for one round of ten drawings.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: Direct drive, belt drive, shaft coupling, sheave, overhung and center hung impellers, bearing pedestal, inlet box, SWSI and DWDI, and the arrangement definitions in Chapter 11: Drives and Standard Fan Arrangements.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Warm-up (2 min): Recall the three questions that make an arrangement number: drive, impeller position, and what carries the bearings and motor.
  2. Round one (8 min): Complete a full round of ten drawings. Before pressing Check Arrangement, say aloud which feature rules out the other highlighted arrangements.
  3. Debrief (5 min): Compare the misses on the results screen. Discuss the common confusions the hints target: not every direct drive fan is Arrangement 4; a coupling alone does not make a fan Arrangement 7; Arrangements 1, 9 and 10 differ only in motor location; Arrangement 2's bearings sit on a bracket carried by the housing, not on a pedestal.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
• Mastery: 8 of 10 arrangements correct on the first attempt in one round.
  • Feature accuracy (out of 30) shows whether a miss came from misreading the drawing or from mapping correct features to the wrong number.
  • Discussion check: explain why drawings 1, 9 and 10 share the same three features but have different arrangement numbers.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Twin City Fan, FanPedia: The Fan & Blower Encyclopedia, pp. 20–23 (centrifugal arrangement drawings and captions), p. 30 (impeller orientation), pp. 162–168 (arrangement technical descriptions). PDF
  2. Air Movement and Control Association International, ANSI/AMCA Standard 99, Standards Handbook: drive arrangements for centrifugal fans (source of the Arrangement 2 definition used here).
  3. Chapter 11: Drives and Standard Fan Arrangements in this textbook.

docs.title: Rotation and Discharge Code Builder
docs.text: Run the Rotation and Discharge Code Builder MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
A centrifugal fan's rotation and discharge code tells the factory which way the wheel turns and where the outlet points, both as seen by an observer on the drive side. The code can be written in letter form (CW THD) or angle form (CW 90). This MicroSim gives you eight job cards, in a fixed order, each describing a fan and its outlet in words. For each card you choose a rotation and one of the eight discharge letter codes, or "Not offered", and submit.

After every submission the sim draws the drive-side outline of the housing with the outlet in the answer's direction, a rotation arrow, a small dial showing the angle measured from straight up in the direction of rotation, and both code forms. The first submission on each card is scored; one unscored retry follows. The running score reads "Codes correct: n of 8", and mastery is 7 of 8 on the first attempt.

After card 8, free practice unlocks. Choose SWSI or DWDI, a rotation, and a discharge angle from 45° to 360° in 45° steps, and the outline and code update at once. On a DWDI fan, 225° (Bottom Angular Down) shows "Not offered on DWDI".

The job cards are illustrative scenarios. Discharge names, letter codes, angle forms and the DWDI discharge list come from FanPedia (PDF pp. 46–49) and Chapter 13.

docs.title: The rule the sim uses
docs.text:
Start with the outlet pointing straight up (360°) and turn it through the discharge angle in the direction of rotation: clockwise for CW, counterclockwise for CCW.

Code Angle CW outlet points CCW outlet points UBD Upblast 360 up up TAU Top Angular Up 45 up and right up and left THD Top Horizontal 90 right left TAD Top Angular Down 135 down and right down and left DBD Downblast 180 down down BAD Bottom Angular Down 225 down and left (SWSI only) down and right (SWSI only) BHD Bottom Horizontal 270 left right BAU Bottom Angular Up 315 up and left up and right

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read the job card: fan type, rotation and outlet direction, all from the drive side.
  2. Choose a rotation and a discharge (or "Not offered") under Your code, then press Submit Code.
  3. Read the feedback and study the drawn housing. Use Retry (unscored) if you want another try.
  4. Press Next Card. After card 8, press Start Free Practice and use the Free practice controls.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: Learners will apply the drive-side rotation and discharge-angle conventions to write the correct rotation and discharge code, in letter form and angle form, for a described centrifugal fan (Bloom's level: Apply).

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Fan sales, application and order-entry staff, and engineering students who specify or order centrifugal fans.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10–15 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: Drive side, clockwise (CW) and counterclockwise (CCW) rotation, discharge position, discharge angle, SWSI and DWDI fans, Bottom Angular Down discharge, and DWDI discharge limits, all covered in Chapter 13.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Predict (8 min): Work through the eight job cards. Before each submission, say the outlet direction aloud and count quarter turns from straight up in the direction of rotation.
  2. Check (2 min): After each card, compare the drawn outlet and the angle dial with your prediction; use the unscored retry on any card you missed.
  3. Explore (5 min): In free practice, fix the angle at 90° and switch between CW and CCW. Note that the outlet mirrors left to right. Repeat at 45° and 315°, then try 225° on a DWDI fan.

docs.title: Discussion Questions
docs.text:
1. Why does CW 90 blow right but CCW 90 blow left, while 360 and 180 are the same for both rotations?
  2. Why must rotation be judged from the drive side and not the inlet side?
  3. A layout calls for a DWDI fan blowing bottom angular down. What could you offer instead?

docs.title: Common Misconceptions Addressed
docs.text:
• The same angle number points the same way for CW and CCW fans.
  • Rotation can be judged from the inlet side.
  • Every discharge is available on every centrifugal fan, including DWDI.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text: Mastery is 7 of 8 job cards correct on the first (scored) attempt. Free practice is exploration and is not scored.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Twin City Fan & Blower. FanPedia: The Fan & Blower Encyclopedia, pp. 46–49 (discharge positions, rotation and DWDI discharges). PDF
  2. Twin City Fan & Blower. FanPedia online.
  3. AMCA International. ANSI/AMCA Standard 99, Standards Handbook (designation for rotation and discharge of centrifugal fans). AMCA

docs.title: Flow Control Power Comparator
docs.text: Run the Flow Control Power Comparator MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
Three common ways to turn a fan down are an outlet damper, variable inlet vanes and speed control. All three reduce airflow, but they need very different shaft power to do it. This MicroSim plots shaft power (% of design) against airflow (% of design) from 50% to 100% for the three methods and asks you to predict their order before you see the curves.

All three curves are labeled illustrative. The speed-control curve is the ideal fan-law relation, power = 100 × (airflow / 100)³, for a system curve that passes through zero. The outlet-damper and inlet-vane values are illustrative values written for this chapter to show the typical ordering; they are not Twin City Fan test data. FanPedia supports the ordering: outlet damper horsepower savings are "usually much less than other methods" (FanPedia p. 182), and inlet box dampers and inlet vanes save horsepower at reduced loads by pre-spinning the air (FanPedia pp. 145, 183, 188). Values between table rows are found by straight-line interpolation. Real speed control has small drive losses, and a system with fixed static pressure saves less than the ideal cube value.

Airflow (% of design) Outlet damper (% power) Variable inlet vanes (% power) Speed control (% power) 100 100 100 100.0 90 96 88 72.9 80 91 77 51.2 70 86 67 34.3 60 80 59 21.6 50 74 52 12.5

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read the challenge (80%, then 70%, then 50% airflow). The chart shows only its axes.
  2. Choose the three methods in order from lowest to highest shaft power, type the saving of the best method compared with the outlet damper in percentage points, and press Check.
  3. A challenge is correct when the ranking is right and the saving is within ±3 percentage points. You get two attempts. When the challenge ends (correct, or missed after the second wrong attempt), the three curves are drawn and the powers at that airflow are marked with their values. Press Next challenge; the curves are hidden again.
  4. After challenge 3 the curves stay visible and the airflow selector unlocks (50% to 100% in 5% steps, starting at 70%). Move it from 100% down to 50% and watch the readout of the three powers and the two savings. Hover any point for its airflow, method and power.

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: New application engineers, inside and outside sales staff, manufacturer's representatives and specifying engineers who discuss flow-control options with customers.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: The learner will differentiate outlet dampers, variable inlet vanes and speed control by the shaft power each needs at reduced airflow, correctly ranking the three methods and estimating the savings gap at a stated airflow between 50% and 100% of design (Bloom level: Analyze; verb: differentiate).

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10-15 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: Flow control, operating point, fan curve, system curve, outlet damper, variable inlet vanes, speed control and brake horsepower, from Chapter 18's "What Flow Control Means" section and Chapter 10.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Predict (6 min): Complete the three challenges in order. Commit a ranking and a saving before each reveal.
  2. Explore (4 min): With the selector unlocked, move from 100% to 50% airflow. Note that the damper curve is nearly flat while the speed-control curve drops steeply, so the gap between them grows as flow falls.
  3. Connect (3 min): Compare the 70% readout with the chapter's worked example "The Same 70% Flow Three Ways" (damper 86%, vanes 67%, speed control 34%) and the 80% value with the Speed Control worked example (51.2%).

docs.title: Common Misconceptions Addressed
docs.text:
• Closing a damper to half flow cuts power roughly in half (at 50% flow the damper still needs about 74%).
  • All flow-control methods save about the same energy.
  • Inlet vanes save as much as speed control.
  • Power falls in proportion to airflow under speed control, rather than with roughly the cube of airflow.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
Mastery is 3 of 3 challenges correct, shown as "Challenges correct: n of 3". Hovering points and moving the airflow selector are exploration, not evidence.

# Airflow Correct ranking, lowest to highest Saving of best method vs. damper 1 80% Speed control, inlet vanes, outlet damper 39.8 points (91 − 51.2) 2 70% Speed control, inlet vanes, outlet damper 51.7 points (86 − 34.3) 3 50% Speed control, inlet vanes, outlet damper 61.5 points (74 − 12.5)

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Twin City Fan & Blower. FanPedia: The Fan & Blower Encyclopedia, pp. 145, 182, 183, 188. PDF
  2. Wikipedia. Affinity laws: the fan-law relation between speed, flow, pressure and power.
  3. Wikipedia. Variable-frequency drive: how motor speed control is applied to fans.
  4. Chart.js. Line chart documentation.

docs.title: Construction Class Advisor
docs.text: Run the Construction Class Advisor MicroSim Fullscreen Edit in the p5.js Editor

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
The advisor presents six illustrative inquiries, in a fixed order, of the kind that reach an application engineer. Each inquiry gives a short description of the fan and the job, and tags for the airstream conditions present: hot, wet, corrosive, explosive, personnel exposure or recirculated gas. Four construction recommendations follow, labeled A to D. One of them is consistent with the FanPedia rules in Chapter 20; the other three each break a specific rule.

The six inquiries cover the decisions a construction line most often gets wrong:

  • high moisture construction for steam in an Arrangement 9 axial fan, with a drain;
  • the rule that high moisture construction cannot be combined with high temperature construction (at 220°F the axial fan needs a high temperature package, so the job goes to engineering review);
  • Type B, not Type C, when a radial bladed fan already has a non-ferrous impeller as standard;
  • the 601°F-800°F centrifugal package plus insulation when workers can touch a 700°F housing;
  • an FGR connection and an insulated inlet box when hot flue gas is returned to the fan inlet;
  • buffer strips or a bolt-on pedestal when stainless steel must not be welded to mild steel.

You commit a recommendation before the reason is shown. The first answer to each inquiry is the one scored; one extra practice attempt is allowed. The summary lists every first answer, the correct answer and the reason, and builds the construction line for inquiry 4 as an example.

The inquiries are illustrative, not customer orders; the rules come from FanPedia.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read the inquiry and its airstream tags. The prompt asks: "What should the construction line say?"
  2. Press A, B, C or D (or the A to D keys) to select a recommendation, then press Recommend (or Enter) to commit it.
  3. Read the feedback. A sound choice reads "Recommended construction is sound." and a wrong one reads "That breaks a rule.", each followed by the reason. After a correct first answer the correct option is marked at once.
  4. After a wrong first answer you may choose again once for practice. The practice attempt is not scored; afterwards the correct option is marked.
  5. Press Next inquiry to continue. After inquiry 6, press See summary for the score "n of 6" and the review list. A score of 5 or more reads "You can turn an airstream into a construction line."
  6. Press Start over to reset all six inquiries and the score.

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: New application engineers, inside and outside sales staff, manufacturer's representatives, distributors and plant staff who write or check the construction line on a fan order. This is an adult professional-development activity.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: Recommend the construction choice for six stated airstream inquiries, consistent with the FanPedia rules in Chapter 20, with at least 5 of 6 correct on the first attempt (Bloom's Taxonomy: Evaluate).

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10 to 15 minutes for one pass, plus 5 to 10 minutes of discussion.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: From Chapter 20 and Chapter 18: construction class, construction material, stainless steel construction, buffer strips, spark resistant Types A, B and C, non-ferrous material, high temperature construction and packages, high moisture construction, housing drain, insulated fan, insulated jacket, double wall construction, flue gas recirculation and inlet box.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. First pass (8 to 10 min): Each learner works all six inquiries alone, without notes, committing each recommendation before reading the reason. Mastery is 5 of 6 on the first attempt.
  2. Name the broken rule (3 to 5 min): For every wrong first answer in the summary, the learner states which chapter rule that option breaks (for example, "high moisture and high temperature construction cannot be stacked").
  3. Discussion (5 to 10 min): Why does a specification that says Type C end with a Type B recommendation in inquiry 3? Why is insulation the deciding item in inquiry 4 when the temperature band is the same in options B and C? What makes an FGR job more than a normal inlet box?
  4. Write a line (optional): Learners write the full construction line for inquiry 5 in the same form as the summary's example for inquiry 4, then compare.

docs.title: Common Misconceptions Targeted
docs.text:
• High moisture and high temperature construction can be stacked (they cannot).
  • Type C is always the lowest-cost answer, even when the impeller is already non-ferrous (use Type B).
  • Insulation is only for heat (it also addresses condensation, sound and personnel protection).
  • A stainless housing can always be welded to a mild steel pedestal (use buffer strips or a bolt-on pedestal when the specification forbids it).
  • An FGR job is just a normal inlet box (it needs an FGR connection on the front of the inlet box, and the hot gas makes an insulated inlet box appropriate).

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
• First-attempt score of 5 or more of 6 shows mastery; the summary reads "You can turn an airstream into a construction line."
  • For each wrong first answer, the learner can name the FanPedia rule the chosen option breaks.
  • Follow-up question: an Arrangement 9 axial fan handles condensing exhaust at 150°F. Which construction applies, and what would change if the temperature rose to 240°F?

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Twin City Fan, FanPedia: The Fan & Blower Encyclopedia: buffer strips and bolt-on pedestals p. 85; spark resistant radial bladed fans p. 107 (note 2); centrifugal high temperature packages p. 110; axial high temperature packages p. 116; insulated jackets p. 119; high moisture construction p. 122; inlet box FGR connection and insulated inlet box p. 145. Source of every rule and reason in the sim.
  2. Chapter 20: Construction Classes, Materials and Spark Resistance in this book.
  3. Twin City Fan, FanPedia (PDF edition).

docs.title: Fan Law Calculator
docs.text: Run the Fan Law Calculator MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
This calculator applies the three fan laws to Curve A, the illustrative fan curve from Chapter 10. The base fan runs at 1,380 RPM on standard air and operates at 10,000 CFM, 4.0 in. wg and 9.0 BHP, at 70% static efficiency, on the system curve P = 4.0 × (Q ÷ 10,000)².

Every point of Curve A is mapped through the fan laws for geometrically similar fans:

  • Airflow: Q2 = Q1 × (N2/N1) × (D2/D1)³
  • Pressure: P2 = P1 × (N2/N1)² × (D2/D1)² × (ρ2/ρ1)
  • Power: BHP2 = BHP1 × (N2/N1)³ × (D2/D1)⁵ × (ρ2/ρ1)

Static efficiency at mapped (corresponding) points is unchanged. The readout panel shows the base and new speed, airflow, static pressure, BHP and static efficiency, with the ratio between them, so you can see at a glance that power moves with the cube of speed and the fifth power of diameter.

The sim starts with four challenges. Each one asks for a single number. You get two attempts; a second wrong answer reveals the model answer and the challenge counts as missed. When a challenge is resolved, the sim sets the matching ratio and draws the new curve (blue) and the new operating point (orange diamond) beside Curve A (gray) and its base operating point (black dot). The ratio sliders are locked until all four challenges are done; then exploration unlocks.

Notes on the model:

  • Curve A is illustrative, not a catalog curve. Its 9.0 BHP is rounded, so Q × P ÷ (6,356 × BHP) gives 69.9%; the sim uses the stated 70% as the base efficiency and carries it unchanged to every corresponding point.
  • A change in air density scales the system's resistance as well as the fan's pressure, so the sim draws a second, density-scaled system curve (orange dashed). The corresponding point stays on it at the same CFM.
  • With a diameter change, the orange point is the fan-law corresponding point. It no longer lies on the original system curve, and the sim says so.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read challenge 1, type a number in Your answer and press Check (or Enter).
  2. If the answer is within 2% of the model value it is marked correct. Otherwise read the feedback and try once more.
  3. Press Next challenge and repeat for challenges 2 to 4. "Challenges correct: n of 4" keeps the score.
  4. After challenge 4, press Start exploring. Move the speed ratio alone and watch the orange operating point slide along the system curve while efficiency stays at 70.0%. Then try the diameter and density ratios. Reset ratios to 1.00 returns to Curve A.

        height="592px"

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: The learner will solve fan-law problems for a new speed, pressure or brake horsepower after a change in speed, impeller diameter or air density, to within 2% of the model value (Bloom: Apply, verb: solve).

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Application engineers, sales engineers and technical students who have read the fan-law section of Chapter 25 and the fan-curve material in Chapter 10.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10-15 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Fan laws, speed change calculation and size change calculation (Chapter 25)
  • Fan curve, system curve and static efficiency (Chapter 10)
  • Density correction factor (Chapter 10)

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Challenges (5-8 min): Solve the four challenges with a calculator before pressing Check. Write down the ratio and exponent used for each.
  2. Exploration (3-5 min): Change only the speed ratio and record airflow, pressure, BHP and efficiency at 0.80, 1.00 and 1.15. Confirm that BHP at 0.80 is 0.512 of the original.
  3. Misconception check (2 min): Set the density ratio to 0.80 and explain why the CFM does not change. Set the diameter ratio to 1.25 and explain why airflow nearly doubles rather than rising by 25%.

docs.title: Common Misconceptions Addressed
docs.text:
• Power rises in proportion to speed (it rises with speed cubed).
  • Doubling the diameter doubles the airflow (airflow goes with diameter cubed).
  • Changing speed changes efficiency on a pure-resistance system (it does not; the point slides along the system curve).
  • Hotter, lighter air changes the CFM a fan moves (it changes pressure and power, not CFM).

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text: Mastery is 4 of 4 challenges answered within 2% of the model value. Moving the ratio sliders during exploration is not evidence of mastery.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Affinity laws - Wikipedia overview of the fan and pump affinity laws for speed and diameter changes.
  2. FanPedia: The Fan & Blower Encyclopedia - Twin City Fan's reference on fan performance, fan laws and system effect.
  3. AMCA International - publisher of the fan application manuals and test standards that use the fan laws to adjust rated performance.

docs.title: Fan Selection Workflow
docs.text: Run the Fan Selection Workflow MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
Fan selection runs through twelve steps in a fixed order, from collecting the application requirements to writing the specification. Each step consumes particular information about the job, and knowing which step uses which fact is what tells an engineer where to loop back when a requirement changes. The flowchart shows the twelve steps, the information that passes from each step to the next, and the dashed loop from the sound and dimension check back to the arrangement when a candidate fails a space or noise limit.

Every step in the flowchart is clickable. Clicking a step opens a short explanation of what that step decides. The panel on the right holds eight information cards from one worked job. For each card you choose the step that uses it. The sim checks the answer immediately, highlights the correct step in green (and your choice in red if it was wrong) and explains why.

The job values on the cards (1,450 RPM table speed, 1,180 and 1,780 RPM motor speeds, 500°F design and 70°F cold start, a 95 dB A-weighted outlet limit and a 10 ft by 8 ft pad) are the chapter's illustrative worked example, not data for a specific catalog fan.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Click any step in the flowchart to read what it does. You can also press Tab to move between steps and Enter to open one.
  2. Read the card in the right panel, choose a step from the list and press Submit.
  3. Read the feedback. Each card allows one attempt and locks once submitted.
  4. Press Next card to continue. After card 8 the panel shows your score out of 8. Below 7, it lists the chapter sections to reread, with links.
  5. Press Restart to sort the same eight cards again.

You can add this MicroSim to any web page by adding this to your HTML:

        height="1042px"
        width="100%"
        scrolling="no"></iframe>

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Adult professional development: new application engineers, inside and outside sales staff, manufacturer's representatives, distributors and specifying engineers.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10-15 minutes

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: The learner will classify eight pieces of application information by the selection step that uses them, with at least 7 of 8 correct on the first attempt (Bloom: Understand, verb: classify).

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: Fan selection, duty point, standard air, arrangement, drive, construction, cold start, accessories, sound data and dimensional data, covered in this chapter and in Chapters 2, 10 and 11.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Exploration (4 min): Click all twelve steps and read each explanation. Trace the information labels on the arrows and find the one loop in the workflow. Ask what would send a selection back along it.
  2. Sorting (6 min): Sort the eight cards. Before submitting each one, say which step uses the fact and why.
  3. Discussion (5 min): Look at the cards you missed and reread the linked sections. Then discuss three common mistakes: thinking selection ends once a size is read from the table; sizing the motor for the hot design temperature instead of the cold start; checking dimensions only after the order is placed.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text: Mastery is 7 of 8 cards correct on the first attempt. Clicking steps to read their explanations is exploration and does not count toward the score. As a follow-up, give the learner a requirement change, such as a lower noise limit, and ask which step the selection loops back to.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. FanPedia: The Fan & Blower Encyclopedia - Twin City Fan's reference covering fan types, arrangements, drives, construction, accessories, sound and selection.
  2. Twin City Fan product catalogs - Current performance tables, dimension tables and sound data used at the catalog sizing and check steps.
  3. Chapter 27: Fan Selection and Writing the Specification - The chapter this MicroSim supports. The step order and card content come from its sections.
  4. Mermaid flowchart syntax - The diagram library used to draw the clickable workflow.
